`term-leverage` row, the instrument, and a test that fails if the default moves. "The evaluation
cannot express this" is a reason to try, not a reason to keep.

Four of my own measurement errors are written up in D264 because each is a reusable trap: a cost
reading that compared two arms playing different games (the real figure, with behaviour held fixed,
is 0.23ms a move); an attribution probe whose `process.env` read dominated what it measured; an
early exit kept for a reason other than the one first claimed for it; and a damage attribution that
read the step before the action and never matched `first-strike-damage`. Plus one about process:
twice I rebuilt `dist` in the middle of a three-seed-set run, and **a measurement that spans a
rebuild is not a measurement**.

### A three-line CSS change that presented as four gameplay failures (#248, D265)

A permanent turns a quarter turn when it taps and everything drawn inside it turns too, so an
attacking creature read "1/2 ATTACKING FRIEND" up the side of the card. Counter-rotating the strip
inside the card fails on geometry — the card's box is portrait, so a child rotated back overflows a
landscape footprint — but the **slot** wrapper is already the right box in both orientations and is
never rotated, so the badges move there and need no transform at all. Vigilance falls out for free.

Then the arena suite went 54/54 to **46/50**, and the four failures were a land not reaching the
battlefield, the mana bar, attackers never being declared and life never moving. None of them
mentions a badge. The move log gave it away: twenty turns of `primary: Pass` where a passing run
shows `chose a play: Play Plains`. `tryToPlayFromZone` decided a card was playable by reading
`textContent` of the **card** and matching /playable/ — and the badges had just left the card, so
every card in every zone read as unplayable and the driver stopped casting anything.

The driver reads the slot and taps the card inside it now, with the failure written into its
docblock. Same family as D262 and D263: a coupling nobody wrote down, failing somewhere other than
where it was made — except this one is load-bearing for all four browser suites at once, and was
loud but misdirected, which sends you to the engine rather than to the layout.

Three suites passed and the fourth found a **second reader**: `tryCommander` in `e2e-pod.mjs`,
which is its own function precisely because the command zone is the one place a spell is cast from
that is not the hand — so the shared driver never looks there and the fix did not reach it. "The
command zone was read 845 times and never said playable." Two readers one suite apart is where
patching call sites stops being the answer, so `slotsIn` now sits beside `cardsIn` with the rule in
its docblock, and the tree was checked for others before fixing.

Why that one cost minutes where the arena failure cost hours: the pod check counts its reads and
prints the text it saw, so the message names the bug. The arena check said a land did not reach the
battlefield. Same class of bug, opposite diagnostic quality, and the difference is entirely in what
each check chose to report on failure.

All four green on the final head: arena 53/53 with the four recovered, table 73/73, solo 24/24, pod
42/42 with the commander cast restored. What is asserted is structural — the strip is outside the
element carrying `--card-rot` — and not photographic: both badge-bearing creatures in the new
screenshots have vigilance, so they attacked untapped.

### The laptop nobody had measured, and a premise that did not survive it (#249, D266)

#249 said a player on a laptop cannot see both boards at once, and called it the single biggest gap
between this and a premium table. It is not true. On a 1440x800 laptop a duel reads **1.16 screens**
and its two creature rows span **229px of the 800px viewport** — both boards on screen together with
571px spare, reproduced across two independent games.

Two things I had not checked before writing the task. The density pass had already happened, and the
comment above the screens-tall budget says so (*"a duel was 1.37 and is 1.18"*) — the task's own last
sentence quotes that number, so I read it off the suite and still wrote the premise from the
screenshots. And that same comment records the one remaining item, the opponents' face-down hands, as
deliberately left alone: *"it is the tabletop metaphor, and style is the player's call."* Still the
position; still Nick's call rather than mine.

What genuinely had never been measured is the laptop. Six of the seven `setViewportSize` calls in the
four suites set 390x844, and the only desktop one is restoring the viewport after the phone check.
Phone width is the right worst case sideways and the wrong one for height — 844px of phone holds more
of this table than 800px of laptop. So the claim nothing could answer is the one the task asserted
hardest, and the absence of a measurement read like permission to assert one.

Both figures are now guards in `e2e-solo.mjs` with budgets set from the readings, printed pass or
fail — **and the pod is asserted too**, which it was not when this section was first written. The
pod reads **1.41 screens with all four creature rows inside 331px of the 800px viewport**: four
boards at once, which is the reading that matters most in the format the product is named for.

Getting that number took three attempts, and the detour is the more useful half. One `SOLO_POD=1`
run played 270 moves in fifteen minutes — 3.3 seconds a move — and never reached the layout block,
which is what made the pod look unmeasurable. Three explanations were ruled out by measurement
rather than argument: the engine plays a four-seat pod in **7–10 ms a move** (now
`scripts/measure/pod-pace.mjs`, so the next "the bots are slow" claim costs one command to refuse);
the driver's own cost is **flat at 253 ms/move** over 220 moves with no growth as the board fills;
and the `stuck` poll that was the leading suspect fires **0.0 times a move**. A later run finished
the game and printed both figures. The outlier is recorded as an outlier (#250), machine contention
being the cheapest remaining explanation and not provable after the fact.

Leaving the pod unasserted rather than guessing a budget for it cost nothing, which was the point:
the gap was recorded as a gap, so closing it was an edit rather than a correction to a shipped
number. A third finding fell out of forcing the checks against a mid-game board instead of a
post-game one — a full four-seat board overflows a phone by 17px, and every layout check in the
suite has only ever measured the emptiest board of the game (#251).

### A check whose premise was wider than its fixture (#251, D267)

One row in `ArenaBar` — mana pips, step, primary action, stops toggle, Concede — was
`flex items-center gap-2` where every other row in that bar wraps. On a phone it sized itself to its
content and pushed the whole table sideways, for the length of every automated game, which is every
game a player using the rules engine has ever played.

The fix was already written down one file away: the tabletop's own bar carries `overflow-x-auto`, and
`PlayTable.tsx` explains why a flex child needs `min-w-0` for it to work at all. The engine's bar
inherited neither when it replaced the manual one.

Finding it needed the right filter rather than more looking. Every element past 390px is 42 of them,
the worst 265px over, all of it cards inside rows that are *meant* to scroll — and an element inside
an `overflow-x: auto` ancestor cannot widen the document. Elements with no scrolling ancestor:
exactly one, the Concede button, `+41px`, the whole overflow. The check reports that now instead of
`overflow 17px`, computed only on failure.

**Why nothing caught it is the part worth keeping.** Every layout check in the solo suite runs after
the game reaches a winner — when the board is emptiest *and* `view.finished` has removed Concede and
the primary action from the bar. The row under test was never on screen when the check ran. That is
the fourth instance this week of one shape, and it now has a name: a check whose premise is wider
than its fixture. D262 named a card by hand, D263 existed and never ran, D266 could not be
contradicted, this one asserted "any board" and only ever saw one. None was a wrong assertion; each
was a correct assertion pointed somewhere it could not fail.

Verified against the failing condition, which took three attempts because a run that finishes inside
its move cap measures a post-game board: a mid-game stop that read `overflow 41px` now passes, arena
53/53 with both control-bar checks, web 226/226. The mid-game screens-tall budgets are deliberately
**not** raised to match — a pod reads 2.88–3.21 screens mid-game against 2.35 set from a post-game
2.23, and raising it would discard the only number protecting the post-game case (#251).

### The same shape in the instrument: an arm that never reached the bot (#254, D270)

`bot-duel` hands `TESTED` straight to `botAction` as `BotOptions`, and `botAction` ignores a key it
does not know — correct for an options bag, and silent. A weight lives at `opts.weights.castable`,
so `TESTED='{"castable":1}'` sets a field nobody reads and **both arms become the stock bot**. Three
seed sets, fifteen minutes each: **467-467, 467-467, 466-466**. That is not a weak signal, it is this
harness's own arithmetic negative control — identical bots play the same games and each is credited
one win per pairing, so the tie is exact by construction. I was composing "level across three seed
sets" as a statement about the term when the perfection of the tie stopped me.

The README already carried the lesson, from the day the ninja holding rule read 467-467: *a reading
identical to the control needs a positive control before you call it level*, and `lookahead: false`
duly came back 90-221. Right question, wrong subject. `lookahead` is a real field, so that control
passes while a *different* arm's key is being dropped on the floor. Fair, connected, and
**this-arm-connected** are three questions, and only the third was at issue.

So the check is now a per-arm pre-flight, and deliberately not a list of `BotOptions` field names —
that would be a second reader of a type that already has one, going quiet rather than wrong the next
time the type grows (D260). Both arms are asked the same ~2000 positions the shipping bot plays; no
disagreement anywhere means a non-zero exit before 936 games are spent. A real arm is found in a
second: `{"weights":{"castable":1}}` diverges at decision 71 on a targeted spell against an X spell.

The part worth keeping is what it cannot tell apart. `holdsNinjas` is a real field, read on every
filter decision, and it trips the guard across all thirteen pairings — because the window never
opens: 19 unblocked attackers, 2 ninjas in hand, **0** both, in 95 declare-blockers steps. So that
rule's 467-467 was a true reading of a rule that almost never fires, and the guard would have said so
in twenty seconds rather than fifteen minutes. Two causes, opposite fixes, so the message names both.

D267's shape, moved from the code into the instrument: **ask what the check would do if the thing it
checks were broken.** The positive control passed identically whether the arm's key was real or
nonsense, which means it was never evidence about the key.

### The hand term was the wrong shape, not the wrong weight (#253, D271)

#227 lowered the weight on cards-in-hand, and D243 closed the subject: the term anti-predicts the
winner at 42%, and a five-fold cut moved 936 paired games by one. The diagnosis was right and it was
about *variation* — what decides a choice is how a term differs across the options on offer, and hand
size barely differs, because nearly every candidate is a cast and every cast moves one card out.

What it did not cover is that **"cards in hand" and "cards in hand I can pay for" are different
terms**, and only the first had ever been measured. The second varies precisely where the first does
not: the candidates at a cast decision differ in what they leave the seat able to do next. #227's
conclusion and "the evaluation is asking the wrong question about the hand" produce the same number,
and nothing could tell them apart until there was a second term to compare.

Both instruments agree. Leverage: 157 of 17451 decisions, nearly the same total as `hand` and
pointed somewhere else entirely — **4.8% of cast decisions** against `hand`'s 2.8%, while `hand`'s own
leverage sits on activations. Win rate, three disjoint seed sets of 936 paired games: **479-454,
469-465, 471-462** — 1419-1381, +1.35 points, sign holding every time. That is D242's bar, and the
first evaluation term to clear it since; D264's `exposed` had no consistent direction and is still
shipped at zero. So `CASTABLE_IN_HAND` goes to **1**: a castable card at 2.5, level with a land and
under a permanent. A hand you can use is nearly a land; a hand you cannot is a hand.

The spread is worth stating rather than averaging away — +25 clears the harness's observed ±6, +4
does not, +9 does — which is the whole reason three disjoint sets are run rather than one long one.
Other weights are unmeasured and the deck table was baselined with the term off; both are recorded at
the constant rather than implied.

The part that nearly went wrong: `term-leverage`'s `castable` arm ran *on* rather than off, because
ablating a term that ships at zero reads a clean 0.0%. Flipping the default turns that arm into an
override that overrides nothing — and the zero-row check added hours earlier would have reported the
term as one the evaluation cannot see, the exact silence it was written to break, on the exact change
it was written beside. **A default and its ablation are one change, not two.** The six arithmetic
tests needed no edit at all, which is the payoff from naming both weights instead of leaning on the
default: they measure the term, not the configuration.

### The pod had never been audited for engine throws (#256, D272)

`unfinished.mjs` exists because thirty-five harnesses here end their move loop with
`try { ... } catch { break; }` and none of them reports catching anything — so a throw truncates a
game, the harness counts it as played, and its number is computed from a game that stopped at an
error. It audited two-seat games only. The three pod harnesses carry the identical catch and had
never been asked, and the pod is where the `nobody to act` end state stops being hypothetical: the
engine's own pod tests exist for CR 800.4a, and a table nobody can move at is worse than a throw.

**234 pods, two deck mixes, every one to a winner.** No throw, no stuck table, no move cap. So the
catch in all three pod harnesses has caught nothing and their published numbers are not short by
games they ate — and it is the strongest evidence yet for the claim the project cares about most,
in the format with three opponents and the 800.4a risk rather than the duel.

Tables, seeds and `ALWAYS` seating are copied from `pod-duel` rather than shared, because the point
is to replay *that* harness's games. One deliberate difference, on its own docblock's authority: it
plays each table four times rotating the arms, and with one bot in every seat all four rotations are
the same game on the same seed — so the audit plays each table once, which is every *distinct* game
it plays rather than every game it counts.

Narrow on purpose. It says nothing about a pod seating a card these tables never did, nor about a
pod a person is sitting at. The audit is as wide as its pairings — D267's shape — and the honest
version of the claim is the narrow one.

### What the term costs, what its weight is worth, and the clock (#255, #257, #258, D273, D274)

Three things D271 left open, closed, and one of them turned into the more useful finding.

**Time.** `canAfford` runs the mana solver per hand card, and the zero short-circuit that used to
skip it stopped firing when the default moved — so the solver now runs at every search leaf with a
person waiting. Measured as an ablation timing both arms on the *same* positions, because running
the file twice compares two different sets of games: about **+0.09 ms per decision** against a
1.2–9.4 ms baseline, with **two of seven readings negative**, which is the tell that the noise is
wider than the effect. Whole-game pace unchanged at 7.0/11.3/9.5 ms/move against a pre-term
8.4/11.3/9.6. A footgun fixed on the way: with the arm set, every move pays for two searches, so
that line's ms/move runs 1.7× a plain run's — 13.0 against the published 8.4, a 60% regression that
does not exist, and I read it as one until the botAction share dropping from 72% to 42% explained it.

**Weight.** 0.5 and 2 against the shipping 1, three disjoint seed sets each: −2/+6/−11 and
+13/+4/−7. Disagreeing signs mean not measured, so **across a fourfold range nothing separates them
from 1**. That is D243's lesson arriving on the term that was meant to be its exception, and
together they close a second avenue: *this evaluation is insensitive to its weights and sensitive to
what it can see.*

**The table.** The published deck table was baselined with the term off, and the argument for not
waiting was that a symmetric change cancels in the relative win rates it reads. Now measured at its
own canonical setting: largest shift **forge-alliance +4 points**, ten games of 288, against a table
always quoted as ±10 a row. Ordering intact, no tier crossed, published numbers not stale. The off
arm reproduces the canonical table within one or two points on all thirteen rows, which is what
makes the comparison a comparison.

**And the clock, built in both shapes because the shape is the question.** `clockRate` is
`exposedPower × startingLife / life` — at full life and weight 1 it is *exactly* D264's rejected
term, asserted as an identity — and it carries **14.2% of attack declarations**, the largest
single-decision-kind figure any term here has posted, nearly double the linear reading. `clockTurns`,
the integer a player says out loud, came in **below** the linear term. Had only that form been
built, the honest conclusion would have been "the clock is weaker than the quantity", which is the
opposite of what is true. Both ship off; leverage is necessary and not sufficient, and `exposed` is
the standing proof of that.

### A noise floor nobody had measured, and a claim retracted twice (#263, D281)

The clock's story ended on a measurement that turned out to be of the harness rather than the term.

Testing D280's symmetric prediction — if caution loses a pod, aggression should win one — meant
running one unchanged arm over three disjoint pod seed sets. It read **60-44, 50-54, 44-60**: a range
of **32 for a setting that did not move between runs**. That is `pod-duel`'s noise floor, ±16 of 104,
fifteen percentage points, and it had never been measured.

Which retracts a number I published twice the same day. The clock's pod readings — 48-56, 52-52,
50-54 — were written up as *"−3.8 points, never once above zero"*. They sit well inside ±16. Three
draws landing at −8, 0 and −4 from a distribution centred near zero is unremarkable, and "never once
above zero" is three coin flips. **D242's three-disjoint-sets rule was applied without its
precondition**: a sign that holds is only believable once you know what one reading wobbles by.

The part that stings is that `pod-duel`'s own docblock says to measure the floor first, and I quoted
that very paragraph earlier the same afternoon — for its *other* warning, about the arithmetic
control — and skipped this half. So the fix is not a resolution to be more careful: **the floor now
lives in the docblock as a number** rather than as homework. A precondition stated as homework gets
skipped; `±16 of 104` does not.

What survives is most of it, and it is the exact stuff rather than the sampled stuff: the duel win
rates (+1.5 at weight 1, −12 at −1, over 2808 games each on a harness whose floor *is* known), the
aggression ablation on identical positions (42% of declarations declined against 24%), the length
figures, and the superlinearity arithmetic. What does not survive is one number — the clock's effect
on who wins a pod, which is **unknown rather than negative**.

The first version of this section ended by warning that every pod win rate in the project was weaker
than it read. **That was the same error again** — a claim wider than what I had checked — and one grep
disproves it. The myriad slot reading says the floor must come from re-running a real arm on disjoint
seeds *and then does it* (4-48 and 2-50 over 52 pods each); `offerPact` says outright that `pod-duel`
cannot price it and ships for a reason that is not a win rate. The practice was already right and
already written down. **The only pod win rate ever published as a result here is the one retracted
above, and it is mine.**

Resolving a four-point pod effect needs about 1000 pods an arm, ninety minutes a reading, three
disjoint sets — four to five hours for one question, which nothing here has ever spent.

### A fact about the game that was a description of a loop (#264, D282)

`exposedPower` — the evaluation's one term about two boards rather than one seat's piles — kept a
single spent-blocker set across the whole table. A blocker that answered seat 1's creature was gone
against seat 2's.

That is not the rules. **Nothing taps a creature for blocking**, and a creature untaps only in its
own controller's untap step, which for me comes after all three of their turns. The same untapped
3/3 blocks seat 1's Bear on seat 1's turn, seat 2's on seat 2's, and seat 3's on seat 3's. Three
opponents fielding a Bear each read as **four points of unanswerable pressure on a board that loses
no life**, and the error grows with the opponent count, so no divisor undoes it. The fix is one
`spent` set per opponent and the sum of what each cannot be stopped from doing; at two seats it is
arithmetically the same function, so every duel number in the project still reads on it.

Two published conclusions go with it. D278 rejected a *minimum* per-opponent clock on a board where
"four damage lands every turn" — no damage lands on that board at all, and the 4 was the bug. The min
is still the wrong object, on arithmetic that holds: three opponents each with an **unblockable** 2/2
cost six a cycle and the min reads two. And D280's explanation of the clock's pod passivity — *"my
blockers are shared, and the same 3/3 answers any one of those 2/2s and cannot answer two"* — is
false in its second half, which was the reason this file gave for needing an attack model it does not
have.

**And fixing it rescued nothing, which is the result worth having.** If pooled blockers were why the
term made a pod bot passive, the caution should have come down toward the duel's. Re-run on the same
851 pod declarations it declined 351 against 358: seven of 851. The duel control reproduced to the
digit, which is what a fix that is arithmetically nothing at two seats should do — measured rather
than argued.

The reason is a gradient rather than a level. An attack is decided by what the term charges for
*tapping* a blocker, and on D280's own board the pooled reading charged 4 for swinging where the
honest one charges **12** — each blocker was answering an attacker on every one of their turns, so
tapping them lets all six through. The level falls to 0 and the price triples; in play the two
roughly cancel. So the passivity is the term's shape, not this bug, and both clock weights stay at
zero.

The lesson is not about blockers. The bug survived three measurements, two instruments and a long
docblock **because it had been written down as a fact about the game rather than as a question about
the code**. "My blockers are shared" reads like domain knowledge; it was a description of a loop.
Every number taken from D276 to D280 was correctly measured on a function that answered the wrong
question, and no amount of pairing, seed discipline or ablation discipline could have caught it —
only reading the loop against the rules.

### Three things a player sees, and none of them were found by a test (#265-#267, D283-D285)

A pass over the things the table says to a person, rather than over what it computes.

**The setup notes had been counting by hand.** `claude/play-realm-setup.md` is what somebody reads
before sitting down: its deck section was headed *"Eleven starter decks"* with all thirteen
described at length underneath, and three places said the engine knows *"three hundred and
thirty-three"* cards where the pool holds **348**. Nobody wrote a wrong number — each was right when
written, nothing connected it to the registry, and two decks and fifteen cards arrived without
touching the prose above them. Fixed, and then made unable to recur: `mechanic-coverage.mjs` prints
the pool in one line and the doc cites that command, `customDeck.ts` no longer carries a count at
all, and a guard reads the registry statically and fails when the doc omits a deck or heads its
section with the wrong number. Four negative controls, because a guard that cannot fail is D263's
trap in a new place.

**The table that is never going to connect said "connecting" for ever.** There was no
`connect_error` handler at all. The server is WebSocket-only, so a network that blocks WebSockets
cannot play — and socket.io retried silently behind a small pill, with the same screen for a server
that is not running and for a wrong `VITE_REALTIME_URL`. The lobby now says so after three failed
attempts, names the address, and deliberately does *not* say which cause it is: pointed at a closed
port in a real browser, every `connect_error` carries the message **`websocket error`** and nothing
else, so a branch on it would have been a guess dressed as a diagnosis.

**And the seat that could not be reclaimed said nothing either.** A refused reclaim called
`writeStored(null)` and left the player in the lobby with no explanation — the same screen as
somebody who had never joined. It now names the table and what happened to it, classified on the
error *code*, which unlike a socket handshake is an enumerated contract.

The browser then said two things the unit tests could not. The server's own prose **won**: the
`pod:error` broadcast arrives after the ack and `state.error` holds one string, so *"pod
BRAVE-OTTER-42 does not exist"* replaced the sentence the ack had just written. That reversed a
documented choice — `showsBroadcastError` kept `not_found` because *"a banner the player can act on
is worth a duplicate"*, and the duplicate replaces rather than adds. And seeding storage to
reproduce the failure showed **zod**: `readStored` checked the three fields were strings, so a seat
left by an older build was sent anyway and the server's validator answered the player. It now
validates against `PodJoinInput`, the schema the server will apply to that exact reclaim, so there
is one reader of the rule rather than two (D260).

The thread between all three: **a failure path with no screen attached to it is not covered by a
test that asserts the state field.** Both silences were in the same forty lines and neither was
found by a test — they were found by asking what a player sees when this fails, and then making it
fail.

### Two rules the engine never enforced, found by auditing a list instead of a card (#269, #270, D287, D288)

`stateBasedActions` carries most of CR 704.5 and had grown one card at a time: a case went in when a
card needed it. So the way to find what was missing was to take the list and check it, rather than
wait for a card to complain.

**CR 704.5q — `+1/+1` and `-1/-1` counters cancel in pairs — was not there.** The size was never
wrong, which is exactly why it survived: `characteristicsOf` reads both kinds and subtracts, so a 2/2
with three plus and two minus has always *measured* as a 4/4. What was wrong is every card that
counts the counters — Hangarback Walker's Thopter per `+1/+1` (three where the rules give one),
persist asking whether the creature had a `-1/-1` and undying whether it had a `+1/+1` (the famous
interaction: a persisted Redcap that gains a plus counter should end with neither and come back
*again*), modular, Walking Ballista. And it is reachable in this pool rather than theoretical,
because `-1/-1` counters arrive here from **infect**.

**The legend rule, CR 704.5j, was not there either.** Two Kalitas sat on one battlefield and nothing
happened. Reachable *inside a single deck*, twice: Forge Alliance runs Blade of Selves, whose myriad
makes token copies of the attacking creature, and its commander Balan pulls every Equipment onto
himself — so a Balan with the Blade attacks a pod and makes two more Balans. Tidal Mind runs Clone,
which can copy its own commander. Implemented keeping the permanent that arrived first, which is a
stated deviation: the rule has the controller choose, and `stateBasedActions` is a pure
`state -> state` function called inside `settle` that cannot stop and ask.

Both fixes made existing tests fail, and both failures were the tests being wrong. Proliferate's two
had built a Chasm Skulker carrying a `+1/+1` **and** a `-1/-1` — one of them saying in a comment that
this made it *"the one permanent here carrying two kinds of counter"* — which is a board the rule
forbids. They now show "one of each kind already there" across three objects instead.

The thread with the blocker bug earlier the same day: **what a test asserts decides what a bug can
hide behind.** D282's pooled blockers hid behind a plausible sentence in a docblock; 704.5q hid
behind a power and toughness that were right either way. The test that catches it reads the counters
rather than the creature, and it is in the file next to one that reads only the size and would have
passed on the broken engine — both on purpose.

### The clock, one more time (#268, D286)

`clockRate` divides by the opponents the table started with, and after the blocker fix the arithmetic
turned against that divisor. At ten life, nine unanswerable power on one seat takes you to 1 and
kills a cycle later; three each on three seats takes you to 7, 4 and 1 and kills on the first of
their turns in the next cycle. **Both die on the same turn** — nine a cycle is nine either way — so
the undivided sum is the honest quantity and dividing by three reads a third of it. `clockCycle` is
that form, at zero and tested, waiting on the same question. And a real pod win rate for the divided
form is finally being spent on: 1040 pods an arm against a floor of about ±5, three disjoint seed
sets.

### The test I was about to add was the weaker one (#269 follow-up, D290)

The CR 704.5 table D288 put into `stateBasedActions` claimed to be the whole rule and had thirteen
of its fifteen cases. Both missing rows turned out to be rows that need no code here — 704.5p
because the pool's only attached creature is a bestowed one the Aura branch already handles, and
704.5e because a copy of a spell *cannot* be put anywhere: it has no instance under its stack id, so
there is no card to bin and no path that could try.

The part worth keeping is what happened when I tried to test 704.5e. The obvious assertion is a
graveyard count — counter the Twincast copy, check there is one Lightning Bolt and not two. It
passed. Then, on the habit D287 left behind, I broke `counterSpell` on purpose so that it would bin
the copy through `source` (which on a copy is the *original's* instance) and ran it again. **It
passed again**, because the original Bolt reaches the graveyard either way. The assertion that
actually pins the rule was already in the test before I touched it: `instances[copy]` is undefined.
Three times this session what a test asserts decided what a bug could hide behind, and this is the
first time the answer was to delete my own test rather than add it.

### A document that contradicted itself about its own opponent (#271, D291)

The player doc describes the computer opponent in two places, and both said it "will not hold a
creature back to block or keep mana up for the counterspell in its hand". The second half stopped
being true at #60 and has been corrected four times since (#148, #149, #152, #218) — and all the
while Tidal Mind's own deck entry, in the same file, carried the measured windows for the rule and
named the switch that turns it off. A reader meeting the summary first concluded the opponent taps
out; a reader meeting the deck entry first concluded it does not.

The other two claims were true and sold wrong. It really does not hold a blocker back and really
does not search your reply, but neither is undone work: both were built, measured and reverted —
D110 for the reply, and for blockers a bonus on untapped creatures that moved nothing at one point,
**cost 26 games in 400 at two**, and made the bot worse at four. In this pool attacking is right.
"Not done" and "done, measured, reverted because it lost games" invite very different things from
whoever reads them next.

The pace figures matched no measurement at all — "under a millisecond a duel, about five a pod"
against D96's recorded 200-pod soak of 2ms median, 7.6ms mean, p99 65ms, one decision in ninety
thousand over two seconds. No guard for any of this: #265's guard works because deck counts are
structured data, and a guard that pattern-matched an English sentence would fail the first time
somebody rephrased it. What the paragraphs carry instead is the symbol name, the file and the
decision numbers.

### The one card that can end a game with nobody winning (#272, D292)

A draw was written into this engine twice — `engine.ts` leaves `winnerSeat` null when the last two
players die together, and `rematch` reads a null winner as "a draw, or a game nobody finished" and
gives the first turn back to whoever had it — and tested neither time. The reason is that a draw
cannot be built out of the actions a test reaches for: `life:adjust` takes one seat at a time, so
the first drop to nought ends the game before the second lands, and conceding every seat fails
because the last concede arrives at a game that is already over.

It needs one effect that kills both players at once, and in this pool that is **Hurricane** — X
damage to each creature with flying and each player. The card has sat in three decks since it was
written, with its symmetry tested; what was never tested was the symmetry going all the way.

Two tests now, off a shared board at 3 life each with X=3. `[0, 0]` is the line that makes it a
*simultaneous* loss: had the seats died one after the other the second would still be on 3 when the
game ended, and `finished`, both `eliminated` flags and the null winner would all read the same —
the D290 trap, caught this time before the test was written instead of after. And the rematch half
was proved by breaking it: `((winnerSeat ?? 0) + 1) % seats`, the obvious wrong implementation,
fails the test with "expected 1 to be +0".

Nothing in the engine changed. Both rules were already right; what was missing was anything that
would notice if they stopped being.

### Every reading of "can you see both boards" was taken post-game (#273, D293)

D266 refuted #249 with two figures at 1440x800 — a duel is 1.16 screens and its two creature rows
sit inside 229px of the viewport — and settled the question. Both are measured **after the last
creature has died**. The question is a mid-game one, and it went unasked because the post-game
answer was so comfortable that nobody thought to.

Measured three times on real mid-game duels at 1440x900, and a fourth from the instrument once it
was in the tree: page height **1.33–1.60 screens**, both creature rows **331–568px of the 900px
viewport**. They fit every time, with 332–569px to spare. So this is a confirmation of D266 rather
than a correction — the conclusion holds where it actually matters.

The near-miss is the part worth keeping. The first number I measured was the creature rows *plus
the hand* — 1019px, does not fit — and for about a minute I read it as though it answered D266's
question. It does not: they are different spans, and nothing has ever claimed the hand fits beside
both boards. That substitution is exactly how #249 produced a confident false premise from a
screenshot, so `table-fold.mjs` now prints both side by side with the second labelled "not the
question".

No budget was added, deliberately: the comment in `e2e-solo.mjs` already rules that mid-game budgets
wait on somebody deciding the table is too tall, and that 1.3 and 2.35 must not be raised to
accommodate a mid-game number. What changed is that the decision now has figures under it.

### The two instruments built to name the next term cannot name one (#274, D296)

#274 was meant to pick the next evaluation term from measurement rather than from a guess: run
`term-leverage` over the whole field, read it beside `eval-calibration`, and take the term in the
interesting cell. Both halves are now run on the current engine, and the answer is that the two
columns do not license the conclusion.

The field, at 312 duels and 34,262 decisions: `creature` 6.4%, `life` 2.3%, `clockCycle` and
`clockRate` 2.1% each, `exposed` 1.5%, `castable` and `permanent` 1.0%, `hand` 0.9%, `clockTurns`
0.6%, `library` 0.2%, `land` 0.1%, and the empty-override control at a clean 0.0%. `clockCycle` and
`clockRate` reading the *same* 731 decisions is the arm's own positive control — the divisor is
`/ opponents` and a duel has one.

Each instrument has now produced a counterexample to itself:

- `castable` has the **weakest calibration of any shipped term** — 51/52/53/54/54/48 against `life`
  and `board` at 51-70 — and earned **+1.35 points** over three disjoint seed sets.
- `clockRate` has the **third-highest leverage of the eleven** and earned **0.00 sigma** over 2434
  decided pods (D295), bound ±4.1 points.

So leverage says a term *can* move a decision and says nothing about whether the decision it moves
is the better one; calibration ranks the players and a search never asks it to. Both instruments
stay — leverage is how `hand` was caught being inert while looking mispriced, and the pair of them
is how `castable` was identified as the right shape for the question `hand` asked backwards. What
changes is what a reading buys: **a reason to spend a win rate, never a substitute for having spent
one.** The standing diagnosis is unchanged — the next gain is a term that sees something new, and no
ranking of the terms that exist can point at one that does not.

One thing stays open and this instrument cannot see it: `clockCycle` differs from `clockRate` only
where there is more than one opponent, and `term-leverage` plays duels. A pod arm would be the cheap
screen before another two thousand pods go on the clock family. It is recorded rather than built,
because nothing is waiting on the answer.

### A player left the game and kept their board, in every pod ever played (#276, D297)

The engine did not enforce CR 800.4a. A seat eliminated mid-pod left its creatures on the
battlefield and its cards in hand, library and graveyard — and a live player's Lightning Bolt listed
a dead seat's creature among its legal targets. Three seats leave in every pod that reaches a
winner, so this was the back half of every pod the engine has played.

Found by probe rather than by a test, which is why it lasted: nothing in the suite asked. And half
the rule was already holding by accident — a dead seat's *abilities* never fire, because `raise`
collects watchers through `apnapSeats`, which filters eliminated seats. A dead player's Chalice of
the Void counters nothing, verified against a live-seat control that does. So the half anyone would
have noticed was correct, and what was left was the objects.

`leaveTheGame` now takes the owned objects wherever they are, the spells and abilities off the
stack, the continuous effects and delayed triggers with them, unattaches and unpairs live cards that
pointed at a departed one, and hands back anything the leaving player held in exile "until this
leaves the battlefield" — otherwise a creature taken by a departing Journey to Nowhere sits in exile
for the rest of the game with its jailer deleted.

Two corrections came from tests rather than from thinking harder. `playout.test.ts` caught a
`pendingChoice` left pointing at a stack object just deleted: **the state that references an object
is part of what has to go with it**, and only a real game found the reference. And the decking test
caught the scope — CR 800.4 is a *multiplayer* rule, a duel ends the moment somebody loses
(CR 104.2a), and wiping the loser's zones there would delete the final board D252 decided stays up.
So the departure only happens while more than one seat survives.

Stated rather than discovered later: every pod figure in `scripts/measure/` predates this, D295's
2434 included. It retracts nothing, but a comparison spanning the commit is not a paired one, and
both files say so.

### Ten undecided pods, six of them one engine throw, four that cannot be replayed (#275, D298)

`pod-duel` collapses five distinct ways a pod can stop into one silent `break` and reports it as
`(N unfinished)`. #268 spent 2444 pods on the clock and ten ended that way.
`scripts/measure/pod-unfinished.mjs` replays those seeds, arms and seating and names each cause,
exiting non-zero on a throw.

A correction first: I had said eight of 2442. The ledger's annotated chunks are 2, 6 and 2, so it is
**ten of 2444 played**. The decided total is 2434 either way, which is what D295 quotes and computes
on, so the conclusion does not move — the wrong number was one stated in passing, not one measured.

Six of the ten reproduce, and every one is the same thing: **the engine refusing a deal the bot
offered on behalf of a player who had left the game.** Two at seed 7830 (shifts 1 and 3, turn 29),
four at seed 11253 (all four shifts, turn 26). Not the move cap, not a seat with nothing to do — an
invariant violation, now isolated to its mechanism in #277: `seatsToAct` names a dead seat whenever
a pending question does, and driving the bot for one produces a refused action in three of five
cases.

The conclusion it was asked to protect survives. The throws removed games rather than mis-scoring
any; all ten were excluded from the denominator. What a throw can do is end a game that would have
been decided, which is bounded by 10 of 2444 — 0.4 points against a 2 sigma bound of ±4.1.

The four that do not reproduce are the finding worth keeping. The candidates are an engine
difference between then and now, or an `ALWAYS=` setting on those runs — and **neither is checkable,
because the ledger records seeds and margins and nothing else.** A long accumulated measurement with
rows that cannot be audited is the same class of problem as a harness that swallows a throw: the
number survives and the thing that would let you check it does not. Before the next long run, a
ledger row needs the arm JSON, the commit, and the full command.

### The engine was waiting on players who had left the game (#277, D299)

D298 traced six of #268's ten undecided pods to one throw — `pact:offer: seat N has been eliminated`,
the engine refusing an action the bot built out of its own rules. The cause is more general than the
card that surfaced it: `seatsToAct` reads a seat off whichever question is outstanding, and none of
its six branches asked whether that seat was still in the game. A question standing on a departed
seat made the engine report a dead player as the one it was waiting on.

Three of the five pending questions then produce an action the engine refuses — `pendingChoice` to
`auto:choose`, `pendingPayment` to `auto:pay`, `pendingOfferedCast` to `pact:offer` — and two produce
one it **accepts**, which is the worse half: a dead player answering a dredge is silent.
`offerPact` was where it surfaced rather than the cause; a departed seat's life is 0, so every
opponent's open board looks lethal and the rule always finds somebody to ask.

The fix is in two halves. `resolveStateBasedActions` **withdraws** a question whose seat has left —
a decision is *resumed* rather than dropped, because the rest of its plan belongs to other players,
and `answerDecision` with an empty answer is what `askOrFinish` already does for a seat eliminated
between two questions. `seatsToAct` and `botAction` **guard** anyway, and both are worth keeping
because the failure modes are not equivalent: a question that slips past the withdrawal becomes a
table with nobody to act, which every harness reports, while an unfiltered one becomes a throw that
35 harnesses swallow in silence. The guard converts the unfindable fault into the findable one.

The lesson is where it was found. This is the first engine bug a *measuring* harness caught before a
test did, and only because #275 built the thing that reads the silence. The counterpart: the
regression test cannot be written from the seeds that found it — two pods out of 2444, and D297
changed the back half of every pod, so those seeds no longer reproduce. The test puts each of the six
questions on a departed seat directly instead. **A test built from the seed that found a bug would
have asserted nothing by the following commit; a test built from the mechanism asserts it for good.**

### The instrument prints its own provenance now (#278, D300)

D298 found four pod rows in the clock ledger that could not be replayed and could not be explained —
an engine difference or an `ALWAYS=` setting, with no way to tell, because a row recorded seeds and
a margin and nothing else. Recording that in a decision entry is not a fix.

`pod-duel` and `pod-unfinished` now print one line before the first pod: the arms as JSON, every
input that changes which games are played, the commit and whether the tree was **dirty** (a hash
pins the build only when it is clean), and when `dist` was built — these harnesses import the built
engine rather than the source, so a stale `dist` is a run of code the commit does not describe.

The point is where the line comes from. `pod-duel`'s own docblock records that *"a precondition
stated as homework gets skipped; a number in the docblock does not"*, and that is exactly what
happened one level up: the ledger header explains the denominator rule carefully and says nothing
about arms or builds, so nobody wrote them down. **A line the instrument prints is a line the ledger
cannot omit.** Printed first, so a run killed halfway still says what it was.

### An Overrun was pumping creatures cast after it resolved (#280, D301)

The rules audit kept going, and the next CR area the engine had never been checked against was
**611 — continuous effects**, cited nowhere in the source. What it found is one of the oldest cards
in the pool doing the wrong thing: Overrun resolved with a 2/2 out, correctly 5/5, and a Centaur
Courser put onto the battlefield afterwards read **6/6** off a printed 3/3, with trample. A
continuous effect from a resolved spell applies only to the permanents that were there when it was
created (CR 611.2c); only a static ability's effect is dynamic (CR 611.3).

The cause is the shape of the code rather than a missing check. `pumpTeam` and `pumpAll` pushed a
`controller-creatures` / `all-creatures` scope, and a scope here is re-read on every characteristics
lookup — exactly right for Glorious Anthem and exactly wrong for a spell that has already resolved.
There was no branch to add: **the scope was being asked a question it answers the same way for two
cases the rules distinguish**, which is why reading the scope was the wrong place to look and why it
survived this long. `duration` is the discriminator — `permanent` is what static abilities use, and
every other duration exists because something resolved to create it.

The sweeps are where it changed games rather than numbers. After a Toxic Deluge a player is entitled
to rebuild that turn; with a dynamic scope every creature they cast afterwards arrived already
shrunk, and a 1/1 entering under a −2/−2 is a dead creature on arrival.

The test's second half is what makes it a test of the rule: an implementation that locked every
scope would pass the Overrun assertion and quietly break Glorious Anthem, so the anthem is asserted
beside it — nothing on the board when it arrives, a creature cast afterwards, pumped anyway.

Not fixed and inherited rather than introduced: a creature that dies and comes back is a new object
(CR 400.7) and should be outside the locked set, but `relocate` keeps its instance id. That has been
true of every "target creature gets +3/+3" in the pool from the start, and wants an object identity
the engine does not have.

### "197 checks clean" was never a number (#281, #282, D302)

Two engine changes that move mid-game state — CR 800.4a and CR 611.2c — meant re-running the four
Playwright suites, which sit outside every automated gate and are the only checks that answer whether
two people can sit down and play a whole game through the real UI. **All four pass**: `e2e-table`
73/73, `e2e-solo` 27/27, `e2e-pod` 41/41, `e2e-arena` 55/55, all exit 0.

That totals 196, and #260's title says 197. The one is the finding. Three consecutive `e2e-arena`
runs on the same build read **55, 53 and 55** — the suite is unchanged since well before #260 and
nothing failed in any of them. It has a dozen checks gated on whether the game it drives actually
produced the mechanic, so **the total is a property of the game that happened, not of the suite**,
and #260 wrote down a denominator that does not exist.

This is the third time this project has found the same mistake in different clothes: a floor quoted
in pods read as a floor in points (D281), a ledger row with a margin and no provenance (D298), and
now a check total read as a constant. Each time a number that moves was recorded as fixed, and the
cost fell on a later reader.

The fix cost almost nothing because the suites were already honest — the parentheticals explaining
each skip were there, just uncounted. Each is now a `skip(why)`, and the summary prints
`54/54 checks passed, 4 skipped` with the reasons listed. A total with its skips beside it can be
compared; a bare total cannot.

### A pump survived a blink, and the previous entry was wrong about the fix (#283, D304)

D301 closed the CR 611.2c work by naming a limitation and not acting on it: a creature that leaves
and comes back is a new object (CR 400.7), but `relocate` keeps its instance id, so an effect locked
to that id finds it again — and that entry said the problem wanted an object identity the engine does
not have. **Probing it took five minutes and the diagnosis was wrong.**

It is reachable with two cards in one deck. Verdant Guard runs Giant Growth and Cloudshift: pump a
Grizzly Bears to 5/5, blink it, and it came back **still 5/5**. Cloudshift is a card players reach
for as a trick, so the engine was making it strictly better than printed — keep the pump, dodge the
removal, re-trigger the entry — and the same hole applied to goad and to an Overrun.

It needed no object identity. What a continuous effect needs is to stop applying when its subject
stops existing, and the engine already knows when that is: the moment a permanent gets a `vanished`
snapshot. So a departing permanent's id comes out of every `cards` scope there, and the effect drops
only when its **last** subject has gone — one creature leaving an Overrun must not un-pump the other
two, which is the second test and the one that makes this a test of the rule rather than of a
deletion.

The id is still reused across a zone change, so this fixes the consequence rather than the
representation. Everything else keyed on an instance is already cleared by `relocate` — counters,
damage, `attachedTo`, `pairedWith`, `castAs`, `enteredTurn` — so the hole had one occupant and now
has none. The shape worth remembering: **a new register keyed by instance id will inherit this bug,
and nothing in the types will say so.**

The lesson is about the first entry. Naming a known gap and estimating it as expensive is worth much
less than spending five minutes finding out whether the pool can reach it.

### An Aura stayed on a land that had stopped being a creature (#284, D305)

CR 704.5m bins an Aura attached to nothing, to something gone, **or to an illegal object**. The
engine had the first two, and both of those are a zone change — which is why they were the two it
had. The missing half is the one where nothing moves: the Aura stays, the host stays, and what
changes is whether the host is still the kind of thing the Aura's text allows.

Two cards reach it and both are real plays. A Mutavault is a land until somebody pays {1} and a 2/2
until end of turn, so an Aura cast on the 2/2 is on a land by the next upkeep. An Etched Champion has
protection from every colour while its controller has three artifacts, so playing the third artifact
is how you shed an Aura — a rule the Champion's own docblock has claimed since it was written while
the engine enforced three of its four clauses.

The consequences ran both ways. A Pacifism answered a Mutavault for the rest of the game instead of
for one turn, which is the same shape as D304's blink: strictly better than printed. And a bestowed
Boon Satyr was *worse* than printed — it should stop being an Aura and stand up as the 4/2
(CR 702.103c), and instead it stayed a non-creature Aura handing a **land** +4/+2.

The check asks the Aura's own `enchant` spec rather than "is it still a creature", so a card added
later with a narrower line gets the rule for free. And the shape of the predicate is the decision:
an attachment is not a target, so hexproof and shroud do not apply while protection does
(CR 702.16e). `isLegalAttachment` is `isLegalTarget` minus exactly those two checks, and the test
that pins it is the one where a Blossoming Defense gives your own enchanted creature hexproof and the
Pacifism stays — three of the four tests pass on the naive fix and that one does not.

### A delayed ability found the replacement of the object it was about (#285, D306)

D304 ended with a sentence about what was left — "a new register keyed by instance id will inherit
this bug, and nothing in the types will say so" — and there was already one. `scheduleDelayed`
stored its subject as a bare id, `relocate` gives a card back its own id, so a delayed ability found
whatever now wore it.

Thicket Basilisk is the reachable case and it is a play rather than a board: the Basilisk attacks,
you block, you Cloudshift your own blocker. The blink takes it out of combat, and the creature that
comes back is a new object the delayed "destroy the creature it fought" cannot find. The engine
destroyed it. The script's own comment claimed the rule — "`destroy` reads the instance and does
nothing for a card that is not on the battlefield" — which is true of a card that left and stayed
gone, and that was the only case in mind when it was written.

The entry now carries the subject's `objectSeq` and `fireDelayed` withholds the subject when they
disagree. The ability still fires (CR 603.7d): the test asserts it on the stack, because "dropped
before it fired" and "fired at nothing" leave the same board and only one is the rule.

Checking the other two users of `subject` was not a formality. Flickerwisp broke at once — it
scheduled the return before exiling the card, so the pinned seq was the permanent's and the card in
exile did not match. Exile-then-schedule now, with the reason written down. Unearth needed nothing:
its subject is itself and it cannot be blinked, because the leave-the-battlefield replacement exiles
it instead.

### The same blink, one window earlier (#286, D307)

D306 pinned the delayed entry's subject and left the window in front of it. The Basilisk's block
trigger sits on the stack where both players can see it, so the obvious moment to Cloudshift is in
response to *that* — and the trigger then resolves after the blink, schedules its delayed ability
about the creature that came back, and pins it to the new object. The creature died anyway.

Worth its own entry rather than folding into the last one, because the failure mode is specific: a
fix aimed at the place a bug was *found* can leave the place it is *used*. The D306 probe cast the
blink after the trigger had resolved because that was the simplest script to write.

`StackObject` now carries `aboutSeqs` for `subject` and `blocked`, the pinning `targetSeqs` has done
for targets all along — a sibling field, because the fizzle rule reads that map and these are not
targets. Blanked only when the object is there and different, which leaves a token's own death
trigger (raised after the token stopped existing) exactly as it was.

The test asserts the board the rules describe rather than the one that merely looks right: after the
blink the trigger resolves and schedules **nothing**. "Scheduled and then missed" and "never
scheduled" leave the same creature alive, and only one of them is the rule.

### An instrument for the rules a comment claims and no test writes down (#288, D308)

Three of the morning's four bugs were found by reading a comment and testing its claim, so
`cr-claims.mjs` collects every `CR <number>` in the engine's sources, every one in its tests, and
prints the rules on the first list only: 90 of 245, ranked by how many places lean on them.

Its precision is low and measured rather than assumed. Of the first three rows read, CR 704.5p and
CR 104.2a were both rules that *are* tested and simply do not have their number written beside the
assertion, and CR 720.6 is a real question this container cannot settle — whether the crown is
cleared or passed when the monarch leaves the game needs the Comprehensive Rules, and
`magic.wizards.com` does not resolve here any more than Scryfall does. So the file says in its own
docblock what it is: a reading list, not a defect count.

### Half of CR 704.5a cannot be tested, and finding that out is the result (#289, D309)

The first row of the cr-claims list that was a real gap: the regeneration block's four tests cover
every way a shield *works* and no way it does not, and CR 704.5a says a creature with toughness 0 or
less is put into its graveyard rather than destroyed — so neither a shield nor indestructible has
anything to replace. The engine has had it right since the shield was written; both saves are guarded
on `ch.toughness > 0`.

Only one half is testable. Take the guard off the regeneration branch and the shield is spent, the
creature is tapped, and the next state-based pass kills it for the same zero toughness: the graveyard
reads the same either way. Take it off indestructible and the creature never dies at all. So the pair
that shipped is asymmetric on purpose — the regeneration test asserts the board a player sees and
says in its docblock that it cannot distinguish the two implementations, and the indestructible test
is the one that pins the rule, verified by breaking the guard and watching it fail.

Third time round for the same thread (D282, D302, and the engine's own CR 704.5e note): a test that
asserts the board can read identically whether the rule holds or not, and the only way to know which
kind you wrote is to break the engine on purpose.

### The doc priced a hybrid card as if it needed both colours (#290, D310)

The player doc quotes a mana cost in one shape, `**Name** ({cost} …)`, eighty-three times. Eighty-two
matched the card. Murderous Redcap's `{2}{B/R}{B/R}` was written `{2}{B}{R}` — both symbols are
hybrid, so the card casts off four Swamps or four Mountains, and the doc told a player they needed
one of each, two sections away from where it teaches hybrid mana. The pool has two hybrid cards and
the other one, Kitchen Finks, was written correctly — which is what a one-off error looks like.

Found by asking in bulk rather than by reading: ten lines of node, 83 matches, one disagreement. The
shape is narrow enough to have no false positives, so it became a guard —
`checkPlayerDocQuotesEveryManaCost`, in the gate, reading the card definitions from `starterDecks.ts`
source because guards run before any build, commanders included. It also fails if the parse finds no
cards or the doc has no quoted costs, because a guard that silently checks nothing is worse than
none.

### Three more claims in the same parenthesis, all understating the card (#291, D311)

The cost was one of three things the doc puts in that parenthesis. The same bulk pass over the other
two found three more errors in 117 claims: Monastery Swiftspear as a 1/1 where the card is a 1/2,
Stormchaser Mage as a 1/2 where it is a 1/3, and Thorn of the Black Rose "in Tidal Mind and Ashen
Rite" where it is only in Tidal Mind.

All three point the same way: two understate a creature's body, and the third sends a player to a
deck that does not have the card. The guard now checks cost, power/toughness and deck membership
from the one shape, skipping a power that is not a plain number because the doc cannot quote one
either. Parsed from source: 338 card definitions, 13 decks, 477 membership rows; each kind of claim
verified by breaking one on purpose.

Four doc errors in an afternoon from two bulk passes, none of which a reader would have found: a
human checks the prose and skims the brackets, which is where a machine is better and where being
wrong costs a player a combat.

### An instrument for self-consistent state, and one real leak (#293, D313)

`state-invariants.mjs` asks whether the state the engine hands back after every action is one its own
rules could describe — the question a throw hunt does not ask, and the one the two invisible bugs of
the morning would have answered (an effect naming a card that had gone, an id outliving its object).

Three of the nine invariants I wrote were wrong, and the reasons are in the file: a zone key rebuilt
by hand instead of imported (43 violations in 52 games, all of them the shared stack), a card total
that counted tokens and then counted a knocked-out seat's deck as a leak, and a delayed-subject check
that CR 603.7d says is not an invariant at all. Three more were rejected before being written.

What survived found something on its first clean pod pass: a living seat's pump still scoped to a
card that had left the game with its eliminated owner. `leaveTheGame` filtered effects by controller
and by source and not by scope. Nothing a player can see comes of it — a scope id with no instance
applies to nothing — but it is the same shape as the three CR 400.7 fixes, and the two places that
prune a `cards` scope now prune it the same way.

### A long game and a stuck table read the same (#294, D314)

`LIST=extort` printed `primary: Pass` for five hundred consecutive moves and the log could not say
whether that was a control mirror grinding through turns or a table deadlocked on one priority. A
re-run finished in sixty moves, 28 of 28 with one named skip, which proves the list can finish and
settles nothing about the first run: a re-run is a different shuffle, and the stalled game was
already gone. That question is unanswerable, and stopping the sequence to ask it cost the eleven
lists queued behind it.

The solo suite's periodic line carries the **turn** now so it will not be unanswerable again — and
the first stall it caught was real, within the hour: a solo pod on turn 20 at move 75 and still on
turn 20 at move 570, which died at the harness's time limit with the game checks never reached. A
turn that eats more than two hundred moves is now a named failure that stops the loop.

### The spectacle row is a 30% shuffle, and both fixes for it were wrong (#295, D315)

`LIST=earned` was failing about one run in four on the row that only exists on a turn an opponent
has lost life. Two explanations were built and both were refuted by measurement: that the driver's
preference for a lit card made the row unreachable (three baseline runs reached it, on deals 1, 3
and 4), and that aiming the burn at the opponent's face would make it reliable (three runs, one
failure — burning the face leaves the blockers alive and closes the combat route to the same
condition). The second one was code, and it is reverted.

What fixed it is arithmetic: a row near p = 0.3 a shuffle misses 17% of the time in five deals and
1.4% in twelve, so the budget is twelve. It costs nothing except on the run that would have been
red.

### Two replacement effects for one event (D316)

The one place this pool can produce two: an unearthed Dregscape Zombie sacrificed under an opposing
Kalitas. One event is replaced once (CR 614.1), the widest wording is asked first, so the Zombie's
own "exile it instead" takes the event and Kalitas never sees a death — no token. Both replacements
exile, so the token is the only thing on the board that says which one won, and the control is half
the test. Two further rules (CR 702.21b, CR 601.2b) came off `cr-claims`'s uncited list by being
read and found already tested: 88 to 86.

## The hour the server was innocent (#297, D319)

`press` in the browser driver returns a boolean saying whether the click landed. `makeMove`
discarded it. So on a stalled table the driver reported **201 passes it never sent**, and the log
read like a player patiently pressing a dead button — which is exactly what it was, except the
button was alive and the press was being refused in the browser.

Everything downstream of that was built on it. #297 had ruled out, each with its own instrument: the
engine (52 headless pods, every one to a winner, no throw and nobody stuck), the pod bots, the rate
limiter, a dropped socket, a human move that bought nothing, and slow writes. All six were honest
results and all six were about things that were never involved. `podwatch` finally caught the state
that proved it — a pod frozen at `stateVersion` 193 with an empty stack, nothing pending and nobody
eliminated. A version that never moves, with no server errors, is a pod nobody asked to do anything.

**The instrument was manufacturing evidence, not losing it**, which is the expensive kind of broken.

Then nearly the same mistake twice. The first diagnostic for the failed press read the DOM
afterwards, and `press` makes two attempts at a two-second timeout — so the read happens up to four
seconds after the refusal, and an overlay that has since closed reads as a perfectly clear button.
Playwright had written the answer already and `press` was dropping it in a bare `catch {}`: the call
log names the element that "intercepts pointer events" from the real markup, at the moment it
happened. That is the primary reading now; the DOM read says whether the obstruction is *still*
there, which is a different and genuinely useful question.

Verified against a button under a `fixed inset-0 z-50` veil and the same button uncovered — the
three readings the stalled table gave sixteen times. Five seconds of checking, protecting a
twenty-four-pod hunt that takes two hours.

## A slow write now says where the time went (#298, D320)

D318 found a write that took 17130ms and played 431 bot moves against a client that waits 8000.
A ten-pod census of every write over 150ms then gave the shape: median 366ms, p90 1476ms, max
7814ms, ten at or above a second, one at or above four.

And it looked like it refuted the obvious fix. **Duration does not track move count** — 215 moves
in 3831ms, 111 moves in 7814ms — so per-decision cost dominates, and I wrote that bounding the moves
per write "only helps the first" of the two faults.

So the report was taught to carry the time spent inside `botAction` and the cost of the single worst
decision, which separates four outcomes where the count separated two. **And then it answered the
question against me** (D321). Across 22 slow writes: deciding is 72% of the write, so the cost is
the bots' search — and the worst single decision in any of them is **163ms**, against a client that
waits 8000. A factor of 49.

Per-decision cost dominates the *variance*, which is why duration cannot be predicted from the
count. But the count still **bounds** duration, because the per-decision cost has a ceiling, and
"cannot predict" is not "cannot bound". That was my error, and the sentence above is corrected
rather than deleted because the reasoning is the part worth keeping.

So the fix is the bound after all: 25 moves a write (8000 over 163, halved for a decision worse than
any yet seen), with `continueBots` picking the table up in further writes until a batch does no
work. The board arrives in pieces instead of freezing for seventeen seconds.

Which turned up something larger on the way. Adding a fourth store callback to check the budget
returned `MAX MOVES IN ONE WRITE: 0` — from a counter that fires on *every* write. `createRealtime`
spreads `...opts.store` and then assigns `onBotStall`, `onNoProgress` and `onSlowWrite` over the
top, so **a caller's version of all three was always discarded** — and the realtime suite passes
exactly those three in and asserts at the end of the whole-game test that the first two are empty.
They could not have been anything else. Its own comment calls an empty list "the claim worth
making" (D322).

With them actually wired and nothing else changed, that test **fails about one run in nine**. So
there is a real bot stall or inert human move in roughly a tenth of games, invisible for as long as
the assertion has existed. Held back rather than pushed: a live assertion that reddens CI one run in
nine is worse than the dead one until the defect it names is fixed.

One defect fell out of reading that code: `emit` in the web client resolves on the ack or at eight
seconds and sets no state between, so the measured *median* slow write — a third of a second, and
the p90 at a second and a half — is indistinguishable from a table that has stopped answering.
Filed as #299, same class as #266 and #267 one layer up.

### The tests, and the four corrections they took (D325)

The bound shipped before anything proved it, because the first pair of tests each stood up a second
`createRealtime` to get its own budget, and that instance's Redis clients, cluster adapter and HTTP
server are not fully released by `close()`. D324 measured the cost: 3 of 6 full-suite runs failed
with broadcast timeouts, 0 of 6 with those two skipped. So the pair was skipped and owed a rewrite.

They are now store-level — a `PodStore` built on the test's own Redis client, no server at all —
and they run in about 700ms. Getting there took four corrections, all of them mine:

- **The budget starved its own fixture.** At one move per write the three server seats cannot settle
  their opening hands inside the write `auto:keep` provokes, so the game had not begun and the first
  move came back `FORBIDDEN: you do not have priority`.
- **The cap test's premise was wrong.** The one move a write spends hands priority back to the
  person, so nothing is owed and no report is made. It failed printing `after 0 round(s)` — proof
  only that I had guessed where the condition lived. It now plays the turn out until a capped chain
  really hits its cap.
- **An assertion that could not fail.** `expect(stalled).toEqual([])` in the budget test: `runBots`
  reports a stranded seat only when its *guard* is spent, which a budget below the guard makes
  unreachable. The seventh such check this session, the fourth of mine.
- **Half the budget was unobservable.** `onSlowWrite` fired only in `applyAction`, so a bound
  applied correctly there and wrongly in `continueBots` would have read as a clean table.
  `continueBots` now reports on the same terms — which is also the right thing for a player, since
  those writes run while the page is already waiting.

The budget assertion is `toBe(1)`, not `<=`: equality carries the bound **and** the proof it was
reached. Proved to discriminate by three deliberate breaks — the guard passed at each of the two
`runBots` call sites, and `reportBotStall` swallowing its report — each of which fails it. The
continuation break fails **only** because of the reporting added above.

### The browser suites, re-run on the changed write path

`pod.ts` changed on the path every player move takes, and the browser suites sit outside the gate by
construction (#245), so they were re-run on the shipping tree:

| suite | |
| --- | --- |
| `e2e-table.mjs` | 73/73 |
| `e2e-arena.mjs` | 53/53, 7 named skips |
| `e2e-pod.mjs` | 41/41, 1 named skip |
| `e2e-solo.mjs` | 28/28, 1 named skip |
| `SOLO_POD=1 e2e-solo.mjs` | 30/30, 1 named skip |

**225 checks, 10 named skips, every suite exit 0.** Every skip is one of the documented
shuffle-dependent rows, each naming the deterministic test that covers it instead.

Stability, which is the whole point: **40 consecutive clean full-suite runs**, 46 passed each,
against 3-in-6 failing before. One earlier run of six failed on the cap test with its message
uncaptured, so a 30-run hunt was armed to catch it rather than calling it a flake; it caught
nothing, and the event stays recorded as one unreproduced failure of unknown cause.

## Which controls does no check press? (#305, D328)

The five browser suites pass 225 checks between them, and every one walks a path a scripted game
happens to take. None of them can answer the other question: of the controls the table *renders*,
which has no check ever clicked? That is where an evening of play breaks first, and green says
nothing about it.

`scripts/surface-coverage.mjs` reads both sides out of the source — every `data-testid` the table UI
renders against every one a suite or the driver presses, looks at, or merely names — and separates
controls from passive elements by the JSX around each testid rather than by its name.

| | first reading | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| controls pressed by some check | 59 | **80** |
| looked at but never pressed | 23 | **10** |
| no check even names | 10 | **3** |

`scripts/check-table-controls.mjs` covers what was reachable, at **26/26**: life up *and* down, the
d6, commander damage by hand, both of the watcher's lobby doors, handing a tabletop game to the
rules engine, "Move by hand", conceding, starting over, and leaving.

**Two of those jumps are the instrument getting more honest, not the coverage changing.** The audit
could not follow the driver's usual shape — build a locator from a prefix selector, tap it two lines
later — so its "never pressed" list was about half false alarm; sampled nine families by hand (five
tapped, four not) and taught it to read six lines on. And the watcher's waiting screen and its Stop
button had **no testid at all**, so they were invisible to the audit as well as to the suites: the
instrument was undercounting itself, and the total moved 195 → 196.

### What it found that no suite could

- **`life-up-*` had never been pressed by anything.** `e2e-table` presses life *down*; the direction
  a player uses for every lifelink hit had only ever been read.
- **`confirm-targets` is unreachable** with the present pool, and the button's own comment now says
  so: a fixed-target spell is sent as its last target is chosen, so Cast appears only for an "up to
  N" spell, and every optional spec in the pool is also `divided`, which the bar declines to draw it
  for. It stays for the first non-dividing "destroy up to two target creatures".
- **The lobby's Watch button only exists before a table is dealt** — `listPublic` lists a pod while
  its status is `lobby`, and readying deals it. So a game *in progress* cannot be found from the
  lobby; the code box is the only way in. Whether it should be findable is a product question, left
  as one.

### Six wrong guesses, and what each one is a fact about

Getting those checks to work cost six corrections, every one mine, and each is a fact about the
product worth having written down: the d6 is in the log rather than the transient feed; the engine
refuses to start on a finished game; "New game" only exists post-game; a reset clears the decks as
well as the board, so the deal button returns *disabled* rather than absent; concede arms on the
first press and fires on the second; and commander damage is two elements — one you press on an
opponent's row, one you read on your own.

Three of the six were found only because the check reported **what it found** rather than that it
did not find what it wanted. "No concede in the log, so the click did not land" is the message that
turned an afternoon into five minutes, and it is the cheapest habit in the file.

## Next

1. More scripts. The vocabulary in `effects.ts` covers far more than the cards currently using
   it, and the four ways a card can ask a player something — a mode, targets, a cost, a
   mid-resolution decision — are all in place. Adding a card is a few declarative lines. Every
   keyword and every static scope now has a card behind it, the subtype scope included;
   **every trigger kind now has at least one card**, `becomes-tapped` included — City of Brass
   since #69, and `mechanic-coverage.mjs` confirms 0 of 78 mechanics are declared with no card at
   all (#223, D239). What this list used to say about `becomes-tapped` being the card-less one is
   stale. And a **clock running out is deliberately not a trigger at all** (#221, D238): nothing
   printed watches one, so it is a fact in the log instead of an event with no listener.
   **A draw is an event now** (`draws`, with `you` and `opponent` halves and no `any`, because
   nothing printed here wants one), which was the most frequent thing in the engine and the one
   nothing could read — so "whenever you draw a card" and its mirror are both a few declarative
   lines.
   **And a cost can now be paid out of the graveyard**, which was the last zone nothing could
   spend: `escape` is a cost and a zone (a mana string plus a count of other cards), `delve: true`
   is a reduction chosen as the spell is cast, and `graveyardFodder` decides which cards go — so
   every card printed with either keyword is a line or two, and the shape beyond them (a cost paid
   by exiling cards from *somebody else's* graveyard, or from exile) is the same primitive with a
   different zone key.
   **A card reaching a graveyard is an event too** (`to-graveyard`, carrying which card it was), so
   "whenever another card is put into a graveyard from anywhere" is a line. **And a card reaching
   exile** (`to-exile`, D225), which was the last destination nothing could see and the one the pool
   has been sending cards to since Journey to Nowhere — so the family is complete: every zone change
   the engine makes is now visible to a card.
   `turned-face-up` has two cards behind it, morph has megamorph and a cost paid in life, target
   redirection has Willbender and Swerve, the three board-watching events carry *which* permanent
   they were about, and an ability on the stack can be pointed at — so exalted, evolve, "that
   creature" and "counter target ability" are all a few declarative lines now. Copying one is there as well:
   `copyAbilityOnStack` builds a second stack object with the first one's targets, its `subject`
   and its division, and **Strionic Resonator** in Rot Harvest copies a triggered ability its
   controller owns. It now also offers the printed "you may choose new targets for
   the copy" (`TargetDecisionSpec`), and so does **Twincast**, which copies a *spell* — an object
   with no card behind it, which is the half of the family that needed the stack to hold something
   that is not a card at all.
   A question whose answer is a **word** now exists too, so "you may", "tap or untap" and "choose
   one —" on a trigger are all a few declarative lines. The *number* half of that family is now
   answered both ways round. A quantity **divided among targets** is announced with the spell and
