   checked as a sum (`divided` on a target spec, Arc Lightning), which covers the shape printed
   cards mostly use — damage or counters split among one, two or three things. And a number with
   nothing to divide it between, chosen **as the spell resolves** rather than as it is cast, is
   `NumberDecisionSpec`: a range the card computes from the board when the question is asked, with
   **Toxic Deluge** in Hollow Tide behind it. (The Chalice of the Void this list used to name as the
   example turned out not to need it: its number is the X in its cost, which is chosen at cast time
   and was already in the engine — see *The spell a trigger is about* above.) And the fourth and last shape, a
   **target** for something else on the stack, is `TargetDecisionSpec`: "you may choose new targets
   for the copy", asked while the copy effect resolves, with **Twincast** in Tidal Mind and the
   Strionic Resonator's printed clause behind it. So all four shapes of mid-resolution question are
   in, and a copy effect is a few declarative lines like everything else.
2. Loading a real Grimore deck into an automated table. **Half answered, and the other half still
   blocked.** A player can now paste a list and play it: names the engine's pool has become the real
   cards and are fully automated, which is the whole of the feature for a list built out of the pool.
   What is still missing is the rest of Magic — a name the pool does not have becomes cardboard the
   tabletop plays by hand, and Arena mode refuses it by name. Closing that needs card data for
   arbitrary names (type lines, mana costs, oracle text), the `cards` table has never been populated
   while this environment cannot reach Scryfall, and a type line is the minimum the engine needs to
   tell a land from a spell. Worth building where the data exists, not here — and the refusal is
   written so that it starts working the moment the data does.
3. **A stronger opponent still — and this item's diagnosis is now settled (D241, D243, D244).**
   The claim below is that *"what is missing is not depth: it is an evaluation worth searching
   with"*, and it stood for months with no evidence about **how** the evaluation fell short. Three
   measurements have now answered that, and between them they rule out the entire family of fixes
   that consists of changing a number:

   - The function is **honest**. Its ladder is monotonic, crosses 50% at a margin of zero, carries
     no systematic bias, and the sum beats every one of its components in every turn band — so depth
     was never being wasted on a function that lies about which side is ahead.
   - It is **blunt early**: 61% sign accuracy at turns 5-8, the only band where a search can still
     change an outcome. No amount of depth repairs that, because every leaf is scored by the same
     blunt function.
   - Its one badly calibrated term is **inert** (cards in hand, 42-46% mid-game: a five-fold cut
     moved 936 paired games by one), and **no term is both decisive and wrong** — the high-leverage,
     poor-calibration cell is empty.

   So the next move is a **term that sees something the function currently cannot**, and the open
   question was what a player reads off a turn-six board that none of life, creatures, lands, hand
   or library can express. **That question now has one answer that shipped and one being measured,
   and both have the same shape — the zone was right and the question asked of it was wrong.**

   - **What of my hand I can actually pay for** (#253, D271). The raw count cannot tell a hand of
     three live spells from three things you have no mana for, and only the count had ever been
     measured — so #227's "cards in hand are worth little" and "the evaluation asks the wrong
     question about the hand" produced the same number. The new term carries 4.8% of **cast**
     decisions against the count's 2.8%, and three disjoint seed sets came back 479-454, 469-465,
     471-462: +1.35 points, sign holding every time. The first evaluation term to clear D242's bar
     since. Shipped **on** at a weight of 1 — and then 0.5 and 2 both measured indistinguishable
     from it, so the weight is flat across a fourfold range (D273).
   - **Whether a seat dies in two turns or in six** (#258, D274). D264 priced the same unanswerable
     incoming power *linearly* and it measured flat three ways; eight power is three turns at twenty
     life and one turn at seven, and a linear term scores those identically. Scaled by urgency it
     carries **14.2% of attack declarations**, the largest single-decision-kind figure any term in
     that table has posted and nearly double the linear reading. The discrete form a player says out
     loud — "I'm dead in two" — came in *below* the linear term, which is why both were built.

     **It ships off, and the reason took three corrections to get right.** +1.5 points over three
     disjoint duel seed sets, and −12 at a negative weight, so the duel response is strongly
     monotone: the term's whole effect is caution and caution wins at two seats. At four it makes the
     bot decline **42% of its attack declarations against the shipping bot's 24%** and run games 1.29x
     as long — exactly measured, on an ablation. Whether that *costs* pod games is **unknown**: the
     −8/0/−4 first written up as a negative result sits inside a noise floor of ±16 of 104 that
     nobody had measured, and D281 retracts it. Shipping a large unmeasured behavioural change to the
     pod is the thing not to do, whichever way the win rate would have gone.

   **And the general lesson is now two for two, which closes a second avenue.** D243 found a
   fivefold cut to the hand weight moved 936 games by one; a fourfold range on its replacement moves
   nothing either. **This evaluation is insensitive to its weights and sensitive to what it can
   see** — so neither depth nor tuning is where the next gain is, and the shape of a term is the
   whole question. The rest of this item stands as written.

   A stronger opponent still. It plays each option out — plays, attacks and blocks — and keeps the
   position it likes best, which is worth better than two games in three against the bot it
   replaced. But one ply is one ply: the simulation stops at the end of the current combat, so it
   cannot see the swing back on the opponent's next turn. "A spell is worth more later than now" has
   been taught by hand instead — the ritual, the Fog, the protection trick, the pump, and now the
   mana an answer in hand is waiting for — and each time it was a fact about the board rather than a
   weight, because the weight cannot be made to work. The counterspell is the clearest case of that:
   the same idea failed twice as a *weight* (D68, D69) and works as a *filter*, and the instrument
   that said why is `held-answers.mjs` — the handicap was never when it counters, it was that it had
   already spent the mana — and with the mana there, the judgement is fine (13 declines in 556
   windows, every one of them spent on another instant, and the spells it lets through cheaper than
   the ones it counters). All three need the *reply*,
   which is this same function recursing with the opponent choosing against it — and the cheap
   substitute for the first of them (scoring an untapped creature above a tapped one) was tried and
   measurably lost games, which is written up in `claude/decisions-log.md`. The reply itself has now
   been built and measured too — level over 240 paired duels, at a quarter more time per decision,
   and clairvoyant into the bargain because the search reads the whole game state (D110). What is
   missing is not depth: it is an evaluation worth searching with.
   **The clairvoyance half of this item was a stale claim and is now measured rather than asserted.**
   It was true of the *reply*, which is why the reply was reverted; the bot that shipped is honest,
   and `hidden-info.mjs` says so by asking it the same position twice with every card it cannot
   identify dealt out again — **0 of 8,945 decisions changed** across 78 games, with 1.58 million
   identities moved by the scrambles, and a deliberate cheat wired in as a control shows up at 26
   of 764 attack declarations. `playout.test.ts` holds the regression test (D186). What a *future*
   deeper search would still need is the honest version of the opponent model: the redacted view
   plus what their deck could be holding and whether their open mana pays for it.
4. The pod interface beyond "it works". Three opponents side by side, combat drawn rather than
   described, a threat read on every seat and on every button that sends an attack, one press to
   send the whole swing at one player, and three preset deals that the table records and never
   enforces. What is still missing is the rest of what a pod is *socially*: no table talk beyond the
   chat panel and those three sentences, and nothing that records who was politically on whose side
   over a game. **Half of that is now built**: every opponent's strip reads `hit you N`, all the
   damage that player has dealt you this game, so the table remembers what people did as well as
   what they promised (D189). **And the other direction is now recorded too** (D227): every strip also reads
   `spared you N`, the attacking power that seat could legally have aimed at you and sent somewhere
   else, which is the one reading that tells a player who chose to leave you alone from a player
   who was never able to attack you. **And the table talks back now** (D232): a bot *offers* a truce
   to the seat whose open board can already kill it, which is the one deal it can price without
   modelling anybody's future — the same board reading `answerPact` uses from the other side. Before
   that nothing at this table had ever spoken to the player first.

   Bot to bot it is near-inert and honestly so, because the two rules are one reading from opposite
   sides: 26 offers across thirteen pods produced 25 refusals, and the winner was identical in 12 of
   13. It is on by default because the value is the table a person sits at rather than a win rate,
   which is a claim made on its own terms. What is still missing is the rest of the conversation —
   asking for help, pointing at a threat, making one, trading a target for a target — and none of
   those is priceable from the present board, which is the line `offerPact` draws.

## Checkpoint — the card data, and what was actually blocking it (#306, D329)

Nick asked how close the Play Realm is to **all Commander-legal cards being scripted and playable
by two people**. The honest measured answer:

| | |
|---|---|
| Unique cards the engine knows and fully automates | **348** (13 starter decks, commanders and extra faces included) |
| Cards legal in Commander | roughly **30,000** |
| Share of them | about **1%** |

The number is small and the reason is not the scripting API. That API covers sixty-odd mechanics,
from cascade and storm to morph, sagas, suspend, levelling and the full CR 613 layer system; it is
not where the shortfall is. The shortfall is that the project **has no card data** to point a
script at. Every name outside the pool is dealt as cardboard — a name and nothing else, moved by
hand — and that is a data problem wearing a scripting problem's clothes.

So this checkpoint is the data path, not more cards.

### What was wrong

`scryfall_cards` had 22 columns. The bulk importer wrote **13**. The nine it skipped were not
decoration:

- `color_identity` — the rule that decides what may legally go in a Commander deck
- `legalities` — how a deck is checked against the format at all
- `keywords`, `card_faces`, `edhrec_rank`

All five of those have existed in the baseline schema since migration 0001 and have been left NULL
by **every sync that has ever run**. Six more fields had no column to go in:

- `power`, `toughness`, `loyalty` — a creature's size and a planeswalker's starting loyalty
- `layout` — which multi-face kind a card is (split, adventure, modal DFC, transform, flip)
- `oracle_id` — the card's identity *across* printings, which is what a decklist means by a name
- `produced_mana` — which colours a source makes, without which every land and rock needs a
  hand-written script to be a mana source at all

### What is in now

Migration **0015** adds those six columns, and the importer's Postgres upsert goes from 13
parameters to 26, refreshing every one of them on re-sync.

The one choice worth repeating here: **`power`, `toughness` and `loyalty` are TEXT**, because
`*`, `1+*`, `?` and `X` are printed values. An `integer` column does not store those badly; it
refuses the row. The cards whose size is itself a rule are exactly the cards that would have gone
missing, which is why the test asserts a `*`/`1+*` creature and an `X` planeswalker, and why that
assertion was proved by typing the column `integer` and watching Postgres reject it.

`SCRYFALL_BULK_FILE` lets the import run from a file already on disk, because `api.scryfall.com` is
not reachable from here. Download `oracle_cards` anywhere, copy the JSON across, point the variable
at it. `claude/play-realm-setup.md` has the one-line command.

### The counter the dry run caught

A dry run against a scratch Postgres from a seven-card fixture — built to carry the awkward shapes
on purpose — came back correct in every column and printed **"Wrote 7 cards"** over six rows.

A filtered card (token, emblem, art series, silver or gold border, digital-only, legal nowhere)
returns from `insertCard` exactly as a written one does, and the loop counted both. On the fixture
that is one row of overstatement; on the real dump it is every token in it.

The number was the smaller problem. The guard that exists to catch a broken import tested
`cardCount === 0` — so **a sync that filtered all 30,000 rows and wrote nothing would have reported
30,000 written, nothing rejected, and raised no error.** The check that was supposed to catch the
worst case could not fire in it. That is the eleventh instrument this session found reporting
success it had not earned, and the ninth of those that I wrote. The two outcomes are counted apart
now, both are printed, and the "wrote nothing" guard is reachable — fired deliberately from a file
of nothing but tokens, and again from a file of nothing parseable.

### Where that leaves the original question

Scripted-and-automated is still 348 cards. What changed is that the thing standing between 348 and
thirty thousand is now **one command on a machine with the file**, rather than a schema that could
not hold the fields and an importer that would not have written them. Whether to run it on the VM,
and whether that machine can reach Scryfall at all, stays Nick's call.

### Also this checkpoint

`check-table-controls.mjs` was printing **26/26 passed** and exiting **1** — `summarize()` set
`process.exitCode` and returned nothing, and two scripts read that nothing as a verdict (D330).
The printed tally and the exit code disagreed, which means it mattered whether a human or a script
was reading. I read the tally twice and called the file done; the background runner read the exit
code. `summarize()` returns a verdict now, counting unlanded presses and taps against it, and both
directions were exercised rather than assumed.

## Checkpoint — a card built from its data, and the measured answer to "how much of a deck is that?" (#308, D331-D333)

Nick's goal for this work is *"an MTG Arena style engine with scripts for each card"*. 348 cards are
scripted by hand. The other question — how much of a deck needs no script at all — now has a number
rather than an impression.

### The probe that moved the problem

Before writing anything, a throwaway probe asked what the engine does **today** with a card nobody
wrote a script for. Three readings, two of which meant the plan was wrong:

| | |
|---|---|
| An unscripted **vanilla creature** | **Already works.** 2/2, cast, resolved, attacking next turn. |
| An unscripted creature reading `Flying, vigilance` | **Already has both keywords.** `printedKeywords` was written for this. |
| An unscripted **land** | **Produces no mana at all.** `manaSources` returned `[]`, potential pool all zeros, with `{T}: Add {G}.` printed on the card. |

The engine reads mana abilities off the script and nowhere else. So a deck of data-derived cards was
never failing on blank creatures — it was failing because its **lands did nothing**, and so it could
not cast anything. One thing had to be generated, and it is the thing printed data states most
exactly.

A fourth reading settled a rejection rule: a `*`/`*` creature cast with no script went **straight to
the graveyard** — correctly, since its size comes from a characteristic-defining ability nobody read,
making it a 0/0 (CR 704.5f). A card that dies on arrival every time is worse than one you move by
hand.

### What it does

`packages/rules-engine/src/fromCardData.ts` takes a card row and returns either a playable card or a
refusal with a reason. The design decision that matters: **parse the printed text; `produced_mana` is
the cross-check, not the source.** That field says *which* colours a permanent makes and nothing
about how many — a Sol Ring produces `["C"]` and taps for **two** — so reading the field and ignoring
the text would ship a card that is wrong in the direction that loses games. A disagreement between
the two is a refusal, not a merge.

`customDeck` then resolves a pasted name three ways instead of two: the pool, then the data, then
cardboard. A hand-written script always wins, which is why all 348 pool cards read exactly as before
— demonstrated by the 1364 pre-existing engine tests passing unchanged rather than argued.

### How much of a deck

`scripts/measure/derivable.mjs`, default arm, over the engine's own 348 cards read back as data:

| | built | of | share |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lands** | 22 | 28 | **78.6%** |
| Creatures | 26 | 173 | 15.0% |
| Instants | 0 | 69 | 0% |
| Sorceries | 0 | 50 | 0% |
| Artifacts | 0 | 18 | 0% |
| Enchantments | 0 | 17 | 0% |
| Planeswalkers | 0 | 5 | 0% |
| **Overall** | **48** | **360** | **13.3%** |

**These are the current figures, which is the point of fixing them.** This table first went in at
17-of-28 lands and 43 of 360, and then cycling moved both — and the table sat directly above a
paragraph saying "lands went 60.7% → 78.6%", so a reader meeting the table first got a stale number
presented as the current one. A progress doc is a statement about *now*, so its numbers get
corrected in place. The decision log is the opposite: it is dated, and D332's 60.7% and D333's
11.9% stay exactly as measured, because rewriting a record's past numbers destroys the only thing a
record is for.

**The by-type row is the reading that transfers**, and the script prints it for that reason: the
aggregate is a fact about whatever set was measured, while the rate within a type applies to any deck
whose mix you know. These thirteen decks were built by hand to exercise sixty mechanics, so they are
far heavier in paragraph-text cards than a list anybody plays — the script prints that caveat itself
and says to read the share as a **floor**.

A Commander deck is about 37 lands and 30 creatures, and a real mana base is basics and simple duals
rather than this pool's Mutavaults and cycling lands. Roughly a third of a hundred-card list, almost
all of it the mana base. Which is the probe's answer from the other side: the value is concentrated
in lands, lands are the largest single block of a Commander deck, and the mana base is the part that
must work before the rest of the deck can do anything.

### Two corrections this phase made to its own work

**The first grouping was not a work queue.** The refusal tally flattens every quoted line to `"…"`,
so all 189 "cannot read the line" refusals landed in one bucket with one example — and the commit
that shipped it claimed the grouping made the bucket mineable. It did not; it was a number and an
anecdote. Fixed by grouping the lines by what they *open with*, which is a queue, and which named the
next increment (morph and echo) that was invisible before.

**`tallyDerivations` was deleted.** It counted a batch by kind — the obvious companion to
`cardFromData`, written because it looked like it would be wanted. Nothing wanted it; the measure
script needs the by-type and by-opening readings, neither of which belongs in the engine package. Its
only caller was its own test, and a test over an export nobody calls is green and proves only that
the speculation compiles.

### Where the line is drawn, deliberately

Morph, megamorph and echo derive from their printed cost — **two cards of 360**, because six of the
pool's morph creatures have a turned-face-up trigger as well, which is the whole reason most morph
cards get printed.

**Cycling derives too, and that one was worth five cards** (D338). It had been left out on a reason
that did not survive re-reading: the objection was that it needs an ability carrying a *function*
rather than a data field, but CR 702.29a *defines* cycling as "Discard this card: Draw a card", so
the effect comes from the rules and only the cost is card-specific — exactly as with morph. Five of
the eleven lands the pool refused were cycling lands, so **lands went 60.7% → 78.6%**, which is the
largest single step this work has taken and in the half of a deck that has to work first.

Typed cycling (`Swampcycling {2}`) is refused: it searches a library rather than drawing, which is
a different ability with a different prompt.

Everything past that is refused on principle rather than on effort. A morph or cycling cost is
**data**: the engine knows what the mechanic does, the card supplies a number, and a misparse is a
refusal. "When this enters, you gain 2 life" is **English**, and turning English into an effect is
the direction in which a card silently does less than it reads — no error, no failing test, and a
player loses a game to the engine rather than to their own misreading. The project's rule for card
text (*inventing the text of a real card is worse than leaving the mechanic out*) has a sibling:
**inventing the effect of a real card is worse than leaving it cardboard.**

### The bug the cycling test found, which is the one worth remembering

Cycling's end-to-end test paid for itself on its first run. The derived ability was **offered
correctly**, the cost was paid, the card went to the graveyard, the ability went on the stack — and
it **resolved doing nothing.** No error, no refusal, no draw: a card that silently did half of what
it reads, which is the precise failure this module is designed to prevent, arriving by a route the
design had not covered.

The wiring in D331 touched five call sites and every one of them is a **battlefield** lookup. It
missed `scriptOnStack`, which is how a resolving spell or ability finds its `effect`. Two things
about that are general:

- **An ability on the stack is the only lookup that can reach a card no longer in play.** A cycling
  cost discards the card as the ability is activated, so by resolution the only thing left is its
  definition. A mana ability never leaves the battlefield and could never have exposed this.
- **Inspecting the derived script would not have found it.** Asserting that the ability's `effect`
  is a function passes either way — the script was always right; the engine's path to it was not.
  Only driving the ability to resolution could tell.

### Nick's calls, untouched

- **Running the Scryfall import.** One command on a machine that can reach it; the `--file` arm of
  the measurement is what turns the floor above into the real figure.
- **How `apps/realtime` should get card rows.** It has no database access at all — only Redis — and
  all three `customDeck` calls sit inside a synchronous compare-and-set write where no query can
  happen. Three options with their costs are in D332. What it must **not** be is the client sending
  rows with the paste: that needs no new plumbing and is a cheating vector.

## Checkpoint — the browser set on the mana-path change (#308, D335)

The derivation touched `manaSources`, `potentialMana`, the ability-offering loop, the arrival hook
and `scriptOf`, which is every path a permanent's abilities reach the table through. The full
browser set on that HEAD: **252 checks, 7 named skips, all six suites exit 0** — `e2e-table` 73/73,
`e2e-arena` 54/54, `e2e-pod` 41/41, `e2e-solo` 28/28, solo-pod 30/30, `check-table-controls` 26/26.

The last one is the D330 fix confirmed by the thing that found the bug: the same background runner
that printed "26/26 checks passed" beside "exit=1" now prints exit 0.

The pod suite ran past 1475 moves of its 2400 cap, almost all passes — the shape of #297's stall.
It was not one: at moves 1225 and 1325 the table was still casting Lhurgoyf and Strionic Resonator,
and it finished 41/41. The slowness was two full gates running alongside it on four cores.

**Across three full passes, every shuffle-gated check has run at least once** — a different handful
is skipped each time. So a single run's skip list says something about that shuffle and nothing
about coverage; only the union across runs is evidence. That retired a prompt-coverage instrument
before it was built, and the first draft of its reasoning was wrong anyway: four prompt kinds read as
"not rendered" because the grep covered two components and they are handled in the interaction
reducer.

## Checkpoint — twelve of twelve on the two-person table (D337)

The question behind all of this is whether two people can play a whole game without trouble, which
is a reliability claim. So the two suites that drive two human browsers at one table ran **six times
each, back to back**, on the HEAD whose change went into the engine's mana and activation paths:

| | |
|---|---|
| `e2e-table` ×6 | **73/73** every time |
| `check-table-controls` ×6 | **26/26** every time |
| exit code | **0**, twelve of twelve |
| `FAIL` lines in the whole log | **none** |

Run with nothing else on the machine, which matters: the earlier single pass ran beside two full
gates on four cores and the pod suite's pace fell from 253ms a move to about 1.6s, making a healthy
long game look like a stall. Timings from a contended run are not timings.

Also audited and clean: 18 checks across the suites have the literal `true` as their condition,
which is the exact shape of the "check that cannot fail" this session keeps finding. None of them
is one. Fourteen are inside an `if (seen.X)` guard with a paired `skip()` — the `if` is the
assertion — and four are labels on a preceding `waitFor` that throws. The grep matched the syntax of
a vacuous check rather than its meaning: 18 hits, 0 findings.

## Checkpoint — the resolution-path fix in six browser suites, and mana that is not a land (#309)

### The full browser set on the `scriptOnStack` fix

The engine change in D338 — `scriptOnStack` was still looking a card up by name, so a derived
ability resolved doing nothing — went through every browser suite there is, on one machine with
nothing else running:

| suite | checks | skipped | exit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `e2e-table.mjs` | 73 | 0 | 0 |
| `e2e-arena.mjs` | 55 | 4 | 0 |
| `e2e-pod.mjs` | 41 | 1 | 0 |
| `e2e-solo.mjs` | 28 | 1 | 0 |
| `SOLO_POD=1 e2e-solo.mjs` | 30 | 1 | 0 |
| `check-table-controls.mjs` | 26 | 0 | 0 |
| **total** | **253** | **7** | all 0 |

### Mana that is not a land, derived (D341)

A Llanowar Elves prints the same line as a Hagra Broodpit, and until now the land derived and the
dork did not: `fromCardData.ts` read mana abilities in its land branch only, and refused a nonland
permanent with any text at all. A Sol Ring — whose whole card is `{T}: Add {C}{C}.` — was cardboard.

All three branches read it now, with the distinction the engine has always drawn and the parse had
flattened: `{T}: Add {G} or {W}.` is a **choice** and becomes one ability per colour, while
`{T}: Add {C}{C}.` is a **sum** and becomes one ability producing two. A five-colour bird built the
other way would make five mana off a 0/1.

The refusal of the sum was my own over-reading of this module's header, corrected in D341: the
header's argument is against deriving from `produced_mana`, which cannot say *how many*. The text
can, and does.

The verification is the part worth repeating, because it is not mine. Sol Ring, Birds of Paradise and
Llanowar Elves are **already in the pool, hand-written from the printed card before this module
existed**, so each test builds a row out of the pool's own `CardDef` and compares the derived script
against `scriptFor(name)`. Mind Stone and Mana Confluence stay refused, from the same pool, which is
what keeps those comparisons honest.

### A cost beyond tapping (D343)

Three more cards print one clause more, and each clause is a field the engine already has: a pain
land's `cost.life` (Mana Confluence), a Lotus Petal's `cost.sacrificeSelf`, and `Morph {2}` on a
land (Zoetic Cavern). All three compared against their hand-written twins, descriptions included —
the printed cost prefix is carried verbatim rather than rebuilt, which is what makes that comparison
exact, because a rebuilt label would have had to choose between the card's name and `this artifact`
and both are printed.

At a table: two spires pay for a two-drop and the life total reads 18; a derived Petal pays for a
Bear and is gone from the battlefield, still gone two untap steps later.

Refused, each one word from an acceptance: `Sacrifice a creature` (a choice, not the card itself),
two clauses in one cost, and a permanent whose mana abilities cost different things.

| | before #309 | after #309 | after #310 |
|---|---|---|---|
| pool, built from data alone | 48 / 360 (13.3%) | 51 / 360 (14.2%) | **54 / 360 (15.0%)** |
| creatures | 26 / 173 | 28 / 173 | 28 / 173 |
| lands | 22 / 28 (78.6%) | 22 / 28 | **24 / 28 (85.7%)** |
| artifacts | 0 / 18 | 1 / 18 | 2 / 18 |

Three cards at a time, and **unrepresentatively few**: this pool was built to exercise sixty
mechanics and holds one rock, two dorks and one pain land, where a real Commander list runs five to
fifteen mana sources that are not lands. It is the first family where the pool proxy understates the
real figure for a structural reason rather than as a general caveat.

**The land branch is now at its honest ceiling for this pool.** The four lands still refused were
read one at a time, and every one is a land that *does something*: Mutavault becomes a creature,
Maze of Ith untaps an attacker and prevents its damage, City of Brass deals you a damage when it
taps, Aether Hub arrives with an energy counter. What is left is not unparsed mana — it is four
different effects, each needing the thing this module refuses to invent.

### The instrument that could not see the change (D342)

Run straight after that change, `derivable.mjs` printed the share from **before** it, to a tenth of
a percent, because it imports `dist` and `dist` had not been rebuilt. An honest measurement of the
previous build is the most misleading thing a measurement can be.

`provenanceLine` already printed `dist`'s build time and its docblock claimed the mtime "is the only
thing that catches it". It is the only thing that *could*; catching it was left to a reader, and the
reader was me. It now compares `dist` against the engine's sources and prints `STALE(src <time>)`,
proved in three directions — fresh build silent, a touched source stale, a touched **test** file
silent, since editing a test does not change what `dist` holds. `derivable.mjs` prints that line now.

Five of the fifty-two scripts that import `dist` print provenance. The rest are a known gap, left
deliberately rather than swept at the end of a long session.

## Checkpoint — the project's own master suite, run for the first time (#311)

CLAUDE.md says to verify every change with `python execution/verify_master_suite_orchestrator.py`.
**Nothing in this effort had ever run it.** Running it found two real things.

### Local SQLite was the broken half (D344)

| | suites passing |
|---|---|
| no server running | 0 of 13 |
| `node server.js` up, before any fix | 8 of 13 |
| after repairing the SQLite schema | 10 of 13 |
| after the guest-auth step | **11 of 13** |

`db.js` builds a different table set per dialect, and its Postgres branch carries two dozen
`ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` statements that the SQLite branch never got. Compared
against `packages/db/migrations/` — this project's statement of what the schema is — a freshly
created local database was missing **twenty-one columns**. On it:

- `/api/decks/discover`, the home feed, answered **500** (`no such column: d.is_public`)
- `GET /api/players/:id/profile` answered **500** (`no such column: profile_theme`)
- `INSERT INTO decks (... is_public, format)` named columns that did not exist, so **creating a deck
  could not work at all**

Fifteen columns are now added, read-then-add via `PRAGMA table_info` rather than the swallow-the-error
pattern already in the file. Six are deliberately left out: they are migration 0015's card columns,
and `CARD_UPSERT_SQLITE` was deliberately left at thirteen columns when that shipped.

This project has a careful record of schema divergence, and every bit of it looks the **other** way
round — what Postgres lacks that `server.js` writes. Nobody had asked what *local* lacks, and local
is the environment CLAUDE.md's workflow names first: *test locally first on http://localhost:3000*.

Verified by endpoint: both routes 500 → **200**. Legacy unit tests 40/40. The legacy Postgres
write-path suite, deliberately run against a scratch database rather than left to skip, **28 of 28** —
so the Postgres branch is verified untouched. v2 gate green.

### A suite that could not pass anywhere (D345)

`verify_full_ui_button_and_modal_suite.py` failed at step 1 of 5 on `/api/auth/guest` → **404**. That
endpoint does not exist in `server.js` or anywhere else in the repository; the only mention of the
path was the test auditing it. The shared guest account it signed you into was **retired on purpose**
(`passwordPolicy.js` blocklists its password, "retired in migration 0012").

So the suite failed in every environment, forever — and since the step is first of five, it exited
before the other four ran. The orchestrator could never report success, which is worse than no suite:
a standing failure cannot be told from a regression.

The step now asserts the endpoint is gone, which is the better check anyway. **The four steps behind
it ran for the first time and all pass**: five section endpoints, the TCGplayer `xJoE0d` attribution
this project's rules require, the A2UI renderer schemas, and the login form.

### What still fails, and why it is left failing

Two suites time out against an external AI advisor service this environment cannot reach — the same
blocked-service class as Scryfall. Left failing rather than made to pass.

## Checkpoint — two front doors, and three corrections of my own (#312, D347-D350)

### The door people will actually use (D347)

Running the legacy server for #311 raised a question nothing had asked: if somebody opens the
address CLAUDE.md names — `http://localhost:3000` — and finds the Play Realm, does it work?

`server.js` mounts the v2 SPA at `/react` whenever `apps/web/dist` exists, so the Play Realm is
there. Driven with a real browser at `http://127.0.0.1:3000/react/play`:

- the lobby renders **completely** — formats, name field, Create table
- the socket opens to `ws://127.0.0.1:3000/socket.io/` and the **handshake succeeds**, because the
  legacy server runs its own Socket.IO on that path
- that instance has **zero** `pod:` handlers
- "Nobody has an open table right now" reads as an empty lobby, and **no connection warning appears
  at all**, because nothing is wrong with the connection
- Create table said `the table did not answer` ten seconds later, and nothing else

This is the mirror of #266 and worse than it: a connection that fails is visible, a connection that
succeeds and goes nowhere looks like an empty room. `silentServerNote` now says the handshake was
taken and the protocol was not answered — and deliberately does **not** say "wrong server", because
a wedged table server produces the same timeout. The operator's remedy goes to the console.

**The VM is unaffected, and that was read rather than assumed (D348):** `Caddyfile` sends
`/socket.io/*` to `realtime:3000` and everything else to `app:3000`, and `deploy-gcp.ps1` builds
`apps/web` and ships `apps/web/dist`. The broken door is specifically port 3000 reached directly,
with no proxy in front — a local shape, not the deployment.

Verified: `e2e-table` 73/73, `check-table-controls` 26/26, `e2e-arena` 53/53 with 5 skips, web
suite 243 tests, gate 17/17.

### Three corrections, two of them mine

- **D349.** I reported `deck_cards.custom_tag` as a column "no schema anywhere creates". Both the
  Postgres branch of `db.js` and `0001_baseline.sql` create it. The grep that established the claim
  ended in `head -8`, and eight `server.js` hits came first — the contradicting evidence was in the
  output I asked for and discarded before reading. The fix (adding it to the SQLite branch) stands;
  the claim about Postgres did not.
- **D350.** `claude/postgres-schema-gap-2026-09-27.md` says `direct_messages` and `password_resets`
  are "the two nothing creates". Migration `0014` has created `password_resets` since that was
  written. Of the nine tables local SQLite lacks, **eight are created by migrations 0007/0008/0009/
  0014** — one cutover decision — and exactly one, `direct_messages`, is defined nowhere at all.
- The docblock of the new audit script documented a `DB_PATH` variable that does not exist. A
  documented flag that cannot work is the same fault as a check that cannot fail, committed in a
  comment instead of in code.

The pattern across all three: **a claim is a claim whether it is in a test, a comment or a
document.** Two of these were caught by verifying rather than after shipping, which is the only
reason they are corrections and not defects.

### Reliability, unchanged

`state-invariants.mjs`: **520 duel games** over 40 passes and **130 pods** over 10, nine invariants
checked after every action in all 650, **zero broken**. Recorded as a negative rather than added to
the code.

And the wire cap, which nothing had watched while a game *ran* (#313, D351):
`scripts/measure/wire-growth.mjs` plays whole four-player pods and reports the peak per-seat view.
Starter decks peak at **29.7%** of the 128 KiB cap; four pasted hundred-card singleton lists peak at
**44.4%**, and the peak arrives at **turn 136** in the longest game — where no single-position test
reaches. Sixteen games, every one to a finish, none over.

---

## Checkpoint — measuring at the bound, and the thirty-sixth swallowed throw (#314, D352-D353)

### Two caps written for one purpose, disagreeing at four seats (D352)

#313 measured a hundred-card deck. Measuring at the **bound** instead — the largest list a player can
paste — did not produce a number. It produced a refusal:

```
EngineError: a table may hold at most 600 cards   (INVALID_DECK)
```

`DECKLIST_LIMITS.maxCards` is 250. `MAX_INSTANCES` is 600 for the whole table, under the heading
"Caps on the card layer, so one action can never blow past STATE_MAX_BYTES" — the same reason the
decklist limits give for themselves. Four seats share the 600:

| cards a seat | at the table | result |
|---|---|---|
| 150 | 600 | dealt |
| 151 | 604 | refused |
| 250 (the paste maximum) | 1000 | refused |

**So the paste says yes and the table says no**, with nothing between the two moments to mention it.
Shipped as a warning rather than a limit — two players may legitimately paste 250 each, so lowering
`maxCards` would refuse a real deck — plus a guard that reads `MAX_INSTANCES` out of the engine's
source and fails if the derived 150 in `packages/shared` drifts from it, because that is a number
copied by hand across a package boundary.

At the engine's own four-seat bound the peak view over four whole games was **27.9%** of the cap —
*lower* than the hundred-card arm's 44.4%. A bigger library is not a bigger view; the board is the
whole of it, for the third time.

### The thirty-sixth harness that swallows a throw, and it is mine (D353)

`wire-growth.mjs` shipped with `try { … } catch { break; }` — the fault D244 found in thirty-five
harnesses, written two days after that entry, in a script whose whole job is to report a number. At
600 instances a swallowed throw would have read "these four games were fine" instead of "this table
cannot make a token". Refusals are now recorded and printed.

The honest run said no refusals, which turned out to be an asymmetry worth knowing:
`MAX_INSTANCES` is checked at the deal and on the **tabletop** token action only.
`createToken`/`addTokens` never consults it, so a card resolving a token is bounded by the card's
text rather than by the constant. Left alone with reasons: the view is measured far from the cap, no
card makes more than a handful of tokens, and throwing mid-resolution would leave a spell
half-resolved that the engine cannot undo.

**Writing down a defect pattern does not inoculate against it.** The `catch` was incidental to what I
was thinking about, and the ones that get written are the ones nobody is thinking about.

## Checkpoint — the advisor that never answered, and a gate that could not fail (#315, D354-D357)

### The rules advisor was never reached (D354)

Two of the fourteen suites in `execution/` reported the rules advisor as "timed out". It is not slow:
the handler races Gemini against a 1500 ms timeout with a heuristic fallback. Reproducing it gave
`HTTP 000 in 8.00s` — **no response at all** — and the server log said
`<rejected> TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'player')`.

The route was registered at line 345. `app.use(session({...}))` is at 467. Express hands a route only
the middleware registered before it, so `req.session` was `undefined`, the handler's first line threw,
and because the handler is `async` that became an unhandled rejection — which Express 4 does not route
to an error handler, so nothing wrote a response.

Moved the whole block below the session and epoch middleware:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| anonymous | `HTTP 000` in 8.00s | `401 Not logged in.` in 0.021s |
| logged in | never reached | `200`, heuristic answer, 0.009s |

Three things hid it: the symptom named the wrong layer ("timed out" points at the endpoint's work),
the epoch middleware's docblock claims it is mounted "before every route" (true of every route below
it), and `if (!req.session.player)` reads as a login check rather than as the crash.

### Both suites were aimed at a door they had no key to (D355)

With the hang gone the advisor answers `401` to an anonymous caller — and both suites POST
anonymously, then assert the answer is non-empty. Independently of the hang, **they could never
pass**. New `execution/grimore_session.py` registers a deterministic throwaway account if absent,
logs in, and returns an opener with the cookie; it **raises** on failure, so a suite cannot proceed
anonymously believing it is authenticated. `verify_account_importer.py` had exactly that bug — it
registered on a login failure and carried on, and `/api/auth/register` sets no session.

**The master orchestrator reports 14/14 for the first time** (0/13 when #311 first ran it, 11/13 after
the schema work). These suites are shallow and one passing suite is not one working feature; what
changed is that the number is earned rather than unreachable.

### The gate read green with Redis and Postgres both stopped (D356)

Ten minutes after that push, a realtime run failed with `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:6379`. Redis was not
running, nor was Postgres — and the gate before the push had printed 1425 + 306 + 46 tests passing,
`17 cached, 17 total`, `462ms >>> FULL TURBO`. Every line was a cache replay.

Turbo is not wrong: a running service is not one of its cache inputs, and my commit touched no turbo
input, so there was genuinely nothing to re-run. The gate was green **because the change could not
affect it**, which is a true statement that looks exactly like a verification.

The sixth form of this file's recurring pattern, and the family is the point:

| form | where |
|---|---|
| a check that cannot fail | #311's guest-auth step |
| a check that cannot pass | D355's anonymous advisor calls |
| a swallowed throw | D244 (35 harnesses), D353 (mine, two days later) |
| a documented flag that does not exist | D352's `DB_PATH=` |
| a skipped suite that reads green | D303, 35 realtime tests without `REDIS_URL` |
| **a cached pass** | **a check that did not run, wearing the output of one that did** |

`scripts/services-up.js` (`pnpm v2:services`) asks the one thing the cache cannot know: an inline
RESP `PING` answered `+PONG`, an eight-byte SSLRequest answered `S` or `N`. No credentials — "is
Postgres listening" and "do these credentials work" are different questions. Proved both ways: exit 0
with both up, exit 1 with Redis stopped, naming the port, `ECONNREFUSED`, and what it costs. The local
gate is now five steps, services first. CI is unaffected: it starts both as containers with health
checks and runs through `pnpm -r`, so there is no cache to restore.

### Three readings of a pasted list, collapsed (D357)

`pod.ts` turned a stored pasted list into a deck in three places — the table's summary, the paster's
ack, the dealt deck — as three `customDeck({ ... })` literals with three copies of the same
conditional commander spread. If one lost it, the table would be told one count while the deal used
another, and **each reading would still be internally consistent**. Collapsed into
`deckFromPastedList`, with a test written against the three observable readings rather than the
helper, because a helper test passes just as happily if a call site stops calling it. Deleting the
spread fails that test and its older sibling; restored, 47 pass.

Two observations that could not say what I wanted: the engine's refusal names only the **first**
unreadable card, so it cannot carry a count; and `libraryCount` after `game:start` is 52 rather than
59, because the deal draws an opening hand. Both now read after the load and before the start.

## Checkpoint — two contracts and a build, each enforced by the thing you cannot skip (D358-D359)

Both of these are the same move: take a check somebody has to remember to run, and put it where the
work already has to pass through.

### The response envelopes (D358)

PR #35's body named ~20 response contracts with no conformance test. Measuring narrowed it: of 26
contracts describing a response or an item in one, **15 are enforced more strongly than a test
would be** — the route calls `MePlayer.parse`, `Collection.parse`, `Deck.parse` as it builds the
response, so a drifted item shape is a 500. Two envelopes already had tests. Six had nothing:
`CardSearchResponse`, `LoginResponse`, `RegisterResponse`, `AuthStatus`, `ForgotPasswordResponse`,
`PlayerProfileResponse`. Every one of those is an object literal in a `res.json({ ... })`, so a
renamed `success` or a `totalCards` that becomes `total_cards` reaches the client unchallenged — and
the envelope is what a client derives its types from.

Each new check drops a declared key and asserts refusal, because a test that only parses a good body
cannot tell a contract that describes the response from `z.object({})`. Proved end to end by renaming
`totalCards` in the route: the test fails and names the field.

**A correction worth keeping.** I asserted `AuthStatus` must *refuse* a signed-in body relabelled
`loggedIn: false`. It does not — zod strips unknown keys rather than erroring, so the false arm
accepts it and drops the `user`. That is the better behaviour and the one worth pinning, so the test
asserts the strip instead. A negative assertion is a claim about the contract, and it can be wrong by
being too strong.

`DraftView` and `SandboxCard` have no route here: they describe the draft endpoints D11 did not port.
A contract ahead of its route, stated rather than tested.

A guard reads every `export const *Response` out of the contracts and fails if one is parsed nowhere
under `apps/`. Proved by injecting `GuardProbeResponse`. `apps/api` 306 → 311.

### The stale engine (D359)

`provenanceLine` prints `STALE(src <time>)` when `dist` is older than the engine source — which is
what D338 needed. But it is opt-in, and **45 of the 52 scripts that import `dist` never called it**,
including the one that burned me, until I added the line by hand. Retrofitting 45 calls is 45 chances
to forget and does nothing about the 46th script.

So `scripts/lib/engine.mjs` re-exports `dist` and warns on stderr, at import, when it is behind. All
49 instruments import from it: **importing the engine is the check.** It does not throw (a harness
mid-sweep that dies on import loses the sweep), writes to stderr so a piped run keeps its measurement
clean, and does not rebuild (a script that silently rebuilds what it measures is worse than a stale
number). `distStaleness` is extracted so the printed line and the warning cannot disagree, tie case
included. A second guard fails if an instrument reaches past the wrapper into `dist`.

Four instruments re-run to confirm the indirection changed nothing: `derivable` 360 cards,
`wire-growth` 25.5%/28.6% of the cap, `mechanic-coverage` 81 of 81, `card-promises` 0 gaps with its
control still reporting 1.

## Hybrid automation, and the badge that was only in one zone (#316, D362-D363)

**The decision (D362).** A pasted deck holding a card the engine has no script for no longer drops
the table out of automation. The engine deals the game, runs turns, priority and combat, and the
cards it cannot read are marked for moving by hand. `coverage.ts` (`manualCards`, `manualNote`) is
the report; `GameView.manual` carries it to every seat; `card:move` and `card:tap` already worked
inside an automated game and already recorded zone-change events, so a hand-moved creature still
raises triggers. Removing the refusal broke **one** engine test of 1425 — which is the evidence that
the two halves were built to coexist.

What it deliberately does not claim: it detects *one* of the two ways a card can fail to be
automated. "No printed data" is certain. "Printed data, unimplemented text" is not detected at all —
the reason code `text-not-automated` exists and nothing emits it. The oracle-text compiler (#317) is
what will be able to answer it.

**The defect that fix shipped with (D363).** "move by hand" was added to `cardBadges` above the
battlefield-only guard, with a comment saying it would therefore show in **every** zone, and naming
the hand as the zone that mattered most. It showed in exactly one: the battlefield. The hand, the
graveyard, the exile pile and the command zone each passed `PlayTable` their own
`badgesOf={(card) => ... ["playable"] ...}` and never called `cardBadges` at all.

Nothing caught it, and each reason is worth keeping:

| Should have caught it | Why it did not |
| --- | --- |
| 8 `cardBadges` unit tests | all passed — the *function* was right; four call sites chose a different one |
| `pnpm v2:typecheck` | a `badgesOf` is `(c: VisibleCard) => readonly string[]` whatever it computes |
| `check-hybrid.mjs` in a real browser | asserted the badge on a deck with 1 unreadable card in 60, which sits in the library ~7 runs in 8, and a library renders nothing |

That last row is the new one for the family: a check whose **true failure reads as a flake**. Every
other member reads as good news. I had written the shuffle dependence into that check's own comment
and then relied on it anyway.

Fixed by making `cardBadges` the only place the rule lives — `playable` moved above the guard, the
four lambdas deleted — plus two regression tests proved to discriminate, and
`checkBadgesAllComeFromCardBadges` in `scripts/guards.js`, also proved to discriminate. A test cannot
catch this and a type cannot either; a grep can, because the defect has a shape.

`check-hybrid.mjs` now runs two tables, because neither deck can carry both claims: a 59/60-readable
deck proves the engine *keeps playing* (four real moves taken), and an all-unreadable deck proves the
marking is *visible* (seven unreadable cards in hand, so the badge cannot be missed by construction).
**11/11**, and in CI's `browser` job as `play:e2e:hybrid`.

## The oracle-text compiler, first stage (#317, D364)

**The thesis.** `fromCardData.ts` asks *is this card's text nothing but its data?* — all or nothing,
and 15% of the pool. The 85% is not a wall: a Murderous Redcap is persist plus one sentence, a
Basilica Screecher is flying plus extort, a Mystic Remora is cumulative upkeep plus one ability. For
almost every card *some* of the text is machinery this engine already has. So the unit is the
**printed line**, not the card. Hybrid automation (D362) is what makes that worth having — before
it, 60% of a card was worth nothing, because one unread line dropped the whole table.

**What shipped.** `printedDef`/`printedRulesLines` split out of `cardFromData`; `compile.ts` above
both it and `scripts.ts` (which imports it, so the compiler cannot live in either); `keywordScriptFor`
with ten keywords; `scripts/measure/compilable.mjs`.

**The compiler can exist because the hand-written scripts were already factored into parameterised
builders.** For a keyword the printed line *is* the argument: `Modular 1` → `modularTrigger(1)`,
`Ward {1}` → `ward(name, '{1}')`, `Undying` → no argument. Nothing invented (D259).

**The unit is a partial `CardScript`, not a trigger** — and reading Calciderm is what showed it.
`vanishingTrigger(4)` is conditioned on a time counter, and the counters come from `entersWith`, and
the declaration lives in `vanishing`. Emit the trigger alone and you get a Calciderm that **never
dies**. Modular and fading are the same three-part shape.

**Three keywords left out**, each because the line does not determine the rule: soulbond (the bonus
is on the next line), level up (its `levelBands` are three blocks of text below it), morph and echo
(already read by `keywordWithCost` — two readers of one line is two places to disagree).

**The test is ground truth, not plausibility**: compile ten pool cards' own printed text and compare
against the scripts a person wrote reading the same cards. Triggers compared by `on` + `description`,
the two fields that come from the builder rather than the card. 20 tests.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| whole-card | 51 — 15.0% |
| **keywords (new)** | **21 — 6.2%** |
| printed-only | 267 — 78.8% |
| **Lines compiled** | **142 of 538 — 26.4%** |

Work queue: 245 distinct openings, 185 from one card each. Biggest: `When ~ enters the battlefield`
(36), `~ deals N damage to` (19), `Draw a card` (7), `Whenever you cast an instant` (6). That is the
pool — thirteen decks built to exercise sixty mechanics — so a **floor**. Scryfall egress is still
refused, so #318 lands source-agnostic.

## The gate needed a gate (D365)

The five-step pre-push gate lived in a session temp directory and, on this run, printed
`GATE FAILED at: node scripts/guards.js (rc=0)` and **exited 0**. `$?` read inside the then-branch
of `if ! cmd` is the status of the successful test, not of the failed command. The `(rc=0)` had been
printed in that message every time; I had never read it because the words before it said what I
expected. Thirteenth member of the family, and the worst shape yet: **a check that reports failure
and returns success.**

Now `scripts/gate.sh` in the repository (`pnpm v2:gate`) — run, capture, then test — plus
`scripts/check-gate.sh` (`pnpm v2:gate:check`), which runs the gate against a step that cannot pass
and fails if it reports success. That check immediately found a second bug pointing the other way:
the gate's summary `grep` exiting 1 under `pipefail` made it exit 1 *after passing every step*. Two
bugs in a twenty-line script whose only job is to report a status, both found by asking it for its
status once.

## The compiler's second stage: sentences (#317, D366)

D364 read keywords, whose fragments are data. This reads the first *sentence* shape, whose fragment
is a closure — which changes what can be compiled and how it can be checked.

One trigger shape (`When ~ enters the battlefield, <clause>`, the biggest bucket by 2x) and seven
untargeted clauses: gain life, lose life, draw, monarch, scry, energy, each-opponent-discards. The
shape and the effect are separate functions deliberately: `untargetedEffect` is shared with every
later trigger shape and with the 114-card instant/sorcery bucket `cardFromData` refuses outright.

**The rule for this stage**: the clause must determine the effect completely, with nothing chosen by
anybody. Targeted clauses need a target-spec vocabulary with its own failure modes, and reading them
badly would aim real removal at the wrong thing — worse than not reading them.

**Two questions settled from the engine's own comments rather than guessed:**

- `draw` vs `drawLater` — the pool uses both for "draw a card", a behavioural difference.
  `drawLater`'s docblock allows itself only for a draw that is the last thing the card does, and
  adds that "the compiler cannot tell the two apart". True of a compiler reading a sentence; not of
  one that matches only when the clause **is** the draw and nothing else. Safe by construction, and
  the better primitive since only a deferred draw can be dredged (CR 702.52a).
- `{kind:'etb'}` vs `{kind:'etb',who:'self'}` — `automation.ts` says `self` is the default, so they
  are the same trigger. The compiler spells it out, because generated scripts are read by people.

**The test had to change shape.** Closures are not comparable, and the obvious fallback — comparing
`description` strings — would have been wrong: Kitchen Finks stores the clause, Aether Hub stores the
whole printed line including the part `on` already carries. So the check runs both effects on one
state and compares the results, which is the actual claim.

Two things that made it honest: a bare `arena()` has empty hands, so Ravenous Rats' discard did
nothing and `toEqual` passed on two no-ops — caught by the non-vacuity assertion, fixed by dealing
seat 1 a card. And `drawsOwed` is a flat list of seat indices, not a count per seat, so my
`drawsOwed[0] === 1` compared a seat to a count with a `?? 0` ready to hide it. Proved to
discriminate: one point of life off fails Kitchen Finks.

| | D364 | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with compiled rules | 21 (6.2%) | **34 (10.0%)** |
| **lines compiled** | 142 of 538 (26.4%) | **156 of 538 (29.0%)** |
| the ETB bucket | 36 | 22 |

The remaining 22 ETB lines are almost all targeted, which is the next increment and the one that
also unlocks removal and bounce on instants.

## Targets and spells (#317, D367)

Two things at once, because they share a prerequisite: targeted clauses need a **target spec**, and
instants and sorceries need a **resolution path**, and both want the effect vocabulary D366 built.
That shared vocabulary was the architecture claim D366 made; this is the increment that tests it.

**Target specs.** `any target` and `target creature` are 47 of the ~95 target phrases in the pool;
the tail is 28 phrasings at 1-2 cards each. The interesting parameter is `friendly`, because **it is
not in the phrase** — "target creature" is identical on a Doom Blade and a Giant Growth. It is a
fact about the effect, so the caller supplies it. D252 added the flag because the bot's default is
"aim at the enemy": a pump that forgets it buffs the creature it was about to kill. Wrong in a way
nothing refuses. The clearest case is a counter on a creature, where `+1/+1` and `-1/-1` differ by
one character and point in opposite directions.

**The bot hints are D364's lesson again.** `Doom Blade` sets `removesACreature: true` and
`Giant Growth` sets `expiresAtEndOfTurn: true`. Emit the effect alone and you get a card that works
and plays badly — worse than an unread line, since an unread line is flagged for a human (D362) and
a badly played one is flagged nowhere. Returned as `spellFlags`, applied only on the spell path,
because "removes a creature" is advice about casting and an ETB trigger is not cast.

**A spell is compiled whole** — its resolution is one go, so a half-read spell would silently do
half of what it prints. **And the first version got that wrong**: it treated *every* line of a spell
as resolution, so Grapeshot (damage + Storm), Sudden Shock (damage + Split second) and Pyromatics
(damage + Replicate) each presented two lines, were refused outright, and **lost a keyword reading
that already worked**. A new path replacing an old one rather than extending it.

The ground-truth tests caught it on the first run and named all three cards. Nothing else would
have: the types were fine and the coverage number went *up*. That is the argument for comparing
against hand-written scripts instead of asserting a shape. Fixed by partitioning — keywords read as
keywords, the remainder as resolution — and pinned by a regression test that checks Grapeshot keeps
both its storm trigger and its damage.

| | D364 | D366 | now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cards with compiled rules | 21 (6.2%) | 34 (10.0%) | **48 (14.2%)** |
| **lines compiled** | 142 (26.4%) | 156 (29.0%) | **173 of 538 (32.2%)** |

Cards with rules have more than doubled since the keyword stage; a third of every printed line in
the pool now becomes rules. Still a floor — the pool is thirteen decks built to exercise sixty
mechanics. 43 compiler tests.

## CI failed where the gate passed (D368)

CI's `v2` went red on `cafa599` while the gate said 17/17 on the same tree. Two defects.

**The test.** `apps/realtime`'s origin allow-list test makes two handshake attempts in sequence,
each with a `setTimeout(..., 4000)` fallback, inside vitest's 5000ms default — **8000ms of internal
budget inside a 5000ms deadline**. It could not pass if either attempt took its slow path, and
passed for months because both normally answer in milliseconds. A loaded runner (the preceding test
took 9.5s) starved it, and it died with `Test timed out in 5000ms` — naming neither origins nor
handshakes, and sending me after a regression in a diff that does not touch that app. A fallback
only reachable *past* the deadline it exists to report inside turns a specific failure into a
generic one. Now 2000ms each with an explicit 15000ms test timeout. Engine import measures 63-84ms,
so the compiler was not the cause.

**The gate, which matters more.** It ran `pnpm v2:*` — turbo tasks. CI runs `pnpm -r`. turbo
**caches by input hash**, so the gate could replay a stored green for a suite CI runs for real;
and CI had three steps the gate lacked (packages build, token-parity test, web production build).
`scripts/gate.sh` is now CI's `v2` job verbatim plus `services-up.js` — eight steps. Slower, and
that is the trade: a gate that is fast and sometimes wrong is worth less than one that is slow and
right.

I had reported `cafa599` as "verified by the gate, 17/17" on a tree CI then rejected. The number was
real; the confidence it implied was not.

## Composition (#317, D369)

The spell path took one resolution clause and refused anything longer — the right safety property
(all of a spell or none of it) reached by a stricter rule than it needs. `readResolution` now
composes: resolution lines together, each split on `, then `, **every** part must compile, state
threaded through them in printed order.

First increment that adds **no vocabulary** and still moves coverage, which is the point:
composition multiplies every reader already present and every one added later. **178 of 538 lines
(33.1%)**, 51 cards, on readers that already existed.

One refusal worth keeping: two parts cannot share one `targets` list, so a spell whose halves each
want their own target is refused rather than silently handed the same target twice.

**Two of my own tests failed, and both were pinning the restriction rather than the invariant** —
one used `Scry 1, then draw a card.` as an "unreadable" example, which it no longer is. The
invariant now uses "Draw two cards, then discard two cards.", real pool text whose second clause has
no reader. The tell for this mistake: the failing assertion was about *how much* the compiler
refuses, not *what it must never do*.

And a comment of mine overclaimed: the ordering test cannot show order-sensitivity, because gaining
life and owing a draw are independent. It proves the state is **threaded** (verified by breaking the
reduce both ways); the comment now says order is untested rather than implying otherwise.

## Keywords, sentences and twelve target phrases (#317, D370-D371)

**204 of 538 printed lines, up from 178 (33.1% → 37.9%). 127 of 339 cards now get a script, up from
102.** Counterspell, Cancel, Disenchant, Naturalize, Krosan Grip, Murder, Mizzium Mortars, Raise
Dead, Gravedigger, Tome Scour, Mind Sculpt, Thought Scour and Returned Centaur among the new ones.

### A keyword nobody implemented was refusing whole cards

`Miracle {R}` refused Thunderous Wrath. The spell path put every line it could not build into the
resolution, and the resolution is all-or-nothing — so a damage clause the compiler reads perfectly
well was thrown out by a line that is not part of resolving the spell at all. Four pool spells were
refused that way (Thunderous Wrath, Staggershock, Rift Bolt, Skewer the Critics).

`isKeywordDeclaration` answers a different question from "can I build this?": **is this line part of
the resolution?** A keyword is a cost or a modifier — a way to cast the card — so leaving it unread
is a *missing option* on a card that plays. An unread sentence is a card that cannot be played at
all. Those are different kinds of incomplete, so `UnreadLine.why` gained `unimplemented-keyword` and
the measure prints it apart: 66 of the 334 unread lines. Anything built on `unread` — the hybrid
badge above all — would otherwise lie in one direction or the other.

Backed by a closed list of CR 702 keyword names rather than a shape rule. **Ability words are
deliberately off that list**: `Magecraft — Whenever you cast …` is a whole triggered ability with a
label on the front.

### Sentences compose, and one composer serves both paths

"Target player mills two cards. Draw a card." is one printed line and two clauses; the reader split
only on `, then `, so Thought Scour went unread whole. Both the trigger path and the spell path now
call one `composeEffects`, which owns the all-or-nothing rule and the one-target rule — they were
two implementations of the same problem.

### The target vocabulary, from two phrases to twelve

`target player`, `target spell`, `target permanent`, `target creature you control`, `target creature
you don't control` / `an opponent controls`, `target artifact`, `target enchantment`, `target land`,
`target artifact or enchantment`, `target creature card in your graveyard`. Each spec stores the
phrase it was read from, which is character-for-character what the hand-written twin stores.

### Three things the tests caught that I had wrong

- **Sentence casing.** Giant Growth prints "Target creature gets +3/+3", so echoing the phrase gave
  `Target creature` against a hand-written `target creature`. Found on the first run.
- **`plain` was unpinned and its comment was false.** Deleting the apostrophe normaliser passed all
  59 tests, and the comment claimed Mizzium Mortars prints a typographic apostrophe — it prints an
  ASCII one. The pool spells the same construct both ways (21 cards `'`, 23 cards `’`), and every
  card the compiler reads today is in the ASCII half. Now pinned on a curly-spelled bounce spell,
  verified red without the normaliser. The corpus #318 imports is the other half.
- **My first deferred-draw guard was too blunt.** `drawLater` owes the card, so nothing after it can
  see what it drew; I refused any composition whose draw was not last, which also broke "Draw two
  cards. You gain 2 life." — a card never in danger. The shape that costs nothing: the clause offers
  **both** readings and the composer picks by position. "Draw a card. Scry 2." really does draw
  first.

### Recorded, not fixed

Five hand-written target filters read the *printed* type line while the compiler's reads the live
one (CR 109.2), and one of them documents the live reading it does not do. Two readings of one
question in one file — task #319, with its own measurement, because it changes which permanents five
shipping cards may point at.

Verified: compile.test.ts 60/60, each of the four new mechanisms proved to fail when broken. Full
gate green (all eight CI steps).

## Trigger shapes (#317, D372)

**217 of 538 printed lines, up from 204 (37.9% → 40.3%). 139 of 339 cards get a script, up from
127.** Ajani's Pridemate, Bloodthirsty Aerialist, Borderland Marauder, City of Brass, Firebrand
Archer, Gelectrode, Goblin Arsonist, Guttersnipe, Longtusk Cub, Ninja of the Deep Hours,
Thermo-Alchemist and Thieving Magpie.

One printed prologue became thirteen. Until now every effect the compiler could read was reachable
from exactly one place on a card — "When ~ enters the battlefield" — so this is the same kind of
increment as composition (D369): almost no new vocabulary, much more coverage, because shapes
multiply every reader already present.

Thirteen prologues (both etb forms including "or dies", dies, leaves, turned face up, attacks,
combat damage to a player, becomes tapped, the two cast triggers, gain life, and the two step
triggers) and one new clause family — a clause that acts on the permanent itself: untap ~, ~ gets
+N/+N until end of turn, put N +1/+1 counters on ~.

Every event is copied off the card that prints the prologue, and the test reads the expected `on`
off the hand-written script rather than from a literal — so a shape copied wrongly fails even if the
compiler and the test agree about the wrong answer.

**"Or dies" is two abilities sharing one effect** (CR 603.1), so a shape carries a list of events.

### Two defects, both caught by deep equality on the board

- Borderland Marauder's `+2/+0` is `{ power: 2 }` by hand and the compiler passed
  `{ power: 2, toughness: 0 }`. Same pump, different *state*, because the bonus is stored as a
  continuous effect.
- Untapping an untapped permanent is a no-op, so Thermo-Alchemist's comparison was two no-ops
  passing `toEqual` — the D366 vacuity family again. The fixture taps it first.

### Not read on purpose: `sacrifice ~`

Ball Lightning sets `leavesAtEndOfTurn` beside its end-step sacrifice, and without it the bot holds
the creature back to protect something it is about to lose anyway. The flag belongs to the *pair* of
prologue and clause, and a clause reader cannot see the prologue — so the clause stays unread, with
a test that keeps the omission deliberate.

### And a reading error of mine

I ran the gate as `bash scripts/gate.sh 2>&1 | tail -6` and called it green. It had failed:
Postgres and Redis died in a worker restart, `services-up.js` refused as designed, and `tail -6` cut
off `GATE FAILED` while the pipe replaced the gate's exit status with `tail`'s. Same shape as D356,
D365 and D368, with the defect moved out of the script and into how I invoked it. Re-run with the
output redirected and `$?` captured: **GATE OK, exit 0.**

## Tokens (#317, D373)

**225 of 538 printed lines, up from 217 (40.3% → 41.8%). 146 of 339 cards get a script, up from
139.** Doomed Traveler, Doomed Dissenter, Mogg War Marshal, Raise the Alarm, Talrand, Woe Strider,
Young Pyromancer.

A token is the one thing in this compiler with nothing to look up: its power, toughness, colour,
subtype and keywords *are* the clause that makes it. The pool's twenty hand-written token constants
are that clause transcribed, so the comparison is the strictest in the file — resolve both effects
and compare whole game states, which covers the created instance and the `CardDef` registered for
it.

**The keywords are validated by the reader that has to read them back.** A token's keywords live in
its `oracleText` and the engine gets them from `printedKeywords` with no script involved, so instead
of keeping a list of keywords the compiler believes in, it writes the text and asks
`printedKeywords` whether that text yields exactly the keywords the clause named. "With flying"
that the engine could not read back would be a 1/1 that silently cannot fly.

Five refusals, each with a test: `create X … tokens`, `… token for each …`, `with "When this
creature dies, …"`, `Create a Treasure token`, and `a token that's a copy of target creature`.

### One guard kept on purpose with nothing pinning it

The reader requires each subtype word to be capitalised, and deleting that check leaves all 82 tests
green — the surrounding regex already carries the weight. It stays because the two ways of being
wrong are not symmetric: the slot becomes the token's *name*, and over-permissiveness on a corpus
nobody has looked at yet is worse than losing a card nobody can name. The comment now says that
instead of implying the check does work it cannot be shown to do.

## The compiler reaches a table (#317, D374)

Seven increments of compiler and none of it had reached a game. `scriptForCard` — the one function
the engine asks "what does this card do?" — still called `cardFromData` and nothing else, so 146
cards' worth of derived rules existed and no table used them.

New module `derive.ts`, above both `scripts.ts` and `compile.ts` (the compiler imports the scripts,
so the answer could not grow a third branch where it was). Precedence: hand-written script, then
`cardFromData`'s whole-card answer, then the compiler. **The hand-written script still wins**, so
all thirteen built-in decks are untouched.

### The half that makes turning it on honest

A compiled script is often partial, and a card that does three of its four printed things with
nobody told which one is missing is exactly the trade D362 refuses. So `coverage.ts`'s
`'text-not-automated'` — reserved since that file was written, *"nothing emits this yet… the
compiler is what will"* — now emits, quoting the line that does nothing.

Three rules keep the report true:

- a card with a hand-written script reports nothing (the script is the authority; otherwise a
  Kitchen Finks would read as partly manual). Pinned by a test over all thirteen decks.
- an unimplemented keyword is not reported — the card plays, and what is missing is one way to cast
  it (D370).
- `manualNote` says "cannot fully play", because the list now holds two different things.

### A bound by arithmetic, because the instrument cannot see it

`wire-growth.mjs` run on this build: worst peak **47202 bytes, 36.0% of the 128 KiB cap** across
three singleton pods of 63-82 turns. But it **cannot measure the new payload** — every deck it can
build is a pool deck, every pool card has a hand-written script, so `manual` is empty in all three
games. That arm needs the imported corpus (#318).

So: a hundred cards each quoting an unabridged paragraph would add ~47 KiB to a 47 KiB peak. The
quote is capped at 120 characters, holding an entry to 227 bytes measured, which brings the same
worst case to ~23 KiB added — 70 of 128.

## The corpus filter, and why no card can reach the database (#318, D375)

The importer was already source-agnostic (`SCRYFALL_BULK_FILE`, D329), so what was left of #318 was
the filter and the report.

**The filter now names the formats.** It used to accept a card legal or restricted in *any* format
Scryfall tracks — a map that also carries Alchemy, Historic, Timeless, Brawl, Oathbreaker and PreDH.
Now: standard, pioneer, modern, legacy, vintage, pauper, commander. Every refusal returns its reason
instead of a bare `false`, and the tally prints a line per reason, because one total cannot tell "the
dump was all tokens" from "the legality list got too narrow". The whole filter is lifted into
`importFilter`, a pure function with five tests — one of which pins the seven format keys as a list,
since a misspelled key reads as `undefined` and silently empties the corpus.

### Then running it found the real blocker

Nobody had ever run this import end to end; no test does, because it needs a database. On a
seven-card fixture it filtered five rows, one per reason — and **rejected both keepers**:

```
column "power" of relation "scryfall_cards" does not exist
```

`packages/db/migrations/0015_scryfall_card_rules_fields.sql` adds the six columns the importer needs
and **has never been applied**: 0 of 18 Postgres databases here have one of them, and `grimore_dev`
has no `schema_migrations` table at all. So the corpus cannot land, and the thing standing between
the compiler and the real card pool is one unapplied migration — recorded as **#320**, because
applying `packages/db`'s migrations to a legacy-created schema and the production cutover are both
Nick's calls.

D329's guard, which turns "wrote no rows" into a thrown error, is what made one run enough to find
this.

### And the instrument that should have caught it read one file

`audit-postgres-schema-gap.js` checks INSERT column lists against the real schema — exactly this
defect — and read only `server.js`, so the card upsert in `scryfallService.js` was invisible to it.
It now reads both. The first run with the second file produced a confident **false positive**
(`scryfall_id`, a column only the SQLite statement names), because the existing guard skipped the
SQLite branch of a ternary and a named constant is not one. Fixed by the declaration name, not by
proximity.

## Attachments, read two lines at a time (#317, D376)

**243 of 538 printed lines, up from 225 (41.8% → 45.2%). 154 of 339 cards get a script, up from
146.** Bonesplitter, Loxodon Warhammer, Basilisk Collar, Darksteel Plate, Blade of Selves, Robe of
Mirrors, Angelic Gift, Pacifism, Rancor.

The compiler's first whole-card shape. `Enchant creature` alone is an Aura that attaches and does
nothing; `Enchanted creature gets +2/+0` alone is a bonus with nothing to attach it to. Neither line
is a unit and the pair is — so `attachmentScriptFor` reads both or neither, and `compileCard`
consults it before the per-line loop.

`equipFragment` is split out of the hand-written `equipment` builder, so the compiled Bonesplitter
and the hand-written one are the same ability.

**`friendly` and `removesACreature` come off the bonus, not the phrase.** Every Aura prints the same
`Enchant creature`; Angelic Gift's target is friendly and Pacifism's is not, and Pacifism is also
removal. A negative size change is harmful by arithmetic.

### A redundant guard, found by trying to break it

The reader had a test for a quote mark, to refuse Ophidian Eye's granted ability. Deleting it left
all 93 tests green: the keyword validation already refuses it, because the quoted sentence splits on
its own commas into fragments `printedKeywords` does not know. Gone, with a comment saying what does
the work. Opposite verdict to the token subtype check (D373), and the difference is which way the
redundancy cut — a duplicate of a *tested* refusal is dead weight.

## Who the trigger watches, and exile-until-leaves (#317, D377)

**253 of 538 printed lines, up from 243 (45.2% → 47.0%). 162 of 339 cards get a script, up from
154.** Angel of Sanctions, Banisher Priest, Banishing Light, Chasm Skulker, Conclave Tribunal,
Impact Tremors, Impassioned Orator, Journey to Nowhere, Soul Warden.

**Ten more prologues, all about `who` and `of`.** "Another creature" is `who: 'another'`; "a creature
