you control" is `who: 'any', of: 'you'`; "~ or another creature" is `who: 'any'` with nothing said
about whose. Soul Warden's own comment makes that load-bearing — a reader that collapsed them would
build a card that triggers off its own arrival where the print says it does not.

**Exile-until-leaves is the second whole-card shape.** The exile and the return are two triggers and
either alone is a broken card. The pool prints it two ways and the difference decides whether the
return exists at all, so a bare `exile target creature` ETB with neither an `until ~ leaves` clause
nor a `leaves` line is refused — that card is permanent exile, and handing the creature back would
be a different, weaker card.

Five new target phrases over one composable `permanentFilter` ("another", "nonland", "an opponent
controls"), replacing what the pool spells as three hand-written filters over the same three tests.

**The vacuity family, third appearance.** Chasm Skulker's clause acts on itself, so with a made-up
source id both effects were no-ops and `toEqual` passed on nothing. Caught by the non-vacuity
assertion, as in D366 and D372 — three for three found by a deliberate guard.

### #320's local half is cleared

Migration 0015's ALTERs are applied to `grimore_dev` and the import is **verified end to end**: the
fixture writes its 2 keepers, filters 5 one per reason, rejects nothing, and the rules columns carry
real values. The production cutover and whether `packages/db`'s runner should own that table stay
Nick's.

## Activated abilities, the third home for a clause (#317, D378)

**265 of 538 printed lines (49.3%). 171 of 339 cards get a script. Unchanged from D377 — and that
zero is the point of this section.** Stage ten's first half picked up nine cards: Blight Mamba,
Drudge Skeletons, Imperious Perfect, Mind Stone, Mutavault, Phoenix of Ash, River Boa, Shivan
Dragon, Skithiryx, the Blight Dragon. Its second half picked up none and fixed two defects.

**A clause now has three homes:** a trigger's resolution, a spell's, and a printed cost. Nearly no
new vocabulary was needed — every effect the compiler could already read became reachable from an
activated ability, and `Regenerate ~` was the one new reader. Mana abilities are answered separately,
with `produces` and **no** effect at all, because that is what makes a mana ability one (CR 605).

**The cost is parsed by classifying its components, not by one pattern.** `{1}, {T}`, `{T}, {1}`,
`{T}, Pay 1 life` and `{1}, {T}, Pay 2 life` are all printed; a single regex over all of them is
where a component gets quietly dropped. Each comma-separated component must classify as something
`AbilityCost` can say, and one that does not refuses the whole line — because an ability that is
free where the print says it sacrifices a creature is a different card, and it would never be
flagged, since it works. `parseManaCost` validates the symbols, which is what stops `{E}` reading as
generic mana and `{X}` as nothing.

**Expressible is not the same as read.** The refusal test first asserted `{T}, Pay 1 life: Add {C}.`
was refused, and failed: `cardFromData` already read it, correctly, with `AbilityCost.life`. So the
life component is now read here too — which is what unlocks a **pain land**, a card the whole-card
reader structurally cannot do, because it folds a permanent's mana lines into one cost and would
rather refuse a land with one free tap and one costing a life than flatten the two.

**`abilities` did not accumulate.** Compiling that pain land found it: the second line read
correctly and was then reported as a `field-conflict`, because only `triggers` accumulated. A
permanent with two activated abilities is ordinary, so `abilities` joins it. Nothing in the pool has
two readable ability lines, which is why the measurement could not have found this.

**One of the five new mechanisms had no test that could see it.** Breaking each on purpose, four
went red and the mana-ability `produces` branch did not: truncated to its first symbol — a permanent
that taps for two reading as one — all 115 tests stayed green, because every sum in the pool is on a
card read whole. A direct assertion was added, and re-breaking it now fails.

## A keyword granted with a pump (#317, D379)

**270 of 538 printed lines, up from 265 (49.3% → 50.2%). 175 of 339 cards get a script, up from
171.** Blossoming Defense, Dive Down, Tainted Strike, Renegade Freighter's attack trigger, and
Skithiryx's haste ability.

**One printed effect, so one `pump` call.** The pump reader used to take the size and refuse any
clause that also granted a keyword. The refusal was right; stopping there was not — `pump` takes
both in one `PumpOptions` and the pool writes them that way, so reading both is the same single call
the hand-written cards make. Two separate continuous effects would expire independently.

**`isKeyword` is what makes it safe.** The engine's keyword list is what `characteristicsOf`
consults, so `gains protection from red` would compile to a creature that gains nothing and a spell
that looks like it worked. An unrecognised word refuses the clause instead.

**The granted keyword decides two bot hints, and the pool draws both lines itself.** Hexproof and
shroud make the spell a protection trick (`protectsACreature`, and deliberately not
`expiresAtEndOfTurn` — "hold until something threatens a creature" is not "hold for the combat").
Infect and haste make the *target* an attacker (`helpsInCombat`, whose own docblock says it is only
for a bonus whose whole value is in the attack and names those exact cards). Indestructible is in
neither set, because nothing hand-written pairs it with either hint.

**Dive Down stored a zero.** The ground-truth check failed on one field, `power: 0`:
`protectFromRemoval` passes both numbers unconditionally, where `sizeBonus` omits a zero component —
two continuous effects that behave identically and compare unequal. Fixed in the hand-written
builder, so one rule has one source.

## The keyword declarations that already had a builder (#317, D380)

**302 of 538 printed lines, up from 270 (50.2% → 56.1%). 190 of 339 cards get a script, up from
175. Keyword declarations with no builder: 57 → 27.** The largest single-stage move so far, and the
cheapest — almost nothing was built, because the engine already had a field for each of these.

**Eighteen rows, one shape.** `Flashback {2}{U}` is `flashback: { cost: '{2}{U}' }` and that is all
of it; so are madness, miracle, foretell, spectacle, buyback, dash and ninjutsu, each with a card in
the pool whose hand-written script sets exactly that field. Beside them delve, affinity, dredge,
suspend, escape, rebound, crew, and morph/megamorph/echo. What the eight alternative costs share is
that each is a **way to cast the card**: reading one adds an option and changes nothing the card
does, which is what makes them safe on a card whose resolution is still unread.

**Morph and echo now go through `fromCardData`'s own reader.** They were listed as deliberately
absent because that module already read them and two readers of one line is two places to disagree.
`keywordWithCost` is exported and imported instead: one parse, two call sites.

**Still refused, each with its reason in the docblock.** Kicker and overload (payoff on another
line, so the declaration alone is paying more for nothing), evoke (the declaration without its
sacrifice trigger is a creature you get cheap and keep — strictly better than printed), embalm,
eternalize and bestow (characteristics the line does not carry), unearth (no single field).

**Three mechanisms no test could see, found by breaking them.** Dropping `echoTrigger` and
`reboundCast` left all 142 tests green, because the table only compares the declared field — both
keywords are a declaration *plus* a trigger. And Rift Bolt is `Suspend 1`, so a reader that always
wrote 1 passed its row; Search for Tomorrow is now a second row. The triggers are pinned by a test
asserting the direction the table cannot: a trigger the hand-written card has must be among the
compiled ones.

## A static, a Fog and a library search (#317, D381)

**309 of 538 printed lines, up from 302 (56.1% → 57.4%). 196 of 339 cards get a script, up from
190.** Glorious Anthem, Judith's static, Fog, Holy Day, Diabolic Tutor, Rampant Growth.

**A static is never resolved, so it is its own reader.** `Creatures you control get +1/+1` is the
commonest static in Magic and the first thing the compiler reads that never goes on the stack —
`characteristicsOf` consults it whenever it computes a creature's size. The word **other** is the
whole difference between the engine's two scopes, and Judith is a 2/2 printing "Other creatures you
control get +1/+0": collapse them and she becomes a 3/2. `statics` also joins the accumulating set
in `merge`, with a fixture test, because nothing in the pool prints two and an untested mechanism
added ahead of need is the one that breaks when the corpus arrives.

**The Fog's second field is the one that matters.** `preventCombatDamage` is the primitive;
`preventsDamage` is the bot hint, and nothing in the engine reads it. A Fog without it works
perfectly and gets cast into an empty board.

**`clausesOf` cuts a search in half.** Both search readers were written against the whole printed
sentence and both stayed unread: ", then " is where clauses are split, and a search prints ", then
shuffle". The readers now match the first clause and the bare `shuffle` reads as the identity,
because `searchYourLibrary` already shuffles — doing it twice would make two boards incomparable.
Both searches are deliberately narrow (no filter for the tutor, `isBasicLand` for Rampant Growth),
and `min: 0` is asserted, because a search you may decline is a different card from one you may not.

## Soulbond, a team pump, and an opponent-only phrase (#317, D382)

**316 of 538 printed lines, up from 309 (57.4% → 58.7%). 199 of 339 cards get a script, up from
196.** Trusted Forcemage, Wolfir Silverheart, Master of Pearls, Ainok Survivalist's turn-up.

**Soulbond was a named refusal and this is the stage it was waiting for.** Its line is the word
alone and the bonus is on the next line, so it is the third whole-card shape after attachments and
exile-until-leaves: both lines or neither, with `soulbondTriggers` alongside, because a pairing that
does nothing and a bonus with no pairing are each half a card. Only the bonus form — Tandem Lookout
hands out an *ability*, declared as `grants: [0]` against a `grantedTriggers` entry nothing here can
build, so it is refused rather than compiled into a pair that gets nothing.

**`pumpTeam`, not `pump` over a list.** "Creatures you control get +2/+2 until end of turn" is a
continuous effect with a scope: a creature that arrives later in the turn is out, and one that
leaves does not take the bonus with it. The same sentence *without* a duration is a static and is
read elsewhere — the duration is the whole difference.

**One phrase, two tests, and the second was not covered until it was broken.**
`target artifact or enchantment an opponent controls` is the first place the type list and the
controller test compose, so `permanentFilter` gained a live-read `types` option. The first draft of
the test put an artifact on each side of the table, which proves the side and says nothing about the
types; dropping `types` left it green. A creature on the opponent's side was the missing row.

## The reset throttle was advisory, and CI found it (#321, D383)

CI failed once on a commit that touched none of this: six password reset emails out of a limit of
five. The test was right and the route was wrong.

**Two writes for one fact.** `/forgot-password` counted `account_events` and then recorded the
request with `auditAccountEvent`, which is deliberately not awaited — a good rule for a *record* and
a wrong one for a **counter**, because the next request reads the table to decide whether to act. A
write still in flight is a request that was never counted.

**The lock, because awaiting is half of it.** A burst of six can all read four and all proceed. The
count and the insert are now one transaction holding `pg_advisory_xact_lock` on the identifier,
released by the commit, keyed on the identifier as supplied — counting before resolving is what
stops the throttle from revealing that an account exists.

**Fails closed**, which is the opposite of the audit rule and right for the opposite reason: a
throttle that throws and reads as "under the limit" is one an attacker removes by making the
database unhappy. The rejection path is byte-identical to the success path.

**The audit trail quietly got worse and a test caught it.** The gate runs before the lookup, so its
row has no `player_id`; the first version dropped the one the old code attached, and the test that
reads the trail by player id failed. `attachPlayerToEvent` puts it back, awaited.

**What the tests prove, stated rather than implied.** The burst test through the route does *not*
discriminate — run against the old code it passed here, because six concurrent requests serialised
far enough apart to count each other, which is why the sequential version only failed in CI once. It
is kept as a stress check with that written into it. The proof is three deterministic tests on the
gate itself: three allowed then one refused in sequence, exactly three of six concurrent calls
allowed, and `allowed: false` from a pool that cannot connect.

## The compiler reached resolution and not the opponent (#322, D384)

`scriptFor(name)` is the hand-written registry — 348 cards, `undefined` for everything else.
`scriptForCard(def)` is the registry first and the oracle-text compiler after. `derive.ts` said it
was "the one place that answers *what does this card do?*". It was not: **44 call sites across four
files asked the registry directly, and were converted**; two more stay, with a reason.

| file | sites | what they decide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bot.ts` | 26 | every bot rule — hold the trick, crew the Vehicle, price the pump that wears off |
| `legalActions.ts` | 9 | whether a flashback, escape, foretell, morph or affinity play is offered at all |
| `autoActions.ts` | 4 | whether a cast, foretell, suspend or turn-up is accepted |
| `automation.ts` | 5 of 7 | saga chapters, an Aura's target, a miracle's cost, a land arriving tapped |

So a compiled card resolved correctly and was then played blind: no abilities the bot could see, no
alternative casts offered, no saga advancing. Nothing said so, which is the worst shape here —
the card *works*.

Invisible to the suite by construction, because every pool card has a hand-written script and the
two lookups return the same object for all 348. That is also what makes the conversion safe: the
precedence is "hand-written wins, always", so it is a provable no-op on the pool.

Two name lookups stay, in `automation.ts`: a granted ability is recorded as the granting card's
*name* plus an index, so there is no definition to ask with — and `grantedTriggers` is the one field
the compiler never emits.

**A source-level test, because no behavioural one can tell the lookups apart on a pool card.**
`derive.test.ts` asserts the three converted files contain no `scriptFor(` call and that
`automation.ts` has exactly two, both on the `grantedTriggers` line, plus one behavioural check that
a compiled-only instant's `protectsACreature` is visible through the right lookup and not the wrong
one. Its first version matched the raw source and failed on all three files, because each one names
`scriptFor` in a docblock; comments are stripped now and the test says why.

## Five filters read the printed type line (#319, D385)

A target filter must read what a permanent **is** (CR 613). Five hand-written ones read the printed
line: Disenchant/Naturalize/Krosan Grip, Ainok Survivalist's turn-up, Wane, Awoken Horror's bounce,
and Galvanic Blast's metalcraft count. `destroyAnArtifactOrEnchantment`'s docblock *claimed* the live
reading the code did not do — true of every artifact creature in the pool, because all of them are
printed as artifacts, which is why it lasted.

Four of the five are live now, each with a test that fails when reverted: a creature made an
artifact, the same creature made an enchantment, and Galvanic Blast's third artifact turning 1
damage into 4.

**Awoken Horror's `Horror` subtype ships with no discriminating test, and the reason is written
down.** `addTypes` appends to `types`, not `subtypes` — probed, not assumed — so nothing in this
engine can make a creature a Horror and no board distinguishes the two readings. It is converted
because the fix is a consistency one inside one expression: the line above already asks for the live
`isCreature`.

**A sixth site stays printed, deliberately.** `conditionMet` is the metalcraft count behind Chrome
Steed's and Etched Champion's conditional statics, and it is called *from inside*
`characteristicsOf` — asking for a live type line there would re-enter the computation for every
other conditional effect on the board. That is a real rules gap (CR 702.105a), now stated at both
ends rather than claimed away. So the two artifact counts genuinely differ, and the test says why it
uses the spell rather than the Steed.

## The compiler had only ever seen 348 rows (#317, D386)

Every coverage figure so far comes from one corpus: the engine's own pool, 348 rows. #318 will hand
the same readers tens of thousands, and two failures live in that gap — a reader that throws on a
line combination the pool does not contain, and a compiler that retains every compilation until the
process dies. Both would surface during the import the corpus plan depends on.

`scripts/measure/compile-at-scale.mjs` has two arms: `--repeat` clones the pool's real rows with
distinct names (pace and memory, real text), and `--shuffled` resamples printed lines across cards
with the owner's name rewritten to the row's (the crash hunt, synthetic text). **240,000 rows
compiled across nine runs and six seeds: zero throws**, at 1,300-1,900 rows/s — so the whole
commander-legal corpus compiles in under a minute, once rather than per game.

**The 495 MB was garbage, not retention.** The unconstrained 30,000-row run grew RSS by 495 MB, which
would be fatal under `node --max-old-space-size=768 server.js`. The same work under a 256 MB cap
survives at the same pace (+108 MB at 30,000 rows, +116 MB at 60,000, +100 MB shuffled), and the
growth is flat between the two row counts, so nothing is held per row. The capped figure is the one
to carry, because it is the condition the server runs under.

**Zero throws is worth only the proof a throw would show.** A `throw` planted in the anthem reader
gave 14 throws over 3,000 rows, each printed with its row. Narrowed to a `+2/+2` anthem it gave
**zero** — the pool prints only `+1/+1` and `+1/+0`, so the reader was never reached. That is the
false green being guarded against, which is why the plant had to be unconditional.

**No coverage figure from this script means anything**, and its own output says so: its rows are real
lines in combinations that are not any real card. D259 is untouched — nothing it produces becomes a
shipped script. The share stays `compilable.mjs`'s to print, against real cards: still **316 of 538
lines (58.7%)**, unchanged by this increment.

## The answers: a counter family, a sweeper, and a discard (#317, D387)

Four openings in the work queue were one shape — "counter target *something*" — and the compiler read
only the bare `counter target spell`. The reader now takes an open target phrase guarded by
`pointsAtTheStack`, the counterpart of `pointsAtAPermanent` on the destroy family: without it
"counter target creature" would compile and hand a battlefield permanent's id to `counterSpell`. Two
synthetic sentences prove the refusal.

Every filter is the function the hand-written card already uses, so the ground-truth test is an
identity and not a resemblance. `isCreatureSpell` came out of Essence Scatter for that — a second
copy would be two filters free to drift, which is the class of bug D385 found five of. On Squelch it
is the card: `kind: 'ability'` without `isActivatedAbility` also answers triggered abilities, which
is a better card than the one printed.

`Destroy all creatures` joins the untargeted sentences and carries **no** `removesACreature`, which
is a decision. That flag is advice about a spell that needs a target; a wrath needs none, and whether
to cast one is the position — right when behind, catastrophic when ahead — which the bot's search
sees by playing it out. Day of Judgment sets no flag either, and a test pins both with Murder as the
control.

"Target player discards two cards" is the first clause read as a **question**: `targets` plus
`decisions`, `who: 'target-player'`. `discardAtRandom` was the shortcut and would have built Ravenous
Rats under Mind Rot's name. The chooser is pinned by name as well as by equality, since equality alone
would follow the hand-written card if it changed too.

**316 → 323 of 538 lines (58.7% → 60.0%), 199 → 205 of 339 cards.** Each of the four mechanisms was
broken on purpose and each break fails a test. Psychic Strike is the near miss: its first clause reads
now, its second needs "its controller" — the controller of the object pointed at — which the clause
vocabulary cannot say, and all-or-nothing keeps the card printed-only.

## Modal spells, chosen as the spell is cast (#317, D388)

A charm is one sentence spread over several lines, and no line of it means anything alone — so it is
read as a whole-card shape before the resolution reader sees the lines, which it had to be: that
reader would hand "Choose one —" to `readEffect`, get null, and refuse the card without ever looking
at the bullets.

**Whole or not at all.** Selesnya Charm, Golgari Charm and Healing Salve each have one bullet with no
reader, and each is refused entirely, header included. Shipping the readable bullets would be a
better spell than the printed one, because the table offers a play per legal combination of modes: a
charm missing its third mode is a charm whose third mode nobody can choose, with nothing to say so.

**Two headers, the rest refused.** "Choose one" (min and max left at their defaults, as Selesnya
Charm stores them) and "Choose one or both" (min 1, max 2, over exactly two modes). "Choose two",
entwine and escalate are each a different number of modes taken, and a header read as the wrong one
is a card that takes the wrong number.

**One hint dropped, the rest refused.** `expiresAtEndOfTurn` and `preventsDamage` travel onto the
mode they belong to — merging a pump's wear-off onto the card would have the bot hold a whole charm
for a combat. `removesACreature` is dropped because a mode combination whose targets cannot be filled
is never offered, so the flag buys nothing on a mode; any other flag refuses the card.

Three shared filters replaced four inline copies (`isCreatureSpell` twice over,
`yourGraveyardLand`), which is what makes the ground-truth comparison an identity, and the graveyard
return became a creature-or-land family.

**323 → 329 of 538 lines (60.0% → 61.2%), 205 → 207 of 339 cards.** Three deliberate breaks each
fail tests.

## Two burn spells could not hit a planeswalker (#323, D389)

Lava Spike and Lava Axe both print "target player or planeswalker" and were both scripted with
`TARGET_PLAYER`, so neither could be aimed at a planeswalker — and the pool has four. The phrase is
"any target" with the creatures taken out, and that omission is the card: a one-mana three-damage
spell is printable because it cannot kill a creature. `player` loses the planeswalker half and `any`
gains a creature the card may not touch, so the fix is a new target kind rather than a filter.

Three lines of `targeting.ts`, both cards repointed, and both resolving through
`damageFirstTarget` — the path that turns damage on a planeswalker into lost loyalty (CR 120.3c),
which a seat-shaped resolution could never reach. The test asserts both directions: the creature is
refused, and three damage kills a three-loyalty Jace. Reverting the card fails one half; deleting the
targeting line fails the other.

The compiler gained the phrase too: **329 → 331 of 538 lines (61.2% → 61.5%), 207 → 209 cards**, with
the compiled spec compared for identity against the hand-written one and a second test keeping "any
target" distinct from it.

## The drain and the edict (#317, D390)

"Each opponent loses 1 life and you gain 1 life" is one effect joined by **and**, not two clauses —
`clausesOf` does not split on that word, because "gets +2/+2 and gains trample" is one effect too. So
it is read whole and in printed order, lost then gained, which is what all three hand-written drains
do. The two numbers are read separately rather than assumed equal: every pool drain prints the same
number twice, so reading one twice would pass every ground-truth test while asserting a symmetry the
text does not promise, and a synthetic asymmetric drain pins it. The tail is optional, and the
pointed form carries `friendly` on the heal and not on the drain — "target player" is the same two
words on both, and the bot's default is the enemy.

"Each player sacrifices a creature" is a **question**: `who: 'each-player'` expands into one per
seat, asked in turn order from the active player (CR 101.4), which is sometimes the card itself — the
second player to sacrifice has seen what the first gave up. "Each player" includes you and "each
opponent" does not, one word of the reader and a different card. The filter decides what may be given
up; without it a player answers an edict with a land.

**331 → 335 of 538 lines (61.5% → 62.3%), 209 → 213 of 339 cards**: Blood Artist, Zulaport
Cutthroat, Cruel Celebrant, Fleshbag Marauder. Four deliberate breaks, four failing tests.

Kambal stays unread on purpose: "**that player** loses 2 life" takes its subject from the event, not
the clause, and means something different under a different trigger.

## The shrinking sweep, the combat filter, and the untapper (#317, #319, D391)

**Golgari Charm compiles whole** — the card this file called "the card that was not scriptable",
because one of its three modes was "regenerate each creature you control". All three read now. The
sweep is `pumpAll` and not `pumpTeam`: "all creatures" includes the caster's own, which is what makes
that mode a decision. The sign is read off the print rather than assumed negative, so the same
sentence with a plus is a mass anthem; hardcoding the minus fails a synthetic test and nothing else.

`target attacking or blocking creature` is the only filter here that reads the combat rather than the
board. It was inline on Divine Verdict and is shared now, so the compiled spec is the hand-written
spec, function included.

The untapper carries **`untapsOnly`**, and that is not a nicety: an ability whose whole effect is an
untap can put the board back where it found it, so a bot that does not know can tap and untap for ever
— the loop #124 was opened for. The flag lives on `AbilityDef` and nowhere else, so `ReadEffect`
gained `abilityFlags` for it, dropped by the spell and trigger paths exactly as `spellFlags` is.

**A sixth printed type line (#319):** Golgari Charm's enchantment mode read the card definition's
type line, so a permanent *made* an enchantment was not a legal target. It uses the shared live filter
now, with its own case in `liveTypes.test.ts`.

**335 → 341 of 538 lines (62.3% → 63.4%), 213 → 216 of 339 cards.** Five deliberate breaks, five
failing tests. Icy Manipulator is the near miss: a three-type target union plus a filter that refuses
an already-tapped permanent, none of which its printed phrase says.

## Counts read off the board (#317, D392)

`tokenEffect`'s docblock named this gap itself: "a count read off the board, not the X chosen at cast
time". `boardCount` reads it once — lands, artifacts, creature cards in your graveyard, +1/+1
counters on this, creatures of a subtype — and two grammars share it: `create X … tokens, where X is
…` and `deals damage equal to … | its power`. Every reading is a function a hand-written card already
used, so the ground truth is exact: `creaturesOfSubtype` was Krenko's `goblinCount`.

The counters read the **snapshot** before the live instance, because a card counts the counters it
had as it died (CR 608.2h). The zero guard is the cards' own: no tokens rather than a request for
none, and no damage event rather than one of zero — this pool's Murderous Redcap is a 1/1, so the
body persist returns deals nothing.

The plural is where this could be wrong rather than incomplete: `-ves → -f`, otherwise drop the `s`,
and refuse anything that does not end in one — which keeps Fungi and Homunculi out, since a subtype
no creature has counts zero and a card that resolves and does nothing is worse than an unread line.

**A correction.** I probed the Squid token with a hand-made state, read `landwalk: []`, and wrote it
up as a shipping defect. It is not: the token has a script found by its name that grants islandwalk,
and a test pins it — my probe built a board that cannot occur. The real gap one level down is that
printed landwalk was never read at all, which matters for a card with no script to declare one: the
corpus. `printedLandwalk` reads it now, the two scripted cards are redundant rather than wrong, and
the Squid clause compiles with the islandwalk it prints.

**341 → 344 of 538 lines (63.4% → 63.9%), 216 → 217 of 339 cards.** Four breaks, four failing tests;
the whole engine suite 1671 green.

## Loyalty abilities (#317, D393)

A planeswalker's line is an activated ability whose cost is a number, not a list of components, so
the cost parse takes it first; `AbilityCost.loyalty` is a field because it carries its own
restrictions (sorcery speed, once a turn, controller only). **The printed minus is U+2212**, and
reading it as a plus would make a planeswalker that gains loyalty for its ultimate — both spellings
are read, and collapsing the sign fails two tests.

Two clause readers came with it: `each player draws N cards` (symmetrical, the opponent included —
that is Jace Beleren's +2, not a better Divination) and `you draw a card`. And one missing row:
`WORD_NUMBERS` stopped at ten, so "mills twenty cards" went unread while the two lines around it
compiled.

**344 → 353 of 538 lines (63.9% → 65.6%), 217 → 222 of 339 cards.** Jace, Memory Adept and Jace
Beleren compile whole — the first planeswalkers read end to end. Garruk is the hybrid test: one
ability automated, two lines reported for a human. Three breaks, three failing tests; the engine
suite 1678 green.

## The grant family, and a hint the team pump was dropping (#317, D394)

**The defect:** `expiresAtEndOfTurn` means "hold this for the combat", and both hand-written cards of
that shape set it — Inspired Charge and Overrun — while the compiled team pump did not. So a compiled
Inspired Charge was a card that works and gets cast in a main phase with nothing to attack with:
D364's trap in the one family whose targeted twin already carried the flag, invisible to every rules
test because the bot reads it and the engine does not.

`grantedKeywordList` now reads one or two keywords joined by "and", each gated by `isKeyword` — so
"soaring", "protection from red" and a list of three are refused and reported for a human. Both
halves travel in one `PumpOptions`, as Ajani's ultimate is written by hand: two effects would expire
independently. And a grant with **no** size change is its own sentence rather than a pump of zero,
because `sizeBonus` refuses `+0/+0` and should.

**353 → 356 of 538 lines (65.6% → 66.2%), 222 → 225 of 339 cards.** Overrun, Inspired Charge and
Ajani compile whole; Garruk is one line short (`+1: Untap two target lands`). Three breaks, three
failing tests; the engine suite 1686 green.

## Every planeswalker in the pool, read end to end (#317, #319, D395)

Three readings, and all five planeswalkers compile whole — worth its own line because a planeswalker
is the shape most likely to compile *partly*: three or four independent abilities, so a card three
quarters read is a hybrid rather than a finished reading.

A **counted target** ("Untap two target lands" — the pool's only `TargetSpec.count`, where the effect
reduces over every target rather than taking the first); **counters on the team** (Nissa's −2, which
is not an Overrun: counters stay and stack, so it is `addCounters` per creature and only the
controller's); and a **count announced in the clause's tail** ("You gain X life and draw X cards,
where X is the number of lands you control" — gain before draw, which matters on an empty library).

**A seventh printed type line (#319):** Garruk's +1 filter read the card definition's type line, so a
Mutavault animated into a creature was not a legal target although it is still a land. It uses the
shared live filter now.

The loyalty refusal test moved to a synthetic walker, having been written against Garruk and outlived
two of his lines: the property is "a line with no reader is reported and its neighbours still
compile", not any particular card.

**356 → 359 of 538 lines (66.2% → 66.7%)**, cards unchanged at 225 of 339 — Garruk and Nissa were
already partly read, and what changed is that they are now whole.

## The count written the other way round, and a drift corrected (#317, D396)

Magic writes one count in two grammars: `, where X is the number of Goblins you control` and
`for each Goblin you control`. The second was listed in `tokenEffect`'s docblock as two separate
missing bullets; it is one gap — the count, not the sentence — so the reader split into an announced
form and a per-thing one over a shared vocabulary.

The two grammars differ in exactly one place, and it matters: the **plural** names a creature
subtype as "Goblins" and has to derive "Goblin", refusing a word that does not end in `s` (there is
no creature type "Fungu"); the **singular** names it as the engine spells it and must derive
nothing, or "Homunculus" becomes "Homunculu". Each grammar now takes only the spelling it prints,
and the pool's one Homunculus is what makes that test discriminate rather than merely compile.

Two cards read as a result: **Lotleth Giant** whole, and **Izoni's** ETB line with her sacrifice
ability left for a human. The Giant's drain had to be read before the flat `each opponent loses N
life`, whose sentence is its prefix — the other order drains one life per opponent and ignores the
graveyard, which is a card that works and is wrong, and the one failure hybrid automation cannot
flag because nothing is unread.

**359 → 361 of 538 lines (66.7% → 67.1%)**, and **223 → 225 of 339 cards**.

**A correction:** the previous checkpoint said the card count was "unchanged at 225". Re-measured on
the clean commit it was 223 — the running figure in these notes had drifted two ahead of the
instrument. Both numbers above come from `compilable.mjs` run on the same tree clean and dirty, and
the per-card output of the two runs was diffed to prove Izoni and Lotleth Giant are the only cards
that moved.

Eight deliberate breaks, eight failing tests. 11,000 rows at scale found no throw. All four browser
suites pass on this engine: **table 76/76, arena 53/53 (7 named skips), pod 41/41 (1), solo 28/28
(1)** — which also replaces the stale solo figure the previous sweep was carrying.

## The counters a permanent arrives with, and a nontoken death (#317, D397)

Two readers for fields the engine already had. `entersWith` was built by three keywords (modular,
vanishing, fading) but never by the printed sentence, so **Endless One** — whose whole card is
"enters the battlefield with X +1/+1 counters on it" — read as nothing at all. And
`Whenever a nontoken creature you control dies` had no prologue, which was **Judith's** other line;
with it she compiles whole.

The counter kinds are an allow-list (`+1/+1`, `charge`, `ice`). `time` and `fade` are refused
because their behaviour lives in the trigger vanishing and fading put on the card, not in the
counters: a sentence read on its own would lay a countdown on a permanent with nothing to count it
down, which is a creature that should leave the battlefield and never does.

Judith's sentence turns on two words a copied shape gets wrong in opposite directions — she
triggers on **her own** death (`who: 'any'`, not `another`) and not on a token's — so both are
asserted as fields, not only compared.

**A fixture defect found on the way, left on purpose (#325):** Chalice of the Void, Walking Ballista
and Hangarback Walker each keep their whole card on one `oracleText` line, ". " where the printed
card has newlines, so every ability on all three goes unread. That is the pool's transcription, not
the compiler — the real text has newlines and the corpus will not have the problem — and fixing it
would move the coverage share, which would conflate "reads more" with "fixtures corrected".

**361 → 363 of 538 lines (67.1% → 67.5%)**, **225 → 226 of 339 cards**, per-card diff showing only
those two moved. Six deliberate breaks, six failing tests; 257/257 in compile.test.ts; gate green.

## A clause joined by "and", and a guard that could not be written (#317, D398)

"and" is usually *inside* one clause, not between two — "gets +2/+2 **and** gains trample" is one
pump — so the conjunction is read as a **fallback**, last in the chain, seeing only clauses every
other reader has refused. What is left is the genuine sequence: Phyrexian Arena's "you draw a card
and you lose 1 life", which is its whole card.

The interesting part is the test that does not exist. The ordering protects "a conjunction one
reader understands keeps that reading", and **that cannot be checked from outside the compiler**:
`compileCard` does not say which reader read a clause, so once the fallback exists "reads whole"
includes the fallback and the sweep reduces to "the fallback exists". Three versions were written
and each was proved unable to fail by planting a reader — one used a stand-in card name (so no
clause naming its own source could read at all), one kept the trigger's prologue (so it asked
whether an instant could be read from a trigger's sentence), and the third was correct and
tautological. The right answer was to delete it and write down why.

What is left is what can be observed: the pool prints four conjunctions both readings can reach, and
on the ones with a hand-written script the two readings **agree** — which is the real reason the
order is safe here, and is asserted against the hand-written card.

**363 → 364 of 538 lines (67.5% → 67.7%)**, **226 → 227 of 339 cards**, with exactly one line
changed in the verbose diff. Five deliberate breaks, five failing tests; 264/264.

## The X a spell was cast for (#317, D399)

Fireball, Savage Twister and Mind Spring — three cards whose whole resolution spends the X they were
cast for, all three with hand-written scripts to check against.

It is a **spell shape**, not a clause reader, and that is the whole safety argument: X is settled as
the spell is cast (CR 601.2b), but a triggered ability's stack object carries no X, so a clause
reader that understood bare X would give some future creature a trigger that draws nothing, for
ever, with nothing unread for a human to notice. A synthetic creature printing "draw X cards" is
refused, and planting the reading in the clause vocabulary turns that test red.

The multi-clause case is refused too, because Exsanguinate's second sentence does not spend X — it
reads the life actually lost, which at a pod is X times the opponents.

**364 → 367 of 538 lines (67.7% → 68.2%)**, **227 → 230 of 339 cards**. Five deliberate breaks, five
failing tests; 270/270; 5,000 rows at scale with no throw. The live game is unchanged — a
hand-written script still wins over a compiled one — so this is entirely about what the corpus will
get.

## X tokens, and one parser for the token (#317, D400)

Secure the Wastes — "Create X 1/1 white Warrior creature tokens" — which D399 named as still
unread. The count belongs to the X spell and the **token definition** belongs to `tokenEffect`, and
that definition is not a small parse: colour words, the optional "artifact", a capitalised subtype,
and the keyword read-back that asks whether the engine can read back the text about to be written
down. So it is parsed once, by `tokenFrom`, which hands back the count word **unread** for each
caller to make sense of.

The refactor landed first and changed nothing (270 tests green before the new reading was added), so
the coverage move is attributable to the reading rather than the shuffle.

**367 → 368 of 538 lines (68.2% → 68.4%)**, **230 → 231 of 339 cards**. Three deliberate breaks,
three failing tests; 273/273; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw.

## Statics that come and go, and the ability word in front (#317, D401)

`while` has two kinds and this reads the English of both: "as long as you control three or more
artifacts" (metalcraft, printed on a size for Chrome Steed and on protection for Etched Champion),
and "as long as ~ is monstrous" — which this engine models as a +1/+1 counter on the creature
itself (D182), the hand-written Fleecemane Lion's own reading rather than one invented here.

"Metalcraft —" and "Battalion —" are flavour with no rules meaning (CR 207.2c), so the word is
dropped before the line is read. A **named list**, not a general "capitalised word then a dash": the
general form would eat a saga's chapter markers too, and a line mis-split is read wrongly rather
than refused. With the word off the front **Firemane Avenger** compiles whole, and its body — "deals
3 damage to any target and you gain 3 life" — is read by D398's conjunction reader inside a trigger.
Two increments meeting on one card.

**368 → 372 of 538 lines (68.4% → 69.1%)**, **231 → 235 of 339 cards**. Seven deliberate breaks,
seven failing tests; 282/282; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw.

## A size that is a count, and the creature that sacrifices itself (#317, D402)

Lhurgoyf and Enigma Drake: a creature whose size **is** a count (CR 604.3). `definesSize` names its
two counts (D57), so the reader takes the two phrases the pool prints and refuses the rest — "the
number of cards in your hand" is a real card and not a count the engine has, and compiling it as one
of the two it does have is a creature of the wrong size every turn. The test reads the live creature,
not only the data: a Lhurgoyf with two creature cards in a graveyard is a 2/3.

Ball Lightning and Hellspark Elemental: "At the beginning of the end step, sacrifice ~", read as a
**whole-line shape** because of the flag. `leavesAtEndOfTurn` is how the bot knows the creature is
dying anyway; without it the evaluation holds a 6/1 back to protect it. The trigger alone is correct
rules and a badly played card — D364's rule in its sharpest form — and "sacrifice ~" behind another
prologue means something else, so the pair is read and anything else refused.

A refusal test from an earlier increment became an acceptance and was rewritten with the churn in
it: the property ("the flag belongs to the pair") is unchanged, only how it is expressed.

**372 → 376 of 538 lines (69.1% → 69.9%)**, **235 → 239 of 339 cards**. Six deliberate breaks, six
failing tests; 291/291; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw.

## Investigate, mana out of a trigger, and damage divided (#317, D403)

Three readers and five cards. **Investigate** is one word for text the card does not print, so it is
read as a call to the engine's own Clue token (D243) rather than transcribed — writing that text here
would be inventing a real card's words. **"Add {R}{G}"** gives Burning-Tree Emissary and, as a side
effect nobody planned, Dark Ritual. **Divided damage** gives Arc Lightning and Pyromatics, where the
sentence holds two numbers that are not the same number: the damage to share and the list of target
counts, which is why Pyromatics is `divided: 1, count: 2`.

**The defect the diff caught:** Dark Ritual arrived without `makesMana`, the hint whose absence makes
the bot cast a Ritual into nothing (#63) — a card that works and plays badly, for the third time
(D364, D394). Found because five cards moved where three were expected. The fix is `spellFlags`,
which reach the spell path only, so the same reader gives Dark Ritual the flag and Burning-Tree's ETB
trigger none — that card's own measured rule. And `makesMana` now does not survive composition: a
spell that adds mana *and* draws a card has a visible effect.

**376 → 381 of 538 lines (69.9% → 70.8%)**, **239 → 243 of 339 cards** — past seventy per cent.
Seven deliberate breaks, seven failing tests; 301/301; 9,000 rows at scale with no throw.

## A target chosen by power, and the exile that is not a destruction (#317, D404)

Selesnya Charm's "power 5 or greater" and Hidden Dragonslayer's "power 4 or greater" — mostly an
increment about **when** a filter asks. `powerAtLeast` reads `characteristicsOf`, not the printed
line, so a 2/2 pumped past five is a legal target and a 6/6 shrunk below it is not, which is #319 in
a new place. The threshold is read off the card, and pinning that needed a creature at exactly four:
two is below both numbers and six above both, so the obvious board cannot tell the two cards apart —
a break run proved it by fixing the threshold at four and passing.

Exile reads as exile and not as destroy, which matters because it is not a destruction (CR 701.19a).
**Selesnya Charm compiles whole**, all three modes.

Three refusal tests from earlier increments became acceptances, each keeping its property: the
unreadable-clause example moved to Rest in Peace's sweep; D377's bare exile now asserts "one etb
trigger and no leaves trigger" instead of "unread"; and the modal refusal moved to a synthetic charm,
exactly as that test had written down it should.

**381 → 386 of 538 lines (70.8% → 71.7%)**, **243 → 244 of 339 cards**. Five deliberate breaks, five
failing tests; 306/306; 5,000 rows at scale with no throw.

**And the live game, re-checked:** nine compiler commits is a lot of engine change to leave
unexercised, so all four browser suites ran on a freshly built stack — **table 76/76, arena 52/52
(6 named skips), solo 28/28 (1), pod 40/40 (1)**. Clean.

## An additional cost, paid as the spell is cast (#317, D405)

Bone Splinters and Village Rites, both whole. The sentence needs its own reader because of *when* it
happens: a spell's sentences all happen on resolution and this one happens as it is **cast** (CR
601.2h), so it cannot be answered and the creature cannot be saved in reply. Read beside the
keywords, where the lines that are not part of the resolution come out before the clause readers see
them.

Only the sacrifice, because that is all `additionalCost` holds. "Discard a card" and "pay 3 life" are
real printed costs the engine cannot express, and dropping one would make the spell **cheaper than
the card** — the clearest kind of card that works and is wrong.

**386 → 390 of 538 lines (71.7% → 72.5%)**, **244 → 246 of 339 cards**. Three deliberate breaks,
three failing tests; 313/313; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw.

## A clause that points at a player, and a reader that was never called (#317, D406)

Sign in Blood — "Target player draws two cards and loses 2 life" — compiles whole, and is read as
**one** clause rather than two because both halves aim at the same player: `targets` is one list per
script, so two targeting parts are refused, and D398's conjunction fallback would hit that refusal.
Drawing comes before the loss, which is the printed order and matters at zero life.

The increment also added a reader for "target player gains N life" that was **dead code** — D390
already read it. Nothing failed and the measurement did not move; the deliberate break found it, by
failing to fail. A break run is usually a check that a mechanism works; this one was a check that it
exists, and a reader with no caller is as invisible as a check that cannot fail. Deleted, with the
near miss written into the test.

**390 → 391 of 538 lines (72.5% → 72.7%)**, **246 → 247 of 339 cards**. Three breaks that failed as
intended plus the one that found the duplicate; 317/317; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw.


## Fate Unraveler drained where its text says damage (#317, D407)

The card prints "Fate Unraveler deals 1 damage to that player" and the script called `loseLife`.
Damage and life loss differ exactly where a player would notice and could not explain it: a
prevention shield absorbs damage and does nothing to a loss of life (CR 120.3, CR 615), damage can
be redirected, and "whenever a source deals damage" sees one and not the other.

**Nothing caught it** because the one test on the card read the life total, which both readings move
by the same amount — a check that cannot fail, by measuring the one quantity the two implementations
agree on. `card-promises.mjs` could not see it either: it reads the text for *structure* and asks
whether the script carries each promise, so "a trigger whose effect does the wrong thing" is outside
what it looks at.

Found the way the other five engine defects were found — by writing a second reading of the same
sentence and requiring the two to agree. Fixed to `dealDamage`, with a prevention shield as the
discriminating test (one point of shielding, two cards drawn: the printed card costs one life, the
drained version two). The `?? c.controller` fallback went too: an event with no actor would have
drained the **controller**, which is the opposite of the card.

The general instrument — resolve the compiled reading and the hand-written script on one fixture for
every card both can read, and report the disagreements — is filed rather than built.

## "That player", which only a trigger has (#317, D408)

Kambal and Fate Unraveler, both whole. "That player" is `c.actor`, the seat whose action raised the
event, and only a triggered ability has one — so the reading lives inside `triggerFromLine` above
the shared clause vocabulary, which is D399's X hazard answered in reverse. A sorcery printing the
same sentence is refused, and a break that moves the reader into the shared vocabulary fails four
tests.

The guard is the cards' own: no actor, or an actor who is the controller, does nothing. Fate
Unraveler's script had `?? c.controller` there until D407 — it would have drained the caster.

**391 → 393 of 538 lines (72.7% → 73.0%)**, **247 → 249 of 339 cards**. Four deliberate breaks, four
failing tests; 322/322; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw. Writing this increment is what found
D407.

## The attack a trigger was about, and a guard copied from the wrong card (#317, D409)

Hellrider and Ichor Wellspring, both whole.

Hellrider's clause names "the player or planeswalker it's attacking", and `c.attacked` carries what
*that* attack was declared against — it travels on the stack object because by resolution the
attacker may be dead and combat may no longer say what it was aimed at. A planeswalker that was
attacked takes the damage instead of its controller; a break that always takes the defender fails
the planeswalker test. Trigger-only for D408's reason: a spell has no attack.

Ichor Wellspring needed the long spelling of "or dies" — `dies` is a creature word (CR 700.4), so an
artifact prints "or is put into a graveyard from the battlefield". One prologue row, both events, one
effect.

Writing that row found the second hand-written defect in two increments: the graveyard half was
guarded on the card still being in a graveyard, copied from Rancor. Rancor **returns itself**, so
the guard is its rule; "draw a card" asks nothing about the source, and a triggered ability on the
stack exists independently of the permanent that made it (CR 603.2, CR 608.2). Corrected, with a
test that moves the card to exile before resolving and asserts the draw on both readings.

**393 → 395 of 538 lines (73.0% → 73.4%)**, **249 → 251 of 339 cards**. Three deliberate breaks,
three failing tests; 327/327.

## The gate's four middle steps ran nothing (D410)

`tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` in the engine exits 2 on four real errors in `compile.test.ts`, on a
tree the gate had called green minutes earlier. The gate's steps are strings run as `$step`,
unquoted, so the shell expanded CI's `./packages/*` filter before pnpm saw it: the first path became
the only filter, the rest positional, and `./packages/db` the script name. pnpm said *None of the
selected packages has a "./packages/db" script* and **exited 0** — for the packages' build,
typecheck, typecheck:tests and test. Four of eight steps, for several days.

`check-gate.sh` could not have caught it: it asks whether the gate fails when a step fails, and a
step that runs nothing really does succeed. D365 one level out.

Fixed with `set -f` for the loop, plus a check an exit code cannot express: each step's own appended
lines are read and either of pnpm's two selected-nothing messages fails the gate. `GATE_STEPS` is
newline-separated now so `check-gate.sh` can inject a real pnpm step, and it does — two of them, one
per message. `bash scripts/check-gate.sh` prints **gate verified**.

The hidden steps were hiding exactly one defect: four `entersWith(...).script ?? {}` call sites
where the `ok: false` arm has no `script`. Everything else was green. The repaired gate runs
**2,577 tests** across every package and app, four typecheck passes, the packages' build, the legacy
token-parity test and the web build.

## A token the card names instead of describing (#317, D411)

Pirate's Prize, whole. "Create a Treasure token" names a token rather than describing one and its
bracketed reminder is not rules text (CR 207.2), so the characteristics are nowhere in the sentence:
the reading is a **lookup** of `TREASURE_TOKEN`, the definition D243 wrote, which is `investigate`'s
argument generalised from one word to a table. The object matters beyond its name — the Treasure's
sacrifice-for-mana ability is what makes the mana solver count it.

Two names, because there are two definitions; Food, Blood and Powerstone are refused, because
reading them would mean inventing their text. Clue is in the table with no pool card behind it, said
out loud, and pinned by a synthetic card against `CLUE_TOKEN`'s own text. The count goes through
`tokenEffect`'s existing machinery, so "two Treasure tokens" needed nothing new.

**395 → 396 of 538 lines (73.4% → 73.6%)**, **251 → 252 of 339 cards**. Three deliberate breaks,
three failing tests; 330/330; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw.

## A colour change in the same pump, and a hint two cards were right to omit (#317, D412)

Crimson Wisps, whole. "Gains haste until end of turn **and becomes red**" is one printed effect, so
the colour rides in the same `PumpOptions` as the keyword — layer 5 *replaces* the printed colours
(CR 105.3), so a colour change outliving its keyword would leave a creature coloured by a spell that
has finished. `colorless` and `purple` are both refused, for different reasons, and both asserted.

Reading it found a defect two increments old: the grant readers gave a **haste or infect** grant
`expiresAtEndOfTurn`, where both hand-written twins carry no spell flag. The flag tells the bot an
instant may wait for blockers, and a haste grant waited out is a card that never did its job. The
hint this family needs is `helpsInCombat` on the target spec instead. Three cases now, at both call
sites — and a test had asserted the wrong value, written from the reader rather than the card.

The other direction too: the compiled reading deferred the draw where the hand-written card took it
immediately. `drawLater` is right for a last-clause draw by its own docblock (CR 702.52a), so the
hand-written card now calls it — one rule, one source.

**396 → 398 of 538 lines (73.6% → 74.0%)**, **252 → 253 of 339 cards**. Four deliberate breaks, four
failing tests; 334/334; engine suite 1,790/1,790; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw.

## A draw that has to happen before the question (#317, D413)

Faithless Looting, whole. "Draw two cards, then discard two cards" composes **correctly and
wrongly**: `clausesOf` splits on ", then ", the two effects run in printed order, and the discard is
a *question* — planned before the resolution runs, so the player would choose out of the hand they
held before drawing. A new failure mode for this module: every refusal so far was a clause nothing
could read, and this is one everything could read and nobody should.

So `lootResolution` is a spell-shape reader like `xSpellResolution`, consulted *before*
`composeEffects` rather than after it, and `ReadEffect` gained `beforeDecisions` — which
`composeEffects` deliberately does not propagate, because a clause cannot know whether a question
follows it. `draw` and not `drawLater` here, for the same reason the reader exists: a card that is
owed is not a card you can be asked to discard.

**398 → 399 of 538 lines (74.0% → 74.2%)**, **253 → 254 of 339 cards**. Four deliberate breaks, four
failing tests; 339/339; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw.

## A blink, which is two clauses about one object (#317, D414)

Cloudshift, whole. The second clause of "Exile target creature you control, then return that card to
the battlefield under your control" is about the **first clause's object** — "that card" is neither a
target nor the source — so no clause reader can be handed it. Reading only the first half would be
worse than refusing both: the exile clause has a reader of its own, so a compiler that stopped there
would turn a blink into unconditional removal of your own creature.

Third spell-shape reader, ahead of `composeEffects` with the other two. The spec carries `blinks`,
because a blink is a help or a hit depending on whose permanent it lands on and the bot cannot read
that off a candidate list. Only "under your control": Flickerwisp's wording returns the permanent to
its owner and at the next end step, which is a different card twice over.

**399 → 400 of 538 lines (74.2% → 74.3%)**, **254 → 255 of 339 cards**. Four deliberate breaks, four
failing tests; 343/343; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw.

## A characteristic read before the permanent leaves (#317, D415)

Swords to Plowshares, whole. The fourth spell-shape reader and the third kind of dependency: not an
order (D413) and not an identity (D414) but a **reading** — "its power" belongs to the creature the
sentence before exiled.

The increment is worth more for what the break runs found. **Two of four breaks passed every test.**
Reading the power after the exile gives the same answer, because `pump` scopes to an instance id and
`relocate` keeps the id across a zone change — a 2/2 pumped +3/+3 and exiled reads power 5 in exile,
probed directly. `pumpTeam`'s docblock has recorded that limitation all along. So the printed order
stays as **fidelity, not correctness**, said that way in the docblock instead of defended by a test
that cannot fail, and the hole is filed as **#326**.

The second: `Math.max(0, power)` cannot be told from its absence, because `gainLife` refuses any
amount `<= 0` on its first line. Deleted, with the behaviour asserted and the reason named.

**400 → 401 of 538 lines (74.5%)**, **255 → 256 of 339 cards**. Four breaks, two failing tests and
two that could not — both diagnosed rather than patched. 347/347; 4,000 rows at scale, no throw.

## A land that turns itself into a creature (#317, D416)

Mutavault's animation, and the first **ability**-shape reader beside the four spell-shape ones. Its
two printed sentences are one reading, and the second decides what the first does: `addTypes` adds a
type where `setTypes` would replace the line, and "it's still a land" is the printed reason to add
(CR 613.1c) — guess wrong and the land cannot be tapped for mana for the rest of the turn. The clause
without that sentence is refused rather than read as either. `setPower` and not a pump, so an anthem
lands on top of a 2/2 base (layer 7b), and `animates` is carried because the bot otherwise animates
for nothing and loses the mana.

**A second figure from here on.** This increment moves no card on the number every checkpoint has
quoted — Mutavault already had a script from its mana ability — but it now has nothing left unread.
Both are real: **cards with a script** is 256 of 339 (it plays, maybe with a line flagged for a
human), **cards with every line read** is 228 of 339 (nothing left for a human at all). The second
ran 220 → 228 across this stretch while the first ran 249 → 256. Neither earlier figure was wrong;
the second was not being printed.

**401 → 402 of 538 lines (74.5% → 74.7%)**, 256/339 with a script, **227 → 228** complete. Four
deliberate breaks, four failing tests; 351/351; 4,000 rows at scale with no throw.

## The compiler, checked against every card the pool can check it against (#317, D417)

Four increments in a row found a defect by reading a card beside its script (D407, D409, D412,
D415), and each argued the reading should be mechanical. `compiled-vs-written.test.ts` is that: it
compares the **whole** compiled script against the hand-written one for every card that has both and
nothing unread — **205 pairs**, where `compile.test.ts` covers about sixty by hand and only the
fields somebody asserted. Functions become `[fn]`, so this is structure and data; behaviour stays
`compile.test.ts`'s job.

**175 agree** after normalising key order, the documented `who: 'self'` default and log descriptions.
**19** differ only by a `keywords` declaration the engine already reads off the printed text — and a
second test proves that reasoning falsifiable by asserting every one of those keywords really is
printed. **11 are real**, listed in the file with what each is and filed as **#327**: Magma Jet's
scry planned before its damage (a general assembly problem, not one card), two missing
`removesACreature` hints for two different reasons, Capsize's missing filter, Garruk's `+1` restricted
to lands you control.

A break run forced the design: comparing **names** only, dropping the `blinks` hint left every test
green, because Cloudshift was already on the list. Each row now carries its differing fields and a
digest of them, so the equality fails four ways — new, fixed, newly different, or differently
different. Five breaks, five failures, plus a row asserting the pair count stays above 200 so the
check cannot hollow out.

This is the instrument #318 needs: an imported corpus has no hand-written script to check against, so
the pool is the only ground truth the compiler will ever have.

## A composition splits at its first question (#327, D418)

The first finding of the new standing check to be fixed, and never one card. The engine asks a
resolution's questions **before** the resolution runs, and `spellScriptFor` put every clause's effect
in `onResolve` — so any card shaped "an effect. a question." asked the player about a board its
earlier clauses had not changed. Magma Jet is the pool's instance and the hand-written script has had
the answer all along.

So `composeEffects` now splits at the first part that asks something, and all three assemblies carry
`beforeDecisions`. `ReadEffect.appliesNothing` closes the last field difference: the scry clause's
effect is the identity, so a resolution that is nothing but questions omits `onResolve` rather than
carrying a function that cannot be told from its absence.

**Two of five breaks passed**, and both were tests that could not fail — slicing past the asking part
(every composed question in the pool is a scry, which applies nothing) and the nested-half refusal
(the fixture never reached it). Both have real fixtures now: a discard that must still move the card,
and a conjunction whose second half asks.

No coverage change — this is about what a compiled card does, not how much compiles. Disagreements
**11 → 10**.

## Five disagreements, and two were real in opposite directions (#327, D419)

Second batch off the standing check's list, and the pattern is the finding: of five rows, **two were
defects, one in each reading of the same card**.

**Garruk Wildspeaker** was wrong both ways. The compiled `+1` carried `untapsOnly`, which that
field's own docblock forbids by name — a `+N` loyalty cost gains a counter, so the untap is never
the whole effect and the anti-loop flag does not apply. And the hand-written spec lacked `friendly`,
which on a card that says "target lands" with no "you control" is the difference between the bot
untapping its own lands and the opponent's. Neither would have been found by reading one of them.

**Cloudshift, Blossoming Defense, Dive Down** carried `friendly` on the compiled side only, beside a
filter that already restricts to your side — written on the hand-written cards too, rather than kept
as a permanent exception.

**Basilica Guards** had a static that restated its own printed `defender`. Deleted, and proved: a new
row asks `canAttack` of the Guards and of a Serra Angel on the same board — one refused, one not —
and deleting the keyword handling fails it and two older rows.

No coverage change. Disagreements **10 → 5**: what is left is Capsize's missing filter, two
`removesACreature` gaps, and ninjutsu and dash as a keyword field versus a hand-written expansion.

## A hint missing from one family, and a guard the engine already had twice (#327, D420)

**Flame Slash**: `removesACreature` was set for a destroy or an exile aimed at a creature and not for
damage aimed at one. Added, and the standing check's value showed: the rule introduced **no new
disagreement**, so it matches every hand-written card it touches rather than being a guess about one.
Not for "any target" — Lava Spike and Magma Jet can be aimed at a face, asserted as its own row.

**Capsize**: a hand-written filter requiring the battlefield, which `legalTargets` (enumeration) and
`isLegalTarget` (validation of a submitted target) both require already. A guard that cannot refuse
anything, deleted, with `legalTargets` asked on a board holding a creature in a graveyard as the
proof.

Disagreements **5 → 3**: Journey to Nowhere's hint needs the trigger path to reach a card-level flag,
and ninjutsu and dash are the keyword-field-versus-expansion question.

## Two keyword fields that were labels, and two cards that did nothing (#327, D421)

The standing check's best find so far: two cards that did not disagree about a key so much as not
work. Both rows asked the same question — is the keyword's script field the implementation, or a
label? — and for both the answer was the label.

**Ninjutsu.** `CardScript.ninjutsu` is audit-only by its own docblock; the play comes from an ability
whose cost carries `returnsUnblockedAttacker`, which is also what tells `collectLegalActions` the
ability is used from the hand and does not spend the card. A compiled Ninja of the Deep Hours could
never be ninjutsu'd.

**Dash.** The haste and the `DASHED` counter are the engine's, but the return to hand is a delayed
ability found by searching the card's own triggers behind an `index >= 0` guard. A compiled Mardu
Scout got haste, attacked, and stayed on the battlefield for ever — silently, because that guard is
what stops a missing trigger being a crash.

The reader now emits the machinery with the declaration (D364's rule, the same way `echo` does one
case below), and the hand-written Ninja shares the compiled card's new `ninjutsuAbility` factory, so
the keyword has one implementation rather than two free to drift. Tested as what the card can do:
the dash return moves a Scout to its owner's hand and leaves a dead one alone, and the ninjutsu
ability arrives tapped and attacking the right seat and does nothing with no attack to join.

No coverage change — these lines were always read, they just did nothing. Disagreements **3 → 1**,
and the one left is Journey to Nowhere, whose `removesACreature` needs the trigger path to reach a
card-level flag.

## The standing check's table is empty (#327, D422)

Journey to Nowhere, the last row. Its removal is an ETB trigger and `removesACreature` is a
card-level field; `triggerFromLine` drops `spellFlags` on purpose, so the hint could not reach the
card. It is read in `exileUntilLeavesShapeFor` now — the whole-card reader that pairs the exile with
the return and holds the `CardDef` — because the flag means "this card's whole effect is to remove a
creature", which is a fact about the card rather than about one line.

Two tests, and the pool prints a card that each one alone excludes: Journey to Nowhere gets the flag,
**Banisher Priest** does not because the host is a creature (a 2/2 worth casting for the body), and
**Banishing Light** does not because its spec is a nonland permanent. Both distinctions were already
drawn by the hand-written scripts, so this reads a judgement the pool had made rather than inventing
one.

No coverage change. **Disagreements 1 → 0**: every card in the pool with both readings now agrees,
and the table is empty — which is the state to keep it in, since the test asserts equality against
it rather than membership.

## Damage with no target, and the kicker payoff (#317, D423)

First increment off the compiler's work queue now the disagreement list is closed. Three cards, two
readers.

**`sweepDestination`** reads *where*: "each creature", "each creature with flying and each player".
A sweep is a destination rather than a target — nothing is chosen and nothing can be made illegal —
so the amount is handed in. One function for both callers, because `xSpellResolution` already
spelled out the bare "each creature" and `damageEffect` read none of it, and two spellings of one
phrase is the defect #319 is a task about.

**`kickerSpellFor`** reads *how much*: a whole-spell shape pairing `Kicker {M}` with "if this spell
was kicked, it deals M damage instead", because the declaration alone is an option to pay more for
nothing — the reason the reader's own docblock had kept kicker out until now. Agonizing Demise has
kicker and is **not** this shape, so it stays unread rather than being forced through a reading about
numbers.

Two things worth recording beyond the cards. The sweep's zero guard, copied from the hand-written
cards, turned out to be **unfalsifiable** — `dealDamage` refuses a non-positive amount itself — so it
is deleted and a test pins the equality instead; that is D415's lesson a second time. And a test
asserting Hurricane's phrase left the card *unread* was recording a gap as a property, the fifth of
that family; it now asserts on the board that the "and" is not a clause boundary.

**407 of 538 lines (75.7%)**, 259 of 339 with a script, 231 complete. Six breaks, six failures.

## Printed protection, and two cards that need no script at all (#317, D424)

Before this, protection was set **only** by a continuous effect — so a card with no script had none
however plainly its text printed it. That is the hole `printedLandwalk` closed for landwalk in #324,
and it matters for the same reason: the corpus #318 imports is unscripted by definition.

The interesting part was why three readers all missed Phyrexian Crusader. "First strike, protection
from red, protection from white, infect" is four printed abilities in one comma list, and
`printedKeywords` and `printedLandwalk` each had their own copy of the whole-line rule, so each
refused the whole line. One classifier now does the parts and the three readers take their own kind
out of it — the rule widened in the faithful direction (parts may mix freely) while keeping the half
that mattered (a part the engine cannot model refuses the line, so a sentence is not a list).

With those lines read, three statics restating them went: River Boa's islandwalk (the standing check
failed the moment the compiler counted the line, exactly as it should), the Squid token's, and the
two protection cards' — so **Paladin en-Vec and Phyrexian Crusader now have no scripts at all**, and
#83's four-rule protection suite exercises the printed reading.

**A correction**: the "cards with a script" figure quoted here since D417 (251 → 256 → 259) was the
measure's `whole-card + lines` categories added together, which over-counts by every vanilla creature
on those paths. Measured directly it is **236 of 339**, and `compilable.mjs` now prints that figure
itself. The line and completeness series were measured all along: **410 of 538 lines (76.2%)**, and
**234 of 339** cards with every printed line read — 25 of them with no script at all.

## Exalted, evolve and battle cry: a keyword whose whole instruction is its own word (#317, D425)

The first keywords the compiler builds a **trigger** from rather than a field. Each is one printed
word with nothing else on the card for it, no number implied and no second line to miss — so the
declaration is the ability, which is what D364 asks before a keyword is safe to read.

Safe because each trigger is written once, in a factory the hand-written card calls too (echo's
arrangement, and `ninjutsuAbility`'s): one implementation per keyword, and the standing check
compares the two readings for free. The three details that are rules rather than effects all come
off the hand-written cards — `alone: true` on exalted, the intervening-if on evolve asked again on
resolution, and the word "other" in battle cry.

**413 of 538 lines (76.8%)**, 239 of 339 with a script, 237 complete, keyword declarations with no
builder down to 17. Five breaks, five failures — two of them caught by the engine tests from #114
and #165, which now exercise the factories.

## The corpus: 33,847 cards, and the first honest coverage number (#318, D426)

#318 was blocked on Scryfall egress and still is — every card-data host answers 403. What is *not*
blocked is GitHub: `git ls-remote` works through the session's git proxy and
`raw.githubusercontent.com` answers 200. So the corpus comes out of `Card-Forge/forge`, which keeps
one plain-text file per card in git — 34,134 of them, a 159 MB sparse fetch.

`scripts/corpus/from-forge.mjs` takes the **printed data** (name, cost, type line, P/T, loyalty,
oracle text) and nothing else — explicitly not Forge's own ability scripts, which are another
engine's DSL and would be a second implementation of the rules that nothing here could check. The
output is the same row shape Scryfall's bulk file has, so `compilable.mjs --file` and the importer
read it unchanged, and the real file replaces it the day egress opens.

**The numbers, pool against corpus:**

| | pool (339) | corpus (33,847) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Printed lines compiled | 413 of 538 (76.8%) | **14,472 of 60,940 (23.7%)** |
| Cards with a compiled script | 239 (70.5%) | 5,506 of 32,948 (16.7%) |
| Cards with every line read | 237 (69.9%) | 3,328 of 32,948 (10.1%) |

Compiling all 33,847 rows without a single throw is also the crash hunt over the whole corpus rather
than a 4,000-row sample.

**And the find that justifies the whole exercise**: the largest systematic miss is the modern
**"enters"** templating. Wizards retemplated "enters the battlefield" to "enters" in 2024; every
reader here was written against the old wording, and so is the pool's own card data — so thousands
of corpus lines fail on a spelling the 339-card pool is structurally incapable of revealing.

**Two gaps, stated**: Forge's oracle text is a community transcription rather than the canonical
feed (second-best source, recorded as such), and format legality is not filtered because Forge
carries none — so silver-bordered cards are still in, which makes the coverage figure pessimistic
rather than flattering.

## "Enters", not "enters the battlefield" (#317, D427)

The first increment off the corpus queue, and the biggest single change the compiler has had: one
aliasing change, **+1,286 printed lines**.

Wizards shortened the phrase in 2024 and made "this creature" how a card refers back to itself.
Every reader here was written against the long form and the card's own name — and so is the pool's
own data, hand-written from memory — so this was invisible until D426 built a real corpus. Two
constants now cover both spellings everywhere: `ENTERS` and `selfRef(name)`.

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corpus lines | 14,472 of 60,940 (23.7%) | **15,758 (25.9%)** |
| Corpus cards with a script | 5,506 (16.7%) | **6,630 (20.1%)** |
| Corpus cards fully read | 3,328 (10.1%) | **3,833 (11.6%)** |
| Pool | 413 of 538 (76.8%) | unchanged |

The over-match was probed rather than assumed: "this creature" inside a spell's *quoted* granted
ability must not be read as the spell's own trigger, and of the 111 instants and sorceries that say
it, five compile at all and all five are a bare keyword declaration. And one break — adding "that
creature" to the list — failed nothing, so that part of the claim is recorded in D427 as untested
rather than left looking covered.

## Enters tapped, and two more steps (#317, D428)

**+438 corpus lines**, and the clearest demonstration of what the pool was hiding. `cardFromData`
has read "enters tapped" since D331 — but only as part of a *whole* card it can account for, so a
land printing one extra line it could not take reported the tapped clause as unread and lost the
other line with it. 347 cards print it; it was the corpus's fourth-biggest bucket for want of a
one-line reader. The conditional arrival ("unless you control two or more other lands") is refused
and asserted.

Two prologues join the upkeep and end step: "At the beginning of your draw step" (part of a
1,168-card bucket) and "At the beginning of combat on your turn" (258). Same trigger shape, steps
the engine has had since #10.

Corpus **16,196 of 60,940 lines (26.6%)**, 6,860 cards with a script, 3,874 fully read; pool
unchanged. Six breaks: three failed outright, one was invalid (deleting a row broke collection, so
vitest reported "no tests" — not a passing break), and one **failed nothing and was right to** —
widening the draw-step prologue to another seat, because the negative row only described the upkeep.
The test now tables all three prologues, and both widening breaks fail.

## Cycling, and landfall (#317, D429)

**+347 corpus lines.** Both are the D421 shape — a keyword whose declaration is what it does, built
through a factory the hand-written card calls too.

Cycling (192 cards): "{2}, Discard this card: Draw a card" is the whole of it. Only *plain* cycling —
the typed cyclings search a library for a named kind of card, which needs a filter this reader would
have to invent, so they stay reported (D259, D362).

Landfall (184 cards): `TriggerDef.what = 'land'` has been there since #163 saying "until a card
asked, nothing could hear it". This is the card asking, and `landfall` joins the ability words so the
prefixed and bare spellings are one row.

**The standing check corrected a fourth hand-written card.** Tatyova's landfall trigger said
`who: 'another'` because "she is not a land"; true of her, not of the phrase. The corpus prints one
land with this trigger (Chocobo Camp), for which `another` misses its own arrival — so the general
reading wins.

Corpus **16,543 of 60,940 (27.1%)**, 7,145 cards with a script; pool **415 of 538 (77.1%)**, 239
complete — Compelling Argument and Tatyova left the incomplete list. Seven breaks, seven failures.

## The question the project is for, asked for the first time (#317/#318, D430-D431)

Nine increments of compiler work had been measured two ways — against the 348-card pool, and against
the 33,847-card corpus as **text**. Neither is the goal. The goal is a deck somebody uploads being
played by the rules, and `scripts/measure/corpus-decks.mjs` is the first thing that asks: two random
60-card decks out of the corpus, resolved through `customDeck` exactly as a pasted list is, played
