bot against bot to a finish, with `applyAction` deliberately unwrapped inside the loop so a throw is
a crash attributed to a seed and a deck rather than a short game (D244).

It found the largest defect in the project to date, and then a second one underneath it.

**D430 — `customDeck` never asked the compiler.** Its `resolve` called `cardFromData`, which answers
the all-or-nothing question *is this card's text nothing but its data?* So **34.3 of the 60 cards in
each random real deck were blank cardboard** — not because nothing could read them, but because
nothing asked. Every reader written since #317 opened was unreachable from the one path a player's
own deck takes. `resolve` now calls `compileCard`; cardboard is left for a row `printedDef` refuses.

**D431 — and every creature it then dealt was a 0/0.** `printedDef` built its `CardDef` with no
`power`, `toughness` or `loyalty`, which was invisible while its only callers added the size
themselves or took the def from elsewhere. `characteristicsOf` reads a missing size as zero, so all
18,603 corpus creatures were arriving for CR 704.5f to bin, and all 327 planeswalkers at zero
loyalty for CR 704.5i. D430 had replaced 34 blanks with 34 corpses.

The printed size is now carried as printed, and a single shared pair of judgements —
`printedBody` and `printedLoyalty` — decides whether it is a number the engine can use, asked by
`cardFromData` and `compileCard` both so the two cannot drift again. A size the compiler *does*
read still counts: Lhurgoyf's `*`/`*` is dealt and is a 2/3 with two creature cards in a graveyard,
while a count `definesSize` does not have is refused rather than dealt as a corpse — the refusal
therefore waits until the text has been read.

| per 60-card deck of random real cards, same six seeds | before D430 | after D431 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cardboard | **34.3** | **0.3** |
| playable from printed data | 1.4 | **35.3** |
| with a flagged line (D362) | 13.2 | **30.3** |
| turns to a finish | 93.3 | **22.5** |

Widened: **40 games, 80 random decks, all 40 finished with no throw and no stall**, 21.8 turns and
70 moves on average. Corpus coverage **16,448 of 60,460 lines (27.2%)**, 7,126 cards with a script —
the denominators move because 223 cards (221 creatures and 2 planeswalkers) are now refused for a
size nothing can read, which is what the 0.3 cardboard per deck is.

## The legality filter, which was never actually blocked (#318, D432)

`from-forge.mjs` had recorded since D426 that format legality was unreachable — "that lives in
Scryfall's `legalities` object and MTGJSON's, both unreachable". True of Forge's *card files*, and
false of Forge's *repository*: its format definitions (`Sets:` allowlists, `Banned:` lists, Pauper's
`Rarities:`) and its per-set card lists are two directories the D426 sparse checkout never fetched.

`scripts/corpus/legality.mjs` reads them and emits Scryfall's own `legalities` object, so the day
Scryfall egress opens the real feed replaces it with no change downstream. Three judgements are
stated because each excludes cards: `Type=Funny` sets (un-cards, which the goal excludes by name),
`Type=Online` sets (Alchemy and digital-only), and the types that are not deck cards at all
(Scheme, Plane, Vanguard, Conspiracy and the rest — 384 cards).

**Its `--check` table caught a defect in the script on the first run.** Two of 13 ground-truth rows
read "(no such card)": schemes and planes were never entering the printings map, because I had
required a plain integer collector number and Forge numbers 345 lines `1★`, 374 `123F`, 310 `M-1`
and 385 `123a`. A card whose only printing carries one of those vanished and read `not_legal`
everywhere — the most damaging direction a legality bug can point. The rarity letter identifies a
card line now; 252 cards came back and all 13 rows agree.

`LEGAL=1` on both measures restricts to the formats the goal names, **off by default** so older
figures stay reproducible:

| | every row | legal in a named format |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cards | 33,847 | **31,654** |
| Lines compiled | 16,448 of 60,460 (27.2%) | **15,869 of 56,421 (28.1%)** |

Filtering raises coverage, because the cards it drops are ones the compiler read worst — so the
27.2% was understating the engine against the decks anybody will actually upload. Legal-only random
decks play: 10 of 10 to a finish, no throw, no stall, 0.1 cardboard per deck.

And it corrects the work queue. The two biggest prologue buckets in all of Magic were "Whenever
chaos ensues" (136) and "When you set this scheme in motion" (81) — Planechase and Archenemy, real
reader work queued against cards nobody can put in a deck. Both gone.

**Where the remaining work actually is**, measured rather than assumed: for each unread
trigger-shaped line, keep the prologue and swap the body for a body that always reads, then
re-compile. Of 12,338 distinct such lines, **10,196 fail on the prologue and only 2,142 on the
body** — and both are long tails (7,060 and 1,489 distinct shapes). So the next increments are
families of prologues.

## The trigger whose subject is the creature it is attached to (D433)

"Whenever equipped creature attacks, put a +1/+1 counter on it" is a shape the compiler could not
express: every trigger it emitted was about the card printing it, and an Equipment is never the
creature the event happened to. One field — `who: 'attached'` on `attacks` and on `combat-damage` —
and it is resolved in `fireTrigger`, where the attachment is known, rather than in `triggerMatches`,
which only sees the event. Armory of Iroas is the hand-written card; the compiler reads its printed
text to the same script.

**Three defects came out of the break run, and two of them were shipping.**

A compiled Armory of Iroas reported `unread: []` — fully automated — and put its counter on the
**sword** instead of the creature. `selfEffect` accepted `(?:<name>|it)` in four clauses and
resolved both alternatives to the source. A line that goes unread gets a badge and a human plays it
by hand; a line read *wrongly* is flagged nowhere, which makes this the worst shape a reading can
take. "it" now means `c.subject ?? c.source` and a clause that names the card still means the card.
411 legal cards print one of those four bodies, 54 print one under a prologue about somebody else,
and the compiler reads the line on **8** of them today — every one of which was aiming at the wrong
permanent.

The `combat-damage` arm **could never be reached at all**: `raise` kept that event in its self-only
watcher set, so it was offered to the creature that dealt the damage and never to the Equipment
printing the trigger. 45 corpus cards print that prologue and all 45 would have compiled clean and
done nothing. Its runtime test is a *compiled* card — Prying Blade's printed row through
`customDeck`, the route an uploaded decklist takes — because that is the path those 45 cards reach a
table by.

And a comment claimed a distinction between the holder and the defining card that does not exist at
either call site; it now says so, and says why its break cannot be made to bite.

**What the break run is actually for.** Of nine breaks, the first six passes failed nothing. Not six
missing tests — one structural hole: the standing compiled-vs-written check skips any card with an
unread line, so every regression that makes a line *stop* reading removes the card from the
comparison rather than failing it. A check that stops looking is not a check. The second lesson is
smaller and sharper: the same increment twice wrote a fix in two redundant places, and redundancy
means no single break can move it. One lever per claim.

## The steps that raised no event (D434)

Eleven of the engine's thirteen steps never raised a step event. `onEnterStep` raised one from
inside its `upkeep` case and its `end` case; `begin-combat` had no case at all and `draw` returned
its deferred draw without raising. For as long as the only cards asking were an upkeep card and an
end-step card, nobody could tell.

Then the compiler started reading "At the beginning of combat on your turn" — the third biggest step
bucket in Magic, 262 legal lines, 19 cards it reads whole — and every one of them compiled with
`unread: []`, was reported fully automated, and **did nothing at all**. A probe confirmed it before
the fix was written: a compiled Luminarch Aspirant reached declare-attackers with no counter on any
creature, nothing on the stack and nothing in the log.

It is one raise now, in `advanceStep`, for every step. Deleting that single line fails 37 tests,
Phyrexian Arena and Ball Lightning among them — which is the measure of how much it was carrying
from two places before.

**Three prologue rows shipped out of twelve candidate spellings, and the deciding number is not how
often the sentence is printed.** A row for a card whose body stays unread changes nothing, so every
candidate was compiled across the corpus and judged on cards finished rather than lines matched:
`end`/any (152 lines, **17** cards), `upkeep`/any (149, **10**), `precombat-main`/you (47, **2**).
The other six spellings have **zero** compilable cards and are not read. `of: 'opponent'` was
written and then taken back out for the same reason — 43 printed lines, no card with a readable
body, so the field would have been machinery nothing exercises. Every count is recorded in the code
so the question is one command to re-ask.

One test had to be retired: `compile.test.ts` asserted that "At the beginning of each end step" stays
unread *"because 'your' is the half that is the rule"*. That described the compiler, not Magic, and a
test that pins a gap fails the day the gap closes.

Legal-only coverage is 15,964 of 56,421 lines (28.3%) and 7,018 cards with a script. The line count
barely moves, which is the point: the 280 lines this fixes were already counted as compiled.

## The cast family (D435)

`spell-cast` has had `by`, `spell`, `self` and `how` since the engine's first Guttersnipe, and the
compiler could read three of the sentences that use them. Seven more rows now — 45 cards — chosen
the way D434 established: on cards whose *body* the compiler already reads, not on lines printed.

| printed | lines | cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| you cast a creature spell | 44 | 11 |
| you cast an enchantment spell | 17 | 9 |
| you cast a spell | 49 | 8 |
| when you cast this spell | 80 | 7 |
| you cast an artifact spell | 21 | 7 |
| a player casts a spell | 35 | 2 |
| an opponent casts a spell | 27 | 1 |

"Historic" (19 lines, 4 cards) and "multicolored" (19, 4) are refused on the **mechanism** rather
than the count: historic is artifact-or-legendary-or-Saga and multicolored is a fact about the mana
cost, so neither is a card type and a reading that pretended otherwise would fire on the wrong
spells. One new field, `ofType`, holds a card type and is kept separate from `spell` because an
artifact creature spell is both at once.

Two findings worth the entry. `spell: 'creature'` was in the union with a comparison in the matcher
and **no script anywhere set it** — a branch with no user is a branch with no evidence. And the
break run caught the hole that mattered: rewriting `ofType` as the creature/noncreature split failed
nothing, because both fixtures agreed with both readings. The case that separates them is an
artifact *creature* spell, so Arcbound Worker is now a test row.

Three increments running, a plausible well-commented claim has turned out to have no test that
could contradict it. Named for next time: when a docblock argues two things must be kept apart, the
fixtures need the case where they overlap, or the argument is decoration.

Legal-only coverage 16,016 of 56,421 lines (28.4%), 7,066 cards with a script.

## The second card drawn each turn (D436)

The biggest remaining prologue family by cards finished — 54 legal lines, **24 cards**, twice the
next candidate — and the smallest engine change, because every entry in `GameState.drew` already
carries the card's place in its seat's turn. Miracle put it there.

The number worth keeping from that measurement is the one at the bottom of the table: **"When this
creature enters" is 337 lines and 0 cards.** Its prologue already reads; what is unread is 337
different bodies. Lines printed has stopped predicting anything, and cards finished is the measure
every increment now uses.

The ordinal travels **on the event** rather than being looked up, and that is the whole of the work:
`cardsDrawnThisTurn` has counted both cards of a `draw(2)` by the time either trigger is matched, so
a reading taken from the running total puts two counters on an Atlantean Cavalry that drew a
Divination — on a card whose entire text is about counting. The break run confirms it: swapping the
filter back to the total fails both runtime tests.

Only "second" is read — 63 of the 65 legal lines that name an ordinal say it — while `onNth` takes
any number, so the field is general and the reader is narrow. Alandra, Sky Dreamer prints "second"
on one line and "fifth" on the next, and is now the test for what the hybrid reading is for: one
line compiled, the other flagged, same card.

Legal-only coverage 16,055 of 56,421 lines (28.5%), 7,097 cards with a script.

## The death the attachment watches (D437)

D433 deferred `who: 'attached'` on `dies` "on a question about ordering". The question had an
answer, and a probe got it before anything was written: a compiled Lead Pipe on a creature killed by
a Lightning Bolt fired **nothing**, with `attachedTo` already `null`. `relocate` detaches everything
pointing at a card as it leaves — it has to — so by the time a death is announced the board has
forgotten the attachment.

Three layers, each needing its own fix and each with its own break:

1. **The fact travels with the event.** `GameState.detached` records what came unattached and the
   `dies` event carries it; `fireTrigger` prefers the event's answer and falls back to the live
   board, so an attack still reads the attachment that is still there. Third increment running to
   need a fact the state no longer holds — after miracle's draw ordinal and D433's attack host — so
   the rule is now written down: if a trigger needs to know something about the instant its event
   happened, the event carries it.
2. **The Aura is not on the battlefield either.** CR 704.5m buries it before the announcement, so it
   was in nobody's watcher list. `raise` splices the event's attachments in *and* the zone gate lets
   them fire from where they went. The splice alone changes nothing, which is why both halves are
   recorded.
3. **The Aura could not be read at all.** Bequeathal — "Enchant creature / When enchanted creature
   dies, you draw two cards" — compiled to a spell with no target that attached to nothing and did
   nothing, because an Aura needed a bonus line. Of 55 legal Auras printing that trigger, **29 have
   no bonus line**. It is optional now, as it has been for Equipment since D433 — and the existing
   "both halves or neither" test immediately caught the first, too-wide attempt: `Enchant creature`
   as the whole card is still refused.

Legal-only coverage 16,262 of 56,421 lines (28.8%) and **7,284 cards with a script**, up 187. Most
of that is layer three: the Aura requirement was blocking every Aura whose second line was anything
but a bonus, not just this family.

## The name a card calls itself by (D438)

A card with a title names itself in full once and in short after. *Alesha, Who Laughs at Fate*
prints "Whenever Alesha attacks"; *Bilbo, Retired Burglar* prints "Whenever Bilbo deals combat
damage to a player". `selfRef` knew the full name and the 2024 "this creature" retemplate (D426) and
nothing between, so those lines were unread — on **924 legal cards** that use their short name in
their own text.

One line in `selfRef`, which about twenty readers share: the entry trigger, the attack trigger,
"enters tapped", "enters with counters", the activated-ability object, the counter readers. It was
found while measuring the next trigger family, when the probe's self-name bucket came back holding
476 unread lines for a prologue the compiler claimed to read.

Two things are worth remembering from it:

- **The space after the comma is the guard, not the letters before it.** *Borrowing 100,000 Arrows*
  and *Guan Yu's 1,000-Li March* both have letters in front of a thousands separator, so a "does it
  contain a letter" check cannot tell a title from a number — and having both checks meant no single
  break could reach either, the trap D433 named. The letter check is gone.
- **The alias is case-insensitive and that is written down rather than fixed.** V8 has no `(?-i:…)`,
  so "Eleven" also matches "eleven". Exactly two legal cards in 33,847 print their own short name as
  an ordinary word (*Eleven, the Mage*, *Storm, Force of Nature*), neither in a clause any reader
  matches, and both are pinned by a test whose job is to fail the day that changes.

Legal-only coverage 16,331 of 56,421 lines (28.9%) and **7,344 cards with a script**, up 60, with
3,997 cards having every printed line read.

## The event that had its own rules (D439)

`combat-damage` was the only board event with a private arm in `triggerMatches` — two values of
`who`, no `of` — so "whenever a creature you control deals combat damage to a player" could not be
written at all, though "whenever a creature you control dies" has been writable since D437. It is 33
legal lines and 9 compilable cards.

It is folded into the branch the other six board events share, and the fold is safe because the
defaults do the narrowing: `who` defaults to `'self'`, which still requires the watcher to be the
subject.

The fold alone did nothing, and the **runtime** test is what said so — the compile table was green on
the trigger's shape before either of these:

- the event now carries `subjectSeat`, which is what `of: 'you'` is answered from;
- and the watcher's `about.subject`, which is what "put a +1/+1 counter on **that creature**" means.
  While the event was its own permanent's business the subject *was* the watcher, so no card had a
  "that creature" to mean; `who: 'any'` is what creates the distinction.

**The plural is refused on purpose.** "Whenever one or more creatures you control deal combat damage
to a player" is 26 lines and 8 cards — more than the row that shipped — and it fires once however
many creatures connected, where this engine raises one event per creature. Reading it would pay Grim
Hireling two Treasures per attacker. It waits for a batched event, with a test that fails if someone
adds the prologue without one.

Legal-only coverage 16,340 of 56,421 lines (29.0%) and **7,352 cards with a script**.

## The count storm cannot be (D440)

"Whenever you cast your second spell each turn" is 47 legal lines and 17 compilable cards — the
largest prologue family left — and it needed a number the engine did not have. `spellsCastThisTurn`
is the **table's** running total, which is what storm counts (CR 702.40a); this line counts only
yours. So `spellsCastThisTurnBy` sits beside it, per seat, and the ordinal travels on the
`spell-cast` event — the third increment running to need a fact at the instant its event happened
rather than at resolution.

`countCast` is one function returning both tallies, called from the two places a spell is cast from
(the ordinary cast and the face-down morph), because the old code wrote `+ 1` out twice and a second
statement of one rule is a place no single break reaches.

Shipped on the measure: "second" (47 lines, 17 cards) and "first" (3, 1). **Declined:** "third" — 2
lines, 0 cards finished, so the row would change nothing.

Along the way: 14 of those 47 lines were unread because `ABILITY_WORDS` did not list `flurry` or
`eukrasia`. Both are on it now, and measuring the rest found **2,129 legal unread lines carrying a
word and an em dash, 56 of which read once the word comes off** — exhaust, alliance, boast, solved,
imprint, and a tail of one-card flavour names. That is the next increment, and it is not just a
longer list: "I", "II" and "III" are also letters before an em dash, so a general rule would eat a
Saga's chapters.

Legal-only coverage 16,363 of 56,421 lines (29.0%) and **7,374 cards with a script**.

## The label in front of an ability (D441)

`withoutAbilityWord` knew three words. The corpus says a list cannot work: **2,733 legal lines**
carry a letters-only label and an em dash, across **540 distinct labels**, and most of the readable
ones are named on one card — "Rosarius", "Keen Senses", "Gae Bolg". Universes Beyond prints a
flavour name where older cards print a shared ability word, and both are flavour with no rules
meaning (CR 207.2c).

So it is a refusal list now: a label comes off unless it has a rules meaning. What does:

- a **keyword ability's name**, matched on the whole label and on its first word, because there the
  em dash joins a keyword to its *cost* — "Cumulative upkeep—Put a -1/-1 counter on Aboroth" would
  otherwise become an unconditional effect;
- **ward** and **channel**, two keywords the keyword list does not name;
- a **Saga's chapter markers**, which are 473 legal lines of letters before an em dash.

The judgement worth remembering: `Exhaust`, `Boast` and `Max speed` print "<keyword> — <activated
ability>", so stripping them *would* finish 28 cards — and they are refused anyway, because the
keyword **is** the restriction (exhaust once only; boast only after that creature attacked). 28 wrong
readings is worse than 28 lines unread.

Most of those refusals cannot be falsified by any printed card — every real line carrying one has a
remainder the compiler cannot read either way — so they are pinned on a probe sentence with a
control, rather than on a fixture that would pass whatever the code did.

Legal-only coverage 16,400 of 56,421 lines (29.1%) and **7,405 cards with a script**.

## One event for the declaration (D442)

"Whenever you attack" is 92 legal lines and 8 compilable cards, and it is not a filter on `attacks`:
`attacks` is about a creature and is raised once per attacker, while this is about the declaration
and fires once however many creatures were in it (CR 508.1). Read off `attacks`, Adeline would make a
token per opponent *per attacker*.

So `{ kind: 'attack-declared' }` is raised once at the end of the declaration handler, only when
something was actually declared. Myriad is already excluded — a myriad token was never declared
(CR 508.4) — because the raise reads the declaration rather than the board.

The test that matters is a count, not a shape: the same board, attacked with one creature and with
three, draws **one card either way**.

Refused, each with its corpus count: "with three or more creatures" (8 lines), "with one or more
<type>" (8), "a player" (7), "with two or more creatures" (6), "with your commander" (2), "while
creatures you control have total power 8 or greater" (2). Each carries a restriction the event cannot
express, and six compile rows fail if a prologue is widened to swallow one.

Legal-only coverage 16,408 of 56,421 lines (29.1%) and **7,411 cards with a script**.

## The batched hit (D443)

D439 measured "whenever one or more creatures you control deal combat damage to a player" — 26 legal
lines, 8 compilable cards — and refused to ship it, because `combat-damage` is raised per creature
and the row would have paid Grim Hireling two Treasures per attacker. D442 built the batched event
for the attack declaration; this is the same move for the damage, and the engine now has both pairs:

| about a creature, raised per creature | about the event, raised once |
| --- | --- |
| `attacks` | `attack-declared` |
| `combat-damage` | `combat-damage-dealt` |

The batch is keyed on **(whose creature, who was hit)**, not on the combat, and the templating is
why: Anowon prints "…deal combat damage to a player, **that player** mills…", and "that player" can
only mean one. A duel cannot tell the two readings apart, so the test is a pod — two creatures, two
opponents, four Treasures.

Legal-only coverage 16,416 of 56,421 lines (29.1%) and **7,419 cards with a script**.

## The question that found the biggest gap (D444)

Six increments of prologue families moved coverage about half a point each. Then the queue was
re-asked a better way: not "which family prints the most lines" but **"which shape is the last thing
standing between a card and a finished script"**. 17,439 legal cards are one unread line from
finished, and the top of that list was not a trigger at all — it was a mana ability:
`{T}: Add {B} or {R}` (252 lines, **67** cards one line from finished) and `{T}: Add one mana of any
color` (112 lines, **55**).

The reader had a comment explaining that a choice of colours "is left to `cardFromData`'s land path
rather than guessed at here". `cardFromData` reads a whole card or nothing — so Akoum Refuge, which
also enters tapped and gains a life, got no script from either path. Deferring to a path that cannot
reach the card is dropping it.

The fix emits the pool's own shape: one ability per colour, exactly as the hand-written Guildgates
and Birds of Paradise are written, with per-colour descriptions because the table puts one on each
button.

**+233 cards with a script in one increment**, against roughly +10 for each of the six before it.
Coverage 16,855 of 56,421 legal lines (29.9%), 7,652 cards scripted, 4,157 fully read.

The lesson is about the instrument, not the mana: a queue ranked by lines printed kept pointing at
trigger prologues whose cards had three other gaps each. `scripts/measure` should keep the
"one line from finished" view.

## A flag that existed and a sentence that did not (D445)

`AbilityDef.sorcerySpeed` has been enforced since planeswalkers (#43). The compiler never read the
sentence that sets it, so "Activate only as a sorcery." made the whole line unreadable — a timing
restriction is not an effect, and the clause vocabulary is about effects. It comes off the end of the
line now, and **23 cards carry a sorcery-speed ability the engine can enforce** where before they
carried none.

**The instrument over-promised by a factor of twelve, and that is the lesson.** A scratch probe put
this sentence first in all of Magic at 213 cards; the change delivered +17. The probe split each
unread line into sentences and counted a card once per *sentence* that failed, so a line with three
unreadable parts was promised three times over. On most of those 213 the **cost** is also unreadable
("Sacrifice a land:", "Tap two untapped artifacts and/or creatures you control:"). `one-line-short.mjs`
does not have that flaw — it counts whole lines — and the sentence-level probe was deliberately not
shipped.

The next increment off this family is the **ability costs**, which is where those cards actually stop.

Coverage 16,876 of 56,421 legal lines (29.9%), 7,669 cards scripted.

## The cost half of the reader, which refused everything (D446)

D445 pointed here, and the stop was total: the activated-ability reader accepted a mana run, one
`{T}` and `Pay N life`, and **refused the whole line** on any other component. "Sacrifice this
creature: …" read as nothing — and after mana, that is the commonest cost in Magic.

Three components already had a field on `AbilityCost` and a payment that charges them; only the
reading was missing. Measured over unread lines whose effect this compiler can already read:
**415** print `Sacrifice <this permanent>`, 143 a filtered sacrifice, 14 `Discard <this card>`.

`selfRef` is why 415 lines are one regex: the corpus spells the same cost as the card's name, "this
artifact", "this land" and "this creature", and D426/D438 already taught that function all four.

**What stays unread is the point.** `Sacrifice a land` (27), `Sacrifice a Goblin` (15), `Tap an
untapped creature you control` (18), `Remove a +1/+1 counter from ~` (35) and `Exile ~ from your
graveyard` (17) have no field to read into. Inventing one would be a cost the payment never charges,
which is an ability that activates for free on a card that otherwise works — nothing at the table
would catch it. Leaving the line unread is the honest half of D362.

Two findings worth keeping:

- **The full suite caught what a targeted run could not.** An older test asserted "Sacrifice another
  creature" was refused. That claim stopped being true; the row was retired in place with the old
  wording quoted, the way D441 retired its allow-list. The rule the test states is unchanged.
- **A disagreement goes on the card, not in a table of excuses.** `compiled-vs-written` failed on
  Shambling Shell because the compiled target spec said `friendly: true` and the hand-written one did
  not. The compiled reading was right, so the hand-written card was fixed — D419's rule.

Coverage **17,419 of 56,421 legal lines (30.9%)**, the first pass over thirty per cent, and **8,029
cards with a script** (+360), 4,552 fully read.

## Two words, 50 cards, and seven cards that had paid for their absence (D447)

"You may" is the commonest pair of words in Magic's trigger clauses, and it made the whole line
unreadable: the clause vocabulary answers *what an effect does*, and this answers *whether it
happens*. 82 legal lines are a prologue this compiler reads, a "you may", and an effect it reads —
**50 cards one line from finished**, among them Gravedigger, Reclamation Sage, Consecrated Sphinx
and Ninja of the Deep Hours.

It is read as what it is: a question with two answers, the shape Ophidian has been written in by
hand since D116. Yes is the first option, which `ChoiceDecisionSpec` documents as the bot's
fallback, and that is right because **all 82 lines are pure upside for the controller** — read, not
sampled. No card in the set costs its controller anything to say yes.

**What is refused:** a may whose effect asks its own question (9 lines, all "you may search your
library for a basic land card"). The engine asks a resolution's questions in order, so a declined
search would have opened the library first — a wrong reading *and* an information leak. Unlocking
it needs a conditional decision in the engine, which is its own feature.

### The pool had been paying for this in card text

The runtime test was first written on printed Gravedigger and passed without the compiler being
involved: the pool hand-writes Gravedigger, hand-written wins the precedence, and its pool text has
no "you may" in it. Checking that against the corpus found **seven pool cards that drop a printed
"you may"** — Goblin Arsonist, Gravedigger, Ninja of the Deep Hours, Ophidian Eye, Gelectrode, Angel
of Sanctions, Yavimaya Granger. All mandatory in the pool, optional in print. Logged as task #328
rather than fixed here, because changing seven shipped cards moves the bot and therefore the deck
win rates that #96, D231 and #268 measured over thousands of games.

Mystic Remora, whose line this increment finished, is settled the other way (D419): its hand-written
question now spells `['Yes', 'No']` like the compiled one, and the `best` that existed only to undo
a confusing option order is gone.

**One process note worth keeping.** The first break run reported ten clean failures against a
**dirty baseline** — a runtime test still answering the Remora's old option word. The verdicts held
once the baseline was fixed, but a break run is only as good as the baseline under it, and that
should be the first thing checked rather than the second.

Coverage **17,500 of 56,421 legal lines (31.0%)**, **8,099 cards with a script** (+70), 4,599 fully
read (+47).

## The same question with a price on it (D448)

D447's queue had a second row: `you may pay <cost>. If you do, <effect>` — 66 legal lines, **39
with a cost the engine can charge**. `payIfChosen` has been that shape since echo (#196), so this
is the free "may" plus one field rather than new machinery.

The words are deliberately asymmetrical with D447's. A free may puts **Yes** first, because all 82
of its lines are pure upside — measured, not assumed. A priced may puts **Decline** first, because
`options[0]` is a bot's fallback and spending mana is not safe. Neither writes a `best`, and the
cost of that is stated plainly: **the bot never pays one of these**. A human is asked properly and
the card is correct either way; whether a generic hint beats the safe answer is a deck-table
question, not a guess.

Everything refused is a cost the engine cannot charge: energy (19 lines), life (4), a mana cost plus
something else (4), and an announced X. `parseManaCost` refuses them all through the same check that
validated D446's ability costs. **Energy is the next obvious question** — a price on an answer paid
in something other than mana.

**The break run earned its keep again.** One lever passed: a guard reading
`whole === null && priced === null` could be broken with all 1,506 tests green, because the ordering
was already decided by the selection below it. Two statements of one rule — removed, and breaking the
real one fails. Third increment running where the break run found a redundant lever rather than a
missing test.

Coverage **17,537 of 56,421 legal lines (31.1%)**, **8,129 cards with a script** (+30), 4,627 fully
read (+28).

## 173 shapes, one mechanic (D449)

Two exact-string readers covered the library search. The corpus prints it in **173 distinct shapes**
over 439 unread legal lines — one mechanic crossed with a filter, an optional reveal, two spellings
of "the card you found", and three destinations. Read as that product, **72 legal cards now read a
search whole**: Demonic Tutor, Eladamri's Call, Call the Gatewatch, Beneath the Sands, Deep
Reconnaissance among them.

The reveal is read as nothing, which the engine had already decided: `miracle` says in its own
docblock that it does not model a reveal, calls it a hidden-information difference in the player's
favour, and says a card that punished the reveal would need it to be real. Here there is one more
argument — the filter is enforced by the engine, so the checking a printed reveal exists for is
already done.

**Printed capitalisation is the guard.** Types and supertypes are lowercase, subtypes capitalised. The
first draft had no lowercase allow-list and was wrong both ways: "a **permanent** card" searched for
a type no card has, and "a **legendary** card" is a supertype, not a subtype. Both would have offered
**nothing**, every time, on cards whose other lines worked — D362's failure exactly.

**The break run's best outing yet: four of thirteen levers passed**, and each named a missing test. A
filter that matches nothing has the same shape as one that works, so inspecting the spec cannot tell
them apart. Two runtime tests now ask what the search *offers*, on a library built to make a wrong
reading loud — the legendary filter has to pick Captain Sisay over Raging Goblin, and both are
creature cards. All thirteen fail now.

**The biggest thing left in the way is one engine feature, not a reader**: `you may search your
library …` is 128 cards one line short, and D447/D448 refuse it because the engine cannot skip a
later question on an earlier answer.

Coverage **17,625 of 56,421 legal lines (31.2%)**, **8,192 cards with a script** (+63), 4,680 fully
read (+53).

## The first engine feature this run needed (D450)

Everything else in the queue was a reader. This was not: "you may search your library …" was the
biggest single thing in the compiler's way — **128 legal cards one line from finished** — and the
engine simply could not express it. It asks a resolution's questions in order, so the only readings
available were "refuse the line" or "open the library before asking", and the second is an
information leak that no board-state check would catch, because the cards go back.

`DecisionSpec.askOnlyIfChosen` is the feature: ask this question only if an earlier answer was this
word. Twenty lines, three decisions worth keeping:

- a skipped question is **answered empty**, not dropped, so answer positions do not shift;
- the word is matched against the **most recent** earlier answer with an option, because a question
  can expand into several entries and "the one before" is not a position a card knows;
- the gate belongs to the reader, not the clause — so the context handed to the inner effect has the
  yes-or-no's own answer **removed**, and the clause is written as if there were no "may".

That last one was a real bug for about ten minutes: the search offered the right cards, the player
picked a Mountain, and nothing arrived, because the clause's `chosenCard(c)` was reading the
yes-or-no's empty answer. The runtime test caught it.

**And the pool shadowed the test again.** The first subject was Yavimaya Granger, which prints this
exact sentence — but the pool hand-writes it with the "you may" dropped (#328), so the test drove a
mandatory search and never reached the compiler. Second time this run (Gravedigger, D447). Pick a
card that is in no deck.

Coverage **17,682 of 56,421 legal lines (31.3%)**, **8,234 cards with a script** (+42, exactly the
sub-shape's measured count), 4,725 fully read (+45).

## Energy as a price on an answer (D451)

D448's largest refusal, closed by one field. `payIfChosen.cost` was a mana string, so the Kaladesh
commons — "you may pay {E}{E}. If you do, create a 1/1 Servo" — named a price the engine could not
charge, even though `AbilityCost.energy` has charged an *activated* ability in energy since #180.
`payIfChosen.energy` is the same price in the other currency, and the affordability question is now
one function asked at both the moments it has to be asked.

**The reader order was load-bearing and only the corpus measure could see it.** `{E}` matches the
mana reader's `\{[^}]+\}`, so putting the energy reader second meant every energy clause went to
`parseManaCost`, was refused, and read as nothing — coverage did not move one card while the compile
table stayed green. Energy first; a row for each side of the pair now pins the order.

**No test-only plumbing.** Printed Aether Chaser gives itself two energy on arrival and offers to
spend them when it attacks, so six runtime tests run on printed text alone — including the one the
break run demanded, where a seat holding **one** energy must not be offered a two-energy price.
Reaching that board needs a card whose gain is exactly one: printed Aether Hub. Without it the
threshold could be short by one and every test still passed.

Honest residual: **19 legal cards** still print an energy-priced may and are not read whole, none of
them because of the price. Six say "**When** you do," which is a reflexive trigger that can be
responded to rather than a continuation of the resolution — reading it as "if you do" would be a
real rules difference, so it stays refused.

Coverage **17,701 of 56,421 legal lines (31.4%)**, 8,237 cards with a script (+3), **4,741 fully
read (+16)** — the fully-read figure is the one this increment was for.

## Surveil: one clause, one field, 92 cards (D452)

The largest clause left in the corpus that needed **no new machinery**. 227 unread legal lines
mention surveil and 120 are a card's only unread line — and every prologue they hang off was already
read, so the whole family was waiting on one reader.

Scry and surveil are the same decision with two destinations (CR 701.18, CR 701.42). So
`CardsDecisionSpec.chosenGoTo` says which, and `surveil(n)` is `scry(n)` plus that field — not a
second zone, because the candidates, the `min: 0`, the no-shuffle rule and the order of what stays
are all identical.

**The scry half is what makes the field mean anything.** Both compile to the same `library-top`
question, so testing surveil alone would pass a reading that sent every scry in the pool to the
graveyard — Preordain and Magma Jet quietly becoming self-mill. The pair is asserted in both the
compile table and the runtime block, and two break levers cross the wires in both directions.

**The break run found one more hole and it needed a probe.** Reading the spec from index 0 instead of
the resume plan's own index left everything green, because on every printed surveil card the
library-top question *is* the first one asked. No corpus card prints an optional surveil, so D450's
gate was used to build the shape that discriminates: "you may surveil 1" puts the surveil second.

Coverage **17,836 of 56,421 legal lines (31.6%)**, **8,329 cards with a script (+92)**, 4,820 fully
read (+79) — the largest increment since D444, and for the same reason: rank the queue by what a card
is *waiting for*, not by what prints most.

## A printed board scope, and the first reader that answers with a set (D453)

"Put a +1/+1 counter on each other Dragon creature you control" — 294 legal cards print a
counter-on-each clause and none of them read. The counter was never the missing piece; reading **a
set of permanents off a phrase** was. Every reader in the compiler until now answered with one
target, one number or one card in a library, so `boardScope` is the first that answers with a list —
its own function, because Magic prints the same scope into a counter clause, a sweep and a pump, and
one reader is what stops it meaning two different sets in two places.

Three parts in printed order: an optional `other`, the type words, an optional controller clause
(`you control`, `you don't control`, `your opponents control`, `each opponent controls`, or none,
which is every creature in the game). Words are classified by **capitalisation** — D449's rule again:
lowercase is a card type or supertype, capitalised is a subtype, so `artifact creature`, `legendary
creature` and `Dragon creature` are three readings of one shape.

**150 cards** print a scope this reads, across 45 phrases. **144** are refused across 80, and that is
the half worth stating: `creature you control with a +1/+1 counter on it`, `Pest, Bat, Insect, Snake,
and Spider`, `creature that convoked it`, `white creature you control`. Each would have put counters
on a wider or narrower set than the card prints, and a counter on the wrong creature is a board a
player cannot argue with.

**The allow-list of types is shorter than the search filters'** on purpose: "each instant you
control" is a well-formed phrase whose set is empty on every battlefield, which is D449's
silent-nothing failure arriving from a new direction.

**The break run deleted a guard and bought two tests.** Eleven levers, three passed. Removing the
*opponents* half of the scope filter left 1,585 tests green, because every scope under test was
"yours", "yours except this one" or "everyone's" — Aku Djinn, whose drawback is that it grows *their*
board, now watches it. Reading two type words as an either-or also passed, because every scope under
test was one word long — Arcbound Shikari, with an artifact creature and a plain creature beside it,
now watches that. The third was a two-word bound kept on theory; measured against the corpus, every
printed scope of three words or more is already refused by a lowercase non-type in it (`with`,
`target`, `and/or`, `you`, `of`), so the bound went and six refusal rows took its place. What
replaced it is the guard that was doing the work: a word has to **be** a word, or `Pest,` becomes a
subtype no permanent has.

Coverage **17,869 of 56,421 legal lines (31.7%)**, **8,354 cards with a script (+25)**, 4,846 fully
read (+26).

## The shrink, which is the pump with one character changed (D454)

"Target creature gets -2/-2 until end of turn" — **265 legal cards print it and none of them read**,
because the pattern above it demanded a `+`. The largest single clause family left in the corpus was
waiting on one character.

The effect was never missing: `pump` has taken a negative bonus since the sweeper. What was missing
is that **the sign decides whose creature it is**. The same sentence one character apart is a trick
you aim at your own board and removal you aim across the table, and `TargetSpec.friendly` is where
that lands (D252) — without the flag the bot's default is "the enemy and the enemy's creatures",
which is exactly right for a shrink and exactly wrong for a pump. So one regex reads both halves,
the size is read first, and the sign picks the branch.

**Darkblast is the ground truth for every field of it.** The pool's one hand-written shrink points
at the hostile `TARGET_CREATURE` and sets `expiresAtEndOfTurn` — on a shrink, wearing off at end of
turn is what kills the creature before the shrink expires. The compiled reading of its printed line
now matches the hand-written script field for field, and `compiled-vs-written` is what says so.

**A mixed size is refused**, and the refusal is about the bot rather than the effect: 14 cards print
`+4/-4`, `pump` would apply it correctly, and what the sentence does not say is which creature it is
for. A `friendly` guessed wrong aims the spell at the wrong half of the table every time.

Nine break levers, nine failures. Coverage **18,010 of 56,421 legal lines (31.9%)**, **8,457 cards
with a script (+103)**, 4,938 fully read (+92) — the second-largest increment yet, from one
character in a regex.

## The library search, widened to the shape the corpus prints (D455)

**416 legal cards were one unread line from finished and that line was a library search** — the
largest family left, and the blockers were exactly the refusals D449 listed: a count, a destination
applied to a set, and a filter of more than one word. The corpus says those are not exotic shapes;
they are how Magic normally prints the clause.

Three more axes on the same product. **The quantity** — `a`, `up to N`, `any number of` — with a
minimum of nought always, because a player may always fail to find (CR 701.19c). **The destination
applied to a set** — both plural pronouns, every printed spelling of the reveal, and five places to
put what was found. **The filter as alternatives of conjunctions**, which is the printed grammar: "a
basic Forest, Plains, or Island card" is one of three, "an artifact creature card" is both at once,
and a leading `basic` distributes over the list. 136 distinct filters now read across 636 lines —
and the ten **fetchlands** come with them, because `a Swamp or Mountain card` was never more than a
compound filter.

**The break run's lesson is worth keeping.** Five of thirteen levers passed, and four of them because
a compile row can only see *that* a line read: AND-ing the alternatives, OR-ing the words inside one,
and dropping the `basic` all still read. What they change is which cards the search **offers**, which
only a game shows — so printed Time of Need, Field Trip and Entomb now play it out. The fifth was two
guards overlapping, and the fix was a row that isolates each.

Coverage **18,113 of 56,421 legal lines (32.1%)**, **8,530 cards with a script (+73)**, **5,015 with
every line read (+77)** — the first time past five thousand cards that read end to end.

## An Aura attaches even when its statics do not read (D456)

**1,240 legal Auras, and 738 of them compiled to no attachment at all** — not castable onto
anything, not attachable, and so nothing for a person to play by hand either. That last part is what
made it worse than an unread line: D362's bargain is that the card plays as far as it was read and
the rest is flagged, and these were flagged *and* unplayable.

Two rules did it. The first was one line, and the file already disagreed with itself about it: an
Aura whose `Enchanted creature …` line could not be read was refused **whole**, while an Aura whose
unreadable line was a *trigger* attached and flagged it. 382 cards turned on that inconsistency. The
bonus is now taken when it reads and the line left unclaimed when it does not, which is what keeps
its badge. The Equipment half had the same rule plus a worse bug: it *claimed* the line it could not
read, so an Equipment printing "has soaring" equipped, granted nothing, and nothing anywhere said so.

The second was `Enchant creature` matched literally. The corpus prints eleven other phrases and 356
Auras named one — `Enchant land` (82), `Enchant creature you control` (54), `Enchant artifact` (19)
and the rest. They go through `targetSpecFrom` now, so the filters are the ones every other target
phrase uses, and the spec wears the printed phrase as its description.

**`Enchant player` is refused on purpose**, although the spec exists: the engine attaches by writing
`attachedTo` with a **card** id, so an Aura aimed at a seat would resolve and attach to nothing —
"works and does nothing", which no badge covers because all its lines read.

Measured across 1,880 legal attachments afterwards: **0 bonus lines neither expressed nor flagged,
0 unclaimed "Enchanted …" lines picked up as card-wide statics**. Nine break levers, nine failures.

Coverage **18,887 of 56,421 legal lines (33.5%)**, **9,213 cards with a script (+683)** — the largest
single increment so far, and Auras with an attachment went **496 → 1,077**.

## Where else does a card come out unplayable? (D457)

D456 found a type where "read nothing" meant "cannot be played", which is worse than an unread line.
Asked of the whole compiler: **23,246 of 30,710 legal cards compile to no script**, and that is
mostly fine. Driven through a real table: a printed Instant this compiler refuses is still offered as
a play, still spends its mana and still reaches the graveyard; a creature with no script is a vanilla
body that casts, attacks and blocks. The Aura was the exception because attaching is the only way the
card reaches where it belongs — and the audit says it was the only one of its kind.

Of the three whole-card readers, only the attachment read two lines as a unit; the exile-until-leaves
and soulbond readers each claim one line, so an unreadable sibling cannot poison them.

**The modal reader is all-or-nothing and stays so.** 526 legal modal cards, 51 read, **161 one mode
short**. A mode is chosen as the spell is cast (CR 601.2b), so the choice *is* the cast: offering two
of three modes does not give the player an incomplete mechanism, it gives them a different card whose
third mode cannot be taken — the first reading here that would remove a legal choice while looking
automated. An Aura that attaches with no bonus is the opposite: complete mechanism, flagged text. So
those 161 stay castable by hand, and the fix is to read the third mode.

Left as task #331: 11 cards whose every mode reads and which still refuse, because of an unknown
header (`Choose one or more —`, `Choose three. You may choose the same mode more than once.`,
`Choose one or both —`).

## The card table, filled from the corpus already on disk (D458)

`scryfall_cards` — what the card search reads, the recommender joins and a legality check would
consult — had **never held a row on Postgres**. D329 found why: the bulk importer named a column the
table does not have and its catch discarded every raise, and the fixed statement still needs a
Scryfall bulk file this container cannot fetch (all four hosts re-tested, all four still `000`). The
data, though, has been on disk since the corpus was built from `Card-Forge/forge`, which git can
reach.

`scripts/corpus/to-postgres.mjs` is the importer's loop over that file, and
`apps/api/src/corpus-to-postgres.test.ts` executes **its** statement — not a copy — against a
freshly migrated database. That is the whole reason the helpers are exported behind a main guard: the
bug D329 found was a statement nothing had ever run, and a copy of it would have passed on the broken
version too.

**Loaded: 33,847 rows, 32,057 with legalities, 31,615 Commander-legal, 10,754 Pauper-legal.** The id
is `sha1(name)` as a UUID, so the load is idempotent — 33,847 names, 33,847 distinct ids, no
collision — and every row is marked `set_code = 'FORGE'`, which is load-bearing: a real Scryfall
import keys by printing id and would otherwise leave two rows per card, the fan-out D23 and D24 both
found.

`color_identity` is derived because CR 903.4 counts the mana symbols in the text box as well as the
cost, and `colors` does not: **4,334 rows have an identity that differs from their colours, 1,166
have no coloured cost at all and a coloured identity.** Ten columns Forge has no data for are left
null and asserted null — a null price falls through to the `COALESCE(…, 0.15)` the product already
uses, while an invented one is wrong and looks right.

Verified end to end: the card search route's own SQL now returns Lightning Bolt and seven more for
`lightning%`, with cost, type line, derived identity and the price floor. First row that query has
ever returned on Postgres.

**Nothing reads these rows for a pasted deck yet**, and that is task #332. `customDeck`'s `data`
parameter is supplied by no production caller — `deckFromPastedList` passes no rows — so a pasted
name outside the 348-card pool is still cardboard. Its three call sites sit inside a synchronous
compare-and-set write where no query can happen, so the rows have to be fetched before it. That is
the next increment, and it is worth 9,213 scripted cards against 348.

Eight break levers, eight failures. One of them earned a change: breaking the FORGE marking failed
two tests, because the test that deletes the FORGE rows was also cleaning up for the next one — so
the file truncates before each test and the counts are equalities now.

## The pasted deck, read out of the card table (D459)

D458 loaded 33,847 printed cards. **Nothing read them for a pasted deck** — `customDeck`'s `data`
parameter, the one that turns a pasted name into a compiled card, had no caller in the product,
because its three call sites sit inside a synchronous compare-and-set write where no query can
happen. So the corpus, the compiler and 9,213 scripted cards were all behind one missing lookup.

Measured through the real `PodStore`, on a list a person could paste — 35 Forest plus 99 distinct
Commander-legal spells of mana value ≤ 5, drawn from the card table itself
(`scripts/measure/pasted-deck.mjs`):

| | cardboard | cast and played, a line flagged | fully automated |
|---|---|---|---|
| no card table | 97 | 0 | 3 |
| card table | **1** | **79** | **20** |

The 79 are cast for their real cost, do what the compiler read, and badge the line that does nothing
— D362's bargain. Before, they were blanks nobody could cast. The one card still unplayable is
Daxos, Blessed by the Sun, a `2/*` whose toughness is a count nothing read: refused on purpose by
D431, because a 2/0 is binned by CR 704.5f before anybody has priority.

**Nothing is stored.** 150 rows is 60 KB of JSON, so a four-seat pod's lists are 240 KB — written
whole on every move if they lived on the pod record, and doubled by the one step of undo. Printed
card text never changes, so `apps/realtime/src/cardLibrary.ts` caches it in the process: `warm`
fetches, `rowFor` answers synchronously. `DATABASE_URL` is now read by this app and is **optional** —
unset, the table boots, deals and plays, and a pasted name outside the pool is cardboard as before.

The warm lives in `PodStore.mutate`, because a list is read three times inside one mutation — the
ack, the lobby summary, the dealt deck — and they must agree. Two more warms came out of the break
run: `setDeck` warms the names it is about to store (the ack is the reading the player sees), and
`get` warms too, because any node can serve any socket and a player joining somebody else's table
was being told the engine could not read 19 of their cards.

`compileCard` is now memoised, which is what makes any of this affordable: 99 cards cost 14.65 ms to
compile, and the table would have paid that five times a move. Keyed on the **whole row**, never the
name — two rows can share a name with different text, and a name-keyed cache hands back a card with
the wrong rules, which reads perfectly well. Cap 10,000, from the measurement that the whole corpus
cached costs 172 MB against a 768 MB heap. A 100-name paste: 587 ms cold, **11 ms** warm.

Twelve break levers on the wiring, twelve failures — but three only after the test was fixed, and
those are the lesson. A fake library that answered unconditionally had no cache in it, so it modelled
the one case that never happens; `libraryCount` is 59 whether the deck is printed cards or blanks;
and a query count read off `pg_stat_database` could not see negative caching disappear, because those
statistics are snapshotted per transaction. Each is now asserted by consequence instead.

## Four people, four of their own decks (D460)

The beta scenario — four-player Commander, everybody on their own deck — had never been measured.
`corpus-decks.mjs` asked the two-seat version of the question; every pod instrument plays the
thirteen built-in decks. So `POD=1` was added: four seats, the `pod` format, singleton 100-card decks
and a legendary commander each, drawn from the same 28,542-card pool as the spells. The duel arm is
bit-identical after the refactor, checked by diffing a 60-game run against the one before it.

**It found an engine throw on its first run.** 3 of 100 pods died with `X is 0 when a spell is cast
without paying its mana cost` — all three on **Bonfire of the Damned**, miracle `{X}{R}`, cast with
X=7. Two halves of the engine disagreed: `legalActions` offers an X whenever the cost *being paid*
has one, and `autoActions` refused any X on an `offered` cast without asking whether a cost was being
paid. Miracle and madness pay one. In the product that is an `illegal_action` on a button the table
had drawn.

The fix is one condition on the refusal; `payFrom` already charges `action.x` on that path. **The
first attempt was in the wrong place** — suppressing the offer — and the break run rejected it:
reverting that change left every new test green, because a free offer has no X to suppress. All it
did was take the miracle's X away, which turns a Bonfire into a card that looks automated and does
nothing. That is what sent me to instrument the throw rather than reason about it.

`playout.test.ts` already asserts "never offers a play it then refuses". It was green and it is a
real check: the pool's two miracle cards cost `{R}` and `{W}`, so the mechanic and {X} never meet.
**An invariant is only as broad as the decks it is asserted over.**

After the fix: **100 of 100 pods to a finish, no throw, no stall**, 66.5 turns and 352 moves on
average. Per 100-card deck: 20.5 scripted, 52.6 with a flagged line, **0.5 cardboard**.

And a better work queue for the compiler, found on the way — **with the numbers corrected in D461**.
The instrument is right: split each trigger-shaped unread line at the comma and ask the two halves
separately, because `one-line-short.mjs`'s top row ("199 cards: Whenever ~ deals combat damage to a")
names a trigger the compiler reads fine. The first probe was not: it tested each effect as the text
of a sorcery under *its own* name, so every self-referential effect read as unreadable. It reported
387 cards short a prologue and 5,535 short an effect, and named the self-subject effect as the
biggest cluster; re-measured under the card's own name it is **690 short a prologue** and **3,509
short an effect**, and the self-subject effect was never missing at all.

## A probe that could not see a self-referential effect (D461)

D460 chose the next increment off a probe that tested each effect half as the text of **a sorcery
under a different name**. Every self prologue and every self-subject effect in this compiler is
written against the card's own name, so that probe read none of them and filed every self-subject
effect as "the effect is the gap". It was never the gap: `Whenever ~ attacks, ~ gets +1/+1 until end
of turn` and `put a +1/+1 counter on ~` have read all along. Corrected split: **690 cards short a
prologue, 3,509 short an effect** (D460 said 387 and 5,535).

The lesson is sharper than "check the probe": a probe that normalises a card's name away cannot see
anything a card says about itself, which in Magic is a large share of all printed text.

From the corrected ranking, two rows shipped — the largest clean prologue families:

- **`When ~ is put into a graveyard from the battlefield`** (27 cards). "Dies" is defined for
  creatures only (CR 700.4), so a noncreature permanent spells the zone change out: Brilliant Halo,
  Audacity, Chromatic Star. `who: 'self'` written out, because this event defaults to `another`.
- **`Whenever ~ becomes the target of a spell or ability`** (8 cards), `by: 'any'` written out
  because the event defaults to `opponent` — a default that is right for ward and nothing else.

That second row needed an engine change. `raiseWard`, now `raiseTargeted`, skipped the controller's
own permanents: one caller's rule written into the engine, when `triggerMatches` already enforces it
from the trigger's side. So a card printing the sentence with nobody named had a trigger the event
never reached — automated-looking and doing nothing, which is the one outcome D362 ranks below an
unread line.

Coverage **9,221 cards with a script (+8), 5,042 fully read (+22), 18,918 of 56,421 lines (33.5%)**.
Small, which is what a prologue row is worth when the effects behind it already read.

**Three families refused with their counts**, all of the block family: "becomes blocked" (52) wants a
batched event, because the engine's fires once per blocker and the printed line fires once;
"blocks or becomes blocked by …" (38) filters the other creature and the event cannot; "blocks" (15)
and "becomes blocked by a creature" (12) say "that creature" meaning the *other* one, which the clause
vocabulary reads as the card itself.

Five break levers, five failures.

A 60-pod run on a fresh seed set after the engine change: **59 finished, 1 unfinished** (seed 30002,
which ran out of the 20,000-move bound rather than breaking), no throw and no stall. Not attributable
to this change — the seeds had never been run and nothing here touches combat, priority or the stack
— and left as task #334, because a pod that cannot finish is the same thing to two people at a table
as a pod that stalls.

> **Corrected by D462:** seed 30002 could not end at all, and that also makes D461's aside wrong —
> the 60-pod set reads **60/60 at 397 moves a game** on the fixed engine, not the 747 D461 quoted.
> That average was the one looping game, reported as grindier decks.

## The pod that could not end (D462)

Task #334, the one pod of sixty D461 left open. Seed 30002 spent all 20,000 moves and reported
`unfinished` — a word that covers two different things, a game that needs more moves and a game that
cannot end, which is why the first move was an instrument rather than a fix.

A `TRACE` arm on `corpus-decks.mjs` prints, every n moves, the turn and step, each seat's life, hand,
battlefield and library, and the commonest action and card. Between move 1,000 and move 12,000 of
seed 30002 **nothing in that line changed**: turn 44, postcombat main, same life totals, same zones,
and `auto:activate` climbing by a thousand each thousand moves — `Umbral Mantle#0 → Air-Cult
Elemental` and `→ Hotshot Mechanic`, in alternation.

**Umbral Mantle** is a real card printed `Equip {0}`. Both creatures were tapped from attacking, and
the bot's `equipMovesSideways` rule read the **host's** tapped state as a reason to move the
Equipment without ever asking the same question of the creature it was moving *to*. Two loops, not
one: tapped onto tapped, where both directions read as fair; and untapped onto a bigger tapped
creature, where the power test sends it across and the tapped-host clause sends it back. A free equip
cost makes either free.

The fix is an ordering — the target's tapped state first and on its own, because a bonus on a tapped
creature buys nothing this turn, and only then is a tapped host a reason to move.

**Why nothing in the project caught it**, which is the part that will matter again: the engine never
threw, because every one of those equips is legal; the stall detector compares consecutive state
versions and an equip bumps one every time; and `playout.test.ts`' standing "never offers a play it
then refuses" invariant was green, because this play is offered *and* taken. Only the move cap
noticed, and a move cap cannot say which of its two meanings applies.

So `corpus-decks.mjs` now answers that itself: it fingerprints what a player would call progress
every move — turn, step, each seat's life and poison, the size of each of their five zones — and
reports **`looping`**, naming the action and the card that filled the window, after `LOOP` (2,000)
moves that move none of it. A different word for a different bug.

The loop *class* is still open and is now task #335: any free activated ability the evaluation scores
at zero can do this, and the seventeen-member "spent on nothing" family answers it one card at a
time. The structural answer — a seat does not take an action that returns it to a position it has
already been at in this step — is its own increment, because it has to be hashed cheaply, must not
catch a Gelectrode pinging twice, and has to be priced per decision.


**Verified**: gate green (rules-engine 2,251, apps/api 325, apps/web 246, apps/realtime 59). Two
break levers against a baseline verified green first, two failures. Seed 30002 finishes on turn 62 in
347 moves. 60 duels 60/60 (20.8 turns, 66 moves — unmoved by the fix). The 60-pod set that held the
failure: **60/60, 69.4 turns, 397 moves** — and that last number corrects D461's 747, which was one
looping game dragging the average; a real four-player pod costs about four hundred moves. A 100-pod
set reads **99/100: 99 finished, 1 threw** — seed 30072 on `the engine cannot divide an activated
ability yet`, which is D460's invariant again in a different place and not a regression from this
change (30000–30059 is 60/60; 30060–30099 had never been run). Three corpus cards carry a divided
activated ability — Mogg Mob, Ral, Caller of Storms and Samut, the Tested — and it is task **#336**.

## The ability the engine offered and then refused (D463)

Seed 30072 of the 100-pod sweep threw on `the engine cannot divide an activated ability yet`. That
refusal was written on a premise its own comment stated — "no ability in the pool divides anything" —
and the corpus has three such cards: **Mogg Mob**, and the -2 of **Ral, Caller of Storms** and
**Samut, the Tested**.

It is **D460's invariant again**: `legalActions` offers the ability, `autoActions` refuses the action
built from it, and `playout.test.ts`' "never offers a play it then refuses" is green because no
built-in deck holds one. Twice in one session, so the lesson is about the assertion rather than the
cards: it is only as broad as the decks it runs on.

Three cards is a line in the compiler, not a feature in the engine, so the ability is no longer
emitted and the line is flagged — unread beats offered-then-refused (D362). Spells keep division,
which the engine implements (#119), pinned by a test on Arc Lightning.

**The half-fix is the part worth remembering.** The first version guarded one assembly site and the
card I checked by hand was correct; the **coverage count** came back one card lower where three were
expected, and that was the whole signal. The compiler builds an activated ability in two places and
the planeswalker loyalty branch is the second, so Ral and Samut were still emitting it. Both go
through one predicate now. A count that moves by the wrong amount is a test.

**Verified**: gate green (engine 2,255, api 325, web 246, realtime 59); two break levers, two
discriminating failures, the spell test green in both; seed 30072 finishes on turn 66 in 270 moves;
coverage 9,221 → **9,219** cards and 18,918 → **18,916** of 56,421 lines (33.5%), which is the price
of the fix and is named rather than rounded away.

## A hundred pods, and the rule that was not written (D464)

`LEGAL=1 POD=1 GAMES=100 SEED0=30000` on the D463 build: **100/100 finished**, no throw, no stall, no
`looping`, 70.6 turns and 408 moves a game. That closes #334 and #336, and it is the first time a
hundred four-player pods of arbitrary real decks have every one reached a finish.

The loop class (#335) is closed too — **by counting rather than by code**. The structural rule was
designed, started and reverted, because `scripts/measure/free-abilities.mjs` answered the question it
depended on: a loop needs a **free repeatable** ability, and over 31,654 legal cards there are
**176**, all covered. 172 are `Crew N` (answered by the crew rules, and self-limiting because crewing
taps creatures); 4 are Equipment with a free equip (answered by `equipMovesSideways` since D462). A
guard with no failing case is a reader written ahead of need, and its break run cannot fail.

**And the cross-check was the thing that was wrong.** An inline probe read 187 against the
instrument's 176; dumping both lists and diffing them named the eleven extras as un-cards — the probe
had skipped the legality filter. A disagreement between two counts says one is wrong, not which, and
one diff settled it where more reasoning would have produced a better-argued wrong answer.

## The reader worth 63 cards was worth 0, and the bounce you choose (D465)

**The retraction first.** D464 named the next increment and measured it: `you may X. If you do, Y`,
63 legal cards, from `may-halves.mjs`. Wrong. That instrument substituted the construct's **prologue**
and its **consequence** and never substituted **X**, the opener — and X reads for **0 of the 63**.
`discard a card`, `sacrifice another creature`, `exile it`, `pay 2 life`: the clause vocabulary has no
reader for any of them, as an opener or as a plain effect. The yield of that reader alone is zero.

That is the **third** wrong answer taken off `one-line-short.mjs`' ranking (after D461's prologue row
and a clause-splitting probe that returned 1,241 artefacts), and three is a method problem: **a probe
that reconstructs part of a line measures the reconstruction.**

`scripts/measure/phrase-gap.mjs` is the method that survives — leave the line as printed, replace one
phrase with an effect known to read, ask the compiler whether the **whole line** now reads. Its top
rows over 31,654 legal cards: `return <permanent> to its owner's hand` **128**, `put a counter on
<permanent>` 94, `sacrifice <permanent>` 81, `you may X. If you do, Y` 66, `discard a card` 55. The
cost-like actions together finish 158, and with the conditional on top, 234 — so the conditional is
the **roof** on an increment, not an increment.

**What shipped** is the top row: a bounce the controller *chooses*. `targetedEffect` has read `return
target <permanent>…` since D366; the commoner printing targets nothing and the controller picks
something of their own as the ability **resolves** — `CardsDecisionSpec` with `from: 'battlefield'`,
which `DecisionZone` already scopes to the chooser's own side, so "you control" is enforced by the
zone. **45 cards**, twelve of them lands (the whole Karoo cycle), plus Kor Skyfisher, Whitemane Lion,
Roaring Primadox, Esperzoa, Denizen of the Deep.

`min: 1` is not a suggestion — Kor Skyfisher with nothing else on your board returns **itself**, and
"another" excludes the source where the card prints the word. That one qualifier needs the source,
which `CardsDecisionSpec.filter` is not handed, so those spellings are the thunk form of
`DecisionSpecOf`. **Named cost:** the bare-`may` reader refuses a spec that is a function, so
`you may return another permanent you control…` stays unread — four cards, filed as #337 with a test
pinning the refusal, rather than bought with a guess.

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,219 | **9,264** |
| cards fully read | 5,041 | **5,086** |
| printed rules lines read | 18,916 / 56,421 (33.5%) | **18,975 / 56,421 (33.6%)** |

Engine suite 2,262 green. Six levers broken one at a time, each failing exactly one test.

## The card that picks itself up (D466)

The other half of D465's family: the same sentence pointed at the card printing it rather than at
something the controller chooses. **About 38 legal cards**, and two kinds of card print it that want
**opposite guards** — `{1}{U}: Return Fleeting Image to its owner's hand` is activated from the
battlefield, and `When Brilliant Halo is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, return Brilliant
Halo to its owner's hand` fires from the graveyard.

CR 400.7 decides it: an ability naming an object that has changed zones does nothing. So a battlefield
self-bounce resolving after its permanent died must **not** pull the card back out of the graveyard,
and a graveyard one must. A guard of "battlefield or graveyard" reads both cards with one rule and is
wrong about the first in exactly the case the rule is for.

The engine does not record where an ability's source was when it went on the stack — but the compiler
knows, because every caller of `composeEffects` knows which trigger shape or ability it is assembling.
So a `SubjectZone | null` is threaded through `composeEffects` → `readEffect` → `selfEffect`, read off
the **event** for a trigger (`dies` and `to-graveyard` → graveyard; `leaves` and `to-exile` → `null`;
the rest → battlefield), `battlefield` for an ability, and `null` for a spell, which leaves the line
unread.

**The break run earned its keep again.** Five levers; four failed a test immediately. The fifth —
answering `graveyard` for every trigger shape — passed everything, because no test covered a *trigger*
whose subject is on the battlefield. Glitterfang is one, it has a test now, and the lever fails.

| | D465 | D466 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,264 | **9,291** |
| cards fully read | 5,086 | **5,126** |
| printed rules lines read | 18,975 / 56,421 (33.6%) | **19,053 / 56,421 (33.8%)** |

Engine suite 2,267 green.

## A guard measured and thrown away (D467)

Not an increment — a refutation worth not re-deriving. Reading `composeEffects` before building the
discard reader, it looked unsafe for two question-asking parts: it concatenates their `decisions`
without offsetting the answers, and a part reads its own by index. So I wrote the guard that refuses
such a composition, and predicted it would cost nothing.

It cost **two cards** — 9,291 → 9,289 — and diffing the per-card verdicts named them: **Cryptic
Annelid** (`scry 1, then scry 2, then scry 3`) and **Fill with Fright** (`Target player discards two
cards. Scry 2.`). Both work today, because a scry's effect is the *identity*: the engine applies a
`library-top` answer to its own plan entry, so nothing indexes anything. The guard deleted two
correct readings and prevented nothing. Reverted.

The hazard is real only where two parts **both** read answers by index, and no corpus card prints
one. Build the reader, then verify a composition at a real table; fix it when there is a card that
fails. Reading code and finding a hole is a hypothesis, and the cheapest test of this one was three
commands.

## The discard, and D467's guard got right (D468)

The largest concentrated family left: measured by substitution, the discard appears on 795
one-line-short cards and **finishes 114** — more than D465 and D466 split between them. Read: the
controller's discard of N cards or their hand, `each player` and `each opponent`, and the `at random`
form of each. Every one is a **question** (`from: 'hand'`), because the discarding player chooses —
`discardAtRandom` is reached only where the words say so, or the compiler would build Ravenous Rats
and call it Mind Rot.

Left out with reasons: `target opponent discards` (no "target opponent" spec exists at all — one spec
lifts the discard, the life loss and the mill together, so it is its own increment), `that player
discards` (needs a `who: 'actor'` the decision machinery has not got), and `discard a creature card`
(finishes nothing — it is a `you may … If you do` opener).

**D467's guard was needed after all, and was the wrong shape.** That entry recorded the hazard —
`composeEffects` concatenates answers, a part reads its own by index — and then refuted it, because
the guard cost two working cards. The hazard is real and this increment made it reachable: Greedy
Rummage (`Draw two cards, then discard two cards. Target player discards a card.`) was already in
`compile.test.ts`, and the full suite caught it on the first run after the reader went in. Both
discards read index 0, so the target player discards nothing.

The right guard is *at most one part that reads answers*, told apart by `appliesNothing` — a scry asks
and reads nothing, because the engine applies a `library-top` answer to its own plan entry. Coverage
unchanged to the line, Greedy Rummage refused, the two scry cards kept.

The method note: D467 consulted the corpus and concluded there was no failing case. The suite's own
fixtures are printed text too, and one of them was it.

| cards with a compiled script | 9,291 | **9,423** |
| cards fully read | 5,126 | **5,214** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,053 / 56,421 (33.8%) | **19,216 / 56,421 (34.1%)** |

## A printed target phrase, parsed rather than enumerated (D469)

The largest family the compiler has had in front of it: target phrases appear on **5,978**
one-line-short cards and substituting one known to read finishes **299**. `targetSpecFrom` is the
single door every targeted reader goes through, so one phrase read there lifts damage, destroy, exile,
bounce, the counters and the discard's `target opponent` form at once.

It also reframed the row above it: `put a counter on <permanent>` finishes 103 cards but over thirty-odd
shapes with the biggest at **4**, and `put a +1/+1 counter on target creature` appears on 47 and
finishes **1**. Never a counter problem — this one wearing a counter costume.

The switch of thirty exact phrases could not grow to cover it, because the phrases are combinatorial.
**The machinery was already there**, checked rather than assumed: `TargetSpec.count` and `optional`
meant the quantifiers (`up to one`, `up to one other`, `each of up to two`, `two`) needed no engine
change, and `permanentFilter` gained colours and negations, tapped/untapped, attacking, blocking,
legendary, basic and a keyword — all read **live** (CR 109.2) except `basic`, which is a supertype and
goes through the `isBasicLand` Rampant Growth has used since #28.

Refusing is the default (D362: a wrong target is a removal spell pointed at the wrong permanent).
Subtypes, "defending player controls" and "that was dealt damage this turn" stay unread with reasons.

Two things worth keeping from the build. **The caller regexes were anchored on the word `target`**, so
the parser never saw a quantifier; five readers now share a prefix built from the quantifier table's own
keys, and the first version of it gave its trailing space to the last alternative only — `two target
creatures` read, `another target creature` did not. And **the Aura reader had been asking this function
what its host could be**, so the parser widened Aura hosts as a side effect and broke two rows of a
refusal table on the first full-suite run. The Aura's vocabulary is now the switch only, stated as an
argument; keeping that refusal cost 26 cards with a script and one fully read, measured.

| | D468 | D469 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,423 | **9,657** |
| cards fully read | 5,214 | **5,436** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,216 / 56,421 (34.1%) | **19,557 / 56,421 (34.7%)** |

Engine suite 2,278 green. Seven levers broken one at a time — and two failed nothing at first, because
the test leant on a phrase the switch answers rather than the parser.

## D470 — Every target the phrase asked for, not the first: a wrong reading D469 shipped

D469 went out at `d1e9680`. Twenty minutes later, re-measuring its own queue, I read the five
