readers it had widened and found that all five end the same way:

```ts
effect: (c) => {
  const id = firstCardTarget(c);
  return id === null ? c.state : destroy(c.state, id);
},
```

`firstCardTarget` is the correct reader while every spec's `count` is one. D469 made that false in
the same commit that relied on it: giving destroy, exile, return-to-hand, untap and counter
`TARGET_QUANTIFIER_PREFIX` let `Destroy two target creatures` compile, so the engine asked the
player to point at two creatures — and the effect killed one.

### Why this is worse than the unread line it replaced

D362's rule is that a line left unread is **badged**, and a human resolves it by hand. D259's is
that inventing a card's text is worse than leaving a mechanic out. A half-read line fails both at
once: the card reports itself fully automated, the player is asked for two targets, one of them is
quietly ignored, and nothing anywhere says so. Before D469 those cards were badged and played
correctly by a person. After it they were silently wrong.

### 18 cards over six families, and the method that found them

Nothing in the repository could have caught this. The engine suite's fixtures are built-in pool
cards and none prints a counted target phrase; the pod sweep plays the thirteen built-in decks. These
are real printings in no built-in deck — the population the compiler exists for, and the only one
neither harness plays. It was found by reading the code the increment had just changed, which is not
a method that scales and is the reason the lever below exists.

Measured over the 31,654 legal rows: **28 cards compile a script asking for more than one target.**
Ten of them are correct by another path — the seven damage-**divided** cards (Arc Lightning,
Electrolyze, Forked Bolt, Twin Bolt, Chandra's Pyrohelix, Flames of the Firebrand, Gang of Devils),
which split one budget between the targets through `dividedAmong` (CR 601.2d), and the three
`Untap two target lands` cards (Argothian Elder, Ley Weaver, Garruk Wildspeaker), read by
`untappedMany`, which has folded over `cardTargets` since the counted untap was written.

The other **18 were resolving one target of two or three**:

- **destroy and exile** (14) — Armaggon Future Shark, Barrier Breach, Curtains' Call, Dust to Dust,
  Into the Core, Numot the Devastator, Peace and Quiet, Petradon, Rack and Ruin, Rain of Salt,
  Reckless Spite, Ulamog the Ceaseless Hunger, Violent Ultimatum, Wicked Pact.
- **untap** (2) — Garruk Curse Breaker and Tezzeret the Seeker, whose `up to two` `untappedMany`
  cannot match: its count is `[\w]+` and `up to two` is three words, so they fall to the open-phrase
  reader.
- **damage** (2) — **a sixth family, and D469 had widened it too.** `Dual Shot` and `Fire Shrine
  Keeper` print "deals N damage to each of up to two target creatures"; `each of up to two` is a
  quantifier `parsedTargetPhrase` accepts, and `damageFirstTarget` dealt the damage to one of them.
  Found by asking which *other* reader takes an open phrase rather than a fixed sentence — the
  question the first five made worth asking again, and the one D469 should have asked.
  `damageEveryTarget` repeats the full amount on each target, which is what "to each of" says and
  why it cannot share an effect with `dividedAmong`. Both of the compiler's damage readers (the
  printed number and the X) now use it; the hand-written cards keep `damageFirstTarget`, which is
  correct for a spec whose count is one.

### The fix, and the one place it is not shared

`foldCardTargets(c, each)` reduces `each` over every card target, which is `untappedMany`'s fold
lifted out so the families share one spelling of it. Four readers use it. Two do not: the **counter**
reader folds inline, because an ability on the stack is an `ability` target and `cardTargets` keeps
only cards, and the **damage** readers use `damageEveryTarget`, because a damage spec can be `any
target` and a player is a legal one.

**The fold is only safe because `composeEffects` refuses a second targeting clause.** `c.targets` is
one list per script, so if two clauses could each point at something, folding destroy over the list
would destroy the other clause's target too. That invariant is written down where it is enforced —
"two target choices cannot share one `targets` list" — and it is what makes "every target in the
list" the same thing as "every target this clause asked for".

It is written `(state, id) => each(state, id)` rather than handing `each` to `reduce`, because
`reduce` passes an index and the array as third and fourth arguments and an effect primitive taking
an options object third would silently be handed a number.

### Which families a real card can actually reach, taken off the corpus

- **destroy** and **exile** — reachable, and the two tests below resolve them (`Curtains' Call`,
  `Into the Core`).
- **untap** — `Join Forces` and `Synchronized Strike` print `Untap up to two target creatures`,
  which reads on its own, but their lines continue `They each get +2/+2 until end of turn`, which
  does not, so the whole line is unread. The two planeswalkers above reach it.
- **counter** — `Double Negative` ("Counter up to two target spells") is the only printing and it
  does not read: the plural stack noun is not in the vocabulary.
- **bounce** — unreachable by construction. The reader's phrase ends `to its owner's hand`; all 38
  multi-target printings in the corpus say `to their owners' hands` or `to their owner's hand`. The
  fold is still written, because a regex is a weaker guarantee than an effect that is right whatever
  it is handed.

### The lever

Two resolution tests on real printings through `customDeck`, asserted via `built.fromData` (D430):
`Curtains' Call` must put **both** creatures in the graveyard, `Into the Core` must exile **both**
artifacts and put neither in a graveyard (CR 701.19a), and `Dual Shot` must kill **both** 1/1s. Break
run: restoring the shipped `firstCardTarget` reading fails each of the three in turn and leaves the
fourth (the spec-level record of what each family accepts) green, which is the right shape — the
defect was never about reading.

Coverage is unchanged, and re-measured rather than asserted: **9,657** cards with a script, **5,436**
fully read, **19,557 of 56,421** printed lines (34.7%) — the same three figures D469 printed, because
this increment changes what a read line *does*, not how many read. Engine suite **2,282** green
(2,278 + the four tests here).

### What this says about the practice

The D468 guard, the D469 Aura refusal and this are three in a row where a reader's reach was wider
than the lines it was written for, and the first two were caught by the full suite. This one was not,
because the suite cannot see cards that are not in a deck. The standing lesson: when an increment
widens what a reader **accepts**, re-read every effect downstream of it in the same pass — the
acceptance and the resolution are two edits, and D469 made only one of them. The sixth family is the
proof that the lesson is not rhetorical: five readers were fixed, and asking the same question once
more found a sixth that the increment had also widened and nobody had listed.

## D471 — A sacrifice the controller chooses, and a measured row that was three readers

The `sacrifice <permanent>` row has sat near the top of the queue since D469 at **81 cards one
unread line from a finished script**. It is not one reader, and finding that out before building was
the whole of the planning.

### The row, classified

Dumped the 81 and read them. Three families share the identical phrase:

| | cards | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sacrifice it unless you <cost>` | **44** | a demanded price with a consequence — echo's shape (#196) |
| `Whenever you sacrifice a <thing>,` | **19** | a *trigger event* this engine does not raise |
| `sacrifice a <permanent>` | **16** | the effect: the print instructs, the controller picks |
| `sacrifice all <permanents> you control` | 2 | the same effect with nothing to choose |

Reading the row as one phrase would have bought a third of what the number promised. This increment
is the third family and the sweep — the only two that are an *effect* — and the other two are now
scoped with their own hazards named:

- The **44** need a cost vocabulary before they can be read at all: the Karoo lands' bounce
  (17 of them), a discard (10), a mana payment (4), a second sacrifice (8), a tap (2). Measured
  which of those already read as effects: the bounce reads for `another creature`/`an artifact` but
  **not** for `an untapped Island`, `a non-Lair land` or `two Forests`; the discard reads for
  `a card`/`at random`/`two cards` but not for `a land card`. So that increment is a qualifier pass
  and then the construct.
- The **19** are an event (`Whenever you sacrifice …`), and every one of their payoffs already
  reads. That makes it a trigger-kind increment, not a clause one.

### The reader

`sacrifice (a|an|another|two|three|up to two|up to three) <permanent>` is a `CardsDecisionSpec` on
the controller's own battlefield — the same shape as D465's chosen bounce, and for the same reason:
nothing is targeted, the pick happens as the ability resolves, and `from: 'battlefield'` already
means the chooser's own side, so CR 701.17a ("a player can only sacrifice a permanent they control")
needs no filter that could disagree with the zone.

Mandatory, with the bounds clamped by `decisionBounds`: **Accursed Centaur with no other creature
eats itself**, a board with none does nothing (CR 608.2 — as much as it can), and a board with
exactly one answers without putting a one-button prompt on anybody's screen.

`sacrifice a creature other than <this card>` is read as `another` wearing the card's own name
(Demonic Taskmaster), and only when the name is this card's: "other than" naming anything else is a
restriction this reader cannot express, so it refuses. `BOUNCE_COUNTS` and `permanentDescribed` are
both reused rather than copied (D441, D438, D465).

**Subtypes are refused**, for the reason D469 refuses one in a target phrase: `permanentDescribed`
is handed a phrase already lower-cased for the prompt's sake, so "a Forest" and "a non-Zombie
creature" cannot be told from a word. Fifteen printed sacrifices name one; they stay unread and
badged rather than read as "any land", which would have Rogue Elephant eat a Mountain.

### What the standing check caught, which is worth more than the increment

`compiled-vs-written.test.ts` went red on **Woe Strider**, a card this change does not mention.

The deck list printed its ability as `{0}: Sacrifice another creature. Scry 1.` The real card says
**`Sacrifice another creature: Scry 1.`** — the sacrifice is the cost, before the colon, exactly how
Bloodthrone Vampire and Izoni are written two hundred lines away in the same file. The script was
always right (`cost: { sacrifice: 'another-creature' }`); the text beside it was a paraphrase nobody
had compared to the printing.

It was harmless until this increment, and then it was not: a chosen sacrifice read as an **effect**
turned the paraphrase into a free, repeatable `{0}` ability that scries whether or not there is a
creature to eat. A different and much better card, compiled out of a typo.

Fixed by correcting the pool's text. The two readings then agree except for an identity `effect` the
hand-written ability carried and the compiled reading does not emit (a scry's work is applying its
own answer, D467), so that field is deleted rather than listed in `DISAGREE` — the same disposal
D419 and D420 gave the same shape of difference. Third defect that check has found in a text nobody
was reading.

### The numbers

| | D470 | D471 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,657 | **9,675** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,436 | **5,449** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,557 of 56,421 (34.7%) | **19,583 of 56,421 (34.7%)** |

+13 fully read against a ceiling of 16 for the family, with the subtype spellings deliberately out.
Engine suite **2,288** green (2,282 + the six tests here).

Three levers broken one at a time on a green baseline, each failing exactly one test: the noun
filter (a land sacrifice stops offering lands), the source exclusion ("other than" stops excluding
the card), and the sweep (`all` takes only the first).

## D472 — `you may X. If you do, Y`, read as what it means

The third row of the queue, and the one that had to be measured three times before it could be
built.

### Why the 77 was never the number

`phrase-gap.mjs` prices this construct at **77 cards** by substituting the whole thing with **Y** —
"you may sacrifice a creature. If you do, draw a card" becomes "draw a card" — and says in its own
docblock that the figure is a ceiling, not a reading, because a reader has to refuse Y when X was
not performed (CR 608.2). Before that, `may-halves.mjs` reported **63** and had to retract it
(D465): it measured halves that are not what a reader would build.

So this increment got its own instrument, `may-if-you-do.mjs`, which asks what a reader can actually
answer. For every legal card one unread line short whose line is this construct — **472 of them** —
it compiles each half on its own under a prologue known to read, and counts **how many questions
each half asks**.

That last column is the whole design, because of one property of the engine's gate.
`askOnlyIfChosen` holds a question back on an **option word** that was chosen (D450). Nothing holds
a question back on "an earlier card answer came back non-empty". So:

| | cards | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| X asks nothing (Y may ask) | **13** | "if you do" *is* "you said yes", so Y's questions ride the same gate |
| X asks once, Y asks nothing | **18** | "if you do" is "that answer named something", read by the effect |
| X asks once, Y asks too | 5 | Y's question cannot be gated on X's answer — refused |
| X asks more than once | 0 | nothing prints it |
| **X unread** | **402** | the opener is a clause this compiler cannot read at all |
| Y unread | 34 | the consequence is |

**The 402 is the real finding.** The construct was never the blocker for most of this family — the
*opener* is, and the openers are a vocabulary of their own: `exile it`, `pay N life`, `reveal it`,
`look at the top card`, `put a card from your hand onto the battlefield`. Reading the construct
finishes the cards whose halves already read, and names the next piece of work precisely rather
than leaving 77 looking like one reader's yield.

### The reading

`sequence` composes the two halves into one `ReadEffect` that the existing "may" wrapper gates
without knowing there are two of them — so the yes-or-no, the prompt, the answer-index shift
(`withoutOurs`) and the `gatable` refusal are all unchanged from D448/D450. X runs through
`immediate` where it has one, for the reason `composeEffects` does on a non-final clause: a deferred
draw cannot be read by anything after it (D387).

"If you do" is then one line:

```ts
const did = xAsks === 0 || chosenCards(c).length > 0;
return did ? y.effect({ ...c, state: after }) : after;
```

Refused rather than guessed: both halves asking, either half pointing at a target (a target is
chosen on the stack, before anybody has said yes — a different machine, D465), and a half that does
not read.

### What the lever proves

`Discerning Peddler` ("When Discerning Peddler enters, you may discard a card. If you do, draw a
card.") through `customDeck`, three resolutions: taken with a card to pitch (discard then draw),
declined (nothing moves), and **taken with an empty hand** — where the discard is clamped to nothing
by `decisionBounds`, so "if you do" is false and no card is drawn. That third case is the one the
ceiling could not price and the one a reader that treated the yes as the condition would get wrong,
handing the player a free card.

The test had to make the hand *exactly* what it says: `advanceTo` walks the draw step, so the seat
holds one more card than `arena` placed, and the empty-hand case would have been quietly untrue.

Three levers broken one at a time, each failing exactly one test: `did` forced true, the
both-halves-ask refusal, and the target refusal.

### The numbers

| | D471 | D472 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,675 | **9,712** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,449 | **5,471** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,583 of 56,421 (34.7%) | **19,629 of 56,421 (34.8%)** |

Engine suite **2,292** green (2,288 + the four tests here).

+22 fully read.

> **The 402 figure above is retracted (D473), and so is the sentence calling it "the real finding".**
> The instrument compiled each half as a bare clause, and `pay {2}` is not a clause this compiler
> reads or needs to — the construct's own reader has read it since D448. So 146 of those 402 were
> mana and energy payments whose openers were never the problem. Re-measured by substitution in
> place, **no** card in this family is held up by its opener or its consequence alone: 47 are
> finished by either half and 425 are held up by the **line around the construct**, overwhelmingly a
> trigger prologue the compiler cannot read. The read of the engine's gate, the reader this
> increment shipped and the +22 are unaffected; the queue it pointed at was wrong. See D473.

## D473 — The 402 was my instrument's artefact, and the real blocker is the prologue

D472's entry quoted its own instrument's biggest number as "the real finding": **402 of 472** cards
in the `you may X. If you do, Y` family held up by the **opener**. That is wrong, and it was wrong
within the hour, found by grouping the bucket I had just published instead of taking its headline.

### What the instrument did

`may-if-you-do.mjs` compiled each half **as a bare clause** under a probe prologue —
`When ~ enters, pay {2}.` — and counted the halves that came back unread. But `pay {2}` is not a
clause this compiler reads and does not need to be: it is read by the **construct's own** reader and
has been since D448. The top two groups of the 402 were `pay {M}` (99) and `pay {M}{M}` (47), so
**146 of them were payments whose openers were never the problem.**

That is the **third** time this family has been mismeasured by asking about a half in a position the
half never appears in. `may-halves.mjs` reported 63 and retracted it (D465); the first clause-level
probe produced 1,241 "several clauses" and 13,006 "prologue gap", both artefacts; and now this. The
method that survives all three is the one `phrase-gap.mjs` settled on and that I did not apply here:
**substitution in place** — leave the printed line as it is, replace one half with something known to
read *in that position*, and ask whether the whole line reads.

### The corrected attribution

The instrument now substitutes in place: X with `pay {1}`, Y with `draw a card`, each on the card's
own printed line. Over the same 472 cards:

| | cards |
| --- | --- |
| the opener alone | **0** |
| the consequence alone | **0** |
| either half alone finishes it | **47** |
| the **line around them** | **425** |

So nothing in this family is waiting on an opener or a consequence. What holds 425 cards up is the
frame, and grouping that bucket says what the frame is:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 49 | `At the beginning of …` prologues the compiler does not read |
| 46 | another clause before the construct on the same line |
| 26 | `Whenever you cast …` |
| 23 | `Whenever a player …` |
| 15 | no prologue at all — a spell, where `you may` has no reader |
| 14 | `Whenever a creature …` |
| 12 | `Kinship —` |
| 7 each | `Inspired —`, `Whenever this creature …` |
| the rest | 50-odd prologue shapes with 3 to 6 cards each |

**The next increment is the trigger prologue vocabulary**, not an opener and not the construct. That
is a different piece of work from everything in D465-D472, which were all about what a clause *does*;
this is about the event a line fires on.

### What this does not change

The reader D472 shipped, its tests, its break runs and its **+22 fully read** all stand — they were
measured by `compilable.mjs` against real cards, not by the instrument that was wrong. What was wrong
is the queue the entry pointed at, which is exactly the kind of error that compounds: the next
increment would have been spent on an opener vocabulary that finishes nothing.

Also dropped: the `grantedTriggers` exemption the first version of the instrument needed in
`scripts/guards.js`. The rewrite reads no triggers at all, so the exemption was a dead entry
describing a file that no longer does the thing — two statements of one rule, which this project
keeps removing (D441, D438).

## D474 — The cast prologue, parsed: one row for a family of eight

D473 said the next increment was the trigger prologue vocabulary, and `prologue-gap.mjs` says which
part of it. Over the legal corpus, **736** cards one unread line from a finished script are finished
by a prologue reader at all, and **168 of them print a cast prologue** — the largest family in the
ranking by a factor of four over the next shape (38).

The eight rows that stood in `TRIGGER_SHAPES` read five of the sentences somebody had measured and
none of the forty-odd the corpus prints. So the cast family is now a **parse**, which is the move
D469 made one level down on target phrases: who cast it, times what kind of spell, times whether a
copy counts.

| printed | read as |
| --- | --- |
| a spell | `spell: 'any'` |
| a creature spell / a noncreature spell | `spell` |
| an instant or sorcery spell | `spell: 'instant-or-sorcery'` |
| an artifact spell / an enchantment spell | `ofType` |
| a white spell / a blue or black spell | `ofColours`, any-of |
| a multicolored spell | `multicoloured` |
| a Spirit or Arcane spell / a Goblin spell | `ofSubtypes`, any-of |
| …with mana value N or less / or greater | `manaValueAtMost` / `manaValueAtLeast` |
| cast **or copy** | `how: 'any'` |

times `you` / `a player` / `an opponent`.

### The engine half: three facts the cast event did not carry

`spell-cast` already had `by`, `spell`, `ofType`, `self`, `how` and `onNth`. It now also carries the
spell's **colours**, its **mana value as cast** and its **subtypes**, each recorded where the event is
raised rather than looked up later — by the time a trigger resolves the object may be gone, and an
{X} spell's mana value counts the X it was cast for (CR 202.3b). Three raise sites had to agree: an
ordinary cast, a **morph** (colourless, mana value 0, no subtypes — CR 708.2, so a Kamigawa Spirit
cast face down does not fire a Spirit trigger), and a **copy** (the copied card's characteristics,
CR 707.2), which also widened `CopiedSpell`.

### Two refusals came off, and one of them was wrong rather than early

"A multicolored spell" was refused twice — D435 and D440 — on the stated ground that it is "a fact
about the mana cost" and therefore not expressible. **That was wrong.** CR 105.1 makes multicoloured
a fact about the card's *colours*, which this engine has always computed; the field was missing, not
the mechanism. It reads now, and the two docblocks and the test that carried the wrong reason have
been corrected rather than quietly edited. "An opponent casts a creature spell" was refused on the
count alone and the parse reads it for free.

### What a subtype is told from, and why it has to be the capital letter

The engine has no list of creature types, and guessing would turn "a kicked spell" into a filter for
a subtype nothing has — a trigger that silently never fires, which is a wrong reading and not a
missing one (D362). The printed line capitalises a subtype and nothing else in that position, so
`Spirit`, `Arcane` and `Goblin` are subtypes and `white`, `creature` and `kicked` are not. Anything
that is neither a known word nor a capitalised one refuses the whole line.

### What it refuses, each read off the dump rather than guessed

 * **"a spell that targets ~"** — 40 cards, heroic and repartee. The cast event does not carry its
   spell's targets, so this is an engine increment and the next obvious one.
 * **"from a graveyard" / "from anywhere other than your hand"** — the zone a spell was cast from.
 * **"during an opponent's turn"** — a fact about the turn, not the spell.
 * **"a historic spell"** (4) — artifact *or* legendary *or* Saga: three fields joined by an `or`
   across both halves of a type line and a supertype, which no field here can ask.
 * **"a white or blue instant or sorcery spell"** — a colour *and* a type in one descriptor, read as
   neither rather than as half of each.
 * **"another spell"**, **"a kicked spell"**, **"a legendary spell"**, **"a spell using teamwork"** —
   one or two cards each and no field for any of them.

### The table grew a second kind of row

`TRIGGER_SHAPES` entries now carry either `on` (the events, when the sentence names them by being
itself) or `from` (the events parsed out of the match, with `null` refusing the line). A parsed row
matches a wide sentence and then has to decide whether it understood the narrow part, which a fixed
`on` never has to — and a refusal falls through to the rest of the table and then to "unread".

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,712 | **9,833** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,471 | **5,570** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,629 / 56,421 (34.8%) | **19,780 / 56,421 (35.1%)** |

`LEGAL=1`, 31,654 rows. D475's gate costs none of them — measured, not assumed. Fifteen runtime
tests on seven real printings, plus twenty mapping rows and eight refusals in `compile.test.ts`.

## D475 — A trigger that fired, resolved, logged and did nothing: "that player" meant nobody

Writing D474's test for **Pyrostatic Pillar** — "Whenever a player casts a spell with mana value 3 or
less, Pyrostatic Pillar deals 2 damage to that player" — the filter worked, the trigger went on the
stack, the log said *Pyrostatic Pillar deals 2 damage to that player resolves*, and nobody lost any
life.

### The cause

`eventRelativeEffect`'s two "that player" readers guarded `who === undefined || who === c.controller`
and returned the board untouched. The second half of that guard was copied off the two hand-written
cards the readers were written for — Kambal and Fate Unraveler, both "whenever an **opponent** …" —
where a trigger cannot fire on its own controller's action, so the clause was unreachable belt and
braces. D474 made "whenever **a player** casts…" readable and reached it.

And the `undefined` half was wrong about what absence means. `fireTrigger` omits `actor` from the
stack object **when the actor is the watcher's own controller**; `EffectContext.actor` documents it,
and Ruric Thar's hand-written script says it out loud: "an absent actor means *me*, and reading it as
nobody is how this card first dealt no damage at all to its own side." That comment was eleven
entries old when D407 wrote the opposite premise into this reader.

### Three cards were being half-read, and they are the reason this is its own entry

`Barbed Wire`, `Copper Tablet` and `Sulfuric Vortex` all print "At the beginning of **each player's**
upkeep, ~ deals N damage to **that player**", and a step trigger passes the **active** seat as the
actor. So on an opponent's upkeep the card worked; on its controller's own upkeep the actor *was* the
controller, was therefore omitted from the stack object, and the guard threw the effect away. These
three have been hitting one side of a duel and not the other for as long as the compiler has read
them — firing, logging and doing nothing every other turn. That is Pyrostatic Pillar's bug with a
different prologue, and it was already shipping.

### The fix, and the gate that replaces the guard

Both readers now take `c.actor ?? c.controller`, where the `??` is the value rather than a fallback.

What the guard was really protecting against is a "that player" whose actor is **not** the player the
sentence means, and that is now answered where it can be answered properly: `eventRelativeEffect` is
handed the prologue's events and reads these two clauses only where `raise` passes the right seat.

| event | the seat `raise` passes | "that player"? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spell-cast` | the caster | yes |
| `draws` | the seat that drew | yes |
| `life-gained` | the seat that gained | yes |
| `step` | the **active** seat | yes — Barbed Wire's "each player's upkeep" |
| `combat-damage` | the attacking creature's controller | **no** — the card means the seat it hit |
| `attacks`, `etb`, `dies` | the watcher's own side | **no** |

**Furnace Scamp** is the sentence the second half is about: "Whenever ~ deals combat damage to a
player, you may sacrifice it. If you do, ~ deals 3 damage to that player" — the damaged seat lives in
`c.attacked.defender`, nowhere near the actor, so `?? c.controller` without a gate would have hit
**its own controller**.

**The gate costs nothing today, and that is measured rather than assumed.** Compiling the 1,482 legal
cards whose text contains "that player", with the gate off and on, reads the same 216 lines either
way: Furnace Scamp's line, and the two other candidates (`Lim-Dûl's Hex`, `Star Athlete`), are
already unread for reasons of their own. So the gate is a guard against a reading that would become
wrong the day the clause around one of those sentences starts compiling — which is the cheapest
moment to put it in, and the one where nobody is watching.

### The test that could not fail

The old assertion required that both an actorless event and an actor-is-controller event do nothing,
on two cards where neither case can arise — so it could not fail for any real card, which is the
shape D415 and D433 each found twice. It now asserts that the two contexts **agree** (they are one
state spelled two ways), that Fate Unraveler's controller really loses the life, and that the same
sentence reads under a cast and an each-player upkeep prologue while a combat-damage prologue leaves
it unread. Copper Tablet's own printing is driven through a game in `scripts.test.ts`: the opponent's
upkeep, then the controller's, which is the half that used to do nothing.

Both halves were break-run: restoring the guard fails Pyrostatic Pillar and Copper Tablet, and
turning `ofColours`' any-of into an all-of fails the two Mold Adder rows.

### Measured

No coverage change in either direction: 216 "that player" lines read before and after, and D474's
9,833 / 5,570 / 19,780 stand. What changed is **behaviour**, on every card whose event can
name its own controller: Pyrostatic Pillar and Eidolon of the Great Revel, which D474 had just made
readable and which now damage a controller who casts a cheap spell, and Barbed Wire, Copper Tablet
and Sulfuric Vortex, which now hit their own controller's upkeep as well as everybody else's. A
coverage instrument cannot see any of that, which is the argument for a runtime test per reader
rather than a mapping assertion.

## D476 — Heroic: the one thing the cast parse had to refuse

D474's parse read every cast prologue the corpus prints except one shape, and that shape was the
largest single thing it left behind: **"Whenever you cast a spell that targets ~"**, 22 cards under
the `Heroic` ability word, 7 under `Repartee`, and 6 that print the sentence bare — *Gnarlback
Rhino*, *Tenth District Legionnaire* and the four *Hero of the …* creatures.

It was refused on a real gap rather than on effort: the `spell-cast` event said what *kind* of spell
was cast and not **what it was pointed at**.

### Three small pieces

1. **The event carries the targets.** `targetIds` on `spell-cast`, set where the cast is raised from
   `object.targets` — **card targets only**, as instance ids. A spell that targets *you* does not
   trigger your creature's heroic, so putting a seat in the same list would make "targets you" look
   like the same question. A face-down cast gets `[]` (it has nothing to target with).
2. **The question is answered in `fireTrigger`.** `targetsSelf: true`, asked beside `self` and the
   attachment and for the reason their comments already give: it is a fact about **which permanent
   is watching**, and `triggerMatches` is not told the holder. An absent `targetIds` reads as "no
   card targets", so the missing-field case refuses rather than fires.
3. **The compiler reads the tail.** `castBound` already handled "with mana value N or less"; it now
   also matches `that targets <selfRef>`, which covers the full name, the short name and "this
   creature" in one alternation. Nothing else about the parse changed — the prologue regex already
   captured the tail and already refused what it could not read.

The targets travel on the event rather than being looked up at resolution for the reason everything
else on that event does: a heroic trigger resolves after its spell may have been countered or have
resolved off the stack, and `object.targets` is gone by then.

### What stays refused

**"A spell that targets you or a creature you control"** — *Reparations*, *Danitha, Spear of Agony*.
A seat and a board filter in one phrase, and the engine deliberately carries card targets only. Two
cards, and reading it as the card half alone would fire on the wrong spells (D362).

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,833 | **9,868** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,570 | **5,601** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,780 / 56,421 (35.1%) | **19,816 / 56,421 (35.1%)** |

`LEGAL=1`, 31,654 rows. +35 cards is exactly the 35 the dump named, which is the first time a
prologue increment has landed on its own prediction to the card.

Three runtime rows on *Wingsteed Rider*'s own printing — a Giant Growth pointed at it, the same spell
pointed at the Bear Cub beside it, and a creature spell that points at nothing — plus two mapping
rows for the full name and "this creature". Break-run: answering `targetsSelf` from "the spell
targeted *something*" rather than from the holder fails the middle row.

## D477 — The board prologue, parsed: the table had no board-watching row at all

With the cast family read, `prologue-gap.mjs` re-ranks: **600** cards one unread line from a finished
script are still finished by a prologue reader, and the biggest cluster left is the one watching the
board rather than the stack.

| printed shape | cards |
| --- | --- |
| whenever **a creature** you control … | 38 |
| whenever **an artifact** you control … | 15 |
| whenever **another creature** you control … | 13 |
| whenever **another artifact** you control … | 8 |
| `Constellation —` / `Eerie —` (an enchantment you control enters) | 8 + 8 |
| an enchantment / a permanent you control, and 30-odd one-and-two-card tribes | ~45 |

And the reason the whole cluster was unread is worth stating plainly: **`TRIGGER_SHAPES` had no
board-watching row in it.** Every shape in the table was the permanent's own arrival, death,
attack or tap. The engine has been able to express "another creature you control enters" since
#29 — three hand-written cards use it — and no printed line could reach it.

### One parsed row

"Whenever a[nother] `<creature|artifact|enchantment|land|permanent>` you control `enters|dies`," —
who (`a`/`an` → `who: 'any'`, which is what "a creature you control" means about itself; `another` →
`who: 'another'`) times what times which of the two events.

`creature`, `land` and `permanent` were already askable. **`artifact` and `enchantment` are new on
the event**, and they are answered from a new `subjectTypes` — the subject's *live* card types — not
from a boolean of their own. The two existing booleans stay, and the field's docblock says why
rather than leaving it to look like duplication: `isCreature` is the characteristics answer, which a
crewed Vehicle and an animated land reach by routes a type line read at face value does not, and
every board-watching creature trigger in the pool is tested against it. Re-expressing those two
filters on the type line would be a behaviour change on all of them, which this entry is not.

### What it refuses

 * **A subtype** — "a Dragon you control", "another Zombie you control", 30-odd shapes with one or
   two cards each. This is the refusal that would do damage if it were taken: `what` holds a card
   type and the event carries no subtypes, so `Dragon` would compile into a filter nothing matches —
   a trigger that never fires, which is worse than one that never compiles (D362). The cast parse
   reads subtypes because *that* event carries them; this one does not, and the asymmetry is the
   point.
 * **A characteristic filter** — "with power 3 or greater", "with a +1/+1 counter on it", "with
   flying", "with power equal to its toughness". **About 18 cards** and the largest thing left in
   the family, so it is the obvious next increment: the event carries the subject's id but not its
   power, its toughness or its keywords, and reading those off the board when the trigger resolves
   is the wrong moment — the permanent may have changed or left (CR 400.7, the same reading D306 and
   D307 each fixed one way round).
 * **"leaves the battlefield"** (5) — a different event whose filters this entry did not widen.
 * **"is put into a graveyard from the battlefield"** on an artifact or enchantment (5) —
   `to-graveyard` is the right event and has no `what` yet.
 * **"a land you control dies"** — refused by the parse itself, because `dies` is defined for
   creatures only (CR 700.4) and nothing prints it.
 * **Two events in one line** — "enters **and** whenever you activate a power-up ability", "another
   creature **or a land**" — which the row's comma does not match.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,868 | **9,902** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,601 | **5,631** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,816 / 56,421 (35.1%) | **19,852 / 56,421 (35.2%)** |

Three runtime tests on real printings, each chosen for what it can tell apart: *Reckless Fireweaver*
separates an artifact entering from a creature entering; *Glaze Fiend* is an **artifact creature**
that watches *another* artifact, so its own arrival must not pump it and a filter answered from the
type line alone would get that wrong; *Favored of Iroas* is constellation, an ability word in front
of an enchantment filter. Ten mapping rows and eight refusals in `compile.test.ts`.

## D478 — The characteristic filter: the event knew *which* permanent and nothing about it

D477's board parse read "whenever a[nother] `<kind>` you control enters / dies" and refused every
filter printed between the kind and the event. That refusal was the largest thing it left behind —
**about 19 legal cards** — and the reason was a real gap rather than effort: the event carried the
subject's seat, its types and (on a death) its counters, and nothing about its **size** or its
**keywords**.

| printed | read as |
| --- | --- |
| with power 3 or greater | `powerAtLeast` |
| with power 2 or less | `powerAtMost` |
| with toughness 4 or greater / 2 or less | `toughnessAtLeast` / `toughnessAtMost` |
| with a +1/+1 counter on it | `withCounter` |
| with flying | `withKeyword` |

### Where the facts come from, and why not the board

`raise` already made one characteristics computation for the three facts D477 needs; the size and
the keywords come off that same call, so the four filters cost two numbers and an array this
function had in hand. **They are asked of the event and not of the board** because by the time a
death trigger resolves the permanent is in a graveyard with no counters and no keywords at all
(CR 603.6e) — which `subjectCounters`' own docblock had already written down, ending "when a card
needs the power it had, or the types, this is where that goes". D477 put the types there; this puts
the power.

**A missing fact fails the filter.** An event raised for something that is not a creature carries no
power, and "a creature with power 3 or greater" is not true of it, so `undefined` is refused rather
than read as a very small number — the lenient direction would have been the wrong one.

### What stays refused

 * **"with power equal to its toughness"** (Symmetry Matrix, Master Symmetrist) — a comparison
   between two of the subject's own characteristics, which no field here asks.
 * **"with power or toughness 1 or less"** (Arnyn) — an **or** across two bounds, where
   `powerAtMost` and `toughnessAtMost` together are an **and**. Reading it as the and would fire on
   strictly fewer creatures than the card: a wrong reading, so the line stays for a human (D362).
 * **"with a counter on it"** (Ray Fillet, Yathan Tombguard) — any counter rather than a named one.
 * **A word this engine has no keyword for.** `isKeyword` is the whole of the check, and it is the
   same refusal the subtype arm makes: a filter for a keyword nothing has is a trigger that never
   fires, which is worse than a line that never compiles.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,902 | **9,931** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,631 | **5,651** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,852 / 56,421 (35.2%) | **19,886 / 56,421 (35.2%)** |

Two of the four filters are driven through a game, chosen as the two a vanilla body can prove:
*Elemental Bond* against Gnarled Mass (3/3) and Bear Cub (2/2), two green vanilla creatures where
the only difference is the power on the event; and *Waterkin Shaman* against Wind Drake and Bear
Cub, two 2/2 vanilla creatures where the only difference is a keyword. Seven mapping rows and four
refusals in `compile.test.ts`. Break-run: dropping either filter fails exactly the row that card
distinguishes.

**Wind Drake is the pool's own flier rather than a fixture**, which the `fromData` assertion states —
D430's trap is that a fixture sharing a pool card's name is silently replaced by the pool's, so a
test about printed data quietly becomes a test about the pool.

## D479 — The tribe: the same parse, one capital letter further in

D477 read "whenever a[nother] `<kind>` you control enters / dies"; D478 read the characteristic
filter printed between the kind and the event. The one thing both refused was a **tribe** in place
of the card type — "whenever a Dragon you control enters" — and that refusal was honest when it was
written: `what` takes a card type, the two board events carried no subtypes at all, and compiling
`Dragon` as a type would have made a filter nothing ever matches, which is a trigger that never
fires rather than a line left for a human (D362).

The **cast** event has carried subtypes since D474, where the same sentence one zone over —
"whenever you cast a Dragon spell" — reads off `ofSubtypes`. So the tribe lands five entries after
the parse that could already have asked for it, and the thing that was missing was never the parse:
it was the event.

### What the board events now carry

`etb` and `dies` take `ofSubtypes`, an **any-of** matched case-insensitively, and the engine answers
`subjectSubtypes` from the characteristics `raise` already computes for D477's types and D478's
size — so the tribe costs one more array off a call that was already being made. As with every
other field in this family the fact is read **where the event is raised**, not off the board at
resolution: by the time a death trigger resolves the permanent is in a graveyard, and a graveyard
card has the printed subtypes but none of the live ones an animation or a type-changing effect gave
it (CR 603.6e, CR 400.7).

**`what: 'permanent'` beneath the tribe, not `'creature'`.** The corpus is the argument: of the 52
distinct tribes printed in this prologue, `Equipment` is an artifact, `Shrine` and `Cartouche` are
enchantments and `Forest` and `Cave` are lands. The tribe is the whole of what the line says, and
adding a card type the card does not print would narrow the trigger to less than its text.

### The discriminator is the capital letter

Magic capitalises subtypes and nothing on the way into the compiler lowercases them, so
`/^[A-Z][A-Za-z'-]*$/` on the printed `what` tells `Dragon` from `creature` — the same test the cast
parse makes, and the only one available: the engine has no list of creature types, and a guess would
compile a filter nothing matches.

### Measured

A corpus scan over the 31,654 Commander-legal rows finds **130 cards** printing a tribe in a board
prologue across **52 tribes** — Zombie 10, Dragon 10, Villain 9, Human 8, then Equipment, Angel,
Shrine, Elf and Cartouche at 5 each, Ally and Forest at 4, and a long tail of ones and twos. That
tail is why this is a parse and not a table: no list of sentences would have been worth writing for
52 tribes, and the parse reads all of them off one row.

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,931 | **9,982** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,651 | **5,686** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,886 / 56,421 (35.2%) | **19,957 / 56,421 (35.4%)** |

**+51 cards on one shape**, the largest single-shape increment of the session, from a change whose
compiler half is six lines.

*Bishop of Wings* drives it through a game, because both of its printed lines read off the one
parse: it gains 4 life when Serra Angel enters and 0 when Eager Cadet enters — two creatures that
differ only in the subtype on the event — and its death half makes a Spirit token. Four mapping rows
and one refusal in `compile.test.ts`, including `When` as well as `Whenever` (the printed Egg and
Ally cards use the short spelling, which is why the row's regex was widened) and a tribe carrying a
D478 filter, where each arm reads its own half. Break-run in both directions: dropping the
comparison fires on Eager Cadet (24 life, not 20); raising an empty subtype list stops firing on
Serra Angel (20, not 24).

**Serra Angel is the pool's own card rather than a fixture** — D430's trap is that a fixture sharing
a pool card's name is silently replaced, so the test asserts `built.fromData` and leaves the Angel
to the pool.

### What stays refused

 * **Two tribes in one prologue** — "a Human or Dwarf you control". `ofSubtypes` is an any-of and
   would read it correctly; `(?<what>[a-z]+)` cannot span the "or", so the line is left whole rather
   than half-read.
 * **The three filters D478 named** — a comparison between two of the subject's own characteristics,
   an **or** across two bounds, and an unnamed counter. `boardFilter` returns `null` for each, and a
   `null` filter refuses the whole line.

## D480 — "That creature" is the other creature, and the block parse that needed it

The block family has been the top of the compiler's queue for several entries, and the docblock
over it said the family was refused for three different reasons. This takes the half of it that is
readable **without** guessing, and the thing that was actually missing turned out to be a referent
rather than a prologue.

### Three spellings, two events, one parse

| printed | read as |
| --- | --- |
| Whenever ~ blocks a creature | `blocks` |
| Whenever ~ becomes blocked by a creature | `becomes-blocked` |
| Whenever ~ blocks or becomes blocked by a creature | both, off one line |

All three carry "a creature", and that phrase is the whole of why these three are readable while
the bare forms are not. The engine raises `blocks` once per attacker blocked and `becomes-blocked`
once per blocker (CR 509.1a, CR 509.1h) — **per creature**, which is what these lines say. The bare
"Whenever ~ becomes blocked" fires **once** however many creatures blocked, so reading it off the
per-creature event would pay an Alley Grifters' discard three times against three blockers: a wrong
reading of a real card, which D362 ranks below leaving the line alone. **92 legal lines** print a
bare spelling — "becomes blocked" 57, "blocks" 24, "blocks or becomes blocked" 11 — and they want a
batched event, the way D443 built one for combat damage rather than reading the batched line off the
per-creature one.

### The referent, which is what was missing

The prologue was never the hard part — `on` has taken a list of events since D134. What stopped
this family was that **almost every one of these cards prints "that creature"**, meaning the *other*
creature in the combat, and the clause vocabulary read "that creature" as `EffectContext.subject`,
which on both of these events is the card whose trigger it is. A row written without that
distinction would have had Aether Membrane return *itself* to hand and Quagmire Lamprey shrink
*itself*.

`EffectContext.blocked` has carried the other creature since D134 and nothing read it. Four clauses
now do, gated on every event in the prologue being a block:

 * `~ deals N damage to that creature` — Ashmouth Hound (6 corpus lines on this clause alone),
   Inferno Elemental, Acolyte of the Inferno;
 * `destroy that creature` — Evil Eye of Urborg;
 * `that creature gets +N/+N until end of turn` — Flailing Drake;
 * `put a +1/+1 or -1/-1 counter on that creature` — Quagmire Lamprey.

**"It" is deliberately left alone.** Acolyte of the Inferno prints "it deals 2 damage to that
creature" in one sentence, where "it" is the Acolyte and "that creature" is the blocker — so this is
a second referent and not a remapping of the subject. A remapping would have had the Acolyte deal
its damage on behalf of the creature it was damaging.

**The gate is D475's rule applied to a creature instead of a player.** Under an `etb` or a `dies`
prologue "that creature" means the permanent that entered or died, which is a different field; the
clause is claimed only where every event in the prologue carries `blocked`. Three rows in
`compile.test.ts` hold that line, and the break run below is what proves they are not decoration.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,982 | **9,996** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,686 | **5,699** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,957 / 56,421 (35.4%) | **19,972 / 56,421 (35.4%)** |

+14 cards from 47 legal lines across the three spellings, which is the honest yield: the prologue
reads all 47, and the clause vocabulary finishes the cards whose effect is one of the four above.
The rest are one clause short, and the clauses they are short of are named below.

Five runtime tests drive a real combat, and the pair that makes them worth more than a mapping row
is **Flailing Drake against Cave Tiger**: one prints "that creature gets +1/+1" and the other
"Cave Tiger gets +1/+1", the same sentence pointed at opposite creatures. The Drake blocks rather
than attacks, because it has flying and a Grizzly Bears cannot block it — the first draft of that
test attacked with the Drake and the engine refused the block, which was the engine being right
about the card.

Break-run, both directions: resolving "that creature" to the subject pumps the Drake instead of the
Bears (2, not 3); dropping the event gate from the counter clause makes a `dies` prologue read
"that creature" as the dead permanent, which the gate row catches.

### What is still refused

 * **The bare spellings** (92 legal lines) — the counting argument above.
 * **A filter on the other creature** (28 legal lines) — "by a non-Wall creature" (Thicket Basilisk),
   "by a green or white creature", "by two or more creatures". Two events from one line is parsed
   now; a filter on the *other* creature is not a field either event has.
 * **A timing on the effect** — "destroy that creature **at end of combat**" (3), "return that
   creature to its owner's hand at end of combat" (2). `scheduleDelayed` is the mechanism and the
   clause reader is the only work, so this is the next bite out of the family.

## D481 — X belongs to the cost being paid, and a pod found the one card where that differs

The pod sweep that follows every compiler increment threw for the first time in five runs:

```
seed 32032: threw — Starnheim Unleashed has no X to choose
```

An engine throw mid-game is the worst failure this project has, because it ends a table rather than
mis-reading a card — and this one was the engine refusing **its own offer**.

### The card, which is not the card I remembered

Checked against the printed data rather than recalled (D259), because memory had it wrong:

```
Starnheim Unleashed — {2}{W}{W} — Sorcery
Create a 4/4 white Angel Warrior creature token with flying and vigilance.
If this spell was foretold, create X of those tokens instead.
Foretell {X}{X}{W}
```

The **printed** cost has no X. The **foretell** cost has two. And foretell *replaces* the printed
cost, so a foretold Starnheim Unleashed is an X spell cast off a card whose printed cost is not one.

### The two halves disagreed, in the direction nobody had tested

 * `legalActions` offers `xMax` whenever **the cost being paid** has an {X} in it — correct, and
   CR 107.3b is why its own comment says so (D460).
 * `autoActions` validated `action.x` against `parseManaCost(def.manaCost)` — the **printed** cost.

So the offer promised an X the payment then refused. The bot took the offer, as it should, and the
game ended on `RULE_NOT_APPLICABLE`.

**The structural reason the check was wrong is where it sat.** It ran about 250 lines above the
chain that resolves which cost this casting actually pays — flashback, escape, foretell, evoke,
dash, bestow, spectacle and overload each replace the printed cost, and the kicker, buyback and
replicate add to it — so at that point in the function the answer was not yet knowable. The check
has moved to just below that chain, where `costText` is the cost being paid, and reads
`payingCost` instead. Nothing has been spent at that point either, so a refusal still costs the
caster nothing.

An **offered** cast (cascade, madness, miracle) keeps reading the printed cost, which is not an
inconsistency: CR 107.3b is enforced where the offer is read, a few hundred lines earlier, and
D460's reading — a cascade'd `{X}{R}` is cast for X=0 rather than refused — is deliberately
preserved.

`xText`, the `(X=n)` the stack shows the player deciding whether to answer the spell, had the same
bug and is fixed in the same place: a foretold Starnheim Unleashed paying five mana used to appear
on the stack with no X at all.

### Verified

Seed 32032 now finishes: *"Every game reached a finish, with no throw and no stall."*

Two tests on the one card, which is what makes the rule legible — the foretold cast takes `x: 2`
(five mana, `xMax: 2` off five Plains, `Starnheim Unleashed (X=2)` on the stack) and the cast from
hand still refuses an X against its printed `{2}{W}{W}`. Break-run: restoring `payingCost =
printedCost` reproduces the production message, `Starnheim Unleashed has no X to choose`, on the
foretold row while the refusal row stays green.

**The sweep is the instrument that found this, and it found it on a card nothing in the pool
resembles.** No hand-written card in the thirteen decks has a foretell cost that differs from its
printed cost in whether it carries an {X}; 31,654 real cards do, and one of them turned up in a
deck built at random on the 32nd seed of a 40-game run.

## D482 — The batched block, and the ten thousandth card

D480 read the three block spellings that carry "a creature" and refused the 92 legal lines that do
not, for a counting reason: the engine raises `blocks` once per attacker blocked and
`becomes-blocked` once per blocker, while the bare "Whenever ~ becomes blocked" fires **once**
however many creatures blocked. `becomes-blocked`'s own docblock had already written down what to do
about it — *"a card that was would want a separate event rather than this one with a flag"* — and
this is that event, built the way D443 built `combat-damage-dealt` beside `combat-damage`.

### Two events, named after the rules

| printed | event | raised |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Whenever ~ becomes blocked by a creature | `becomes-blocked` | once per blocker |
| Whenever ~ becomes blocked | **`blocked-creature`** | once, per creature that became blocked |
| Whenever ~ blocks a creature | `blocks` | once per attacker blocked |
| Whenever ~ blocks | **`blocking-creature`** | once, per creature that blocked |

The names come from CR 509.1a ("becomes a blocking creature") and CR 509.1h ("becomes a blocked
creature"), which is also the clearest way to say what distinguishes them from the pair above: those
are about the *other* creature, these are about this one.

Neither carries a `blocked` field, deliberately. There may be several blockers, and the cards that
want them say "each creature blocking it" — a question about the board when the ability resolves,
not a fact about the declaration. A `blocked` field here would invite exactly the per-blocker
reading the event exists to avoid, and `eventRelativeEffect`'s gate keeps "that creature" to the
per-creature pair for the same reason.

### Why the yield is high for an event with no new clause readers

The bare forms print, overwhelmingly, **clauses the vocabulary already had**: a corpus scan over the
92 lines finds "it gets +2/+2 until end of turn" 7 times, "+1/+1" 6, "+0/+2" 3, and a dozen more
sizes behind them, plus "untap it", "you gain 2 life" and "you may draw a card". Every one of those
resolves on the card itself, which the self readers have handled since the beginning. So the work
was the event and the parse; the effects were already there.

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 9,996 | **10,031** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,699 | **5,731** |
| printed rules lines read | 19,972 / 56,421 (35.4%) | **20,010 / 56,421 (35.5%)** |

**Ten thousand cards now compile to a script**, from 9,712 at the start of this session's run of
increments.

### The tests measure the count, and the first draft did not

Five runtime tests through a real combat, and the assertion that matters is the number of triggers
the declaration puts on the stack — read before anything resolves. That is a change of method
forced by a break run: the obvious test, Chub Toad's "+2/+2" against two blockers, **cannot fail**,
because raising the event twice puts two identical pumps on the stack and a pump from one source
does not stack with itself. The Toad came out a 3/3 either way.

So the count is asserted three ways instead: the stack holds one trigger for two blockers,
*Deepwood Tantiv* gains 2 life rather than 4 (a life gain does stack with itself), and *Ashmouth
Hound* — D480's card, unchanged — puts **two** triggers on the stack in the same position and
damages both blockers. Break-run: raising the batched event per blocker fails the stack count on
both bare cards and leaves the per-creature card green.

One more thing the tests learned: two blockers on one attacker can owe a damage-assignment order
(CR 509.2), and until it is given **nobody holds priority**, so the triggers sit unresolved. The
first draft drained straight after the block and read zero damage off both Bears — the engine being
right and the test forgetting to answer it. The order is asked for conditionally, because the engine
only asks when the answer can matter: a 1/1 Chub Toad cannot kill either 2/2 whatever the order.

### A live bug in a shipping pool card, found by the new event

Two of the gate's standing checks failed on the first run of this change, and both were right.

**`compiled-vs-written` reported a disagreement on Ichorclaw Myr** — a card in the infect deck,
printed `{2}` for a 1/1 with infect and *"Whenever Ichorclaw Myr becomes blocked, it gets +2/+2
until end of turn."* That is the **bare** spelling, and its hand-written script was
`on: { kind: 'becomes-blocked' }`, the per-blocker event. **So the Myr had been getting +4/+4
against two blockers and +6/+6 against three, for as long as it has been in the pool** — in the one
deck where every point of power is a point of poison, and against the obvious answer to a 1/1,
which is to block it with two creatures.

Nothing could have found this before: the compiler had no reading of the bare prologue to disagree
with, and no test blocked the Myr with two creatures. The card is corrected to `blocked-creature`
with a test that blocks it with a Grizzly Bears and a Centaur Courser and asserts one trigger on the
stack and a 3/3, and a break run that puts it back on the per-blocker event and reads two.

**This weakens Blight Vector, and the amount is unmeasured.** The deck's win rate was measured with
the Myr paying double against two blockers, so the correction takes something real away from it in
exactly the spot the deck wants it. The honest statement is that the balance figures for that deck
predate this fix; re-measuring it is its own task rather than a rider on a rules correction, because
a balance number is only worth having with the seeds and the arms written down (D263).

**`has a card behind every mechanic it declares` reported both new kinds as orphans**, which is
D229's rule and D442's exemption procedure doing their job. `blocked-creature` needs no exemption
now — Ichorclaw Myr prints it and is in a deck. `blocking-creature` takes one, with the evidence the
procedure demands: 24 legal corpus lines, and the runtime test on printed Chub Toad's blocker half.

### What is still refused in this family

 * **A filter on the other creature** — 28 legal lines, "by a non-Wall creature", "by a green or
   white creature". Still not a field either event has.
 * **A count of blockers** — "becomes blocked by two or more creatures". Neither event carries how
   many, and the batched one deliberately carries nothing about them at all.
 * **"A creature you control becomes blocked"** — 10 legal lines, somebody else's creature rather
   than this one. The events take `who` and `of` already, so this is a prologue row rather than
   engine work, and it is the next bite.
 * **A timing on the effect** — "destroy that creature at end of combat" (3), "return that creature
   to its owner's hand at end of combat" (2), on the per-creature pair.

## D483 — "~ or another Ally you control": the subject, parsed

With the board prologue's *event* parsed (D477), its filters read (D478) and its tribe read (D479),
the biggest prologue family left is the one that names **the card and its kind in one breath**.
Measured over the legal rows: **151 lines across 52 shapes**, which is more than the previous three
entries put together.

| printed subject | lines |
| --- | --- |
| Ally | 39 |
| enchantment (constellation's own wording) | 23 |
| creature (enters) | 13 |
| creature (dies) | 8 |
| artifact | 5 |
| Human | 4 |
| nontoken creature | 4 |
| Pirate, nontoken creature (dies) | 3 each |
| Zombie, Vampire, Dragon, Cat, Goblin, legendary creature | 2 each |
| a tail of 34 shapes | 1 each |

No new engine work. D477 gave the board events their `what` and D479 their `ofSubtypes`; this entry
is a parse of the sentence's **subject** where those two parsed its event. A tribe followed by the
type it is a tribe of — "another **Human creature** you control" — fills both fields at once.

### Two events, and an honest account of why

The row reads `[{ who: 'self' }, { who: 'another', of: 'you', <filter> }]`: the card itself, **or**
another permanent that matches. One event with `who: 'any'` and the same filter would be shorter.

**On today's corpus the two are identical**, and that was measured rather than assumed: a scan of
the legal rows finds **zero** cards that name a tribe or a type their own type line lacks. So the
filter never excludes the card's own arrival, and this is not a bug fix dressed as a parse.

The two-event form is still what shipped, because it is what the sentence says — the card is named
unconditionally and the filter governs only the "another" — and because a card printed tomorrow whose
own type line lacks the tribe it names reads correctly here and would not under `who: 'any'`. The
pair cannot double-fire: `another` excludes the subject and `self` requires it.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,031 | **10,076** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,731 | **5,768** |
| printed rules lines read | 20,010 / 56,421 (35.5%) | **20,057 / 56,421 (35.5%)** |

Two printed cards drive both arms through a game. *Beregond of the Guard* ("or another **Human** you
control enters, creatures you control get +1/+1 and gain vigilance") grows the team when an Eager
Cadet arrives, does **not** when a Serra Angel does, and grows a Cadet already on the board when
Beregond itself arrives — which is the `self` arm doing work the filter must not eat. *Eidolon of
Blossoms* does the same for a card **type**: it draws on its own arrival and again when a Rancor
(the pool's own Aura, and an enchantment) comes down.

Ten mapping rows and nine refusals in `compile.test.ts`. Break-run both ways: dropping the `self`
arm fails exactly the two own-arrival tests, and dropping `ofSubtypes` makes Beregond fire for an
Angel.

Two test drafts were wrong about mana rather than about the parse, and both are noted where they
were fixed: a Grizzly Bears cannot be cast off five Plains, and lands tapped for the Eidolon are
still tapped when the next spell wants them.

### A second pool card changed shape, and the check that insisted

`compiled-vs-written` failed once on this change too, on **Zulaport Cutthroat** — printed "whenever
~ or another creature you control dies, each opponent loses 1 life and you gain 1 life", and
hand-written as a single `{ kind: 'dies', who: 'any', of: 'you', what: 'creature' }`.

Unlike D482's Ichorclaw Myr this is **not a bug**: a Zulaport Cutthroat is itself a creature, so the
two shapes fire on exactly the same deaths. It is a representational disagreement, and that table's
own rule is that a new disagreement is *settled* rather than listed. The hand-written side moved to
the two-event shape, because the parse is the half that matches the sentence.

Worth saying plainly: two increments in a row, the first thing the new parse did was disagree with a
hand-written card. Once it was a live bug and once it was a shape — and the check cannot tell them
apart, which is why each one has to be read rather than waved through.

### What it refuses

Every refusal is a **filter** on the subject rather than a type, and each would compile into a
trigger looser than the card (D362): `nontoken` (a field `dies` has and `etb` does not), a colour
("another **black** creature"), `legendary`, `snow`, `historic`, a negated subtype ("non-Human"), and
two types in one subject ("creature **or** planeswalker"). Together they are most of the 52-shape
tail — and `nontoken` is the one worth taking next, because the field exists on one of the two events
already.

## D484 — One word on the wrong event: `nontoken` on the entry

`dies` has carried a `nontoken` filter since the beginning — *"whenever a nontoken creature you
control dies"* is how nearly every death payoff is printed, and its docblock says why: a deck of 1/1
tokens would otherwise drain the table to zero by accident. `etb` did not carry it. That one-word
asymmetry was the whole of what stopped **101 legal lines**:

| printed subject | lines |
| --- | --- |
| nontoken creature (dies) | 39 |
| nontoken creature (enters) | 22 |
| ~ or another nontoken creature | 7 |
| nontoken artifact | 7 |
| nontoken tribes (Dragon, Spirit, Zombie, Vampire, Wizard, Sliver, …) | ~19 |
| subjects still refused (modified, historic, legendary, "Elf or Berserker", …) | 7 |

The change is three lines of engine and a word lifted off the front of the subject in two parses:
`subjectIsToken` is set on an entry as well as on a death, the matcher asks for it on both kinds, and
`boardTrigger` and `orAnotherTrigger` take `nontoken` off the subject before reading the rest. On the
"or another" shape the filter goes on the **another** half only — the card printing the line is a
card rather than a token, so its own arm needs no filter.

### The card that shows what the word is for

*Blessed Sanctuary*: **"Whenever a nontoken creature you control enters, create a 2/2 white Unicorn
creature token."** Without the filter the Unicorn is a creature entering, which makes another
Unicorn, which makes another. The word is not a nicety on this card — it is the difference between a
trigger and a loop, and the break run says so in the plainest terms available: dropping the entry
half of the filter produced **30 Unicorns** off one Eager Cadet, bounded only by the test harness's
resolution budget rather than by anything in the rules.

A second runtime test puts *Arni, Humble Scribe* ("whenever another nontoken creature you control
enters, untap Arni") on the board beside the Sanctuary, which is the pair the filter is about: one
Cadet is one nontoken entry, so Arni untaps once, and the Unicorn that arrives in response is not
Arni's business either.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,076 | **10,091** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,768 | **5,775** |
| printed rules lines read | 20,057 / 56,421 (35.5%) | **20,077 / 56,421 (35.6%)** |

+15 cards for three lines of engine, which is the best ratio of any entry in this run — and the
reason is that the parses were already there. Nine mapping rows across the two prologue describes.

**The yield understates the change.** 101 lines now read where 0 did, and only 15 cards crossed from
"one line short" to "finished", because most of these cards are long: Bane, Lord of Darkness and
Brenard, Ginger Sculptor are short a clause rather than a prologue. The prologue being readable is
what lets those clauses be worth writing.

### What is still refused

The subject words that are filters no field expresses: `modified` (a defined condition about
counters and attachments, CR 701.x), `historic`, `legendary`, and two types in one subject
("artifact creature or Vehicle", "Elf or Berserker"). Seven lines between them, and each would
compile into a trigger looser than the card (D362).

## D485 — The counter clause, parsed — and the stuck table it found

`phrase-gap.mjs` put "put a counter on &lt;permanent&gt;" at the top of the clause queue: **150 cards one
line short, across 115 distinct shapes**, where the largest single shape is *six* cards. A row per
shape is not a strategy for that.

The shapes differ in three places and only three: the **count** ("two +1/+1 counters"), the **kind**
(`+1/+1`, `-1/-1`) and the **target phrase** — and D469 already built a parse for the third. So the
clause now asks `targetSpecFrom` the question every other targeted reader asks, instead of listing
`target creature` and `target creature you control` as the only two subjects it knew. The family
comes along with it: "another target creature you control", "up to one target creature", "each of up
to two target creatures", "target creature with flying", "target creature an opponent controls".

The count stops at three, which is what the corpus prints. `X` and "that many" are refused: both name
a number from elsewhere in the sentence, and a reader that guessed would be wrong rather than silent.

### The defect this found, which matters more than the clause

The first runtime test refused its own target: **"too many targets chosen"**, on a card whose trigger
had just asked for one.

`abilityTargetSpecs` — the function that tells the validator what an ability on the stack may be
pointed at — resolved its script with `scriptFor(name)`, the **hand-written registry**. For a
compiled card that returns nothing, so the spec list was empty, so a chosen target was one too many.
And because nobody holds priority while a choice is owed, the table does not continue:

> **every compiled card whose trigger targets would have hung the game at the moment it was
> answered.**

Not a mis-read card — a stuck table, which is the failure this project has ranked worst since #297.
The engine's own rule for this was already written down in `automation.ts`, two files away:
`scriptForCard` and not `scriptFor`, *"because a card nobody wrote a script for still has whatever
the compiler could read"*. `derive.ts` imports `scripts.ts`, so that function cannot be imported
back; the two callers that matter pass it in, and both already had it to hand.

**One narrow gap is left stated rather than hidden.** `soleTargetSpecOf` keeps the registry lookup,
so a *compiled* card's ability cannot be redirected by a Spellskite. That is a card doing less than
it could, not a table that cannot continue, and it is written into the function's docblock.

### And a bug of my own, caught by the second test

The reader applied the counters with `firstCardTarget`, which takes one. "Each of up to two target
creatures" is **one spec with a count of two**, so Gavony Silversmith put its counter on the first
creature and nothing on the second — `['3/3', '2/2']` where the card promises one each. It reduces
over `cardTargets` now, the same list the count let the player choose.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,091 | **10,145** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,775 | **5,801** |
| printed rules lines read | 20,077 / 56,421 (35.6%) | **20,145 / 56,421 (35.7%)** |

Three printed cards drive it, each exercising a different part: **Skinrender** (a count of three, and
a 2/2 that dies to it — the death is the assertion, because a card leaving the battlefield takes its
counters with it), **Gavony Silversmith** (two targets, one counter each) and **Plague Belcher**
(a *harmful* counter on a creature *you control*, which is the case that shows `friendly` is read off
the kind and the filter off the phrase — two different questions). Ten mapping rows and six refusals.

Break-run, both halves: putting the validator back on the registry refuses all three cards' targets
with the production message, and putting the effect back on `firstCardTarget` fails exactly the
two-target row.

### A row that was waiting for this reader

The gate failed once on a **stale refusal**: D453's scope family asserted that "put a +1/+1 counter
on each of up to two target creatures" stays unread, and its row said why — *"the support/bolster
shape, which is a targeted clause and belongs to a different reader."* That reader is this one. The
row is deleted rather than kept, which is the rule that family's own comment states: a stale row
fails the test, and that is the point of asserting an equality rather than a subset.

### What the parse still refuses

 * **A subtype target** — "target Merfolk you control", "target Wall". `targetSpecFrom` lower-cases
   its phrase before the parse sees it, so the capital letter that tells a subtype from a qualifier
   is already gone. That is a change to *that* function's contract and the obvious next increment:
   it would lift this clause, the pump, the damage and every other targeted reader at once.
 * **"enchanted creature"** — the Aura's host, which the Aura reader answers with a different
   question (D469 says so in as many words).
 * **A counter kind with its own rules** — a loyalty counter, a stun counter. `addCounters` would
   store the name happily, and the rules attached to it are not implemented, so a card that looked
   automated would do nothing (D362).

## D486 — A subtype in the target noun position, and the disjunction it is spelled with

`targetSpecFrom` is the chokepoint every targeted reader goes through — destroy, exile, bounce, the
damage family, the pump, the counter clause, the discard's `target opponent`. D469 made it a parse
instead of a list of thirty phrases, and `parsedTargetPhrase`'s docblock has carried one deliberate
omission ever since: **subtypes**. "target Equipment", "another target Soldier you control",
"{T}: Untap target Forest". The signal needed is a capital letter, and the function could not see one,
because `targetSpecFrom` lower-cases its phrase at the top for the description's sake before the
parse begins. That docblock said fixing it was "a change to that function's contract rather than a
line here", and this is that change.

### What it cost to make the contract change

The parse is handed `trimmed` — the phrase with its printed capitalisation — instead of `printed`,
and lower-cases **each word where it is compared**: the quantifier lookup, the `opponent` test, the
`with <keyword>` word, the controller clause, every qualifier in the run. `printed` is still what
the description is built from, because a player reads "choose target creature" mid-question and not
"Target creature". The noun position is never the first word of a target phrase — the first word is
always `target`, `another` or `up to` — so lower-casing the first character costs the parse nothing,
which is what makes the two forms separable at all.

The noun position then reads two shapes, which are one shape:

* **One capitalised word** — a subtype, classified by `permanentWordMatch`, the reader that already
  owns that rule for printed board scopes ("each Ooze you control"). Sharing it is the point: a word
  that is one thing in a scope is the same thing in a target.
* **A disjunction** — "target creature or Vehicle", "target Scarecrow or Plains", "target Bird, Cat,
  Dog, Goat, Ox, or Snake", read before the qualifier run because a disjunction's words *are* the
  noun; popping one off the end would leave `creature or` to be read as qualifiers.

Both land in one new `permanentFilter` option, `anyOf`, which is a list of predicates rather than a
list of words — because the words are not one vocabulary, and because "creature or Vehicle" is a
**disjunction** where every other field on that factory is a test the candidate must pass. Each
predicate reads the live type line (CR 109.2, #319).

### The measurement, and where it paid out

| | 77806da | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,145 | **10,278** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,801 | **5,928** |
| printed rules lines read | 20,145 / 56,421 (35.7%) | **20,337 / 56,421 (36.0%)** |

Scoped by substitution in place before it was written: 290 lines on 285 cards carry a capitalised
noun position, and swapping the word for a noun known to read finished 48 lines and 33 cards — the
rest are unread for a **second** reason (regenerate, tap, the copy clause, characteristic-setting),
which this increment does not touch. The disjunction half measured 21 lines and 16 cards the same
way.

Afterwards, the breadth is what the chokepoint promised: **88** lines with a capitalised noun
position now read, spread across at least twelve clause families — destroy 28, the counter clause
26, bounce 5, regenerate 3, untap 3, attach 1, and a tail. And the larger payer was the half with no
capital in it at all: **242** lowercase disjunctions read, because "destroy target artifact,
enchantment, or land" (Acidic Slime, Aftershock) was a three-way run the switch's exact phrases never
covered. The disjunction branch was ten lines of code and came free with the parse.

### The plural, which this increment got wrong first and corrected

The first draft kept the printed word as spelled, on the argument that three of the corpus's
capitalised noun positions are singular subtypes ending in `s` (`Plains`, `Fungus`, `Bolas`) and
de-pluralising would read `Fungus` as `Fungu`. A `compile.test.ts` row written to assert that
`target Sagas` stays unread **failed**: it reads. `permanentWordMatch` guards a word's *shape*, not
its membership in any vocabulary, so `hasSubtype(line, 'sagas')` is simply false on every board ever
printed — the line reads, the spell can never be cast, and unlike an unread line **nothing flags it**
for a human to play by hand. That is the silent-nothing failure D449 found in the search filters and
the exact case D362 calls worse than an unread line.
