So a capitalised word ending in `s` is refused. It costs the three singulars and buys back four
plurals as lines a human is told about. The guard has its own break run: deleting it fails three
rows, two of them the ones that record the cost.

Measured rather than reasoned, against the corpus's own type lines: of the **80** distinct
capitalised noun positions in the legal corpus, **72** are subtypes some printed card actually has.
Four of the eight that are not are those plurals. The other four — `Charix` (a card naming itself),
`Contraption`, `Attraction`, `Reflection` — read and match nothing, four lines of 290, and want a
subtype vocabulary the engine does not have. Recorded as **#341**, not guessed at here.

### Vraska's Contempt, and the bot hint the disjunction nearly dropped

`compiled-vs-written.test.ts` went red on one card the moment the disjunction began to read, in two
fields: `removesACreature` and `targets`. Both were settled rather than added as a row, which is that
table's own rule.

`kind` first. "Exile target creature or planeswalker" has to read as `kind: 'permanent'`, because
`targeting.ts` turns `kind: 'creature'` into "and the candidate is a creature *now*" and an uncrewed
Vehicle is a legal target for Daring Demolition that is not one. The hand-written card said
`kind: 'any'` with a filter that threw players away — the only one of the pool's nine `kind: 'any'`
specs that was not the printed phrase "any target", and `legalTargets` enumerates every seat for
`any` only for the filter to refuse each one. The hand-written side moved to the compiled shape: the
same legal targets by a shorter route.

`removesACreature` second, and this is the one that mattered. `targetedEffect`'s own docblock argues
that a compiled card which *works* and *plays badly* is worse than an unread line, because a line
left unread is flagged and a badly played one is not. The flag had been derived from
`spec.kind === 'creature'` at three sites, and the disjunction can no longer carry it there. So all
three now ask `mayRemoveACreature(spec, phrase)`, which adds one case: a `permanent` spec whose
**printed phrase** names a creature. The word is in the card's own text. "Destroy target Equipment"
and "destroy target artifact or enchantment" still answer no, and "destroy target Scarecrow or Plains"
answers no as well — a true miss, since nothing in the file can tell a creature subtype from a
Vehicle's, which is #341 again.

### What is still refused, and why each

* **A capitalised word ending in `s`** — above.
* **A negated subtype** — "target non-Human creature" (44 lines) and "target non-Aura" (5). The
  qualifier run refuses `non-human` because it is on none of its lists, which is the right answer
  until there is a reader for it.
* **A disjunction carrying a qualifier** — "target tapped Goblin or Elf". None is printed; refusing
  rather than reading it with the qualifier dropped is the honest default either way.
* **A conjunction** — "target Goblin and Elf" is not one target.

### The tests

Four runtime tests through `customDeck`, on two printings pulled from the corpus rather than typed
from memory (D259): Aeronaut Cavalry for the filter and Daring Demolition with Consulate Dreadnought
for the disjunction. The first two are not the shape they were drafted in — answering the trigger
with an explicit `auto:choose` got "nothing is waiting for a choice", because the subtype filter had
already cut two creatures down to **one** legal target and the engine does not ask a question with a
single answer. That is the better assertion: with `anyOf` deleted the Bears are legal too, the
question has two answers, the engine stops, and `drain` never reaches the counter. The break run
fails exactly those two.

Plus 24 compile-side rows: 14 printed lines that read, 6 refusals, and 4 on the `removesACreature`
hint. And the stale row from D485 — "a subtype target: the target parse lower-cases its phrase before
it could tell" — deleted, because that is what this increment was.

### A second stale refusal row, found by the gate

`compile.test.ts` had D485's row — "a subtype target: the target parse lower-cases its phrase before
it could tell" — and deleting it was expected. The full gate then found a second one in
`scripts.test.ts`: D469's own refusal table asserts `destroy target Wall` returns `null`, with the
same reason in its comment. `target Wall` is 11 printed lines in the legal corpus and reading it is
what this increment is.

Both rows were records of *this* omission rather than refusals on their own merits, which is why the
list of refusals in `parsedTargetPhrase`'s docblock is the thing to keep current: two test files were
quoting it, and a row that quotes a reason outlives the reason unless the reason is somewhere one
file owns. The phrase moved up into the mapping table, and the row's slot now holds the three
refusals this increment does make — the trailing `s`, the negated subtype, and a qualifier inside a
disjunction.

`destroy target squirrel` stays on the refusal list and is more useful than it was: the same word
with a capital now reads, so the pair is what proves the capitalisation is load-bearing rather than
decorative.

## D487 — A spell's lines that are not its resolution

`readResolution` is **all-or-nothing** by design, and its docblock says why: a spell that resolves
and silently does half of what it prints is worse than one left unread, because an unread card is a
manual object inside an automated game and says so (D362), and a half-read one says nothing. So
`spellScriptFor` compiles a spell whole or not at all.

The consequence is that **any** line it cannot read refuses the card — including a line that is not
about the resolution. `isKeywordDeclaration` exists because of exactly that: `Miracle {R}` was
refusing Thunderous Wrath, whose other line, "deals 5 damage to any target", this compiler reads
perfectly well. That function's argument is the one this increment extends: "every keyword a spell
can carry is a **cost or a modifier** — a way to cast the card, not a step of resolving it."

Three more families are the same thing, and were measured by setting one line aside and asking the
compiler again:

| | lines | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a cost modification | 64 | "This spell costs {3} less to cast if it targets a tapped creature" |
| a triggered ability | 36 | and on a spell these function elsewhere: from the graveyard (Punishing Fire, Spit Flame, Reach of Branches), from the library (Creeping Chill), out of a discard (Gorilla Tactics, Psychic Purge), on cycling (the Resounding cycle, Decree of Justice, Slice and Dice) |
| an activated ability | 6 | Hammer of Bogardan, Geistblast, Wither and Bloom — all paid from the graveyard or a discard |

All 106 were read individually before the list was written, not sampled.

| | 242358d | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,278 | **10,364** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,928 | 5,928 |
| printed rules lines read | 20,337 / 56,421 (36.0%) | **20,440 / 56,421 (36.2%)** |

"Every printed line read" is deliberately **unchanged**, and that is the honest shape of this
increment rather than a shortfall: the ability line is still unread and still reported, so these
cards are playable with one line flagged for a human — which is what `compile.ts` already says a
keyword declaration means, and why it tags the two reasons apart.

### The safety property, which is not "this line is not the resolution"

It is: **the spell read without this line gives its controller no more than the printed card does.**
Three families next door break it, so they stay in the resolution and the card stays unread.

* **A casting restriction** — "Cast this spell only if you control two or more Vampires" (9 lines),
  "Cast this spell only during the declare attackers step" (the Assassin's Blade cycle). Dropping it
  lets the engine cast a card the rules forbid: the clearest widening of the three, and the only one
  that is a rules violation rather than a price.
* **`costs {X} more to cast`** (13) — Fireball's "for each target beyond the first", and Strive.
  Dropping it makes the spell *cheaper* than printed. The regex that reads the cost modification had
  to be split in two for this; matching `less|more` together would have shipped a free Fireball.
* **"When you cast this spell, …"** (14) — the one family where the shape does not decide. Empyrial
  Storm, Show of Confidence, Storm of Forms and Mentor's Guidance copy the spell, which is a
  benefit; **Dash Hopes** lets any player pay 5 life to counter it, which is the card's drawback and
  the reason it is printed at {B}{B}. Nothing in this file can tell those apart, so all fourteen are
  refused rather than five read and one turned into a strictly better Counterspell.

Both halves have break runs. Removing the routing fails 9 rows; letting a casting restriction
through fails 2 — and the second is the one worth having, because it is the test that would catch
somebody widening the classifier by one regex later.

### Where this came from, and the bigger thing it replaced

The queue said the biggest remaining structural gap was the **multi-sentence line**: 9,760 unread
lines on 9,381 cards carry more than one sentence, and 2,262 of them read in part. Reading those in
part looked like the largest increment the compiler had ever had in front of it.

It is not an increment, it is a rule this project already decided against, and the reason is written
in `readResolution`'s own docblock. The audit made the cost concrete:

* "`{1}: Add {W}, {B}, or {G}.` **Activate only once each turn.**" — dropping the second sentence is
  an unlimited mana ability and a bot loop (#124, D463).
* "Exile target creature. **Return it to the battlefield under its owner's control at the beginning
  of the next end step.**" — becomes permanent removal.
* "**Sacrifice it at the beginning of your next end step**" — becomes permanent reanimation.

A first pass flagged 787 of the 2,262 as restrictions and called 1,475 safe; reading the population
by opening phrase (888 distinct, 1,756 sentences) found the second class — the printed **downside**
— which that list missed entirely. The compiler cannot tell an upside delayed trigger from a card's
printed cost, and the bot does not read flags (#322): a human at the table polices an unread
sentence, the bot plays the partial reading as the whole card.

So that family is **refused, deliberately**, and the measurement is recorded rather than the code
written — #342 holds it. What the audit did turn up on the way is this increment: of the spells that
read once one line is set aside, 106 are refused by a line that is not their resolution at all, and
that is the same defect `isKeywordDeclaration` was written for, two years of card design wider.

Of those 106, 35 looked at first like the sentence-split family — "Feast of Blood :: Destroy target
creature. You gain 4 life." reads as two sentences and was still refused. Probing the card showed
the sentence split was never the cause: its other line is "Cast this spell only if you control two
or more Vampires". The right fix was the line classifier, and Feast of Blood is one of the nine that
still refuses, correctly.

## D488 — Prevent the next N damage

Top of the clause queue by cards finished (D434's ordering): **105 printed lines on 50
Commander-legal cards**, in 27 distinct destination forms, every one of which was listed from the
corpus before the reader was written.

It is the cheapest increment of this run because the engine already had everything: `preventDamage`
has been the primitive since #85, `shieldFirstTarget` is the wrapper the two hand-written prevention
cards already call, and `ContinuousEffect.preventsDamageAmount` is where the points go. So this is a
**reader**, not an engine change.

| | 44db9d2 | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,364 | **10,412** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,928 | **5,976** |
| printed rules lines read | 20,440 / 56,421 (36.2%) | **20,511 / 56,421 (36.4%)** |

Every one of the 48 cards is fully read rather than playable-with-a-flag, which is the difference
from D487: a prevention ability is usually the whole of what its card does beyond a body.

One reader for the whole family rather than a row in each of `untargetedEffect`, `selfEffect` and
`targetedEffect`, for the reason `damageDestination` is one function: the sentence is fixed and only
its **destination** varies, so three readers would be three copies of one parse differing in a
clause. The three destinations:

* **A target phrase** — "any target" (61 lines), "target creature" (16), and the narrower ones:
  "target artifact creature", "target player or planeswalker", "target legendary creature".
  Whatever `targetSpecFrom` can express, which is why this reader is 40 lines long.
* **`you`** (7) — a shield on the controller. Not a *side*: "you and/or permanents you control" is
  `preventDamageToSide` and a different printed phrase.
* **The source itself** (7) — Rock Hydra, Ethereal Champion, Opal-Eye, Rasputin Dreamweaver and the
  rest print their own name in the destination slot.

### What it refuses

* **`X` instead of a number** (11 lines). X is chosen as a spell is cast (CR 601.2b), and on a
  trigger or an activated ability `c.x` is zero — so a clause reader that understood bare X would
  build a card that *works and prevents nothing*, with nothing left unread for anybody to notice.
  That is `xSpellResolution`'s argument for keeping X on the spell path, and it holds here.
* **A scope** — "each creature and each player" (Kitsune Palliator), "each creature you control".
  `preventDamage` pushes one effect per target, so reading these would shield the first and silently
  drop the rest.
* **"enchanted creature"** — the Aura host, which D469 says in as many words is a different question.
* **"that permanent or player"** — an event-relative destination, so it belongs to whatever raised
  the event.
* **"this creature by Torrent of Lava"** — prevention from one named source, which the shield has no
  field for: `preventsDamageAmount` absorbs the next N points from anywhere.

### Two bot hints, and a card that compiled for the first time

`compiled-vs-written.test.ts` went red twice on this increment, and both were the check doing its
job on a field no runtime test would have missed.

**Samite Healer** carries `preventsDamage: true` on its **ability** and Healing Salve on its
**mode** — a hint nothing in the engine reads and the bot does: do not spend a shield on a board
with no damage coming. The compiled reading had the effect and not the hint, which is the failure
`targetedEffect`'s docblock names — a card that works and plays badly, and nothing flags it. Both
keys are set now, because the two paths take it from different places: `modalScriptFor` lifts it off
`spellFlags` onto the mode, and the activated-ability path reads `abilityFlags`.

**Healing Salve** is the more interesting one. Its second bullet prevents damage, so the card has
never compiled at all — and the moment it did, the check found its **first** bullet disagreeing.
"Target player gains 3 life" has been read as `friendly` by the life clause all along; the
hand-written card said plain `TARGET_PLAYER`, so the bot could offer three life to an opponent. The
compiled reading is the better one, so the hand-written side moved to a new `TARGET_PLAYER_HELPED`
beside `ANY_TARGET_HELPED` — a constant rather than a change to `TARGET_PLAYER`, which has sixteen
users and most of them point at a player the card is doing something *to*.

That is a defect found by a reader for an unrelated clause, in a card whose other half this
increment never touched, and it is the second time the standing check has paid for itself this run
(Vraska's Contempt was the first, in D486).

### A row that inverted, and a claim of mine that was wrong

`compile.test.ts` had a row asserting Healing Salve is **refused whole, all three lines**, with a
note saying it was "the last pool card holding the property" and that the synthetic row below it
would hold the property when that one went. That has now happened — Golgari Charm left when
regenerate was read, Selesnya Charm with D404's exile-by-power, Healing Salve with this. The row is
inverted rather than deleted, so it now asserts the whole card reads and the note's history stays
attached to the card.

And one claim of mine was simply wrong. I wrote Wandering Mage's "target Cleric or Wizard creature"
as a **mapping** row on the argument that D486 reads a disjunction in the noun position. It does
not read that one: D486 splits on `or` and then requires each part to be a single type or subtype
word, and "Wizard creature" is two. The capability I claimed is not the capability that shipped.
One printed line, moved to the refusals with the real reason, and left as the shape to read next —
a disjunction whose parts share a trailing noun changes what the parts mean, so it is not a
widening of the existing branch.

### #246's check earned its keep again

The first full gate on this increment failed at `typecheck:tests`, not at a test: `compile.test.ts`
declares its own local `Mode` interface for reading a compiled modal, and the new assertion read a
`preventsDamage` field that interface did not list. `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json` is clean on that
file either way, because the test tsconfig is a separate project — which is the whole reason #246
added `typecheck:tests` to the gate, and the second time this run that a check written for an
earlier increment caught something the one before it would have let through.

### The clause queue, ranked by cards finished — and why that ordering matters

The instrument that picked this increment (`clause-pick.mjs`) substitutes each candidate clause for
one the compiler certainly reads and counts the cards whose **whole text** then reads. Run over the
eight largest candidate families:

| cards finished | lines | family |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **50** | 105 | prevent the next N damage — *this increment* |
| **30** | 121 | search your library for a `<card>` |
| **28** | 93 | counter target spell unless its controller pays {X} |
| **26** | 143 | `you may pay {M}. If you do, …` |
| 7 | 199 | add one mana of any color |
| 2 | 271 | sacrifice a `<permanent>` |
| 1 | 323 | deals N damage to each `<scope>` |
| 0 | 145 | `~` gets +N/+N as long as `<condition>` |

The bottom half is the point. **`sacrifice a <permanent>` is 271 printed lines and finishes two
cards**; `deals N damage to each …` is 323 lines and finishes one; the as-long-as static is 145
lines and finishes none. Those cards have other gaps, so reading the clause buys a line in the
percentage and no playable card — which is D434's rule stated with numbers rather than as a
principle, and a correction to the queue this loop was working from, which had `sacrifice a
<permanent>` (87 cards) and the cost-like family near the front on line counts.

Ranked this way the next three are the library search, the counter-unless-they-pay, and the
`you may pay {M}` offer, in that order.

## D489 — Counter target spell unless its controller pays {N}

81 unread "Counter target … unless …" sentences on 81 Commander-legal cards, and **50 of them are
one shape** with no spell filter at all (Force Spike, Convolute, Jwari Disruption, Censor). Measured
from the corpus before anything was written, with every distinct form listed.

| | ed81b7e | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,412 | **10,438** |
| cards with every printed line read | 5,976 | **6,003** |
| printed rules lines read | 20,511 / 56,421 (36.4%) | **20,553 / 56,421 (36.4%)** |

### It is ward, from the other side of the table

The engine already had the whole mechanism and it took one reading of `pendingPayment`'s docblock to
see it: "`seat` here is never the controller of the ability that set it — which is the whole reason
it could not be folded into `pendingDecision`". That field was built for a question asked of
somebody who is **not** resolving anything, which is exactly this card. Ward asks the player who did
the targeting; this asks the player whose spell is being answered. Both are the same question — pay,
or this object leaves the stack — and the half that is **not** a choice is already shared:
`settlePayment` counters without asking when the cost cannot be afforded, because a prompt with one
outcome is a table that has stopped.

So `counterUnlessPaid` is a second raiser of an existing field rather than a new kind of pause. The
one difference is **when**: ward raises its payment from a triggered ability, this one from the
counterspell's own resolution. That was the single design question, and it was checked rather than
assumed — the three places the engine clears a pending payment are a seat leaving, the game ending
and a reset, and none of them fires at the end of a resolution. The question has to outlive the
spell that asked it, because the spell is gone by the time the answer arrives.

### A latent lie in a shared path, which a second raiser exposed

`settlePayment` built its own log line for the unaffordable case, with the word **ward** hard-coded:
`${warded}: ward ${cost} was not paid — …`. Correct while ward was the only raiser, and a card
announcing a keyword it does not have the moment there were two — "Force Spike: ward {1} was not
paid". The wording now comes from whoever raised the payment, as `pendingPayment.unpaidNote`, which
each raiser builds for itself. Nothing can change between the raise and the settle (nobody holds
priority while a payment is outstanding), so building the words early costs nothing and keeps the
shared path from having to know which card asked.

That is asserted, not assumed: the third runtime test checks the log says "Force Spike" and does
**not** say "ward", and it is the reason the field was added rather than a nicety.

### What it refuses, and all of it is about where the number comes from

* **`{X}`** — Clash of Wills prints "unless its controller pays {X}", and that X is the
  counterspell's own, chosen as it was cast. `pendingPayment.cost` is a printed string priced by
  `parseManaCost` at settle time, so an `{X}` left in it would be priced as one generic and the card
  would ask for the wrong amount every time. `xSpellResolution`'s argument, in a new place. This one
  was a correction: the first draft's guard was `parseManaCost(cost).generic + 1 > 0`, which is
  vacuously true, and Clash of Wills went straight through it.
* **A computed cost** — "{1} for each card in your graveyard" (Circular Logic), "for each creature
  you control", "plus an additional {1} for each…". The regex takes a literal mana cost and nothing
  else, so these fall through to the plain counter arm, fail their target phrase, and stay unread.
* **A cost that is not mana** — Perplex's discard, Grip of Amnesia's graveyard exile, Molten
  Influence's four damage. `pendingPayment` prices mana.

And two that are refused **by their target phrase** rather than by this arm: "target instant or
sorcery spell" and "target artifact or creature spell". Checked both ways before the rows were
written — neither reads in the plain "Counter target instant or sorcery spell" either, so this is a
pre-existing gap in the *spell*-kind vocabulary, about ten lines in the corpus, and the natural
sibling of D486's noun position for stack objects. It is the next thing to do in this family.

### Three test mistakes, all mine, all in the harness rather than the card

The runtime tests took four attempts and every failure was a fact about the engine I had assumed:

1. **The caster keeps priority after casting** (CR 117.3c), so seat 1 had to pass before seat 0
   could respond. The first draft cast straight over the top.
2. **Turn parity is not what I guessed.** `firstSeat: 1, turn 4` is seat 1 active; I "fixed" a
   failure by flipping it to `firstSeat: 0` on a guess and made it worse. Printing `activeSeat`
   settled it in one run — which is what I should have done first.
3. **`tapAllLands` needs priority**, so pre-tapping seat 0's Islands on seat 1's turn threw in the
   *setup*, before anything the increment is about. `auto:cast` taps for its own cost.
4. **`replacements` is drained onto the provoking action's message**, as its own docblock says, so
   the field is empty again by the time a test looks at it. The note is read off the log.

### `typecheck:tests` again, and why the field stayed required

The first full gate failed there a second increment running: `automation.test.ts` builds a
`pendingPayment` by hand, in the table that checks a pending question is cleared when its seat
leaves, and that fixture had no `unpaidNote`.

Worth saying that the answer was to fix the fixture rather than make the field optional. An optional
`unpaidNote` with a fallback would put the hard-coded "ward" back in `settlePayment` as the default,
which is the exact lie this change removed — and it would be a default that is right for one raiser
and wrong for every future one. Required means a new raiser cannot compile without saying what its
card says, which is the property worth having.

## D490 — The kind of spell a target phrase names: "target blue instant spell"

The sibling D489 named as the next thing to do, and it is D486's noun-position disjunction again for
objects on the stack instead of permanents. `targetSpecFrom` had exactly two spell filters, both
exact-match switch cases: `target creature spell` and `target noncreature spell`. Everything else
Magic prints in that position — a card type, a colour, a count of colours, a negation, or a
disjunction of any of them — fell through to `parsedTargetPhrase`, whose noun vocabulary has no
`spell` in it, and was refused.

Measured before it was built, by substitution in place: swap each unread `target <words> spell` for
`target spell`, which reads, and ask the compiler again. **302 unread lines on 295 cards** carry
such a phrase, and **41 lines on 32 cards** are refused by *nothing else* — the rest have a second
problem in the same sentence. The phrases, by count: `instant or sorcery` 8, `artifact` 3,
`artifact or creature` 3, then `enchantment`, `red`, `instant`, `sorcery`, `blue`, `black` at 2 each,
and thirteen singles.

### The grammar is a disjunction of conjunctions, and one card forces that

`or` separates alternatives; nothing separates the words *inside* one. So `instant or sorcery` is two
one-word alternatives and `blue instant` is one two-word alternative. **Guttural Response** is the
card that makes the distinction load-bearing: it counters a spell that is **both** blue and an
instant, and read as a flat disjunction it would counter every instant at the table — a strictly
better card than the one printed, which is the failure class D259 is about.

Split with the same expression D486 uses, because printed text spells a disjunction three ways:
a comma, `, or`, and a bare `or`.

### The vocabulary, and the two words that are not colours

Each word is read as a card type, the one supertype printed in this position (`legendary`, on Icy
Reception), one of the five colour words, `colorless`, `multicolored`, or a `non` negation of any of
them. The last two are not colours but counts of them (CR 202.2): no mana symbols, and more than
one. `non` is one rule over the whole vocabulary rather than a second table — only `nonartifact`,
`nonblue` and `noncreature` are printed, and a negation that worked for two of the three would be
the kind of partial rule this file keeps finding bugs in.

Read off **live** characteristics, not the printed type line, for the reason #319 gave when it
corrected five hand-written filters: a spell whose colour or type an effect has changed is the spell
the phrase is about.

### `land` is left out on purpose, and that is the interesting refusal

A land is played, never cast (CR 305.1), so there is no such thing as a land spell. A phrase that
*read* would compile, match nothing on any stack, and make its card silently uncastable — which is
exactly the failure #341 is open about for subtypes, and the trade D486 refused a whole shape
(capitalised nouns ending in `s`) to avoid. Nothing in the corpus prints it. Refusing it costs
nothing and keeps the rule stated rather than accidental.

### One unknown word refuses the whole phrase

D362, applied one word at a time. **Consign to Memory** is the real card behind it: "Counter target
triggered ability or colorless spell" reaches across two kinds of stack object, and reading it as
"target colorless spell" would print a card that cannot answer the triggered ability it exists to
answer. `triggered` and `ability` are not in the vocabulary, so the phrase stays unread.

### The two exact phrases stay in the switch, and the reason is a test

`targetSpecFrom` runs its switch first, so `target creature spell` and `target noncreature spell`
are still `isCreatureSpell` and `isNoncreatureSpell` — the *identical functions* hand-written Essence
Scatter and Negate carry. This parse would read both to the same answer through a different
function, and `compiled-vs-written.test.ts` compares specs by identity, which is the argument
`isCreatureSpell`'s own docblock makes. Two test rows assert the switch still wins.

### The break run found a test that was not testing what it said

Five breaks, four caught on the first pass. The one that was not: deleting the per-word refusal left
every "unknown word" row still passing, because all three were a term of **one** unknown word and a
separate guard ("a term with no readable word refuses the phrase") turned them down on its own. The
row that separates the two rules is a term that *mixes* a known word with an unknown one —
`target blue historic spell`, which without the per-word refusal reads as "target blue spell" and
counters every blue spell at the table. Added, and the break then failed as it should.

The other four: the conjunction read as a disjunction (Guttural Response's runtime test), the
negation dropped (Frazzle's), `land` added to the type list (its refusal row), and the filter
deleted outright (three runtime tests).

### What it bought

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,438 | **10,476** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,003 | **6,040** |
| printed rules lines read | 20,553 / 56,421 (36.4%) | **20,603 / 56,421 (36.5%)** |

Fifty lines against a probe that predicted forty-one: the extra nine are knock-ons, lines that were
already readable in a modal or a second sentence whose *other* half was this phrase.

Two of D489's own refusal rows moved to its mapping table, since the gap they recorded is the gap
this closed. The history is kept in a comment rather than the rows deleted, because the pair is the
evidence that the unless-paid arm never cared about the spell filter in front of it.

### Still open in this family, named rather than guessed

**A mana-value clause on the spell**: Change the Equation prints "Counter target red or green spell
with mana value 6 or less", and the colours now read while the clause does not. Its refusal row says
which half is the reason.

## D491 — A mana-value clause on a search filter, and the word `permanent`

### The measurement changed the increment

The standing note said this was "a mana-value clause on a search filter, 82 lines on 82 cards". The
first probe (`scratchpad/mv-filter.mjs`, substitution in place) said something different: the clause
is **cross-cutting**, not a search feature. Its shape list has these in it beside the tutors —

```
Destroy target creature or planeswalker with mana value N or less
exile target artifact or creature an opponent controls with mana value N or less   (Annex Sentry)
Counter target spell with mana value 2 or less                                     (Change the Equation)
Whenever … another creature you control with mana value 4 or greater dies          (Caldaia Guardian)
```

— which is four different readers of one printed phrase: `parsedTargetPhrase`'s permanent scopes,
D490's new `spellTargetPhrase`, `libraryFilter`, and a trigger's subject scope. So a second probe
(`mv-split.mjs`) priced each context on its own, because the whole arm measured 46 cards and the
question was whether that is one increment or two:

| arm | cards finished | lines |
| --- | --- | --- |
| mana value in a **search** filter only | 6 | 9 |
| mana value **not** in a search (target / spell / trigger) | 21 | 35 |
| the word `permanent` in a search only | 5 | 5 |
| **search: mana value and `permanent` together** | **25** | **32** |
| everything at once | 46 | 66 |

The two halves are exactly additive — 21 + 25 = 46 — so they are separable, and **they are separated
on purpose**. A card in a library has a printed mana value; a permanent on the battlefield and a
spell on the stack have a live one. One function answering both is the shape #319 found five bugs
in. This is the library half, which is also the bigger of the two.

It also says the two additions have to ship **together**: `permanent` alone finishes five cards and
the clause alone six, but the Rebel and Mercenary tutor chains print both at once ("a Rebel permanent
card with mana value 3 or less" is nineteen lines between them), so together they finish 25.

### The clause is peeled in a wrapper, and one card is the reason

`libraryFilter` is now a wrapper that peels ` with mana value N or less|greater` off the end and
hands the rest to the old body, renamed `cardFilterBody`. Not an arm inside the body, because of
**Behold My Grandeur**: "a card with mana value 6 or greater". The body reads "a card" to
`filter: null`, which means *any card* — so an arm that applied the clause per-body would leave that
phrase searching the whole library, a strictly better card than the one printed. Peeling first makes
the clause apply to every body uniformly, including the one with no filter of its own. The runtime
test for it is the one with 47 Forests in the library.

`filter` is optional **as well as** nullable, so the guard tests both: "any card" arrives as `null`
or `undefined` depending on which arm answered.

### `permanent` is not a type, and that was already a recorded bug

`cardWordMatch` refused `permanent` deliberately — its own docblock records that the first draft
compiled "a permanent card" into a filter asking for a type line containing the word, which no card
has (CR 205.2a), so the search offered nothing on a card that otherwise worked. It is read now as
what CR 110.1 says a permanent **is**: any of the six permanent types. The list is the
`PERMANENT_TYPES` that `permanentWordMatch` already had, shared rather than copied, because "is this
a permanent" has one answer and now two callers — and the difference from `SEARCHABLE_TYPES` is the
point, since `instant` and `sorcery` are searchable and never permanents.

### What it refuses, and all of it is about where the bound comes from

The same rule D489's unless-paid arm needed, for the same reason.

* **`{X}`** — Lin Sivvi, Defiant Hero: "a Rebel permanent card with mana value X or less", where X is
  chosen when the ability is activated.
* **A bound that is a fact about the board** — Sisay, Weatherlight Captain: "with mana value less
  than Sisay's power". The regex requires a digit, so both of these fall through and stay unread.
* **A bare equality** — "with mana value 3". Magic prints `or less` and `or greater` here; neither
  alone is read.

And the vocabulary still missing in this position, each a real printing, each left unread rather
than read loosely: a `non` negation (`a nonland permanent card`, Guardian Sunmare), a colour word
(`a colorless creature card`, Conduit of Ruin), both at once (`a nonlegendary green creature card`,
Woodland Bellower), a filter that reads another object (`with the same name as target nontoken
creature`, Bifurcate), and a three-way disjunction across filters (Search for Glory). Those are the
next increment in this family, not oversights — the compile test has a row for each.

### The break run, and one test that is weaker than it reads

Five breaks, all five caught: the comparison inverted, the bound made exclusive, the clause peeled
and then discarded, the body filter dropped so only the number is read, and `permanent` read as a
word on the line.

Worth recording that break 4 — dropping the body filter — failed only **three** of the five runtime
tests. "4 or greater" passed it, because nothing else in that library has mana value 4 or more, so
the type filter was doing no work in that one case. The other three catch it, so the suite
discriminates; the single test does not, and saying so is cheaper than discovering it later.

### `typecheck:tests` again, for the third increment running

`#246`'s target caught it again, and the plain typecheck is clean on it: a `DecisionSpecOf` may be a
**function** of the state — that is how a question whose shape depends on the board is declared — so
`decisions[0].prompt` does not typecheck. Narrowed with an assertion rather than cast, because an
`as` would have turned "this compiled to the wrong kind of decision" into a runtime `undefined` that
the prompt assertions would have read as a missing prompt.

### What it bought

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,476 | **10,504** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,040 | **6,065** |
| printed rules lines read | 20,603 / 56,421 (36.5%) | **20,635 / 56,421 (36.6%)** |

25 cards and 32 lines, which is what `mv-split.mjs` predicted for this arm to the card.

### Still open, and now sized

**The other half: a mana-value clause outside a search** — 21 cards, 35 lines, on target phrases,
D490's spell phrases and a trigger's subject scope. It reads a *live* mana value, which is why it is
its own increment and not this one.

### Addendum: the gate found four stale refusal rows, and one of them was a test I had written myself

The first full gate run failed in `compile.test.ts` with four failures, all of the same kind — rows
asserting that the compiler **refuses** exactly what this increment makes it read:

| where | row | what it said |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D449 | `a Rebel permanent card` | "`permanent` is not a type (CR 205.2a)" |
| D449 | `refuses "a permanent card"` | a standalone test, with a paragraph on why accepting it would be worse than an unread line |
| D455 | `a mana value condition` | "a filter this module cannot build" |
| D455 | `a category that is not a type` | "the D449 guard still refuses it" |

This is the third increment running where the gate caught a stale row rather than a defect (D469's
`destroy target Wall`, D489's two spell-kind rows), and it is worth saying why that keeps happening
and why it is a good sign: this suite writes its *refusals* down with the reason, so closing a gap
makes the old reason fail loudly instead of quietly becoming untrue. Four rows is four places the
project would otherwise now be lying about what it can read.

Each was moved rather than deleted, with its history in place — D449 already had a "retired rows"
table from D455, so this is the fourth entry in it. The D449 standalone test is the interesting one:
its reasoning is still entirely correct ("permanent" is not a type, and reading it as one offers
nothing, silently), so the test keeps the paragraph and inverts the assertion, because what changed
is the *reading* and not the rule. A reader that matched `permanent` against the type line would
still be the bug that test was written to forbid.

One row left behind in D449 on purpose: `a green creature card`. A colour is not on the type line at
all, so it needs a filter over `CardDef.colors` — the next increment in this family, and now the
only row in that table.

## D492 — A mana-value clause on a target phrase

The other half of D491, and the measurement **corrected my own framing of it twice** before any code
was written. Both corrections are the point of the entry.

### First correction: the clause is not a search feature

D491's probe found `with mana value N or less|greater` printed in four different places, not one. So
`mv-context.mjs` priced each context separately, by substitution in place, ranked by cards finished
(D434):

| reader | cards finished | lines | cards touched |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **battlefield permanent target** | **17** | 29 | 155 |
| **spell on the stack** | **3** | 5 | 10 |
| graveyard/hand **card** target | 1 | 2 | 90 |
| cast-trigger condition | 0 | 0 | 26 |
| library dig | 0 | 0 | 4 |

### Second correction: the biggest printed block is nearly worthless

I had said the graveyard-card block was the thing to build, because it prints ~91 lines across four
shapes (`target creature card with mana value N or less` alone is 47). By **cards finished** it is
**one card**. It touches 90 and unblocks almost none of them, because those lines — the reanimation
and return-to-hand shapes — fail on something else that this clause is not holding up.

That is precisely the error D434 was written about, after the clause-queue ranking made it. I made it
again, from a line count, and the only reason it cost nothing is that the probe was run before the
code. Worth stating plainly: **a line count is not a work estimate in this compiler**, because a line
with two problems counts once in the family of each.

So the increment is the top two rows — 20 cards, 34 lines — and the bottom three are recorded rather
than built.

### One peel, two numbers, and that is the whole subtlety

The clause is peeled in `targetSpecFrom` and the rest of the phrase is **re-read by the same
function**, one level deep. That is why it works for every shape at once: the switch's exact phrases,
D486's noun-position disjunction, D490's spell kinds, and the controller clauses all keep working with
a clause bolted on, and nothing downstream learns about mana value. It has to be peeled *first*
because the clause sits **after** the controller clause — "target creature an opponent controls with
mana value 3 or less" — and `parsedTargetPhrase` strips `an opponent controls` by matching the end of
the body.

Where the number comes from depends on the spec's `kind`:

* **A permanent** — the mana value of its **printed** mana cost, where X counts as nought
  (CR 202.3b). Despark does not see an X creature as a seven-drop because its controller paid seven.
* **A spell on the stack** — `manaValueOnStack`, which exists for exactly this: X is the announced
  value while the spell is being cast. Disdainful Stroke would never be able to answer an X spell if
  this read the printed cost.

Endless One is the card that makes both testable, and the runtime pair is the best thing in this
increment: printed `{X}`, cast for X=4, it is a 4/4 on the battlefield with mana value **0** and a
mana value of **4** while on the stack. So "destroy target creature with mana value 1 or less" may
point at the resolved 4/4, and "counter target spell with mana value 4 or greater" may point at the
same card on the stack. The break run confirms they are independent: using the printed cost for both
fails only the stack test, and using the stack value for both fails only the battlefield test.

### What it refuses

Where the **bound** comes from, which is the rule D489 and D491 both needed: Lin Sivvi's `{X}`, a
bound that is a fact about the board, and a bare `with mana value 3` (Magic prints `or less` and
`or greater` here and this reads neither alone). Plus two refused by their **phrase** rather than the
clause, each a real printing: Divide by Zero's "spell or permanent", which reaches across the stack
and the battlefield at once, and Exile into Darkness, where the clause is on a *sacrifice* and not on
a target.

### The break run asked for a test I had not written

Five breaks, five caught — but break 4, dropping the inner filter and keeping only the number, passed
every test in the block on the first pass. "Target creature" carries no filter of its own, so there
was nothing for the break to shadow. The row that catches it is Baffling End's shape, "an opponent
controls **and** mana value 3 or less", asserting that a two-drop of your own is within the bound and
still not a legal target. Added, and the break then failed as it should.

### `typecheck:tests`, for the fourth increment running

`Compilation` is a union whose failing arm has no `script`, so `instant(text).script` does not
typecheck. Narrowed once in a helper rather than cast at five call sites. The plain
`tsc -p tsconfig.json` has been clean on every one of these four.

### What it bought

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,504 | **10,527** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,065 | **6,085** |
| printed rules lines read | 20,635 / 56,421 (36.6%) | **20,665 / 56,421 (36.6%)** |

### Found while probing this, and bigger than it: "This spell can't be countered"

Abrupt Decay's resolution line reads perfectly on its own and the card still does not compile,
because `This spell can't be countered.` is an unread line and a spell needs every line read. Sized:
**85 legal cards touched, 95 lines, 24 cards finished outright.**

It is **not** a parse. Dropping the line makes the card strictly worse than printed — answerable when
it should not be — and that is still a wrong reading even though it errs conservatively. It wants a
`CardScript` flag that `counterSpell` and `counterUnlessPaid` respect, which is an engine feature with
its own tests, so it is recorded as its own task rather than bolted onto this one.

### Addendum: a fifth stale refusal row, and this one was mine from two increments ago

The gate failed on one row, in D490's own table:

```
['Counter target red or green spell with mana value 6 or less.',
  'Change the Equation: the mana-value clause, not the colours'],
```

D490 wrote it deliberately, with a comment calling it "the clause family that is still open rather
than closed by this increment" and naming which half of the phrase was the reason. D492 closes that
half, so the row failed — loudly, in the gate, saying exactly what had changed.

That is now **five refusal rows in five increments** that a later increment turned into a reading
(D469's `destroy target Wall`, D489's two spell-kind rows, D491's four in D449/D455, and this one),
and the third I wrote myself. It is worth stating as a property rather than an annoyance: this suite
writes the *reason* beside every refusal, so closing a gap cannot quietly make a test's stated
rationale untrue — the test fails and names the half that moved. A suite that only asserted "this
does not read" would have gone on passing while its explanation rotted.

The row moved to D492's mapping table; the note stays where the row was.

## D493 — "This spell can't be countered": built, measured, and held back for a pool card

Written, tested, gated — and **reset off the branch**, because the gate found a real gap rather than
a defect. Recorded here in full so the work is not lost with the session that did it.

### What it was worth

`This spell can't be countered.` was an unread line, and a spell needs every printed line read or
declared, so it refused the **whole card**. Abrupt Decay's resolution line reads perfectly on its
own and the card still did not compile.

Measured first: 85 legal cards touched, 95 lines, 24 cards finished outright. Delivered, with the
suite green: **10,527 → 10,604 cards with a compiled script, 6,085 → 6,110 fully read, 20,665 →
20,767 of 56,421 lines (36.8%)**. The +77 against a predicted 24 is because the probe counted only
cards where *everything* became readable.

### The design, in four pieces

1. `CardScript.cantBeCountered?: true`.
2. `spellStaticFromLine()` in `scripts.ts`, wired into **both** line loops — `spellScriptFor` and
   `lineScriptFor`. Both are needed and the first draft had only the first: Abrupt Decay and Dovin's
   Veto are spells, while Carnage Tyrant, Thrun, Blurred Mongoose and Great Sable Stag print the
   same line on a **permanent**, which goes through the other loop. Probing real printings is what
   caught that; an assumption would have shipped half the family.
3. `StackObject.cantBeCountered?: true`, copied off `scriptForCard` at the cast site. It has to
   travel on the object: `counterSpell` is in `effects.ts`, which cannot import `derive.ts` —
   `derive → compile → scripts → effects` is a cycle. It is also the honest shape, since it is a
   fact about *this casting*.
4. A guard at the top of `counterSpell`, the single chokepoint for ward's unpaid settle, the bot and
   every scripted counter.

Not a skipped line, on principle: a spell that can be countered when its text says it cannot is
**worse than printed**, and a reading that errs generously is still wrong (D259, D362). Refused with
test rows: `Spells your opponents cast can't be countered` (a permanent's static about *other*
objects — collapsing it in would be wrong in both directions at once) and the narrower
`can't be countered by spells or abilities your opponents control`.

### Why it is not on the branch

The gate failed one check: **`deck coverage > has a card behind every mechanic it declares`**.

That check is right, and it is the only thing in the suite that could have caught this. It enforces
D229's rule — *a mechanic needs a card in a deck to exist in the pool* — and reads the declared
surface straight out of `scriptTypes.ts` so that a field added for an engine change whose cards
never arrive cannot slip through. No card in the thirteen built-in decks prints the line, so the
mechanic would have shipped unexercised at a real table.

**The field was not added to that test's `plumbing` exemption set**, and that is the decision worth
recording. The exemption would have made the gate green in one line. The test's own docblock argues
against it — a list there is "a second place to forget the next mechanic" — and weakening a check to
pass a change is the one move that makes every future green meaningless.

### What finishing it costs, and why that is its own change

A real card that prints the line, hand-written, with a deck slot. **Dovin's Veto** is the candidate:
`{W}{U}`, "Counter target noncreature spell. This spell can't be countered", both halves already
supported (`isNoncreatureSpell` is what hand-written Negate uses), and the white-blue answers deck is
the obvious home.

That is a **balance change**, and this project measures those (#96, #139, #231). Doing it in passing
would have meant an unmeasured deck swap riding along inside a compiler increment — which is the
thing the increment loop exists to prevent. So it is split out rather than smuggled in.

### One lesson from its break run

Four breaks, four caught — but only after fixing one of the breaks. Break 3 looked uncaught, and the
real explanation was that the `sed` anchor did not match the file, so **nothing had been broken**.
Written correctly it failed three tests.

*A break that silently fails to apply is indistinguishable from a test that does not discriminate.*
Check the edit landed before concluding anything about the suite. This nearly cost two good tests.

## D494 — An instrument for which shape to read next, and two things it corrected

Twice in two increments I ranked work by **lines printed** and was wrong. The graveyard mana-value
block prints about 91 lines and finishes **one card** (D492). D434 already said to rank by cards
finished; the earlier attempt at that ranking over-counted, because it replaced whole clauses
including their destinations. So this is the instrument, built properly.

### How it works, and why it cannot over-count

`scripts/measure/one-away.mjs`. A card with **exactly one** unread line is one shape away from
compiling completely, so that line is what blocks it. Normalise the line into a shape — the card's
own name, numbers and mana costs generalised — and count the cards per shape. No per-family
substitution logic, so there is nothing to get wrong in the swap; the only judgement is how wide the
shape is.

Over the legal corpus: **30,710 cards compile, 16,101 of them have exactly one unread line**, in
13,140 distinct shapes.

### The instrument's own first answer was wrong, and probing caught it

The first version truncated each line to seven words. Its top row read "204 cards —
`Whenever ~ deals combat damage to a`", which looked like the biggest family ever measured here.
It is not a family. The trigger *event* already reads:

```
READS   Whenever ~ deals combat damage to a player, draw a card.
READS   Whenever ~ deals combat damage to a player, you gain 2 life.
unread  Whenever ~ deals combat damage to a player, that player discards a card.
unread  Whenever ~ deals combat damage to a creature, destroy that creature.
```

What is unread is the **effect clause after** the trigger, and it differs card by card. A seven-word
shape grouped cards by shared *prefix* — which is the line-count error again, wearing a better
disguise. An instrument built to stop me mis-ranking was mis-ranking.

Fixed by widening the shape to fourteen words, which splits the prefix buckets into real families.
Recorded rather than quietly corrected, because the lesson is about instruments and not about this
one: **a grouping is a claim, and a claim about what blocks a card has to be checked against a card.**

### The queue it gives, which is the useful output

| cards | the one line that blocks them |
| --- | --- |
| 29 | `~ can't block.` |
| 29 | `~ attacks each combat if able.` |
| 29 | Threshold — as long as there are seven or more cards in your graveyard, … |
| 25 | `{M}: Add {M} or {M}. ~ deals N damage to you.` (the painlands) |
| 25 | `~ can't be blocked.` |
| 23 | `{M}: ~ gets +N/-N until end of turn.` |
| 22 | `{M}, {M}: Tap target creature.` |
| 22 | `~ can block only creatures with flying.` |
| 21 | Changeling |
| 18 | Bushido N |
| 16 | Fear / Soulshift N / enter as a copy |

The top of that list is a cluster worth **105 cards**: four one-line combat statics, all four already
modelled in `Characteristics` as `cantBlock`, `mustAttack`, `cantBeBlocked` and
`cantBeBlockedByWalls`. And the reason they are unread is precise: `characteristicsOf` initialises
all four to `false` and only ever sets them from `state.effects`, while printed **landwalk** and
printed **protection** are seeded from the oracle text a few lines above, because they are *base*
characteristics that "loses all abilities" should clear (CR 613.1f). The four combat statics belong
in exactly that place and are not there. Two precedents, one new reader.

### Also measured and deliberately not built

A **colour word** and a **`non` negation** in a library-search card filter — the last two rows of
D449's refusal table. **5 cards, 6 lines** between them (1 and 3 alone). It would need
`cardWordMatch` widened from a type-line predicate to a whole-card-definition one, across both of
its call sites, because a colour is not on the type line. Against D490's 38 cards, D491's 25,
D492's 23 and D493's 77, it does not earn that. The rows stay as refusals.

### Addendum: a guard I did not know about, pointing at every number in this session

The gate failed before a single test ran, on `scripts/guards.js`:

```
[guards] 1 script(s) import the engine's dist directly:
[guards]   scripts/measure/one-away.mjs
[guards] Import from scripts/lib/engine.mjs instead. It re-exports the same
[guards] module and warns on stderr when dist is older than the engine source.
```

The reason is the one this instrument needed most. `scripts/lib/engine.mjs` compares `dist`'s mtime
against the newest engine source on import and warns if it is stale, because a harness run after a
source change but before a rebuild "measures the previous build — and prints a number that is not
wrong, merely about code that is no longer there". D338 is the precedent: a measure printed the
pre-change share **to a tenth of a percent** off a stale `dist`. The guard exists because
`provenanceLine` was opt-in and 45 of 52 scripts never called it — "a warning you have to remember
to ask for is a warning that is missing from exactly the script nobody was thinking carefully
about".

This lands on more than the one file. Every number in this session came from a scratchpad probe
importing `dist` directly, outside the guard's reach. I rebuilt `dist` before each measurement and
the re-run through the wrapper gives **identical** figures — 30,710 compiling, 16,101 one-away,
13,140 shapes — so the numbers stand. But they stood by habit rather than by check, and the habit is
exactly what D338 says is not enough.

Fixed by routing the instrument through `../lib/engine.mjs`, with the reason in its own docblock:
this harness reports *which shape to build next*, so a number about the previous build would send the
next increment at the wrong family.

## D495 — The three one-line combat statics, which the engine already knew and could not see

D494's queue put this at the top of the list: four one-line combat statics worth 105 cards. The
reason they were unread is the sharpest kind there is — **the engine already implemented all of it.**
`Characteristics` has had `cantBlock`, `cantBeBlocked` and `mustAttack` since #76, the pool's
hand-written cards set them through `statics`, `canBlock` and `forcedAttackers` enforce them, and a
dozen tests cover the rules. What was missing was the only path an **imported** card has: its
printed text. `characteristicsOf` initialised the three to `false` and set them from `state.effects`
alone, while printed landwalk and printed protection are seeded from oracle text a few lines above,
because they are *base* characteristics that "loses all abilities" must clear (CR 613.1f).

So Aesthir Glider blocked, Aether Figment was blocked and Akoum Firebird sat at home — each in flat
contradiction of its own card, on a board where the rule it needed was running for somebody else.

### A scope cut found by reading, before writing anything

The queue's 105 cards are **four** shapes, not three:

```
  88  ~ can't block.                                  [Aesthir Glider]
  59  ~ attacks each combat if able.                  [Akoum Firebird]
  58  ~ can't be blocked.                             [Aether Figment]
  28  ~ can block only creatures with flying.         [Ascending Aven]
```

`Characteristics` has a field for the first three and **none** for the fourth. "Can block only
creatures with flying" is not `cantBlock` narrowed, it is a new restriction with its own predicate
inside `canBlock`, and reading it onto any existing field would be a wrong reading rather than an
unread line (D362). It is 22 cards and a separate increment; a refusal row in `compile.test.ts` names
it so the next reader knows it was seen and left.

Scope: the **three** the engine already models — 83 cards by the queue, 205 printed lines.

### The reading, and the one thing about it that is not obvious

`printedCombatLine` runs on the **whole line, before the comma split**, and that is not a stylistic
choice. The subject of these lines is the card's own name, and **11 of the 192 cards have a comma in
theirs**: "Etrata, the Silencer can't be blocked." comma-split is "Etrata" and "the Silencer can't be
blocked", and neither half is anything at all. The other three printed-ability readers (keywords,
landwalk, protection) are comma-part readers because their lines are comma-separated *lists*; this
one is a sentence.

The subject must be the card itself, in the three spellings printed text uses:

- its **full name** — "Aesthir Glider can't block."
- its **short name** — "Bilbo can't be blocked.", on *Bilbo, Luckwearer*. 9 of the 192 print only
  this, and the corpus confirmed the convention rather than my memory of it: *Ares, God of War*,
  *Hulk, Always Angry* and *Hulk, Brutal Brawler* all use the short name in **every** line they
  print, not just this one.
- **"this creature"** — the 2024 retemplate's second reference. 9 cards, plus one *"This land can't
  be blocked"* on a land that becomes a creature.

`shortName` already existed, in `scripts.ts`, where `selfRef` builds the engine's one self-reference
pattern out of it. It **moved to `characteristics.ts`** rather than being copied, because the import
between the two modules only runs one way — `scripts.ts` imports `characteristics.ts`, never the
reverse — and the vocabulary of "this ..." words moved with it as `SELF_TYPE_WORDS`, which `selfRef`
is now built from. Two lists would have been two places to forget a word; D433's thousands-separator
rule (*70,000 Light-Years from Home* must not offer "70" as a name for itself) now has exactly one
home.

Everything else is refused, and the refusals are the reading:

| printed | why it is refused |
| --- | --- |
| `Enchanted creature can't block.` | an Aura **granting** the restriction to its host |
| `Equipped creature can't be blocked.` | the same, for Equipment |
| `Creatures can't block.` | a one-sided Fog |
| `Blue creatures you control can't be blocked.` | a team-wide static |
| `~ can't be blocked except by creatures with flying.` | the predicate is not one of the three |
| `~ gets +2/+2 and can't block.` | a pump welded on — read the clause alone and the creature gets the restriction without the compensation printed beside it |
| `Threshold — As long as ..., ~ gets +2/+2 and can't block.` | behind a condition |
| `Wraith Form — ~ can't be blocked.` | an ability word prefix, unpeeled |

Handing an Aura the restriction it only grants is the exact mistake the whole-line rule exists to
prevent (D487): strictly worse for the player than leaving the line to a human.

### The break run, and a break that applied and still proved nothing

Five breaks, each **verified to have changed the file** before the tests ran — D493's lesson, where a
`sed` anchor silently failed to match and the tests "passed" against unbroken code.

The table is in the addendum below, because the first run of it had a defect of its own.

**The first break was wrong twice before it discriminated.** My first version made the subject
optional — accept any subject at all — and **every test still passed.** The reason is worth keeping:
for "Enchanted creature can't block.", the *predicate* lookup refuses it anyway, because the leftover
clause is "enchanted creature can't block" and that is not one of the three phrases. The subject check
is not what refuses an Aura's line; the predicate is. What the subject check actually buys is refusing
a **loose prefix strip** — a reader that threw away everything before the first "can't" would read
"Enchanted creature can't block" as a restriction on the Aura. Rewritten that way the break fails 12
rows.

Which sharpens D493's rule rather than repeating it: a break that *applies* can still be a no-op,
and a passing break run is only evidence once each break has been shown to move a specific row for a
reason you can state.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed rules lines read | 20,665 / 56,421 (36.6%) | **20,870 / 56,421 (37.0%)** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,085 | **6,171** |
| of those, needing no script at all | (not taken) | **1,077** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,527 | 10,527 |

The last row does not move, and it should not: these lines are counted **compiled and emit nothing**,
exactly as a printed keyword is, so a card whose only line is one of them needs no script at all —
which is what the fourth row counts. 86 cards finished rather than the queue's 83, the difference
being short-name cards with other lines that were already read.

### Addendum: the gate caught a break that never got reverted

The gate failed with 3 of the 5 runtime tests red — the `cantBlock` and `mustAttack` ones, with
`cantBeBlocked` passing — on a tree where those same tests had passed in isolation an hour earlier.

The cause was not in the engine. I had run the break harness as
`python3 break495.py 2>&1 | head -8`. `head` closes the pipe after eight lines, Python raised
`BrokenPipeError` on its next `print`, and the process died **mid-run, with break 4 applied** — the
one that removes the seeding. The revert never ran. So the candidate tree counted all 209 lines
compiled and set none of the three fields: the compile half green, the table half broken, and the
coverage numbers unchanged because they do not depend on the seeding.

This is D493's lesson arriving from the other side. There, a break silently failed to **apply**, so a
passing run proved nothing. Here, a break silently failed to **revert**, so a passing run was measured
against code that was still broken. Both read identically from the outside: tests that pass.

Three things changed as a result:

- The harness registers its revert with `atexit` and ends by comparing a SHA-256 of the file against
  its backup, printing the verdict. It now reads `final sha matches backup: True`. A stateful script
  does not get piped into `head` again.
- **One assertion was too weak, and break 4 is what exposed it.** The Inkfathom Infiltrator test
  pointed their Infiltrator at mine, which is refused by *either* half of "can't block and can't be
  blocked" — so it passed on the evasion alone while `cantBlock` was dead. It reads against an
  ordinary Grizzly Bears now, and the seeding break fails **4** tests rather than 3.
- The coverage figures were re-measured after the restore: **identical** — 20,870 lines (37.0%), 6,171
  cards fully read, 1,077 needing no script. They are a function of `compileCard` alone, and the
  seeding is not on that path. Expected, and now checked rather than assumed (D494).

The re-run break table, with every break verified both to apply and to revert:

| break | compile.test | scripts.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| strip everything before the predicate instead of naming the card | 12 fail | 1 fail |
| keep only the first clause, dropping the `and` | 1 fail | 1 fail |
| full name and "this X" only, no short name | 3 fail | pass |
| count the line compiled but seed nothing | pass | 4 fail |
| don't strip the trailing period | 17 fail | 5 fail |

### Addendum: the gate then failed twice on a runner error, and it was not a flake

With the seeding restored, the gate failed again — this time with **2637 tests passing, 15 of 15
files green, and one unhandled error**:

```
Error: [vitest-worker]: Timeout calling "onTaskUpdate"
Test Files  15 passed (15)
     Tests  2637 passed (2637)
    Errors  1 error
```

vitest exits non-zero on a run error, so the gate is red on a suite where nothing failed. It
reproduced **identically on a second run with nothing else on the machine**, which is what separates
this from the flake it looks like.

It is not a new problem and it is not mine, but the trigger was. `vitest.config.ts` carries the
measurement that chased this down once already: four mitigations that did not work (a worker cap, the
`dot` reporter, `--concurrency=3`, `singleFork`), and then the cause — **a worker that spends ten
seconds inside one synchronous test body cannot answer the reporter's RPC inside its timeout.** The
fix was `breathe()`, one `await` that defers to the event loop once per game, applied to "the five
tests long enough to matter".

Adding 35 tests to this package is what brought it back, and the durations say why: seven more test
bodies had grown past the point of mattering, the longest being **44 seconds** of uninterrupted
game-playing in "answers the questions cards ask mid-resolution". `breathe` is now in twelve places
rather than five — once per seed in six of those tests, and every 400 moves in the one that is a
single 20,000-move pod. The gate is green: `GATE_RC=0`, no unhandled errors.

The part worth keeping is in both files' comments now: **"long enough to matter" is not a fixed
list.** It grows with the suite, so the response when this error reappears is to read the per-test
durations in the failing run and give the yield to whichever long body lacks one — not to re-run, and
not to read 2637 passing tests as a pass.

### Verified at the table

Gate green on the third run: `GATE_RC=0`, no unhandled errors, every suite passing.

Pod sweep on a fresh seed set, run on the pushed commit (`0f01863 clean`, `dist` built from it):

```
GAMES=40 SEED0=34601
Games: 40    finished 40
Of the games that finished: 57.0 turns and 283 moves on average
Per deck of 100 (160 decks built):
  distinct cards the engine was given a script for: 23.5
  cards with at least one line nothing could read:  50.3
  cards playable only because of the printed data:  61.9
  cardboard — nothing could make them playable:     0.5
Every game reached a finish, with no throw and no stall.
```

40 of 40, as the three previous sweeps (34001, 34201, 34401) were. These statics are restrictions
rather than new actions, so the thing they could have broken is a stall — a board where every
creature must attack and none may block is one a naive implementation can wedge. It did not.

## D496 — Tap target, and a self-pump that shrinks: two siblings nobody wrote

Both readings were found by **asking the compiler** rather than reading it. D494's queue named its top
shapes; a probe compiled a synthetic card for each and printed which read. The answer had the two
findings sitting next to each other in the output:

```
READ    {G}, {T}: Untap target creature.
unread  {G}, {T}: Tap target creature.
READ    {G}: Probe Beast gets +1/+1 until end of turn.
unread  {G}: Probe Beast gets +1/-1 until end of turn.
```

Neither is a missing mechanism. `tap` is one primitive with its boolean either way round, and
`sizeBonus` has always accepted negatives — it refuses only `+0/+0`. In both cases every piece behind
the reader worked and the reader itself asked for too little, which is exactly why neither was
noticed: nothing failed, nothing threw, the cards simply came out unread.

### Tap target

`Untap target …` had two readers — a counted one and a single-target one — and `Tap target …` had
none, while **26 legal cards print `{W}, {T}: Tap target creature.` exactly** and 24 more print it
against an artifact, a Wall, or Icy Manipulator's three-way phrase.

The pool has carried a hand-written version of this clause since #52. **Icy Manipulator** —
`{1}, {T}: Tap target artifact, creature, or land.` — now compiles completely, and the standing
`compiled-vs-written` check says the compiled reading **agrees with the hand-written script field for
field**. That is the strongest confirmation available here: the ground truth was written by a person
reading the printed text, months before the reader existed.

Two things differ from the untap beside it, and both are deliberate:

- **`friendly` is `false`.** Untapping your own land is the point of a Kiora's Follower, and the
  untap's own comment says so; tapping your own creature throws the card away. Icy Manipulator's
  hand-written filter draws the same line.
- **No `untapsOnly`.** That flag exists because an untap can put the board back exactly as it was
  found, so the bot can loop for ever (#124). A tap moves the board one way. Carrying the flag would
  be *wrong* rather than redundant — it would mark a real play as a no-op.

### A self-pump that shrinks

The self-subject pump demanded a `+` on both halves. That is the **same oversight D252 found in the
targeted pump**, a few hundred lines further down, where its own comment still reads: *"265 legal
cards print the second \[sign\] … unread because the pattern above it demanded a `+`."* One reader
later, the same character.

The family it refused is `{B}: ~ gets +1/-1 until end of turn.` — Breathstealer, Darklit Gargoyle,
Cavern Crawler: 23 legal cards trading toughness for power. Unlike D252's reader the sign changes
nothing else, because the subject is the card itself: no `friendly` to flip, no second branch. The
regex was the whole of it.

The runtime test is the one that matters: Breathstealer is a 2/2, so two activations make it a 4/0
and it dies to a state-based action (CR 704.5a). A reader that dropped the negative half would leave
a 4/2 standing there.

### A refusal row I wrote and the test deleted

I expected `Tap two target creatures` to be turned down, reasoning that the untap needs a *separate*
`untappedMany` reader to set `TargetSpec.count`, so the single-target path must drop the number. It
does not: `TARGET_QUANTIFIER_PREFIX` carries "two" into `parsedTargetPhrase`, the count lands on the
spec, and `foldCardTargets` folds the effect over every target the engine filled in. **The untap's
extra reader predates that and is redundant for this.**

The row became an assertion rather than a deletion, because "it reads" was never the question: a
count silently dropped would tap one creature out of two and look like a working card (D362). Nomad
Decoy's printing is now pinned at `count: 2`.

### The break run

Five breaks, each verified both to **apply** and to **revert** (the harness registers its revert with
`atexit` and ends by comparing a SHA-256 against its backup — the D495 lesson):

| break | compile.test | scripts.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the tap reader, deleted | 8 fail | 2 fail |
| `friendly: true`, aiming the tap at its own side | 1 fail | pass |
| `untapsOnly: true`, telling the bot the tap buys nothing | 1 fail | pass |
| the boolean: untap instead of tap | pass | 1 fail |
| the pump sign: back to a plus on both halves | 6 fail | 1 fail |

`typecheck:tests` (#246) caught two things again — the fifth increment running, and `tsc -p
tsconfig.json` was clean on both: the action field is `abilityIndex`, not `ability`, and
`LegalActions` has no `activations` list, so a test that inspected the bot's offered aims could not
exist in that shape. The second became a test that asks the **engine** to refuse an illegal aim
instead, which is a better question anyway.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed rules lines read | 20,870 / 56,421 (37.0%) | **21,079 / 56,421 (37.4%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,527 | **10,673** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,171 | **6,316** |

Two regexes, 209 lines and 145 cards finished. Still unread in this family and named as refusal rows:
`non-Human creature` and `noncreature artifact` (a `non` in front of a capitalised type), Amber
Prison's second clause, and `Activate only once each turn.` — 13 cards, the next shape in the queue.

### The instrument's own interface

`one-away.mjs` read `process.argv[2]` alone, which no sibling in `scripts/measure/` does:
`compilable.mjs` and `corpus-decks.mjs` both take `--file`. Called the way the others are, it failed
with `ENOENT: open '--file'`. It takes both now, with a usage line and exit 2 rather than a stack
trace. A harness whose calling convention differs from its neighbours' is a harness that gets called
wrongly.

### Addendum: the increment's own sweep found the loop it created

The pod sweep on `SEED0=34801` came back **39 of 40**:

```
  seed 34819: looping — 2000 moves with no progress in precombat-main of turn 94,
              2000 of them auto:activate (Hyalopterous Lemure#0)
```

`{0}: Hyalopterous Lemure gets -1/-0 and gains flying until end of turn.` A real card, free and
repeatable, whose line was **unread until this increment** — so the loop could not have existed
before and is mine. It is #334's Umbral Mantle shape with the sign reversed: every activation is
legal and changes the board, so no stall detector that compares states can see it; the power simply
walks down for ever inside one step, the step never passes, and the game cannot end.

The fix is the **fourteenth member of the "spent on nothing" family**, and the second about a loop
rather than a card: `AbilityDef.selfShrink`, set by the compiler because it is the only thing that
knows the sign while it is reading the clause, carrying the keywords the ability grants in exchange.

**It took three attempts, and two of them are worth more than the fix.**

1. **Before and after.** The first version measured the board either side of the activation —
   `untapBoughtSomething`'s shape — and did nothing. An instrument said why in one run:
   `[shrink] no: stack`, **2001 times**. An activated ability goes on the stack, so `simulate`
   returns a board where the pump has not happened. The before/after approach cannot see an
   activation's effect at all. That is a fact about the whole family worth knowing.
2. **"Does it already have the word?"** The flag-reading version asked exactly the right question
   and the seed still looped, with the flag read correctly 2000 times. The reason is the first
   version's finding again from the other side: **the bot never passes priority**, so none of the
   abilities ever resolves, so the flying never arrives, so "does it already have flying" is
   permanently false and the stack goes 2000 deep. The rule needs the stack clause: one of these
   already waiting to resolve *is* the loop.
3. Both clauses, and seed 34819 finishes.

Neither was reasoned out. Both came from printing what the predicate actually saw (D489): the first
from a line of `no:` reasons, the second from the flag being read correctly while nothing changed.

**The rule is not "never shrink yourself."** Hyalopterous Lemure's first activation buys flying — a
4/3 the ground cannot block for a 3/3 it can — and that is the card. The bot takes the first and
declines the rest.

One of the three breaks exposed a weak assertion, as in D495. "Refuse every self-shrink, the first
one included" passed, because the test asked the **engine** whether the activation was legal, and a
bot filter does not change legality. It asks the bot's own choice now, walked forward a few moves
because the bot plays its land first and that is right.

Re-run on the same seed set: **40 of 40 finished, no throw and no stall**, 57.1 turns and 301 moves
on average.

## D497 — A mana ability that deals you damage, and eleven lands that tapped for nothing

The pain lands: `{T}: Add {W} or {U}. Adarkar Wastes deals 1 damage to you.` — 34 printed lines on
37 legal cards, the top unread shape in D494's queue after the two D496 closed.

### Three rules wear almost the same words, and the pool already had two of them

`scripts.ts` has carried the distinction in a comment since #69, and it decided how this was built:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **City of Brass** | **triggers.** "Whenever City of Brass becomes tapped, it deals 1 damage to you." The damage uses the stack and the table gets a window. |
| **Mana Confluence** | **costs.** `{T}, Pay 1 life`. A player on one life is never offered the mana, because a cost you cannot pay is not a cost you may choose to pay (CR 118.4). |
| **a pain land** | **effect.** One mana ability whose effect is both halves. It resolves immediately without the stack (CR 605.3a), nobody gets a window, and a player on one life may tap it and die. |

Building it as either of the other two would be a card that plays differently from its text (D362):
as a cost it would refuse the player who wants to kill themselves for the mana; as a trigger it would
hand the table a response window Magic does not give them. All three are now pinned by a runtime
test each.

That needed an engine change: `autoActions`'s mana branch added the mana and **returned**, so an
`effect` beside `produces` was silently dropped. Nothing in the pool had one, which is why it went
unnoticed — the pain lands are the first cards to need it. The effect runs before `settle`, so the
state-based action that kills a player on one life fires in the same breath.

### The damage is a fact about the line, not about the card

Adarkar Wastes prints two lines:

```
{T}: Add {C}.
{T}: Add {W} or {U}. Adarkar Wastes deals 1 damage to you.
```

Tapping for `{C}` costs nothing and tapping for `{W}` costs a damage. `foldManaLines` flattened both
