lines into one cost and one set of colours, so whichever line came first decided for all of them —
**the first version of this reader gave every pain land's colours no damage at all**, which is a card
that plays better than it reads. The colours are grouped by their own line's damage now, and a colour
printed on two lines with different damage is refused rather than guessed.

### What the refusal rows found, which is worse than what the increment set out to fix

Two synthetic refusal rows came back **read**: `{T}: Add {R}. ~ deals 1 damage to any target.` and
`{T}: Add {R}. ~ deals 0 damage to you.` Following that to real cards found the real thing.

`cardFromData` only answers when it can read the *whole* card, so a pain land with a second ability
falls through to `compile.ts`'s line-by-line path — and **that path had no mana reader at all.** The
general activated-ability reader claimed the line, built an ability out of the damage clause, and
dropped the `Add {U}` entirely:

```
Cephalid Coliseum  abilities: [{"d":"{T}: Add {U}. Cephalid Coliseum deals 1 damage to you."}]
                                                                        produces: undefined
```

**The compiled Coliseum tapped for nothing.** Eleven legal lands were in that state — Cephalid
Coliseum, Barbarian Ring, Cabal Pit, Centaur Garden and the rest of the Odyssey threshold cycle —
and it is strictly worse than an unread line, because the bot plays a land that makes no mana and
then cannot use it. This predates D497; what D497 added was the machinery to notice and to fix it.

Two changes, and the second is the general rule the first implies:

- `manaAbilitiesFromLine` is exported for the per-line path, asked **before** the general reader.
  Order is the whole fix: asked after, the general reader wins and the mana is lost again.
- A line that `isManaAbilityLine` says promises mana and that the mana reader cannot read is
  reported **unread**, full stop. It never reaches the general reader. That costs 4 lines and 3
  cards against the honest count — lines that were "read" while losing their mana — and it is the
  right trade.

### The break run

Six breaks, each verified to apply and to revert:

| break | compile.test | scripts.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the damage sentence is never read | 6 fail | 3 fail |
| the subject check: any "deals N damage to you" counts | 1 fail | pass |
| one damage for the whole card, as the fold used to | 3 fail | 3 fail |
| the engine never runs a mana ability's effect | pass | 3 fail |
| the per-line mana reader, removed | 1 fail | pass |
| an unreadable mana line falls through to the general reader | 2 fail | pass |

**The fifth break is why the Coliseum test exists.** Removing the per-line reader left every other
row green, because they are all single-line cards `cardFromData` reads whole — the same weak-coverage
lesson as D495's Inkfathom row and D496's legality assertion, three increments in a row.

A **sixth stale refusal row** was retired: `compile.test.ts` had Adarkar Wastes listed as a line that
"stays whole" because "the damage is not read". True of the reader as it stood, wrong now; moved to
a mapping row with its history kept, the third such row I wrote myself.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed rules lines read | 21,079 / 56,421 (37.4%) | **21,102 / 56,421 (37.4%)** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,316 | **6,340** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,673 | 10,672 |

+23 lines and +24 cards from the reading, less the 4 lines and 3 cards the honest refusal gives back,
and one card short on the script count for the same reason. The number that matters here is not in
the table: **eleven real lands now produce the mana they print.**

### Verified at the table

Gate green (`GATE_RC=0`, no unhandled errors). Pod sweep on a fresh seed set, on the pushed commit:

```
GAMES=40 SEED0=35001
Games: 40    finished 40
Of the games that finished: 67.2 turns and 346 moves on average
Every game reached a finish, with no throw and no stall.
```

40 of 40, as every sweep this stretch has been. The turn count reads higher than the 57.1 of the
previous sweep, and that is **not** a result: it is a different seed set, which is a different 160
decks. A pain land's damage would be expected to shorten games rather than lengthen them, so if the
difference were real it would point the wrong way — which is exactly why it is left as a number
about one seed set and not reported as a change.

## D498 — Printed restrictions on who may block, and a measured negative before it

### First, the increment that was not worth building

D494's queue put `Threshold — As long as there are seven or more cards in your graveyard,` at the
top, 29 cards, and the obvious cheap move was to **peel the ability word**: CR 207.2c says an
ability word has no rules meaning, so `Word — ` ought to come off the front of a line and leave
something readable. Measured before building, across every unread line in the legal corpus:

```
unread lines with an "<Word> — " prefix: 2006
of those, the remainder alone reads:       92
  21 Channel      17 Exhaust      11 Boast      9 Max speed      1 each: 14 others
```

**92 of 2006, and almost all of them are not ability words at all.** Channel, Exhaust, Boast and
Max speed are *keyword abilities* with real rules meaning — Channel is activatable from your hand,
Exhaust is once only, Boast needs the creature to have attacked, Max speed needs the speed counter.
Peeling them would read each card as doing strictly more than it prints, which is the wrong-reading
failure D362 is about. The genuine ability words in the list are about five one-off cards.

So: **not built**, and the reason is in the numbers rather than in a judgement. The `Threshold`
family needs the *condition* read, not the prefix dropped; the prefix is the cheap half and the
cheap half buys nothing.

### What was built instead

244 printed lines in 126 shapes say something about who may block this creature. The two sentences
that carry most of it:

```
~ can't be blocked by creatures with power 2 or less.      31 printed lines
~ can't be blocked except by creatures with flying.        the allow-list half
```

The fifth printed-characteristic reader, after keywords, landwalk, protection and D495's combat
statics, and the first that needs a **vocabulary** rather than a flag. `BlockerClause` is
declarative — power with a comparison, a colour, a card type, a creature type, a keyword — because
`Characteristics` is data that the view packs, the bot copies and the tests compare; a predicate in
it would be a closure crossing every one of those boundaries.

Two fields, not one:

- `cantBeBlockedBy` — a **ban**: a blocker answering any clause may not block.
- `blockableOnlyBy` — an **allow list**: a blocker must answer at least one, or it may not block.

They are opposite quantifiers over the same vocabulary, so a card printing both is **refused rather
than merged**. Nothing in 33,847 prints both, and the merge rule would be a judgement the printed
text does not settle — does the ban narrow the allow list, or does either alone let a blocker
through? Refusing leaves it to a human.

Enforced in `canBlock` off the **attacker**, where protection and the Wall clause already live: a
sentence about who may block this creature is a fact about the creature printing it. The refusal
message says the clause back in printed words, because "can't be blocked" alone is the least useful
thing the engine could say about an Amrou Kithkin.

**Counts are deliberately out.** "Can't be blocked by more than one creature" (17 lines) and "can't
be blocked except by three or more creatures" (6) are about how *many* creatures block, not which —
a fact about the whole declaration rather than about one blocker, which is `menaceSatisfied`'s
family. Named as refusal rows so the next reader knows they were seen.

### One reading was wrong twice before it was right

`creatures with power 3 or greater` read as nothing, because `blockerFilter` split the phrase on
"or" before trying it whole: `creatures with power 3` and a bare `greater`. The comparison words are
part of one clause. **Amrou Kithkin and the whole 40-line power family were refused for it**, and
the fix is to try the phrase whole first and treat only a phrase that is not itself a clause as a
list.

Then `creatures with flying or reach` was refused for the mirror reason: one noun carrying a list
*inside* it, which naive splitting turns into `creatures with flying` and a bare `reach`. That is its
own branch now, gated on every word being a keyword the engine actually has — which is why
`creatures with shadow` is still refused, shadow not being in `KEYWORDS`.

### The break run

Eight breaks, each verified to apply and to revert:

| break | compile.test | scripts.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the whole-phrase attempt, so "power 3 or greater" splits on "or" | 5 fail | 2 fail |
| the keyword-list branch inside one noun phrase | 1 fail | pass |
| the ban/allow conflict rule: merge instead of refusing | 1 fail | pass |
| the subject check: any sentence about blocking counts | 2 fail | pass |
| the lose-all-abilities reset | 1 fail | pass |
| the ban is never enforced | pass | 3 fail |
| the allow list is never enforced | pass | 1 fail |
| `blockerMatches` reads power the wrong way round | pass | 2 fail |

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed rules lines read | 21,102 / 56,421 (37.4%) | **21,187 / 56,421 (37.6%)** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,340 | **6,382** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,077 | **1,111** |

+85 lines and +42 cards. The "needing no script" row moving by 34 is the shape of this family: these
are creatures whose whole text is one sentence about blocking, and the engine now plays them off the
card definition with nothing to run.

**These three numbers are corrected.** The first reading of this table said 21,184 / 6,379 / 1,109,
and it was taken off a `dist` built before the last of D498's own edits went in — the ones a python
script dropped on the floor when it asserted after writing, and which had to be re-applied by hand.
D338 is the standing precedent for exactly this and `scripts/lib/engine.mjs` warns about it; the
warning is only as good as the rebuild that follows it. The figures above are the ones the committed
tree produces, re-measured twice (D499).

### Addendum: D495's exception-clause refusal row is retired

D495 refused `~ can't be blocked except by creatures with flying` for its **predicate** — an
allow-list is not one of the three statics and `Characteristics` had no field for it — and wrote
that refusal down as a row of its own. D498 gave it the field, so the line compiles now and the row
asserted an empty `unread` where there is nothing left unread. The gate caught it, which is the
whole reason the refusal rows are tests rather than comments.

It is retired the way the five before it were: the row leaves the refusal list, a paragraph in its
place says what it claimed and why that stopped being true, and the sentence itself — Aesthir
Glider's name and all — becomes an assertion in this file's D498 block. **The seventh stale refusal
row in this series, and the fourth I wrote myself.** The sixth was Adarkar Wastes, three increments
ago; a refusal row going stale is what progress through this queue looks like from inside the test
file, so the count is worth keeping rather than quietly resetting.

The row below it stays refused and is a different question: `Ascending Aven can block only
creatures with flying` is the *other* direction — a restriction on what this creature may block
rather than on who may block it — and it needs its own field and its own `canBlock` branch (#344).

## D499 — Five readers re-parsing the same string a few thousand times a move

D498's gate failed on a timeout, not an assertion: `playout.test.ts > answers the questions cards ask
mid-resolution` ran past 60s. It is the longest playout body in the file and it had been at 42.8s,
so the obvious reading was the one D495 already dealt with — a test body grown long enough that the
worker stops answering the reporter, fixed with `breathe()`.

**That reading was wrong, and the measurement is what said so.** The same test, alone, on the tree
with D498's two source files reverted:

| tree | that one test |
| --- | --- |
| before D498 | 42.8s |
| with D498 | over 60s, timed out |
| with D498 and this cache | **18.2s** |

A 40% jump from one reader is not a test that needs more room. `characteristicsOf` calls
`printedParts` three times on every read — once each for the combat statics, the blocker limits and
the landwalk — and the bot calls `characteristicsOf` thousands of times per decision, because every
position the search looks at re-reads every creature on the board. So each reader added to
`characteristics.ts` re-splits and re-regexes the same unchanged oracle text a few thousand times a
move, and **the cost lands on the whole engine rather than on the reader that added it**. D498 was
the fifth reader and the one that crossed the line; the four before it had been charging the same
rent unnoticed since each shipped.

### The fix is the one a pure function allows

`printedParts(oracleText, name)` is a pure function of two strings. It is memoised on them, keyed
name-then-text with a NUL between — either string may contain any other character, so a separator
that cannot appear in a card name or in oracle text is the only one that cannot collide.

**The key must carry the name**, and that is the one real hazard here rather than a precaution.
`~ can't be blocked by white creatures` is a self-subject restriction when the subject is the
card's own name and somebody else's restriction otherwise (the whole-line subject rule, D495,
D362). Key on the text alone and the first card to ask decides the answer for every card printing
that sentence — a creature that blocks when it may not, which is exactly what D362 says is worse
than not reading the line. A test asks it in both orders, since a one-way check passes on a cache
that never stores anything.

The value is shared, so nothing may mutate it: `printedParts` returns `readonly PrintedPart[]` and
every reader below builds its own result from it. A second test reads one card through all three
readers twice and checks they still agree.

The cap (200k entries, cleared rather than evicted) is a long-running server's bound, not a tuning
knob. The key space is the distinct (name, text) pairs a process sees — about 34k for the whole
corpus, plus one entry per distinct line from `isPrintedAbilityLine` during a compile sweep — so the
map cannot grow without end. Clearing is correct at any moment, which is the merit of memoising a
pure function and the reason no invalidation rule is needed.

### The break run

| break | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| the name dropped from the cache key | the collision test, both orders |
| a reader consumes the array it was handed (`parts.length = 0`) | the shared-value test |

Both verified to apply and to revert, the revert checked against a SHA-256 of the backup — the
habit D495 earned.

### Proved behaviour-neutral, not assumed

A cache that changes an answer is a bug wearing a speed-up, so the check is the coverage sweep with
the cache's *read* disabled — every call recomputes, every call still stores — and the two runs
compared:

| | with the cache | cache read disabled |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,672 | 10,672 |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,382 | 6,382 |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,111 | 1,111 |

Identical on all three, across 30,710 legal cards. That is also what caught D498's stale `dist`:
running the sweep twice on purpose is what made the three-line discrepancy visible at all.

### What this does not claim

It does not claim the engine is 2.3x faster in play. It claims one playout body is, and that body
is bot-search heavy, which is where `characteristicsOf` is hot — a position the bot never looks at
twice pays the parse once either way.

What the gate's own clock says, though, is larger than the one test:

| rules-engine suite | |
| --- | --- |
| the failing D498 tree | 540.23s, 2 failed of 2705 |
| with this cache | **137.71s, 2707 passed** |

**3.9x, on the same 15 test files.** The suite is mostly engine simulation, so that is the closest
thing here to a measurement of the engine rather than of one test — but it is still a test suite,
not a table with people at it. The honest claim is: five readers were re-parsing the same strings,
they have stopped, and everything that calls `characteristicsOf` in a loop got cheaper by roughly
that factor. The number to compare against is the next gate's.

## D500 — The mirror: what a creature may block

D495 refused `~ can block only creatures with flying` and said so; D498 refused it again, named the
count, and left it for its own increment. This is that increment. **#344 closed.**

### Why it is two more fields and not a reuse of D498's two

This is the whole decision, and getting it wrong would have been expensive:

| sentence | who it restricts | field |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `~ can't be blocked by creatures with flying` | fliers may not block **it** | `cantBeBlockedBy` (D498) |
| `~ can block only creatures with flying` | **it** may not block a non-flier | `blocksOnly` (D500) |

A Cloud Pirates is a 1/1 flier with no evasion whatsoever and a very bad blocker. Fold the two
directions into one pair of lists and all 29 cards in the allow-list half silently become
unblockable from the ground — evasion they do not print, on cards a player would then lose games
to. That is the D362 mistake committed 29 times over, and worse than leaving the line unread.

So `Characteristics` gains `cantBlockThese` and `blocksOnly` beside D498's pair, seeded in
`characteristicsOf` with the other printed characteristics and cleared by "loses all abilities"
(CR 613.1f), and `canBlock` reads D498's two off the **attacker** and these two off the
**blocker**. One test asserts the separation from the reader's end and one from the table's.

### The family, and what read for free

39 printed lines, all of them read:

```
~ can block only creatures with flying.              29 lines — the entire allow-list half
~ can't block creatures with power N or greater.      6
~ can't block creatures with power N or less.         2
~ can't block artifact creatures.                     1   Hinterland Drake
~ can't block black creatures.                        1   Gibbering Hyenas
```

The last two cost **no new parsing**. The filter vocabulary is D498's `blockerFilter`, unchanged, so
the moment the subject-and-verb shape read, every clause D498 could already parse read with it. That
is the argument for having built D498's filters as a vocabulary rather than as one sentence's regex,
and it is the first time that has paid.

`blockerMatches` is now `clauseMatches`, because it is asked about the attacker here and its
parameter was called `blocker`. Same body, honest name.

### What stays refused, and the one that is only half-read

Every other `can block only` printing hands the restriction to somebody else — an Aura's "Enchanted
creature", Chaosphere's "Creatures with flying", or a spell quoting the sentence onto a token it
creates — and the whole-line subject rule refuses all of them, as it does for D495 and D498.

`~ can't block` and `~ can't block and can't be blocked` are **D495's** statics and stay there:
`printedParts` asks the combat reader first, and a test pins that this reader claims neither, since
the ban regex is `can't block (.+)` and "and can't be blocked" is a `.+`.

**Orgg and Goblin Mutant are read in half and that is the right answer.** Each prints trample, a ban
this reads, and `~ can't attack if defending player controls an untapped creature with power 3 or
greater` — a condition nothing reads. Two lines compile, one is reported unread. The whole-line rule
is per line precisely so that a card like this is more useful than all-or-nothing in either
direction.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed rules lines read | 21,187 / 56,421 (37.6%) | **21,224 / 56,421 (37.6%)** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,382 | **6,411** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,111 | **1,135** |

+37 lines and +29 cards. The reader answers 39 lines across the whole corpus; 37 of those are on
cards inside the sanctioned-format filter, which is the number that counts here.

### The break run

Nine breaks, each verified to apply and to revert, the revert checked against a SHA-256 of the
backup:

| break | compile.test | scripts.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the subject check: any sentence about blocking counts | 2 fail | pass |
| the allow list and the ban swapped | 8 fail | 4 fail |
| the both-ban-and-allow refusal | 1 fail | pass |
| the lose-all-abilities reset for the new two fields | 1 fail | pass |
| the reader is never wired into `printedParts` | 10 fail | 4 fail |
| the ban is never enforced | pass | 3 fail |
| the allow list is never enforced | pass | 1 fail |
| both lists asked about the blocker instead of the attacker | pass | 3 fail |
| the restriction written into D498's fields as well (the mirror collapse) | pass | 1 fail |

The last row is worth reading twice: the compile-level mirror test asks `printedBlockerLimit`
directly, so a break at the *seeding* site leaves it green and only the table-level test catches it.
Two tests for one claim, at two different levels, and only together do they cover it.

### A test that passed for the wrong reason, caught before it shipped

The first version of the table-level mirror test attacked with Cloud Pirates and blocked with
Grizzly Bears, expecting the block to be legal. It is not — Cloud Pirates has flying. **Nearly every
card in the allow-list half is a flier**, which is the point of the sentence, so a test built on one
is decided by the flying rule rather than by anything D500 does.

Gibbering Hyenas is the card that can prove it: no evasion at all, so a black Gravedigger blocking
the Hyenas is refused only if the ban leaked onto the wrong side. The Cloud Pirates case is kept as
a second test asserting *which rule* refused the block — "can't block a flier", not "can't be
blocked except by" — which is all the flying rule leaves room to say. Third increment running in
which a break run or a failing assertion exposed a test that would have passed on half the
behaviour.

### Named and left

`Creatures with power less than ~'s power can't block it` — **9 cards** (Aura Gnarlid, Battering
Wurm, Den Protector and six more). D498's direction, not this one, but it needs a clause kind whose
answer depends on *both* creatures, and `clauseMatches` deliberately sees only one. That is a
signature change to a matcher two field pairs now depend on, so it is its own increment rather than
a rider here.

## D501 — Three keywords whose rules text is the list D498 and D500 just built

The payoff increment. **#346 closed.**

```
fear          37 printed lines   CR 702.36a   except by artifact creatures and/or black creatures
shadow        39                 CR 702.28b   can block or be blocked by only creatures with shadow
horsemanship  25                 CR 702.5b    except by creatures with horsemanship
```

101 legal lines, and not one of the three was in `KEYWORDS`, so `printedKeywords` could never return
one and a card whose entire text is the word `Fear` — six of them — read as nothing.

**Every one of these rules is already expressible.** Fear is an allow list of
`{type:'artifact'}` and `{colour:'B'}`; horsemanship is an allow list of one keyword; shadow is an
allow list in **both** directions at once, which is exactly the half D500 added three hours ago and
the first rule in this engine to need it. Shadow is where D500 pays for itself a second time: read
it in one direction only and a Dauthi Marauder blocks a Grizzly Bears, which it may not.

### Why the rules are a separate table, and the card that decided it

The obvious implementation is to seed `blockableOnlyBy` from the keyword. **Dauthi Horror says no.**
Its text is

```
Shadow
Dauthi Horror can't be blocked by white creatures.
```

— a keyword allow list and a printed ban on one card. D498 *refuses* a card printing both a ban and
an allow list, because merging them is a judgement nothing in the corpus asks for. Seed shadow into
`blockableOnlyBy` and that refusal fires on Dauthi Horror, and the card loses **both** restrictions:
no shadow, no white ban, a 2/1 anyone can block.

And the two are not in conflict. A white creature with shadow may not block it, for two independent
reasons. So `KEYWORD_BLOCK_RULES` is its own table, `canBlock` applies it **alongside** whatever the
card prints, and each list is satisfied on its own terms. That is also the right rule for a creature
carrying two of these at once: every list must be answered, and the clauses inside one list are
alternatives.

The rules derive from `keywords`, which "loses all abilities" already clears, so this adds no fourth
thing to remember to reset — the argument for deriving them rather than copying them into fields.

No white creature with shadow has ever been printed, so the test that proves the independence grants
shadow to a Serra Angel with the engine's own `pump`. It then answers the keyword's list and is still
refused, by name, by the printed ban.

### Horsemanship is asymmetric, and a test says so

CR 702.5b restricts who may block the creature and says nothing about what it may block, so a
Barbarian General may block whatever it likes. A rules table invites symmetry — shadow is symmetric,
and two of three entries having both halves would make the third look like an omission — so the
asymmetry has a test of its own: the block horsemanship *permits*. The break run confirms it,
because adding `blocksOnly` to horsemanship fails exactly that test and nothing else.

### The semicolon that was hiding five printings

`Vigilance; horsemanship` is how Zhang Fei prints two keywords, and `printedParts` split keyword
lines on commas alone — so the line came out as one part that is not a keyword and **a card whose
entire text is two keywords read as nothing.** 33 legal lines use a semicolon.

Found while reading the horsemanship printings, fixed by splitting on `[,;]`, and safe because the
whole-line rule is untouched: every part still has to be a part, so `First strike; banding` is still
refused whole (10 of the 33 lines name banding, which this engine has no keyword for). A test pins
both halves — the lines that now read, and the banding lines that must not.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed rules lines read | 21,224 / 56,421 (37.6%) | **21,364 / 56,421 (37.9%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,672 | **10,689** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,411 | **6,490** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,135 | **1,170** |

**+140 lines and +79 cards**, split by running the sweep again with the semicolon disabled:

| | lines | cards finished |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the three keywords | +128 | +70 |
| the semicolon split | +12 | +9 |

The keywords beat their own 101-line family count because a word in `KEYWORDS` also reads inside a
comma list (`Flying, fear`) and in a granting effect, not only on a line of its own.

### The bot is not told what these are worth, on purpose

`KEYWORD_VALUE` in `bot.ts` prices flying at 1.5, deathtouch at 1.5, reach at 0.25 — every one of
those numbers measured on the paired bot-against-bot instrument. Fear, shadow and horsemanship are
left unpriced (the lookup is `Partial` and defaults to 0), because **a weight nobody measured is a
guess wearing a number**, and this file has retracted two of those already (D258, D263).

They are not invisible to the bot regardless: `canBlock` refuses the blocks they forbid, so the
search sees the consequence in every position it looks at. What is missing is the bot *valuing*
evasion it cannot be blocked through, and D144's contextual-evasion term is the shape that question
needs. Named here rather than answered.

### The break run

Ten breaks, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256 of the backup:

| break | compile.test | scripts.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fear's artifact clause dropped | 1 fail | 1 fail |
| fear's colour clause dropped | 1 fail | 1 fail |
| shadow's `blocksOnly` half removed | 1 fail | 1 fail |
| shadow's `blockedOnlyBy` half removed | 1 fail | 2 fail |
| horsemanship made symmetric, which no rule says | 1 fail | 1 fail |
| the attacker-side keyword loop never runs | pass | 4 fail |
| the blocker-side keyword loop never runs | pass | 1 fail |
| the printed list wins over the keyword (the Dauthi Horror merge) | pass | 1 fail |
| the semicolon split reverted to commas only | 1 fail | pass |
| the whole-line rule made lenient, so an unreadable part is dropped | 1 fail | pass |

### Two more stale refusal rows, and a standing check that had to be answered rather than edited

D498 and D500 each carried a row reading "a keyword the engine lacks" and naming **shadow**. True
when written; not any more. Both are retired to `banding`, which this engine genuinely does not have
and which is the most tempting wrong read in the game, being a keyword about blocking. **The eighth
and ninth stale refusal rows in this series.**

The harder one was `deck coverage > has a card behind every mechanic it declares`, which went red
the moment the three words joined `KEYWORDS`: it requires a card in the thirteen built-in decks for
every declared mechanic. The pool has no fear, no shadow, no horsemanship.

D442 already settled the shape of the answer and its own docblock says what not to do — "the honest
answer is not to add a card to a measured deck to satisfy a test", and #96 and #231 both moved win
rates by a single slot. So the three keywords join `compilerOnly`, and the bar that entry carries is
the one it has always carried: each **names its corpus count and the runtime test that drives a real
printing through `customDeck`**. The test's own control still runs — the exemptions must *still* be
orphans in the pool — so one of these left behind after a card carrying it arrives in a deck is
reported rather than quietly carried for ever.

## D502 — Threshold: a static that is on while your graveyard is big

The queue head by cards finished (D434), re-measured after D501 moved everything: **31 cards** whose
only unread line says "there are seven or more cards in your graveyard". **#347 closed.**

108 legal lines print that phrase. **33 of them are a static about the card itself**; the rest are
activated abilities ("Activate only if there are seven or more…"), abilities the card grants itself
in quotes, and one-shot spell effects ("If there are seven or more…, instead…"), each of which
belongs to another reader or to nobody.

### Nothing new in the effect machinery, which is the point

#142 built the conditional continuous effect for metalcraft: `ContinuousEffect.while`, asked in
`effectApplies` every time a creature's size is computed rather than stored, because — as its
docblock says — **there is no moment at which it turns on.** Threshold is a third `while` kind
beside the artifact count and monstrosity's counter, and it is the cheapest of the three to answer
honestly:

| kind | what it reads | the caveat |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `controller-artifacts` | the battlefield's **printed** type lines | a permanent *made* an artifact does not count (CR 702.105a) |
| `source-has-counter` | the source's own counters | none |
| `controller-graveyard` | the length of one zone list | **none** |

The artifact count has to read printed types because it runs inside `characteristicsOf` and asking
for a live type line would re-enter the whole computation — two conditional effects reading each
other's types would not terminate. A graveyard count reads a list of ids, so none of that reaches
it and the number it gives is simply correct.

### Two things the reader had to learn

**The condition is printed on either side of the predicate.** Nine lines put it last, as metalcraft
does (`~ gets +2/+2 as long as there are seven or more cards in your graveyard`); fifteen put it
first (`As long as there are seven or more cards in your graveyard, ~ gets +1/+1 and has flying`).
Same sentence, same rule, and a reader handling one position would read a third of the family.

**The predicate is a list**, where metalcraft's is a single thing. So it is split on "and" and each
part read on its own, which is `thresholdPredicate`. Five kinds of part, every one a real printing:

```
gets +N/+N                       Krosan Beast, +7/+7, whose whole card is the one line
has <keyword>                    Mystic Visionary — flying and no pump at all
has protection from <colour>     Mystic Familiar
can't block                      Childhood Horror, Dirty Wererat, Frightcrawler, Putrid Imp
can't be blocked                 Cephalid Inkmage
attacks each combat if able      Otarian Juggernaut
```

One object, not one per part: the print is one ability, and two continuous effects would be two
things to expire.

`countFrom` reads the number, so "seven" and a digit are the same thing. Every threshold card prints
"seven" and the constant would have worked — until the first card printing any other count read as a
threshold card. A test pins three and ten.

### Masked Gorgon is the card the whole-line rule is for

"has protection from green and from white" splits into a part this reader understands and a bare
"from white", which it does not. So the Gorgon stays unread (D487): **a Gorgon with protection from
one of the two colours its card names is worse than a Gorgon a human plays by hand** (D362).
Nantuko Blightcutter refuses for the same reason — "+1/+1 for each black permanent your opponents
control" is a count, and `sizeBonus` takes numbers.

The condition refuses too, and that is what keeps this reader from eating its neighbours: `if there
are seven or more` is a one-shot spell effect (Cabal Ritual, Cleansing Meditation, Demoralize — some
twenty lines), `unless` is Deep-Sea Terror's attack restriction, and a graveyard that is not yours is
somebody else's count.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed rules lines read | 21,364 / 56,421 (37.9%) | **21,392 / 56,421 (37.9%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,689 | **10,712** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,490 | **6,512** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,170 | 1,170 |

+28 lines and **+22 cards finished**, against the queue's 31. The gap is honest and worth naming:
the instrument buckets by the line's first fourteen words, so `Threshold — As long as there are
seven or more cards in your graveyard,` collects the cards whose *tails* are a quoted ability
(Bloodcurdler, Boneshard Slasher, Centaur Chieftain, Cephalid Sage, Chlorophant, Decaying Soil,
Hunting Grounds) alongside the ones read here. Those need the engine to grant a permanent an ability
written in quotes, which it cannot do at all — #230's note says so — so they are a different
increment and not a shortfall in this one.

The "needing no script" row does not move, and should not: every card in this family emits a
`statics` entry, so none of them is a card the engine plays off the card definition alone.

### The break run

Ten breaks, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256 of the backup:

| break | compile.test | scripts.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the leading-condition form (fifteen lines) | 4 fail | 2 fail |
| the trailing-condition form (nine lines) | 8 fail | 2 fail |
| the count is hard-coded to seven | 1 fail | pass |
| the predicate list is read as one part | 5 fail | 2 fail |
| an unreadable part is dropped instead of refusing the line | 1 fail | pass |
| `can't block` is not read | 1 fail | 1 fail |
| protection takes every colour instead of the named one | 1 fail | pass |
| the condition is never evaluated, so the static is always on | pass | 5 fail |
| the boundary is off by one | pass | 4 fail |
| the count reads every graveyard, not the controller's | pass | 1 fail |

**One break came back green and found a hole in the tests**, which is the fifth increment running
in which that has happened and the reason every break gets run rather than reasoned about. Dropping
an unreadable part instead of refusing the line left both suites passing: the two refusal rows that
should have caught it happen to refuse for *other* reasons — Masked Gorgon's bad part never reaches
that line, and a bare "has banding" ends with an empty result either way. The row that discriminates
is `gets +1/+1 and has banding`: a readable part beside an unreadable one, which is the only shape
leniency actually changes. Added, and the break now fails.

## D493 — "This spell can't be countered", as a flag the engine acts on

**Built two days ago, held back, and shipped now.** The work was finished then: the flag, the stack
object, `counterSpell`'s guard, four compile rows and two runtime tests. What blocked it was the
standing mechanic-coverage check — `deck coverage > has a card behind every mechanic it declares`
requires a card in the thirteen built-in decks for every `script` field, and no pool card is
uncounterable. The note left at the time said the increment needed a hand-written pool card and a
deck slot.

**D501 is what unblocked it, and the answer was already in the file.** D442's rule allows an
exemption for a mechanic the *compiler* reads that the hand-written pool does not print, provided
the entry names its evidence: the corpus count, and the runtime test that drives a real printing
through `customDeck`. D501 used it for three keywords an hour ago. This increment has both, so it
takes the same road — and the pool's decks, which #96 and #231 each moved by a single slot, are left
alone.

### Why it is a flag and not a skipped line

Skipping the line is a two-character change and the wrong one. A spell that can be countered when
its text says it cannot is **worse than printed**, and a reading that errs in the generous direction
is still a wrong reading (D259, D362). Every other member of the family this compiler skips — cost
modification, a graveyard trigger, an activated ability (D487) — is skipped because running it would
change the *resolution*; this one changes what happens to the spell **on the stack**, which is a
thing the engine can actually enforce.

So it is read into `CardScript.cantBeCountered`, copied onto the `StackObject` as the spell is cast,
and honoured by `counterSpell`.

### Where it lives, and the import cycle that decided it

`counterSpell` is in `effects.ts`, and the script lookup is `scriptForCard` in `derive.ts`. Effects
cannot import derive: `derive → compile → scripts → effects`. So the flag travels on the stack
object, the way `x`, `flashback`, `answering` and `castNumber` already do — settled at the moment the
caster has the script in hand, which is also the honest shape, because it is a fact about *this
casting*. The face-down cast deliberately does not copy it: a face-down spell has no text at all
(CR 707.2).

`counterSpell` is the single chokepoint: ward's unpaid settle, the bot, and every scripted counter go
through it, so one guard covers them all. A "can't" beats a "does" (CR 101.2), so the spell stays on
the stack and resolves — and the counterspell is still spent, which is the whole point of the card
that printed this. The guard writes to `state.replacements`, the channel the engine already drains
onto the provoking action's message, rather than a log entry, because nothing else in `effects.ts`
logs directly.

### Probing real printings found a gap an assumption would have shipped

The first draft wired it into the **spell** line loop only, and the probe showed exactly half the
family reading:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Abrupt Decay, Dovin's Veto | read |
| Carnage Tyrant, Thrun, Blurred Mongoose, Great Sable Stag | **still unread** |

A permanent card goes through `lineScriptFor`, a different loop — and the line is about the spell on
the stack *before* the permanent ever arrives, so it belongs in both. D259's rule ("probe the real
printings, never work from memory") is what caught it; the four compile rows for a creature exist so
it cannot regress.

### What stays unread, on purpose

A permanent's static about **other** objects — "Spells your opponents cast can't be countered",
"Creature spells you cast can't be countered" — is a different reader with a different scope.
Collapsing it into this flag would be wrong in both directions at once: the permanent itself would
become uncounterable, and the spells it exists to protect would not be. Also refused: "can't be
countered **by spells or abilities your opponents control**", which is a narrower "can't" than the
flag can express. 35 legal lines in that group, against 86 that print the plain sentence.

### The break run, and a lesson about break runs

Six breaks on today's tree, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256 of the backup:

| break | compile.test | scripts.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `counterSpell` ignores the flag | pass | 1 fail |
| the flag is never copied onto the stack object | pass | 1 fail |
| the line is not read on a permanent card | 2 fail | 1 fail |
| the line is not read on an instant or sorcery | 3 fail | pass |
| the reader also claims a permanent's static about other spells | 3 fail | pass |
| the note is never written, so nothing says why it resolved | pass | 1 fail |

The original run, two days ago, is the reason this file now checks that every break *applied*: one
break looked uncaught and the real explanation was that its anchor did not match, so **nothing was
broken at all**. *A break that silently fails to apply is indistinguishable from a test that does
not discriminate.* That near-miss is why the harness in use since D495 registers its revert with
`atexit` and compares a SHA-256 before it exits.

### What it bought

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed rules lines read | 21,392 / 56,421 (37.9%) | **21,494 / 56,421 (38.1%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,712 | **10,789** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,512 | **6,539** |

**+102 lines and +77 cards with a script**, against a family of 86 printed lines — because an
instant or sorcery needs *every* line read or declared before it compiles at all, so reading one
static unlocks the whole card's lines. Abrupt Decay is the card that showed it: a resolution line
that read perfectly, on a card that did not compile.

Measured two days ago as +77 cards as well, on a tree five increments younger. The same number from
the same family, re-measured rather than carried over — which is the point of re-measuring.

## D503 — Bushido N, which cost one regex and the right pair of events

Queue head after D502: **35 legal printed lines**, 20 cards whose only unread line is `Bushido N`.
**#348 closed.**

CR 702.44a: "Whenever this creature blocks or becomes blocked, it gets +N/+N until end of turn."
One printed sentence, **two** events, because blocking and becoming blocked are different things
that happen at different moments to different creatures.

### Everything it needed was already here, and D482 is why the right pair exists

| event | fires |
| --- | --- |
| `blocking-creature` | once for a creature that blocked at all |
| `blocked-creature` | once however many creatures blocked it |
| `blocks` | once **per attacker** it blocked |
| `becomes-blocked` | once **per blocker** |

A Samurai wired to the second pair would get **+2N/+2N against two blockers**. That is not a
hypothetical: it is precisely what D482 found shipping on Ichorclaw Myr, in the infect deck, where
every extra point of power is an extra poison counter. So the batched pair is the correct one, and a
compile row asserts the kinds by name rather than trusting the choice.

Both events default to `who: 'self'`, so neither trigger needs a subject and the pump points at
`c.source`. The two `TriggerDef`s are separate objects on purpose: the engine puts a resolved
trigger on the stack by identity, and two abilities that were one object would be one ability firing
once. A break proves it — sharing the object fails three runtime tests.

No script field. Modular, vanishing and fading each carry their number into a field the engine reads
elsewhere; bushido is the pair of abilities and nothing else, which is why the reader sits beside
that branch rather than in it.

### The test the suite did not have

Ichorclaw Myr is the pool's only reader of this family and it prints the becoming-blocked half
alone, so **`blocking-creature` had never been exercised on a compiled card.** A reader wired to one
event would have passed two of the three runtime tests here. Jade Avenger — a printed 2/2 whose
entire text is `Bushido 2` — blocks a Grizzly Bears, becomes a 4/4, and lives through a trade it
would otherwise have died in.

The fourth runtime test is the control and is not redundant: bushido is **not** "whenever this
creature attacks", and a reader wired to `attacks` would pass the becoming-blocked test by accident,
because the attack trigger fires first and the board would read 4/4 either way. So an unblocked swing
has to leave it a 2/2 and put two damage through, not four.

### The three printings left unread, named

All three are a different mechanic wearing the word:

- **Fumiko the Lowblood** — "bushido X, where X is the number of attacking creatures": a count read
  on resolution, not a printed number.
- **Sensei Golden-Tail** — *grants* bushido 1 with a counter, which is handing another permanent a
  triggered ability (#230, which the engine cannot do at all).
- **Takeno, Samurai General** — "+1/+1 for each point of bushido it has". This engine has no notion
  of *how much* bushido a creature has; the keyword is two triggers, not a number on the card.
  Reading it would mean inventing a field to answer a question one card asks (D57).

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed rules lines read | 21,494 / 56,421 (38.1%) | **21,529 / 56,421 (38.2%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,789 | **10,817** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,539 | **6,559** |

+35 lines — the family exactly, one line per card — and **+20 cards finished**, which is what the
queue predicted. The first increment in this stretch where the prediction and the measurement agree
to the card, because the shape is one line on one card with nothing else to unlock.

### Not priced for the bot, and said rather than left

`KEYWORD_VALUE` in `bot.ts` has no entry for this, because bushido is not a keyword in
`KEYWORDS` at all — it is two triggers, and the bot's three readers of `script.triggers` see them
like any other. What the evaluation does *not* do is value a creature more highly for having them,
and that is the same gap D501 named for fear and shadow: a weight nobody measured is a guess wearing
a number, and this file has retracted two of those (D258, D263).

### The break run

Seven breaks, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256 of the backup:

| break | compile.test | scripts.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the blocking half is dropped | 5 fail | 1 fail |
| the becoming-blocked half is dropped | 5 fail | 2 fail |
| the per-object events instead of the batched ones | 5 fail | 1 fail |
| the two triggers share one object | 5 fail | 3 fail |
| the bonus is hard-coded to one | pass | 3 fail |
| the pump points at nothing instead of the creature itself | pass | 3 fail |
| the number is optional, so a bare "Bushido" reads | 1 fail | pass |

The fifth row is worth reading: the break changed the pump and left the trigger's `description`
alone, so the compile rows — which assert the description — correctly saw nothing. Only the board
can tell a +1/+1 from a +2/+2, which is the division of labour these two files are supposed to have.

### A test that passed the wrong card's name

The first draft of "reads it beside the rest of a real card" gave the card the name
`Araba Mothrider` and the second line Battle-Mad Ronin's sentence, so the self-subject did not match
its own card and the line read as unread. The test caught it immediately, which is the point — a
self-subject sentence is read against the name it is printed on, and a fixture that mixes two cards
is testing nothing.

## D504 — Wither, which is infect's creature half and nothing else

**26 bare `Wither` lines** in the legal corpus (Boggart Ram-Gang, Cinderbones, Duergar Cave-Guard,
Harvest Gwyllion and 22 more), plus a dozen printings that grant it. **#349 closed.**

CR 702.78a: "Damage this source would deal to a creature is dealt in the form of -1/-1 counters."
That is **word for word** what infect already does to a creature in this engine. What infect adds is
the *player* half, where its damage is poison rather than life (CR 702.90b).

So the whole increment is **one word in `KEYWORDS` and one `||`**:

```
const infect  = sourceKeywords?.has('infect');
const withers = sourceKeywords?.has('wither');   // new
…
next = infect || withers ? -1/-1 counters : marked damage;   // creature branch
…
next = infect ? poison : life;                               // player branch, untouched
```

Two locals rather than one, because the two part company in that second branch — and that
separation is the entire risk in this increment.

### The test that decides it

A Boggart Ram-Gang hits you for **three life**. A Glistener Elf hits you for three **poison**, and
ten poison ends the game. Putting the keyword into the player branch as well would have turned all
26 of these cards into infect creatures, and would have passed **every other test in the block
without a murmur** — the creature behaviour is identical by definition.

So "deals its damage to a player as LIFE, not poison" is the assertion this is really about, and the
break run confirms it discriminates alone: the player-branch break fails exactly one test.

### A test that proved nothing, and what fixed it

The first draft of the creature test attacked a 3/3 Centaur Courser with a 3/3 Boggart Ram-Gang and
read the blocker's counters afterwards. The Courser **died**, and a permanent that leaves the
battlefield takes its counters with it (CR 400.7) — so the assertion read `undefined` and said
nothing at all about where the damage went.

A 2/4 Harvest Gwyllion is the board that works: three counters leave it a 0/1, alive, and still a
0/1 a turn later, which is the only way to *see* the difference between a counter and marked damage.
Marked damage is wiped in the cleanup step; a counter is not.

### Read off the source, and the third test says so

Wither is a fact about the creature **dealing** the damage, not about the one taking it — the same
shape as deathtouch and protection. A 2/4 Gwyllion blocking a 3/3 Courser leaves the Courser with
two permanent counters and takes three *marked* damage itself, so it is a 2/4 again next turn. A
break that reads the keyword off the target fails two tests.

### What came free, and what did not

Every reader that hands a keyword to something asks `isKeyword`, so `Target creature gets +1/+1 and
gains wither until end of turn` read the moment the word was in the list — the same free ride D501's
three keywords got, and a runtime test checks the granted word actually *works* rather than merely
being stored.

**`Equipped creature gets +1/+0 and has wither` does not read, and the test says why it is not
wither's fault**: the same sentence with *flying* in it is unread too, because no reader handles a
size bonus and a grant in one equip line. Writing that row as a wither test would have claimed a gap
that is somewhere else entirely.

Refused on purpose: **Everlasting Torment** ("All damage is dealt as though its source had wither")
hands the ability to every damage source in the game, which is a global replacement and not a
keyword on a permanent. Reading it as the enchantment *having* wither would give an enchantment an
ability that does nothing and leave the rule it prints unenforced — wrong twice over (D362).
"Black creatures you control have wither" is refused for the same reason D500's class subjects are.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed rules lines read | 21,529 / 56,421 (38.2%) | **21,555 / 56,421 (38.2%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,817 | 10,817 |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,559 | **6,573** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,170 | **1,179** |

+26 lines — the bare family exactly — and **+14 cards finished**. The "compiled script" row does not
move at all, and should not: a printed keyword emits no script (D424), so every one of these cards
is played off its own card definition. Nine of the fourteen need no script whatsoever.

### The break run

Four breaks, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256 of the backup:

| break | compile.test | scripts.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the word is not in `KEYWORDS` | 3 fail | 2 fail |
| the creature branch does not read it | pass | 3 fail |
| the **player** branch reads it too, so wither becomes infect | pass | 1 fail |
| it is read off the target instead of the source | pass | 2 fail |

### The pool has no wither, so the mechanic-coverage check gets a fifth exemption

Same road as D501's three keywords and D493's one script field: the entry names its corpus count and
the runtime test that drives a real printing through `customDeck`. Adding a wither creature to one of
the thirteen measured decks to satisfy a test is what D442's own docblock says not to do.

## D505 — Two pods in forty looped for ever on Basalt Monolith

Found by the pod sweep that verified D503, not by a test:

```
seed 36210: looping — 2000 moves with no progress in precombat-main of turn 36,
            2000 of them auto:activate (Basalt Monolith#1)
seed 36221: looping — 2000 moves with no progress in precombat-main of turn 81,
            1002 of them auto:activate (Basalt Monolith#1)
```

**#350 closed.** Not a D503 regression: bushido adds two combat triggers, Basalt Monolith is an
artifact with no combat role, the loop is in precombat-main, and seeds 34001 through 36001 were all
40/40. These are simply the first seeds that built a deck containing the card. Pre-existing, and
reproducible to the move.

The card taps for {C}{C}{C} and spends {3} to untap itself, for ever. Every step is legal, and the
board after each pair of activations is the board before — the Kiora's Follower cycle with both
halves on one permanent.

### The engine already had the rule, and two things kept it away

#124's eleventh "spent on nothing" rule is written for exactly this shape: `untapsSomething` asks
whether the ability's whole effect is an untap, and `untapBoughtSomething` asks what the untap
bought. Neither could see the Monolith:

1. **`untapsOnly` was set by the two *targeted* untap readers and not by the self-untap one.** The
   flag lived beside `Untap target permanent` and `Untap two target lands`; `Untap ~` — the same
   clause pointed at the card printing it — returned a bare effect. So `untapsSomething` said no and
   the rule was never asked. Confirmed by compiling the real card rather than reading the code:
   `ability[1] = {"cost":{"mana":"{3}"},"description":"{3}: Untap this artifact."}`, no flag, where
   Kiora's Follower's carries one.
2. **`untapBoughtSomething` found the untapped permanent through `action.targets[0]`**, which a
   self-untap does not have. With the flag set and this fallback missing it would have refused
   **every** self-untap outright — Horseshoe Crab's included, which is a different wrong answer and
   the reason both halves had to change together.

### Nothing else was needed, and that is the part worth stating

With the flag set and the fallback in place, the question already answers this card correctly:

- **mana**: tapping for {C}{C}{C} and spending {3} to untap leaves the same three mana available, so
  no cast becomes affordable;
- **a body in a combat**: it is not a creature;
- **an ability handed back**: the only one is its own **mana** ability, and `pointlessToHandBack`
  excludes mana abilities precisely so that a cycle cannot be its own justification.

Grim Monolith is the same card at {4} and is fixed by the same change. So are Retrofitter Foundry,
Staff of Domination and Staff of Compleation, which print the same self-untap.

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| seed 36210 | looping, 2000 moves in one main phase | **finished**, 55 turns |
| seed 36221 | looping, 2000 moves in one main phase | **finished**, 110 turns |
| the whole sweep, `SEED0=36201 GAMES=40` | 38 finished, 2 looping | **40/40**, no throw and no stall |

Re-run on the same seed set rather than a fresh one, which is the only run that proves anything
about this fix.

### Two tests, because the fix is two halves

- *does not untap a Basalt Monolith it has just tapped for mana* — the loop, in the position it
  loops from, with the hand emptied so the mana cannot be for anything else.
- *but untaps a Horseshoe Crab to block an attack already on the table* — the control, and the
  reason the fallback exists: a tapped 1/3 is not a blocker, one mana makes it one, and that is
  `untapBoughtSomething`'s third clause asked of a permanent with no target.

Both use real printings through `customDeck`'s `data`. A compile test pins the flag on the untap
ability, its **absence** on the mana ability beside it, and its absence on a tap — because D505
widened where the flag is set, and widening it one card too far costs the bot a real play.

### The break run, and two breaks that did not discriminate

Four breaks, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256:

| break | compile.test | playout.test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the self-untap reader does not set the flag | 2 fail | 1 fail |
| the bot has no source fallback, so every self-untap is refused | pass | 1 fail |
| the mana ability carries the flag too | 1 fail | pass |
| a `tapped` check is dropped, so untapping an untapped permanent counts | pass | pass |

**The third break had to be rewritten twice, and both misses are the same mistake**: I patched a
builder the card does not go through. First `selfEffect`'s untap branch (mana abilities do not reach
it), then `tapAbilities` (Basalt Monolith's `{T}: Add {C}{C}{C}` is three of one type, so it is
`sumAbility`). The test was right each time; the break was aimed at the wrong code. That is the
D493 lesson again — *a break that silently fails to apply is indistinguishable from a test that does
not discriminate* — wearing a new hat: a break that applies to the wrong function is the same thing.

**The fourth break genuinely does not discriminate, and it should be recorded rather than patched
around.** Removing `!inst.tapped` leaves every test green, because the guard is a fast path rather
than a correctness gate: untapping an already-untapped permanent buys no mana, no body and no
ability, so the four questions below it answer "no" anyway. The guard stays — the rule's own
docblock says 36 of 57 surviving activations were this case, which is about how often the bot
*presses the button*, not about whether the answer is right — and this paragraph is why there is no
test for it.

### What this says about the sweep

The pod sweep has now found three loops that no test could have: #334's Umbral Mantle equip,
D496's Hyalopterous Lemure self-shrink, and this one. All three are the same shape — a free or
mana-neutral repeatable ability the evaluation scores at zero — and all three arrived with the
increment that first made the card readable. **The sweep is the instrument for this class, and
running it on a fresh seed after every increment is what keeps catching them.** It is also why the
seed is advanced rather than reused: 34001 through 36001 would never have found this card.

## D506 — Changeling, and the layer it has to be applied in

Changeling (CR 702.73a) is "this card is every creature type", and the queue ranked it first by
cards finished: **61 legal corpus cards** print the bare line, three of them (Woodland Changeling,
Impostor of the Sixth Pride, Universal Automaton) with nothing else in the text box at all.

### One place, which is the whole design

Subtype matching is spread across eighteen call sites in the engine — `clauseMatches`'s Wall and
Wizard clauses (D498, D500), the `controller-subtype` effect scope every tribal lord uses,
`canBlock`'s Wall clause, three counts in `scripts.ts`, two filter builders that receive only a
`TypeLine` and could never see a flag. Changeling is therefore **not a flag**: it extends the
subtype list that all eighteen already read, and none of them changed.

That needed a vocabulary the engine did not have, and **the derivation was wrong twice before it
was right**:

| attempt | rule | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | every word in the subtype section of a Creature-headed line | 325 — polluted with Equipment, Saga, Food, Treasure, Clue, Background, Book, Forest, Shrine, Aura |
| 2 | attempt 1, minus every word seen on a noncreature line | 298 — but **dropped eighteen real tribes** |
| 3 | heads containing Creature, Tribal **or Kindred**, minus noncreature subtypes | **316**, correct in spot-checks |

Attempt 2's eighteen casualties were Goblin, Elf, Wizard, Demon, Elemental, Soldier, Warrior,
Merfolk, Kithkin, Faerie, Giant, Shaman, Shapeshifter, Rebel, Rogue, Treefolk, Eldrazi and
Lhurgoyf — every one of them a word that also appears on a *Tribal* or *Kindred* line (Tribal
Instant — Goblin, Kindred Sorcery — Elf), which the second rule read as evidence that it was not a
creature type. `Kindred` is the rename Tribal got in 2024 and the word that fixed it.

**This was caught by checking the output against expected names, not by trusting the count.** A
list of 298 looks just as plausible as a list of 316, and a changeling that is not a Goblin is the
bug nobody would have found at the table for weeks. `Time` and `Lord` are in the list as the two
halves of the two-word "Time Lord", which is the one known imprecision and costs nothing: no card
asks whether something is a Time.

### The layer, and the test that found it

The first implementation extended the subtype list **after the effects loop**, on the final keyword
set — which reads as obviously right (lose-all-abilities has already cleared the keyword, so a
frogged changeling is a Shapeshifter again) and is wrong for a reason the reader cannot see:

> *Every later layer's scope is judged against the layer-4 type line.*

Written after the loop, the extended line was handed to callers and invisible to the one reader
that matters most. **An Imperious Perfect did not pump a changeling**, because the lord's
`controller-subtype` scope had already been matched against a bare Shapeshifter. Nine compile
tests passed; `hasSubtype` answered Goblin, Elf, Wall, Wizard, Spirit, Dragon and Zombie correctly;
the whole increment looked finished. The *runtime* test for the lord is what said otherwise.

The fix is `withChangeling`, called inside layer 4 beside `withAddedTypes` (CR 613.1d — changeling
is a characteristic-defining ability, CR 604.3). It reads the keyword off the printed text and
pre-scans for a "loses all abilities" effect, which is CR 613.8 **dependency** rather than plain
layer order: layer 6 is after layer 4, so the type-changing application is dependent on the ability
still being there and is applied after the removal. Judging that scan against the pre-changeling
line is the same simplification `withAddedTypes` already documents for its own scopes, and it costs
nothing in practice — **no printing in the corpus grants changeling to another creature.** The two
that come close (Moritte of the Frost, Omni-Changeling) copy a permanent and add the keyword to the
copy, which is layer 1 and arrives as a printed keyword on the thing being read.

Only creatures are extended. A changeling card is every creature type in every zone (CR 702.73a),
but the only question this engine asks of a noncreature object is about artifact and enchantment
subtypes, and those are not creature types. `def.typeLine` is untouched, so a player still sees
"Creature — Shapeshifter", and the printed subtypes stay at the front of the live list.

### The tests

Nine compile tests, including: the bare keyword read; Avian Changeling, Changeling Sentinel and
Changeling Outcast compiling whole; `hasSubtype` true for seven tribes and false for Equipment,
Aura, Saga, Vehicle, Food and Forest; `subtypes[0] === 'Shapeshifter'`; `def.typeLine` unchanged;
lose-all-abilities clearing it; a noncreature permanent unaffected; and `CREATURE_TYPES` pinned at
316 names.

Two of those nine were rewritten. **Mistform Ultimus** ("is every creature type") is a *refusal*
row, not a second reading: its sentence is a list of words rather than a keyword, so the line stays
unread and inventing a reader for it would be D259. And a row asserting that "create a 2/2
colorless Shapeshifter creature token with changeling" refuses turned out to be false — the token
reader asks `isKeyword` for the words after "with", so the keyword made it compile. That row is now
the positive assertion it should always have been: **Irregular Cohort** compiles whole.

Four runtime tests through `customDeck`'s `data`, on printed **Woodland Changeling** — chosen
because its whole text is the word, so nothing else can account for an assertion. Each asks a rule
that *already* reads a creature type, and **each has a Grizzly Bears beside it as the
discriminator**: a 2/2 green creature with no keywords on the same battlefield, so a changeling
that gained nothing and a board where the rule fires for everybody both fail.

| rule | the changeling | the Bears |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Juggernaut's `cantBeBlockedByWalls` (D495) | may not block it — it is a Wall | may block it |
| Imperious Perfect's `subtype: 'Elf', other: true` | **3/3** | 2/2 |
| Bog Rats, "can't be blocked by Walls" (D498 ban) | may not block it | may block it |
| Elven Riders, "… except by Walls and/or fliers" (D498 allow) | **may** block it | may not |

The last row is the one a filter that merely refused everything would fail, and the Imperious
Perfect row is the one that earned its place: it failed on the first implementation and is what
moved the extension into layer 4.

`keyword changeling` joins the `compilerOnly` exemption set, with its evidence named per D442: 61
legal corpus cards, not one in the pool's thirteen measured decks, the keyword not grantable, and
the four runtime tests above.

### The break run

Six breaks, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256 of the original:

| break | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| the keyword is not in `KEYWORDS` | 10 tests + `tsc` |
| the subtype list is never extended | 5 tests |
| the creature guard is dropped, so a noncreature is every creature type | 1 test |
| the lose-all-abilities pre-scan is dropped | 1 test |
| the extended line reaches callers but is hidden from every later layer's scope | 1 test |
| `CREATURE_TYPES` carries an artifact subtype | 2 tests |

The fifth break is the original bug, isolated: the line is correct everywhere a caller looks and
wrong in every scope. **One test catches it, and it is the lord.**

### Coverage

| | before D506 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 21,555 / 56,421 (38.2%) | **21,615 / 56,421 (38.3%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,817 | **10,821** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,573 | **6,598** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,179 | **1,191** |

**25 cards finished** — the whole point of ranking the queue this way (D434).

### Named and left: a changeling in a graveyard

`cardWordMatch`, which reads a *printed* card rather than a battlefield permanent, does not consult
`characteristicsOf` and so does not see the extension. A changeling card in a graveyard is not a
Spirit for soulshift. That is correct today only by accident — soulshift's "return target Spirit
card with mana value N or less from your graveyard" is **not read yet** (it is 17 cards in the
queue), so nothing asks the question. When it is read, the printed-card path needs the same
extension, and this paragraph is the note that says so.

## D507 — The free ability the bot pressed two thousand times

The pod sweep on `SEED0=36401`, run straight after D506, came back 38 of 40. Two games looped, and
neither card has anything to do with changeling:

    seed 36402  2000 moves, precombat-main of turn 33, all auto:activate (Blinking Spirit)
    seed 36406  2000 moves, precombat-main of turn 29, all auto:activate (Flowstone Hellion)

| | printing |
| --- | --- |
| Blinking Spirit | `{3}{W}` 2/2 — "{0}: Return Blinking Spirit to its owner's hand." |
| Flowstone Hellion | `{4}{R}` 3/3 — "Haste / {0}: Flowstone Hellion gets +1/-1 until end of turn." |

### Both cards work, which is what makes this a bot rule

The first guess was a no-op effect, and it was wrong. Probed one activation at a time through
`customDeck`:

- the Spirit's ability resolves and the card is in its owner's **hand**;
- the Hellion goes 3/3 → 4/2 → 5/1 → **graveyard**, dying on the third activation with its toughness
  at nought (CR 704.5f).

Neither card could spin if anything ever resolved. **The bot does not pass priority.** So the first
activation sits on the stack, the board the second activation is judged against is the board the
first was judged against, and the question "is this worth doing" gets the same answer for ever. The
stack ended two thousand copies deep. The harness's stall detector could not see it either, because
every one of those moves was legal and bumped the state version — the same blindness D462 recorded
for Umbral Mantle.

### The idiom already existed twice, scoped to one family each

`animationCouldMatter` (D242's Mutavault) and `shrinksItselfForNothing` (D496's Hyalopterous Lemure)
both refuse an action whose own copy — same source, same ability index — is already on the stack, and
both docblocks say the same thing in their own words: it is the honest version of "has this already
been done". Two families had the check. Every other free ability in the engine did not.

So it is hoisted into a rule of its own, the **fifteenth** of the "spent on nothing" family and the
third about a loop rather than a card: `freeActivationAlreadyPending`.

**Free, specifically**, and that is the whole scope decision. A cost is what bounds the repetition: a
`{1}` ability runs out of mana, a `{T}` ability runs out of permanent. Only a cost of nothing can
spin. Written wider — "never repeat an activation already on the stack" — the rule would refuse a
Gelectrode pinging twice in a step, which `untapBoughtSomething`'s own docblock defends as entirely
right. **41 legal corpus cards print a `{0}:` activated ability**, which is the whole blast radius.

`costIsNothing` asks all fourteen members of `AbilityCost` by name rather than counting the object's
keys, so a cost component added later makes an ability look **paid** rather than free — the direction
that costs the bot a play instead of hanging a game.

### The tests, and the one that pins the scope

Five, through `customDeck`'s `data` on all three real printings:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| presses the Hellion once | the control — `+1/-1` is real material to `evaluate`, and the search should have it |
| and not twice | the loop, in the position it loops from |
| presses the Spirit once | a different effect entirely: this one leaves the battlefield |
| and not twice | the sharper half — a second "return this to its owner's hand" is not merely worth nothing, it is meaningless |
| **but presses a Merfolk Coralsmith twice** | the too-wide direction |

**Merfolk Coralsmith is the test that decides the rule's shape.** `{2}{U}` 2/3, printing the
Hellion's clause word for word at `{1}` instead of `{0}`. Three Islands is three activations and then
the question stops being asked, which is what a cost is for — so a rule that refused it would be
wrong, and this row is what says so.

### The break run

Five breaks, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256 of the original:

| break | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| the rule is never asked in the options loop | 3 tests |
| an explicitly printed `{0}` counts as a paid cost | 3 tests |
| the free gate is dropped, so a paid activation is refused too | 1 test (the Coralsmith) |
| a tap counts as no cost | **nothing** — see below |
| the stack is asked about any pending object, not this ability's own copy | 1 test |

**The fifth break was not caught by the first run**, and the sixth test exists because of it. Widened
to "refuse a free activation whenever anything at all is pending", every test still passed — in each
of them the only thing on the stack *was* the ability in question. So a row was added: the Hellion's
pump waiting and the Spirit's own button still worth pressing, because nothing about *it* has been
done. A break nothing catches is a suite that does not pin the shape it is meant to pin.

**The fourth break genuinely cannot be caught, and that is recorded rather than patched around.**
Dropping `cost.tap` from `costIsNothing` makes a `{T}` ability look free, so the rule would refuse
re-activating one while its first copy waits — but the engine refuses that anyway, because the
permanent is tapped. No board can distinguish the two, so there is no test to write. The member
stays, because `costIsNothing` has to be a true statement about costs rather than a true statement
about the boards that happen to be reachable today. Same shape as D505's `!inst.tapped` guard.

The `src/bot.test.ts` mistake is worth recording: the first version of the harness ran
`vitest run src/playout.test.ts src/bot.test.ts`, and **there is no `bot.test.ts`**. Vitest exits
non-zero on a path that matches nothing, so every break would have reported "caught" without a single
assertion failing — a break run that passes when it should fail, which is the thing a break run exists
to prevent. Caught by checking the file list before trusting the result, and the run was stopped and
redone.

### The sweep

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| seed 36402 | looping, 2000 moves in one main phase | **finished**, 47 turns, 189 moves |
| seed 36406 | looping, 2000 moves in one main phase | **finished**, 55 turns, 222 moves |
| the whole sweep, `SEED0=36401 GAMES=40` | 38 finished, 2 looping, 396 moves a game | **40/40**, no throw and no stall, 301 moves a game |

The moves-per-game figure is worth keeping: it fell by a quarter across forty games, so the rule is
trimming free button-presses the sweep never flagged as loops, not only the two that hung.

Re-run on the **same** seed set rather than a fresh one, which is the only run that proves anything
about this fix.

### Four loops, one shape

The pod sweep has now found four loops no test could have: #334's Umbral Mantle equip, D496's
Hyalopterous Lemure self-shrink, D505's Basalt Monolith self-untap, and this pair. Every one is a
free or mana-neutral repeatable ability the evaluation scores at zero or better, and every one
arrived with the increment that first made its card readable. **Running the sweep on a fresh seed
after every increment is what keeps catching them**, and advancing the seed is why: 34001 through
36201 would never have found either of these two cards.

## D508 — "Activate only once each turn", and the queue head that was not one

### The measurement that moved the queue

`one-away.mjs` printed its head as **Threshold — As long as there are seven or more cards in your
graveyard,** at 19 cards. Breaking that shape down card by card (`scratchpad/thresh.mjs`) showed it
is not one shape at all:

| cards | sub-shape |
| --- | --- |
| 17 | `has "<quoted ability>"` — needs the compiler to turn arbitrary quoted text into a `TriggerDef` |
| 16 | `Activate only if there are N or more cards in your graveyard` |
| 14 | assorted one-offs (an attack trigger, a cast restriction, an Aura's "all creatures able to block") |
| 3 | `Enchanted creature …` — an Aura subject rather than a self one |

So **the printed head was 17 cards behind the hardest job in the family**, and the queue's own
normalisation had hidden a cheaper neighbour inside the same bucket. That is the second time a shape
count has needed to be re-cut by hand before it meant anything (D434 is the first), and the lesson
is the same: a shape is only as good as its normaliser.

Re-measured the whole restriction family instead (`scratchpad/actonly.mjs`), by taking the trailing
sentence off and asking whether the line then compiles whole:

    519 legal cards are one line away on a line carrying "Activate only …"
    143 of those, the restriction is the ONLY thing unread

| cards finished | clause |
| --- | --- |
| **38** | **Activate only once each turn.** |
| 18 | Activate only during your turn, before attackers are declared. |
| 8 | Activate only during your turn. |
| 6 | Activate only during your upkeep. |
| 5 | Activate only if this land entered this turn or if you control a basic land. |
| 4 | Activate only if you control a Swamp. |

**38 is twice the printed head**, and it is the clause this increment reads. The four timing clauses
below it are deliberately left: "when" is a different question from "how often", and bundling them
would double the surface for no shared mechanism.

### Three clauses, one sentence, a list rather than a regex

D445 already read `Activate only as a sorcery` (213 cards) by stripping the sentence off the end
before the effect is read. The printings combine the two clauses freely:

    Activate only as a sorcery.
    Activate only once each turn.
    Activate only as a sorcery and only once each turn.
    Activate only once each turn and only as a sorcery.

So `activationRestriction` splits on "and only" and reads the parts as a list — four shapes in three
regexes rather than four patterns — and **a clause it does not know refuses the whole line**, which
is D487's rule where it matters most: a restriction read in half is an ability the table offers at a
moment the card forbids, which is worse than an unread line (D362).

### Declarative, not another predicate

`AbilityDef` already had `activateOnlyIf?: (state, source, controller) => boolean` — monstrosity's
field, checked in `legalActions` and again in the activation path. It could not carry this, for three
reasons, and the third is the one that decided it:

1. The predicate is handed `(state, source, controller)` and **not the ability index**, so it could
   not tell which of a card's abilities it is guarding. Basking Rootwalla's pump and its madness
   cost are different questions.
2. The engine has to **record** the activation, and only something that knows the restriction exists
   can do that.
3. The refusal can **name the rule** — "Azimaet Drake has already used that ability this turn" —
   instead of `activateOnlyIf`'s generic "cannot be activated right now", which is what D67 asks of
   every refusal.

So `AbilityDef.onceEachTurn?: true`, checked beside `activateOnlyIf` in both places and recorded as
the cost is paid.

### The state, and why nothing resets it

`CardInstance.abilityUsedTurn?: Readonly<Record<string, number>>` — the **turn number** each ability
index was last used on. `=== state.turn` is the whole question, so there is no cleanup-step reset to
write and none to forget: exactly the shape `loyaltyUsedTurn` has had since #43, one index deeper.
`spellsCastThisTurnBy`, `lifeLostThisTurn` and `cardsDrawnThisTurn` all need clearing in the cleanup
step; this does not, and that is worth preferring.

A separate field rather than a generalisation of `loyaltyUsedTurn`, because the two rules differ:
