CR 606.3's restriction is per **planeswalker** (two different loyalty abilities on one card are still
one activation a turn), where CR 602.5f's is per **ability** (two "once each turn" abilities are one
each).

On the instance rather than in `GameState`, which makes CR 400.7 fall out: a permanent that leaves
and comes back is a new object with a new id and its ability back — the rule a blink is about (#283).

### The tests

Eleven compile tests, including Darkthicket Wolf's whole card, three more real printings, both
combined orders, D445's clause still read on its own, a control asserting the flag is **not** set on
an ability that does not print it, and four refusal rows naming the next four clauses in the queue.

Five runtime tests through `customDeck`'s `data` on printed Azimaet Drake and Darkthicket Wolf. The
Drake is the card to measure with precisely because its ability costs `{U}`: on a board with five
Islands the mana is not what stops the second activation, so a test that passed because the mana ran
out would have proved nothing.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| the first works and the second is refused, with the rule named | both halves, because a restriction that refused everything would pass the second alone |
| it is not offered a second time either | D67/D89 — an option offered and then refused is worse than one that was never there |
| it comes back next turn | the reset, which is the turn number doing its job |
| per permanent, not per card | two Drakes are two abilities a turn; the mistake a map keyed by card name would have made |
| does not restrict an ability that does not print it | a pool Llanowar Elves taps as often as it is untapped |

### The break run

Eight breaks, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256 of all three source files:

| break | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| the reader never sets `onceEachTurn` | 9 tests |
| an unreadable restriction clause is dropped instead of refusing the line | 5 tests |
| the reader sets the flag on every ability | 2 tests |
| the activation path does not refuse the second | 3 tests |
| the activation is never recorded | 4 tests |
| the record is a boolean rather than the turn, so it never comes back | 4 tests |
| `legalActions` still offers it | 1 test |
| the record is keyed by nothing, so one ability spends them all | 4 tests |

Every one caught. The harness now treats an unapplied break as a hard failure rather than a printed
note — D507's lesson, applied the first time it could be.

### A stale refusal row, the eighth

`compile.test.ts` carried a row asserting that Basking Rootwalla's line stays unread, with a comment
calling it "the next shape in D494's queue" and putting it at **13 cards**. D508 reads it, so the row
is retired — and its figure was this family's own count rather than the queue's: re-measured, it is
**38 cards finished** and 519 lines carrying some restriction.

Eighth stale refusal row in this series, and the pattern is now named in the file: a row that says
"this is the next increment" becomes a lie the moment that increment ships. That is the row doing its
job, and it is why each one names what would retire it.

### Coverage

| | before D508 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 21,615 / 56,421 (38.3%) | **21,661 / 56,421 (38.4%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,821 | **10,859** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,598 | **6,637** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,191 | 1,191 |

**39 cards finished**, against the 38 the measurement predicted — the extra one prints both clauses,
which only the combined reading finishes.

## D509 — The three "Activate only during …" clauses, and what the declare-attackers step taught

D508's sibling, and the rest of the restriction family. After that increment the family re-measures
at **480 cards one line away** on a line carrying "Activate only …", **104** of them with the
restriction as the only unread thing, and these three clauses are 32 of those:

| cards finished | clause |
| --- | --- |
| 18 | Activate only during your turn, before attackers are declared. |
| 8 | Activate only during your turn. |
| 6 | Activate only during your upkeep. |

Thirty-two beats every shape in the printed queue, whose head is still the 19-card threshold bucket
— 17 of which are the quoted-ability job D508 records as the reason that bucket misleads.

### One field, three values

`AbilityDef.timing?: 'your-turn' | 'your-upkeep' | 'before-attackers'`. One field rather than three
booleans, because the clauses are mutually exclusive readings of the same question — *when* — and a
card prints exactly one. Three flags would have let a script say "during your upkeep" **and** "before
attackers are declared" at once, which no printing says and which the engine would then have had to
decide about.

The reader is three more clauses in `activationRestriction`'s list, and **the order inside that chain
is load-bearest**: the long clause starts with the short one, so a chain that tried "during your
turn" first would read Alaborn Veteran as restricted to the whole of its turn — a card that can tap
in its second main phase, which it cannot. A second timing clause on one ability refuses the line
rather than overwriting the first, because a silent overwrite would take the *second* clause, which
is the one a reader would least expect.

### Not `atSorcerySpeed`, which was the shortcut on offer

Sorcery timing is four conditions: your turn, your main phase, an empty stack, and priority. A card
that says only "during your turn" means **one** of them. Reusing the sorcery check — the obvious
thing, and it already existed — would have refused a Cinderhaze Wretch in its own upkeep and during
its own combat, both of which the card allows. `atActivationTiming` asks the active seat and then
the clause, and asks nothing about priority, because the generic machinery around every activated
ability already requires it and folding it in would make the same mistake one layer down.

### What the declare-attackers step taught, and why the step index is exact

The first version of the runtime tests failed for a reason worth keeping. In the declare-attackers
step **`state.priority` is `null` until attackers have been declared**, so *every* activation there
is refused for want of priority, whatever its clause — the tests would have passed on the priority
refusal rather than on anything this increment does, which is a test that proves nothing.

The engine already had that right: it is CR 508.1, and nobody gets priority in that step before the
declaration. Which is what makes the step-index reading **exact rather than an approximation**: the
only reachable moment inside declare-attackers is *after* the declaration, by which point "before
attackers are declared" has passed. So `STEPS.indexOf(step) < STEPS.indexOf('declare-attackers')`
and the printed clause are the same window for anybody who could act, and the comparison reads
`STEPS` — which is in turn order — so a step inserted later lands on the correct side of it with
nothing here changing.

The tests now declare an empty attack on the way through combat, and the helper's docblock says why.

A second test failed the same way from the other end: on an opponent's turn the active player gets
priority first, so seat 0's activation came back "you do not have priority" — again a refusal that
would have been there with no clause at all. Seat 1 passes once, which hands seat 0 priority *inside*
seat 1's main phase, and that is the only board on which the clause is the thing being asked.

**Both are the same mistake:** a refusal that arrives for the right reason by accident. The fix in
both cases was to reach the state where the clause is the only thing left that could refuse.

### The tests

Ten compile tests, including all three printings, the long-versus-short ordering asserted directly,
a control that an unrestricted ability gets no timing, the combination with D508's once-each-turn,
the two-timing-clauses refusal, and three rows for clauses still unread.

Seven runtime tests through `customDeck`'s `data` on printed **Cinderhaze Wretch**, **Alaborn
Veteran** and **Dwarven Weaponsmith**. All three abilities are mana-free, which is deliberate: a
`{3}` cost would mean every refusal could be the mana running out, or the seat not holding priority
to tap a land in that step, rather than the clause under test. A tap is paid from the permanent
itself, so the only thing that can refuse these is the restriction. (Disrupting Scepter is on the
battlefield anyway, as the artifact the Weaponsmith sacrifices.)

**The Wretch is the discriminator for all three clauses.** Every other assertion would also pass
with the three collapsed into one; the rows that pair it against the Veteran on the same board, in
the same step, with opposite answers are what say they are three.

### The break run

Eight breaks, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256 of all four source files:

| break | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| the short clause is tried before the long one | 5 tests |
| a second timing clause overwrites the first instead of refusing | 1 test (after a rewrite — see below) |
| the timing is reused as sorcery speed | 3 tests |
| the upkeep clause reads the wrong step | 2 tests |
| `before-attackers` includes the declare-attackers step | 3 tests |
| the active-seat check is dropped, so an opponent's turn passes | 1 test |
| the activation path does not refuse an out-of-window activation | 4 tests |
| `legalActions` still offers it outside its window | 1 test |

**One break had to be rewritten, and the miss is instructive.** "A second timing clause overwrites
the first" stripped the guard from the *upkeep* branch only; the test's clause order is "upkeep and
only during your turn", so the second clause hit the `your-turn` branch, whose guard was still there,
and the line was still refused. The break applied, changed real code, and discriminated nothing.
Stripping all three guards — which is what "the guard is gone" actually means — fails the test.
Third time in this series that a break has been aimed at the wrong branch of the right function
(D505 twice, now this), and the tell is the same every time: zero failures from a break you expected
to hurt.

### Coverage

| | before D509 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 21,661 / 56,421 (38.4%) | **21,705 / 56,421 (38.5%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,859 | **10,899** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,637 | **6,670** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,191 | 1,191 |

**33 cards finished**, against the 32 the measurement predicted.

Across D508 and D509 together the restriction family has gone from 0 of its 143 one-away cards read
to **72**, for two fields, one predicate and one list of five clauses.

## D510 — Soulshift N, and the version that compiled and did nothing

CR 702.46a: "When this creature dies, you may return target Spirit card with mana value N or less
from your graveyard to your hand." **25 legal corpus cards print the bare line and 17 of them were
one printed line from a finished script** — the queue head once D508 and D509 cleared the restriction
family.

Chosen over the printed queue head (the 19-card threshold bucket, 17 of which are the much larger
quoted-ability-to-`TriggerDef` job) for a second reason: **it is the first thing in the engine that
asks whether a *card* has a creature type**, which is exactly what D506 named and left.

### Mostly parts that already existed

A counted keyword like Bushido N (D503): one regex, and `soulshiftTriggers` assembling a
self-subject `dies` trigger (#157), a graveyard target (#23) and `bounceToHand`. What is new is a
graveyard filter that reads **two** things about a card — the subtype and a mana-value ceiling —
where every graveyard filter before it read one.

`Soulshift 4, soulshift 4` — Forked-Branch Garami, the only card that prints it — is refused. Its
reminder text merges the two into **one ability with two targets**, which is a different rule from
two copies of this one, so reading it as either would be a guess (D487). The anchored `\d+$` is what
does that, and a break run row confirms an unanchored version reads the line.

### The version that compiled and did nothing

The first implementation put `optional: true` on the target. The reasoning was tidy: the printed
"you may" is a choice, `optional` is the engine's "up to", every other declinable target here is
written that way. **The runtime tests said no in the clearest possible way — nothing was ever
returned.**

An optional target with nobody to ask is a target the engine declines, so every soulshift in the
game silently did nothing. And **no reader test could have caught it**: the script compiled, the
trigger was there, the count reached the description, the filter was correct. The compile block even
asserted `optional: true` and passed. It took putting a creature on a battlefield and killing it.

That is the sharpest instance so far of the rule this project keeps relearning — a reading that
*looks* right in the script is not a reading that works at the table — and it is why every increment
in this series pairs a compile block with a runtime block driven through `customDeck`.

The target is mandatory now, which is also what the rules say: the Spirit is chosen as the trigger
goes on the stack, and CR 603.3c removes the trigger entirely when there is no legal choice — which
the engine already does, so an empty graveyard is not a stuck table (asserted).

**What is left out, stated plainly:** the resolution-time decline. A player who would rather leave
the card in the graveyard cannot say so, and it always comes back. That is a choice the controller
loses and never an illegal play; it is the same gap the seven pool cards in **#328** have; and
`decisions` is where the fix for all of them belongs. The docblock says so at the point somebody
would otherwise reach for `optional` again.

### D506's note, closed

`cardHasSubtype(def, subtype)` is the printed-card twin of `hasSubtype`. A card in a graveyard has no
continuous effects applied to it — which is why `TargetSpec`'s `graveyard-*` kinds exist — but
changeling is not a continuous effect. It is a characteristic-defining ability (CR 604.3), so it
works in every zone, and a **Woodland Changeling card in a graveyard is a Spirit for soulshift**.

D506 extended the live type line inside layer 4 and recorded this hole in the same breath: nothing
asked the question of a printed card, so the omission was correct only by accident. Soulshift asks.

**The general reader still cannot**, and that is named rather than fixed: `cardWordMatch` builds
filters of the shape `(line: TypeLine) => boolean` from a printed word, and a bare type line cannot
carry a keyword, so every *compiled* "target Spirit card" filter that goes through that path is still
blind to a changeling. Widening it means widening the signature at nineteen call sites. This function
is where that change will land, and the filters that can call it today do.

### The tests

Nine compile tests: the count read at 3, 5 and 8 and reaching the description; beside fear and
beside trample on real printings; the doubled printing refused; a numberless soulshift refused; and
four assertions on `cardHasSubtype` directly — a changeling card is a Spirit and a Goblin but not an
Equipment, an ordinary Wolf card is a Wolf and not a Spirit, and a noncreature card that prints the
word is still not a Spirit.

Six runtime tests through `customDeck`'s `data` on printed Crawling Filth, Burr Grafter, Kami of the
Painted Road and Woodland Changeling:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| returns a Spirit inside the limit | the mechanic, end to end |
| will not return one above it | **the discriminator** — Burr Grafter's soulshift 3 against the same {4}{W} Kami, so a reader that dropped the number fails here and passes everything else |
| will not return a non-Spirit | the other half of the filter: Grizzly Bears is inside every limit and the wrong type |
| returns a changeling card | D506's note, paired with the Bears row so it passes because of the keyword and not because the filter is loose |
| does not reach an opponent's graveyard | "from *your* graveyard" |
| an empty graveyard is not a stuck trigger | CR 603.3c |

### The break run

Nine breaks, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256 of both source files:

| break | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| the keyword is not read at all | 7 tests |
| the regex is unanchored, so the doubled printing reads as one | 1 test |
| the target is optional again, so the engine declines every time | 5 tests |
| the mana-value ceiling is dropped | 3 tests |
| the subtype is dropped, so any card inside the limit comes back | 1 test |
| the ceiling is strict, so a Spirit at exactly N is refused | 1 test |
| the filter forgets whose graveyard it is | 1 test |
| a printed card's changeling is ignored | 2 tests |
| changeling extends a noncreature card too | 1 test |

Every one caught. Two are worth naming: *the target is optional again* is the bug this increment
actually had, kept as a permanent guard; and *the ceiling is strict* is the off-by-one that would
make Soulshift 5 refuse a five-drop, which only the Kami-at-exactly-N row can see.

### Coverage

| | before D510 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 21,705 / 56,421 (38.5%) | **21,730 / 56,421 (38.5%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,899 | **10,920** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,670 | **6,687** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,191 | 1,191 |

**17 cards finished**, exactly the measurement's prediction.

## D511 — A quoted triggered ability an Aura or Equipment grants, and the three sites that looked it up by name

`Enchanted creature has "At the beginning of your upkeep, create a 1/1 white Human creature token."`
— Commander's Authority. The grant is a quotation: the host gains an ability whose text is printed
on the Aura, and CR 113.6 says that ability is the **host's**, not the Aura's. The engine has had the
machinery since #230 (`CardScript.grantedTriggers` holding the table, `ContinuousEffect.grants`
holding indices into it so the effect stays serialisable), and the compiler has never been able to
reach it. It can now.

### The reader is `lineScriptFor` called on the quotation

`grantedTriggerFrom(quoted, name)` hands the inner text straight back to `lineScriptFor` — the same
per-line reader the card's own lines go through — and then demands the result be **exactly
triggers**:

```ts
const { triggers, ...rest } = read;
if (triggers === undefined || triggers.length === 0) return null;
if (Object.keys(rest).some((key) => (rest as Record<string, unknown>)[key] !== undefined)) {
  return null;
}
```

Recursion rather than a second grammar is the whole point: every trigger shape the compiler learns
anywhere becomes a grantable ability for free, and a quotation the compiler cannot read refuses the
**line** rather than compiling a weaker version of the card (D487). The `rest` check is what keeps
that honest — a reading that is triggers *plus* a flag would otherwise be installed with the flag
silently dropped, which is the failure D362 names.

In `attachmentBonus`, the quote is split off the front of the keyword grammar:

```ts
const quoted = /^has\s+(?:(.+?)\s+and\s+)?"([^"]+)"$/i.exec(tail);
```

Two printings exist and both are read: `has "X"` (Commander's Authority) and
`has <keyword> and "X"` (Cathar's Call, Power Fist). It is done before the `has` branch because the
quoted text contains commas and that branch's splitter would shred it — which is exactly why these
cards were refused before.

The Aura's effect and the Equipment's equip ability then carry `grants: [0, 1, …]` and the fragment
carries the `grantedTriggers` table, so **one** reader serves both attachment kinds.

### The bug the runtime test found: three lookups by card name, the third silent

Writing the runtime test turned up a real engine bug that had nothing to do with this increment's
new code. `grantedTriggers` was looked up in three places by the grantor's **card name**, through
`scriptFor` — a lookup in the hand-written registry — and all three carried a docblock explaining
that this was deliberate because "it is also the one field the oracle-text compiler never emits".

That sentence stopped being true the moment an Aura's quoted ability compiled. A compiled card has
no registry entry, so all three lookups returned `undefined`:

| site | what it decides | how it failed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `automation.ts` collection (~1637) | whether the trigger fires at all | the grant was installed and never fired |
| `scripts.ts` targets (~5910) | what the trigger may point at | an empty target list |
| `automation.ts` `abilityOrTrigger` (~4009) | **what the trigger does** | the trigger went on the stack, was announced, "resolved" in the log, and did nothing |

The third is the one that matters: it is a silent failure wearing the appearance of a working card.
Fixing one or two of three would have been worse than fixing none, because it buys a grant that
works everywhere except where it counts. The fix is a `defKey` on `GrantedTriggerRef` — populated in
`grantedTriggersOn`, where the grantor instance is in hand — and `scriptForCard(defs[defKey])`
preferred at all three sites with the name kept as the fallback, so #230's hand-written grantors
(Ophidian Eye, the soulbond pair) keep working unchanged. `abilityOrTrigger` gained an optional
`defs` parameter, passed at all five of its call sites.

This is #322's bug — "the bot reads the hand-written registry, so every compiled card is played
blind" — surviving in the one corner that change did not reach, a month later, found by a test that
played the card rather than inspected it.

### The tests

13 compile tests on real printings. Commander's Authority and Cathar's Call for the two quote
shapes; Combat Research for the same reader on an Equipment; Sixth Sense, Sticky Fingers,
Necrosynthesis, Pillory of the Sleepless and Nurturing Presence as a row each. Then five refusals:
Power Fist ("that many", which the reader cannot carry forward), Withercrown (an "unless" on a step
trigger), Idolized (an X that counts the board), a quotation that is an **activated** ability
(`{T}: Add one mana of any color.`, Karametra's Favor's text) and a quotation that is a bare keyword
(`Flying`). The last two are both refused by the same check — the recursive reading has no triggers
at all — and the "exactly triggers" check below them is a different, unreachable guard.

4 runtime tests through `customDeck`, all driven by **real plays** — `auto:cast` with a card target
for the Aura, `auto:activate` with a card target for the equip — because the first version wrote
`attachedTo` by hand and every assertion failed: the field records the attachment, the continuous
effect is installed by the resolution path. They prove the host fires the granted trigger, that it
stops when the Aura leaves, and that the trigger's **source is the host and not the Aura** (CR
113.6) — the assertion a name-keyed grant fails.

### The break run

Eleven breaks over three files, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256:

| break | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| the quote branch removed | 10 tests |
| the Aura effect stops carrying the `grants` indices | 8 tests |
| the Aura fragment stops carrying the `grantedTriggers` table | 8 tests |
| the Equipment ability stops carrying the indices | 2 tests |
| the Equipment fragment stops carrying the table | 2 tests |
| `grantedTriggersOn` stops recording the grantor's `defKey` | 2 tests |
| the collection site back to the name-only lookup | 2 tests |
| `abilityOrTrigger` back to the name-only lookup (the silent one) | 2 tests |
| `grantedTriggerFrom` stops requiring *exactly* triggers | **nothing** |
| `grantedTriggerFrom` accepts an empty trigger table | **nothing** |
| the targets site back to the name-only lookup | **nothing** |

Three uncaught, and rather than argue about them they were measured. Across all 87 distinct
quotations the corpus prints inside an attachment line:

- **0** read as triggers *plus* another field, so nothing printed can reach the `rest` check;
- **0** read as an empty trigger table, so nothing printed can reach the length check;
- **0** of the 8 readable ones carry targets, so a compiled grant never reaches the targets site.

All three stay. The first two are guards against a silently half-read grant and cost three lines;
the third is the same fix as its two siblings and becomes live the moment an inner text with a
target reads — 19 of the 51 refused quotations name one ("tap target permanent", Ghostly Touch).
This is D507's precedent, now with a corpus count behind each instead of an argument: a break that
applies, reverts, and that nothing printed can reach is recorded, not patched around.

### Coverage

| | before D511 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 21,730 / 56,421 (38.5%) | **21,738 / 56,421 (38.5%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,920 | 10,920 |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,687 | **6,693** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,191 | 1,191 |

**6 cards finished**, against a prediction of 25 — and the gap is the useful part. The script count
did not move at all, which is the shape of this family: these Auras and Equipment already compiled
(enchant, equip), they just left the bonus line unclaimed, so the increment finishes cards rather
than starting them.

### What the family actually needs next, measured instead of guessed

The prediction was wrong because the grant was never the bottleneck — the **inner** vocabulary is.
Every quotation the corpus prints inside an attachment line, by what `lineScriptFor` makes of it:

| | distinct texts | legal cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reads as triggers (ships now) | 8 | 8 |
| reads as something other than triggers — all of them activated abilities | 28 | 38 |
| the reader refuses outright | 51 | 50 |

So the quoted-attachment family is 96 legal cards, not the 583 the earlier count suggested (that
number was every quoted grant, including the creature and Sliver grants this increment does not
touch). The 28 are one engine gap, not 28 reading gaps: `{T}: This creature deals 1 damage to any
target` (Fire Whip, 7 cards) and `{T}: Add one mana of any color` (Karametra's Favor, 4 cards) are
*activated* abilities, and `ContinuousEffect` has no `grantedAbilities` to put them in. That is the
next increment in this family, and it is worth more than the 51 refusals, which are 51 separate
trigger shapes.

## D512 — Granting an **activated** ability, and the two cards that quote their own name

D511 measured the quoted-attachment family and found the gate was the inner text, not the grant: of
the 87 distinct quotations the corpus prints inside an `(Enchanted|Equipped) creature has "…"` line,
8 read as triggers, 51 the reader refused, and **28 were activated abilities** — with nowhere to put
one. `ContinuousEffect.grants` carries indices into `CardScript.grantedTriggers` and there was no
`grantedAbilities` beside it. This increment is that field and everything downstream of it.

### The engine side, which is most of the work

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `CardScript.grantedAbilities` | the table, beside `grantedTriggers` |
| `ContinuousEffect.grantsAbilities` | indices into it, beside `grants` |
| `PumpOptions.grantsAbilities` | carried through `modsFrom`, so all five grant sites reach it for nothing |
| `grantedAbilitiesOn` | `grantedTriggersOn` with the other field read |
| `LegalPlay.grantedBy` / `AutoActivateAction.grantedBy` | which card *defines* the ability |
| `grantedAbilityFor` / `abilityUseKey` | one lookup and one record key, shared by `legalActions`, `autoActions` and the bot |

**Two arrays rather than one tagged list**, because the two are used at different moments: a trigger
is collected when an event happens, an activated ability is offered in `legalActions` and paid for in
`autoActions`. A single list would make every reader ask which kind each entry was — and
`abilityOrTrigger` already has the answer for free, in the stack object's `kind`.

**`grantedBy` on the action rather than an index into an assembled list.** The obvious shortcut was
to concatenate printed and granted abilities and let `abilityIndex` run past the printed ones. That
list renumbers itself whenever an Aura arrives or leaves — which is to say, between a bot composing
an action and the engine applying it. So the action names the grantor and the index in *its* table,
and `autoActions` re-derives the grant from the board before it pays for anything: a reference to an
Aura destroyed since the play was offered is refused, not honoured.

**One loop in `legalActions`, not two.** The granted abilities are appended to the printed ones and
the same fifteen checks run over both — a granted `{T}` taps the host, a granted sorcery-speed one
is still sorcery speed, a granted one on a creature that arrived this turn is still summoning-sick.
A second loop would have been a second copy of those checks, which is how two paths that must agree
stop agreeing.

**And the mana half**, which is easy to forget because the activation path works without it: a
granted `{T}: Add one mana of any color` has to appear in `manaSources` (what the auto-tapper taps)
and in `potentialMana` (the dimmed pips). Without it the engine would offer a player the ability and
refuse the spell it was paying for in the same breath (D67). `tapSources` needed nothing — it taps
the permanent and adds the mana itself — so the entry carries `grantedBy` only to keep its
`abilityIndex` unambiguous.

### The two cards that quote their own name

Found by probing real printings rather than by reading, and it is the one place where granting an
*activated* ability is harder than granting a trigger:

```
Ninja's Kunai     "{1}, {T}, Sacrifice Ninja's Kunai: Ninja's Kunai deals 3 damage to any target."
Trusty Boomerang  "{1}, {T}: Tap target creature. Return Trusty Boomerang to its owner's hand."
```

The compiler binds a card's own name to **the ability's source**, and the source of a granted ability
is the host (CR 113.6). Both read, both compiled, and both were wrong in the worst available way:
Ninja's Kunai's granted ability would have sacrificed the **creature**, and Trusty Boomerang's would
have returned the creature to its owner's hand. Two cards that look read and eat your board.

There is no field meaning "the permanent that granted this", so `namesItsGrantor` refuses the line
(D362, D487) — and the guard is applied to the *trigger* reader too, whose D511 docblock had argued
that no printed quotation names its grantor. It was true of the triggers and false of the family.

### The tests

13 compile tests: Fire Whip and Viridian Longbow (the two attachment kinds through one reader),
Karametra's Favor as **five** abilities one per colour (the Birds of Paradise shape, which is what
proves the index list is a list), a row each for printed Midnight Covenant, Dragon Mantle, Sadistic
Obsession, Presence of Gond, Ocular Halo and Sinstriker's Will, the two self-naming refusals,
Leyline Immersion as a quotation the reader cannot read, and the D511 regression row.

9 runtime tests through `customDeck`, every Aura **cast at its host**: the ability is offered on the
host carrying the card that defines it; `{T}` taps the host and leaves the Aura untapped; it
disappears when the Aura leaves; a reference to a departed Aura is refused; **two** Auras on one
creature each grant their own index-0 ability and both resolve (+1/+0 and +1/+1, which is the row a
grantor-blind index would fail); a granted mana ability reaches `manaSources`; the dimmed pips agree;
a creature that arrived this turn cannot use a granted `{T}` ability (CR 302.6); and a Frogged host
loses the button (CR 613.1f).

One retired row: D511's "refuses a quoted ability that is not a trigger at all" was asserting the
absence this increment filled in. It now asserts that the ability reads *and* that the trigger table
stays empty.

### The break run

23 breaks over six files, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256. **14 caught**, and
the nine that were not were measured rather than argued — across all 87 attachment quotations the
corpus prints:

| break | why nothing catches it |
| --- | --- |
| `namesItsGrantor` ignores the short name | **0** grantors in the family have a comma in their name |
| `grantedAbilityFrom` drops the exactly-abilities check | **0** quotations read as abilities *plus* another field |
| the off-battlefield cost guard is dropped | **0** granted abilities carry a discard, exile, graveyard or loyalty cost |
| `abilityUseKey` keys a granted ability like a printed one | **0** quotations contain "Activate only once each turn" |
| the bot resolves a granted ability off the host's own list | the two rules that would discriminate are about a **free** ability, and **0** granted abilities cost nothing |
| `sameActivation` ignores which card granted it | same: it is a rule about a free ability already on the stack |
| `legalActions` offers granted abilities from hand and graveyard | the collector returns nothing for a card outside the battlefield, so the zone check is a short-circuit, not a rule |
| `grantedAbilitiesOn` ignores lose-all-abilities | all three callers skip a permanent with no abilities first; its sibling's clear **is** load-bearing, because the trigger loop does not skip |
| `abilityTargetSpecs` ignores the object kind | 14 granted abilities do carry targets, but an *activated* ability's targets travel on the action — the only route to that site is Spellskite-style redirection, which `soleTargetSpecOf` already leaves out for compiled cards by its own docblock |

The last two are the ones worth keeping in mind. Both are **correct** answers nothing can currently
ask for, and one of them — the layer-6 clear — had a test that looked like it covered it: the Frogged
host row passed with the line deleted, because `legalActions` had already skipped the creature. That
row's docblock now says so, which is the difference between a test and a claim.

### Coverage

| | before D512 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 21,738 / 56,421 (38.5%) | **21,768 / 56,421 (38.6%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,920 | 10,920 |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,693 | **6,718** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,191 | 1,191 |

**25 cards finished**, exactly the number the probe predicted (30 legal cards compile a granted
ability — 24 Auras and 6 Equipment — and 25 of them have no unread line left). The script count did
not move, which is this family's shape: the Auras already compiled their enchant line and left the
bonus unclaimed.

The remaining 51 refused quotations are the family's whole future: 19 of them name a target, and
every one is a separate trigger or ability shape rather than a shared mechanism.

## D513 — The threshold quoted tail, and the guard that had to be turned off

`Threshold — As long as there are seven or more cards in your graveyard, Fledgling Dragon gets
+3/+3 and has "{R}: Fledgling Dragon gets +1/+0 until end of turn."` — the head of the one-away
queue, and the increment that spends what the last two built.

40 legal cards print the threshold line. **22 are exactly one line short, and 17 of those have a
quoted tail**: the card handing *itself* an ability for as long as the condition holds. Three printed
shapes, all of them a self grant:

```
Cephalid Sage       ~ has "When ~ enters, draw three cards, then discard two cards."
Fledgling Dragon    ~ gets +3/+3 and has "{R}: ~ gets +1/+0 until end of turn."
Possessed Aven      ~ gets +1/+1, is black, and has "{2}{B}, {T}: Destroy target blue creature."
```

### Nothing new under the reader

D511 built the recursive quoted reader, D512 added the activated table beside it, and
`ContinuousEffect.while` has carried the threshold condition since D502. This is those three parts
meeting on a `scope: 'self'` static: `thresholdEffect` takes the quote off the front of the part
splitter, reads it with the same two readers, and hangs `grants` / `grantsAbilities` on the static's
own effect instead of on an attachment's bonus.

Two things *were* new, and both are small:

- **The quote comes off before the splitter runs.** A quotation contains commas and the word "and",
  and `thresholdPredicate` splits on exactly those — the same lesson `attachmentBonus` learned in
  D511, arriving in the one other place that splits a predicate.
- **`is black` is a part.** Five legal cards print `gets +1/+1, is black, and has "…"` (the Possessed
  cycle and Wayward Angel), so the splitter now splits on commas too and a colour change is a
  readable part. It is not decoration: Possessed Aven's own granted ability destroys a **blue**
  creature, and a reader that kept the printed colour would leave a blue creature pointing a gun at
  itself.

### The guard that had to be turned off

D512 taught both quoted readers to refuse a quotation that **names the card granting it**, because
the compiler binds a card's own name to the ability's *source* and for an attachment that is the host
rather than the Aura — Ninja's Kunai's granted ability would otherwise have sacrificed the creature.

Here the grantor **is** the source, so the same sentence that was a bug on an Aura is exactly right
on a self grant: Fledgling Dragon's "{R}: Fledgling Dragon gets +1/+0" means the Dragon. So the
readers take a `selfGrant` flag, and **8 of the 17 printings name themselves inside the quote** — a
copy of the attachment branch would have refused half the bucket and looked like a reading decision
rather than a mistake. The break run's second row is that flag, and it fails 8 tests without it.

### The tests

9 compile tests on real printings: Cephalid Sage (the quote as the whole predicate, with no pump at
all — an empty bonus is a real reading), Fledgling Dragon (pump plus a self-naming activated ability
— the `selfGrant` row), Possessed Aven (three parts including the colour change), Wayward Angel (four
parts, the longest printing in the family), Centaur Chieftain and Pardic Arsonist as quoted triggers,
two refusals whose inner text is unread, and the D502 regression row for a threshold line with no
quote.

5 runtime tests through `customDeck`, each run **twice — at six cards and at seven**, because "it
works at seven" and "it is always on" are the same reading of one board: the Dragon's ability is
offered at threshold and not below it (with the pump as the control); activating it pumps the Dragon;
the ability **goes away mid-turn when a card leaves the graveyard**, which is the row a static
installed at entry would fail; the Aven turns black and its ability is offered against a blue
creature across the table; and a granted **enters** trigger fires for a creature that arrives while
the condition holds, which says the engine applies statics before it raises the arrival.

Two rows elsewhere were retired rather than left to rot: D502's "leaves a line unread: a granted
ability" asserted the absence this increment filled, and the comment in its place records what
replaced it.

Three test-writing corrections, each worth the line it costs:

- the Aven's ability was *not* offered at first, and the grant was not why — `legalActions` will not
  offer a play whose target cannot be filled, and the board had nothing blue on it. The row now puts
  a Cephalid Sage across the table and says why.
- Cephalid Sage's discard is **asked, not done**: "then discard two cards" compiles to a decision, so
  the hand is three up and a question is owed. The row answers it rather than asserting a net hand
  size that would have hidden either half.
- the first version asserted `pendingDiscard`, which is a different mechanism (the cleanup-step
  discard) from `pendingDecision`.

### The break run

13 breaks over `scripts.ts`, each verified to apply and to revert against a SHA-256. **13 of 13
caught** — the first clean sweep in this series, which is what a reader built out of parts that
already have tests looks like. The ones worth naming: *selfGrant is not passed* (8 tests), *the
quoted branch drops the threshold condition* (26 tests, because a permanent grant breaks every
board), *the colour change uses the wrong colour* (4), and *an unreadable head no longer refuses the
line* (1 — the Boneshard Slasher row, which is the whole-line rule doing its job on a card whose
pump reads and whose drawback does not).

### Coverage

| | before D513 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 21,768 / 56,421 (38.6%) | **21,780 / 56,421 (38.6%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,920 | **10,932** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,718 | **6,728** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,191 | 1,191 |

**10 cards finished** and 12 new scripts — the first increment in a while to add scripts rather than
only finish cards, because a threshold line is sometimes the whole of a creature's text box.

The bucket is down from 17 quoted tails to 7, and the seven name their own next increments: a
"becomes the target of a spell or ability" trigger (Boneshard Slasher, and the 13-card Frost Walker
bucket is the same shape), an ETB that pumps a colour-defined group (Gloomdrifter), an opponent-cast
trigger (Hunting Grounds), and an optional counter (Chlorophant).

## D514 — The Illusion drawback, and what a clause is worth next to a line

`When Frost Walker becomes the target of a spell or ability, sacrifice it.` — **15 legal cards**, 13
of them with no other unread line, and the whole family was held up by three small things.

### Three small things

1. **The prologue read `Whenever` and not `When`.** CR 603.1 makes no distinction; the split is
   historical — the old Illusion drawback says "When", the modern upside printings say "Whenever".
   One word was read and the other was not.
2. **The opponent-restricted printing had no row at all.** `… becomes the target of a spell or
   ability an opponent controls` is what Old Fat Spider, Battle Mammoth and Ruric Thar print, and it
   differs in `by` — written as its own row rather than an optional group, because a card that fired
   off its own controller's Giant Growth would be a different card.
3. **The tail `sacrifice it` had nowhere to go.** `sacrifice <permanent>` elsewhere in the file is
   the sacrifice the **controller chooses** from their battlefield; sending this clause there would
   ask a player which of their creatures to sacrifice when the card names one.

Also read: `mill N cards` with nobody named, which means the controller (CR 701.13a) — Cephalid
Aristocrat and Cephalid Illusionist.

### `by: 'any'` is the whole of the card

The event's default is `by: 'opponent'`, because **ward** was the only thing that used it and ward
never triggers off its controller's own spells. The Illusion drawback has no "an opponent casts" in
it: you cannot pump your own Illusion, and that is the card. So the unrestricted row says `any` out
loud, and the two runtime rows are each other's discriminator — the Illusion dies to its own
controller's Giant Growth, and Old Fat Spider draws **nothing** off its controller's.

### What a clause is worth next to a line

| | before D514 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 21,780 / 56,421 (38.6%) | **21,901 / 56,421 (38.8%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 10,932 | **11,033** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,728 | **6,791** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,191 | 1,191 |

**63 cards finished and 101 new scripts** — four times the bucket this increment set out to read,
because `sacrifice it` and `mill N cards` are **clauses rather than lines**: they turn up in ETB
triggers, activated abilities and spells as readily as in the trigger that led here. The last few
increments finished cards without adding scripts; this one did both, and the difference is the level
the reading sits at.

### Two tests that were refusals, and one from the increment before

The clause's arrival changed three standing rows, and each one is worth more as a pair than as a
quiet edit:

- **`does not read the same sacrifice behind a different prologue`** asserted that `Whenever ~
  attacks, sacrifice ~` went unread. It reads now (28 legal cards print that shape), and what had to
  stay true is the other half: the trigger carries **no** `leavesAtEndOfTurn`, because a sacrifice
  behind another prologue is not a creature that leaves at end of turn, and a bot holding one back
  to protect a creature it is about to sacrifice would be reading a flag the card does not have.
- **`does not read "your end step" as "the end step"`** was a refusal for the same reason, and once
  the clause read, the choice was between the pair reader that carries the bot hint and the generic
  trigger path that does not. So `At the beginning of your end step, sacrifice ~` is read **here**,
  with `of: 'you'` taken from the printed word rather than defaulted — 11 legal cards print it
  against 25 for "the", and the two are different cards. Coverage did not move for this one: the
  generic path already read those lines. What moved is the hint.
- **D513's Boneshard Slasher refusal** became a reading one increment later: its threshold
  quotation is this exact trigger, so it came along for nothing. The row is kept as a positive
  assertion, with the pair recorded — refusing the whole line in D513 is what left the card correct
  to finish rather than wrong and finished (D487).

### The tests, and the break run

7 compile tests (the three Illusion printings through one `it.each` with the `by: 'any'` assertion,
the opponent-restricted row, the bare mill, and two refusal rows for the neighbours that stay
unread: an optional draw, which needs #337's "you may" gate, and `sacrifice it unless you discard a
land card`, which needs the 44-card cost vocabulary).

6 runtime tests through `customDeck`: the Walker sacrificed by its own controller's spell and by an
opponent's; a spell that targets nothing leaving it alone (the control that makes those two about
*targeting* rather than about a spell resolving); the Spider's opposite restriction in both
directions; the bare mill milling its controller with the Octopus still standing; and the CR 400.7
guard — a permanent already gone when the trigger resolves does nothing rather than being dragged
back out of exile.

One test-writing correction, and the engine was right: the first version called `tapAllLands` for
seat 1 on seat 0's turn and was refused for want of priority. An instant is castable with priority on
anybody's turn and `payFrom` taps the caster's own lands, so the row passes priority and casts.

**10 breaks over `scripts.ts`, 10 of 10 caught** — including both halves of each `by` (the
unrestricted row taking the default, and the restricted row taking `any`), the missing zone guard,
the wrong permanent sacrificed, and the mill reading the wrong number or the wrong player.

## D515 — Devoid, and 132 cards the engine was playing the wrong colour

`Devoid (This card has no color.)` — CR 702.114a, and **132 legal printings** say it. Every one of
them arrives from card data with a *non-empty* colours array, because that field is derived from the
mana cost: Abstruse Interference costs `{2}{U}` and the row says blue.

So this was not an unread line. It was **132 cards played as the wrong colour**: a Counterspell for
blue could counter one, protection from black turned aside a devoid Eldrazi, and every colour filter
counted them. The line sat in the unread column, which is what made it look like a gap rather than a
defect — the queue measures what is unread, and a wrong reading that comes from *data* rather than
from a reader is invisible to it.

### One place, because that is where the question is asked

The reading is two lines: a `devoid` member of `PrintedPart` so the word is recognised, and one check
at the top of `printedColors`. That function is the single place this engine asks what colour a card
is — `characteristicsOf` calls it for every permanent and every spell on the stack, and `copySpell`
calls it for a copy's characteristics (CR 707.2).

Two places it deliberately does **not** go:

- **`printedDef`.** Setting `colors: []` there would leave anything holding a def built another way
  still wrong, and doing both would be two sources for one fact.
- **`Characteristics.keywords`.** Devoid says nothing about how a permanent behaves on the
  battlefield, which is what that vocabulary is for; a `devoid` entry there would be a word no rule
  reads (D57). It is a fact about the *card*, in every zone.

Colour **identity** is untouched (CR 903.4): a devoid card's identity still comes from the mana
symbols on it, which is why a Commander deck may not run one outside its colours. Nothing in this
package computes identity, and the field this reads is not it.

### The tests

3 runtime tests through `customDeck`, and the pair is the point: **Blinding Drone and a control
creature with the same `{1}{U}` cost**, one printing the word and one not. The Drone is colourless
and the control is blue; a Bears with protection from blue is protected from the control and **not**
from the Drone; and `isPrintedAbilityLine` reads the word as a line (so `compile.ts` counts it and
emits nothing) while refusing it inside a sentence.

**4 breaks, 4 caught.** Worth naming the third: *devoid strips every card's colours* fails **31**
tests, which is the measure of how much of this engine runs on colour — and the fourth, *the word is
matched anywhere rather than as a whole part*, is caught by exactly one assertion, the whole-line
rule's.

### Coverage

| | before D515 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 21,901 / 56,421 (38.8%) | **21,998 / 56,421 (39.0%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,033 | 11,033 |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,791 | **6,802** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,191 | **1,192** |

97 printed lines and **11 cards finished** — and the number that matters is not in the table: 132
legal printings now have the colour their own card gives them.

## D516 — The Act of Treason sentence, read as one group; and devoid on a spell

`Gain control of target creature until end of turn. Untap that creature. It gains haste until end
of turn.` — the queue head after D515, with **15 legal cards** one printed line away on it and
**38 printings** carrying the first sentence.

### Why it is read as a group and not clause by clause

Every other reading in this compiler splits a resolution on its full stops and reads each clause on
its own. That is exactly what must not happen here, and the reason is D362 rather than tidiness:

- `Untap that creature` and `It gains haste until end of turn` both refer to the **target**, and
  this file's referent machinery reads those words as something else. "That creature" is the other
  creature in a combat (D480); "it" through `selfEffect` is the card itself — so `it gains haste`
  compiled clause-wise hands the **spell** haste and does nothing at all. A card that resolves and
  silently buys nothing is worse than an unread line.
- The three parts cannot be allowed to drift apart. Without the untap a stolen tapped creature does
  nothing; without the haste it is summoning-sick for its new controller (CR 302.6), which is the
  entire point of the card; without the duration it never goes home.

So `stealPrefix` matches all three sentences or none, and one function — `stealUntilEndOfTurn` in
`effects.ts` — owns the whole mechanism: `gainControl`, `tap(..., false)`, a single `end-of-turn`
pump carrying haste and anything else the tail grants, and a separate `controlRevertTo` effect that
sends the creature home. The pool's own hand-written Act of Treason was rewritten onto the same
function, so there is one implementation rather than two free to disagree.

### The grammar, measured rather than guessed

Over the 38 printings the third sentence comes in three shapes and no others:

```
It gains haste until end of turn.                   Act of Treason, 20 printings
It gains haste and menace until end of turn.        Lose Calm; Traitorous Blood's "trample and haste"
It gets +2/+0 and gains haste until end of turn.    Malevolent Whispers, Mascot Interception
Until end of turn, it gets +2/+0 and gains haste.   Traitorous Instinct
```

The keyword list therefore goes through `grantedKeywords`, which validates it against
`printedKeywords` — the function the engine uses to read a keyword line back — rather than matching
the literal word *haste*. The duration is accepted at either end of the clause. And the list must
*contain* haste: `stealUntilEndOfTurn` adds haste itself, so a tail that does not ask for it is a
clause this reader has no business answering for, and letting one through would hand a creature
haste its card never promised.

`grantedKeywords` is also what refuses the two printings whose tail is a quoted ability — Furnace
Reins and Shackles of Treachery, `it gains haste and "Whenever this creature deals combat damage to
a player or battle, create a Treasure token."` Granting a quoted ability to a creature you do not
own needs a `grants` index this function cannot build, and the quotation splits into fragments
`printedKeywords` does not recognise, so the **line** refuses (D487) rather than the steal
compiling and the grant disappearing.

Anything after the third sentence goes back to the ordinary composer, which is why Bond of Passion
(a second, independent target) and Bloody Betrayal (a Blood token) still refuse the line rather than
shipping half of what they print.

### The hand-written card was refusing a legal target

`ACT_OF_TREASON` filtered its target to `creatureYouDontControl`. The printed text says `target
creature`, and the narrowing bought nothing: `TargetSpec.friendly`'s own docblock says the bot
already prefers the enemy and the enemy's creatures, and untapping your own tapped blocker and
giving it haste is a real play. A shipping card that refuses a legal target is a defect, not a style
choice (D362), so the filter went and the standing test row that asserted the refusal was retargeted
to assert the play — the Hill Giant untaps, gains haste, and stays on its own side.

### Devoid on a spell was reported unread, having become read

Found while probing the family: Turn Against is one of these cards, and its only unread line was
`Devoid`. D515 made devoid real — `printedColors` returns no colours for a card that prints it — but
only the **permanent** compile path said so. A permanent's lines go through `isPrintedAbilityLine`,
which counts the word compiled and emits nothing. A spell's lines go through `spellScriptFor`, where
a keyword declaration nothing can *build* lands in `declared` and is reported unread. After D515 the
same printed word was compiled on a devoid creature and unread on a devoid instant, while the engine
played both colourless.

`isDevoidLine` in `characteristics.ts` closes that, and is deliberately narrow: the other members of
`PrintedPart` — landwalk, protection, the combat statics, the blocker bans — are facts about a
permanent on the battlefield and cannot appear on an instant or a sorcery, so widening it to "any
part read off the def" would buy nothing and would let a genuinely unread battlefield line through
on a card type that cannot have one. **Five legal spells** had `Devoid` as their only unread line:
Turn Against, Consuming Sinkhole, Oblivion Strike, Reality Hemorrhage and Unnatural Endurance.

### The tests

**14 compile tests** and **8 runtime tests through `customDeck`**. Worth naming three:

- the runtime rows check the four facts the card is made of separately — it changes sides, it
  untaps, it has haste, and it **goes home at end of turn** rather than dying in the thief's
  graveyard — plus the pump riding and expiring with the same effect;
- a refusal row for a steal whose tail grants *flying* rather than haste. No legal card prints it;
  it is the guard, not a card;
- three refusal rows for D487 in its three variants (the quoted grant, the Blood token, the counter
  before the untap), each of which *starts* with a sentence this reader knows.

### The break run

**15 breaks, 13 caught — and the two that were not are recorded here because the *breaks* were
vacuous, not the tests:**

- *isDevoidLine answers for every printed keyword* widened the predicate to `part.kind === 'keyword'`.
  But `Islandwalk` reads as a `landwalk` part and `Protection from red` as a `protection` part, so
  the widening left both of those answers false and nothing could notice. Re-run as
  `|| part.kind === 'landwalk'` and again as `printedParts(line).length > 0`: **both caught.**
- *the pump has no duration* deleted the explicit `duration: 'end-of-turn'` from
  `stealUntilEndOfTurn`. `pump` defaults `opts.duration` to `'end-of-turn'`, so that line restates
  the default and deleting it changes nothing. Re-run as `duration: 'permanent'`: **caught.**

So **16 real breaks, 16 caught.** The ones worth naming: *the tail after the group is thrown away*
(`rest: []`) is caught by the three D487 refusal rows, and *the hand-written Act of Treason does
nothing* is caught by the pool-card rows — which is the check that the hand-written card and the
compiled reading are still the same mechanism.

### Coverage

| | before D516 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 21,998 / 56,421 (39.0%) | **22,044 / 56,421 (39.1%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,033 | **11,043** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,802 | **6,817** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,192 | 1,192 |

46 printed lines and **15 cards finished.** Fourteen of them are named and verified by probe:
nine on the steal reader alone (Act of Treason, Involuntary Employment, Limits of Solidarity, Lose
Calm, Malevolent Whispers, Portent of Betrayal, Sarkhan Vol, Traitorous Blood, Traitorous Instinct),
Turn Against on both halves of the increment, and four on the devoid correction alone (Consuming
Sinkhole, Oblivion Strike, Reality Hemorrhage, Unnatural Endurance). The fifteenth is not attributed:
`grantedKeywords` and the clause readers are not scoped to this family, so a card outside it can
finish on them, and guessing which one would be a number with nothing behind it. Measured on a
freshly built `dist` with no stale-engine warning, `LEGAL=1` over the 31,654-row corpus.

## D517 — The Unearth keyword line, and the index that was in the way

`Unearth {cost}` (CR 702.84). **56 distinct legal names print it; 25 had it as their only unread
line** — Dregscape Zombie, Hellspark Elemental, Corpse Connoisseur, First-Sphere Gargantua, Grixis
Slavedriver, Hell's Thunder, Shambling Remains, Viscera Dragger, Vithian Stinger, the three
Scrapworks, Simian Simulacrum, Tocasia's Onulet and the rest.

### The mechanic was never the gap

This engine has played unearth since D183 and the pool carries two hand-written unearth cards. The
ability, the haste, the end-step exile and the leave-the-battlefield replacement all existed and all
had tests. What stood in the way was the **shape**.

The printed card schedules a one-shot: "exile it at the beginning of the next end step". D183 built
that as a delayed trigger (CR 603.7) — `delayed: true`, which `raiseTrigger` uses to keep the
ordinary event path from firing it — scheduled by `scheduleDelayed` with the trigger's own **index**
into the card's `triggers` list. An index is only knowable once that list is finished, so the ability
builder took a `() => CardScript` thunk and read the index back off the completed script:

```ts
const unearth = (cost: string, script: () => CardScript): AbilityDef => ({ … })
// DREGSCAPE_ZOMBIE: abilities: [unearth('{B}', () => DREGSCAPE_ZOMBIE)]
```

A compiled card has no such thunk. `compile.ts` assembles its `triggers` from *every* line of the
card, so while this line is being read the index it would need does not exist yet. That is precisely
what the standing note in `keywordScriptFor` said — "written out as an ability plus `unearthExile()`
per card rather than as a field, so there is no one fragment to emit" — and it is why 25 cards sat
behind a mechanic the engine already had.

### The exile is read off the body instead of scheduled onto it

`unearthExile` is now an **ordinary** end-step trigger gated on the `UNEARTHED` counter the ability
already puts on the body — the same counter the leave-replacement has read since D183. No index, no
thunk, so `unearthFragment(cost)` is one builder, and the pool's two hand-written cards are built
from it alongside the new `keywordScriptFor` row. There is no second implementation to drift, which
is what `compiled-vs-written.test.ts` would otherwise eventually catch.

**Why it is the same card and not an approximation.** A one-shot and a repeating-but-conditional
trigger differ only if the condition can survive the first firing, and it cannot: the first end step
exiles the body and the counter goes with it. The one way to tell them apart would be removing the
counter from a living unearthed creature, and nothing in this engine does that — `addCounters` is the
only writer of `UNEARTHED` and no card removes a counter by that name. Stated rather than hidden,
because it is the one real difference: a future card that stripped counters would leave the body
where the printed one exiles it.

Two things it fixes on the way:

- `of: 'any'` is now what the trigger **is** rather than what the scheduling asked for, so a body
  that reached the battlefield on another seat's turn is exiled at the end of *that* turn without the
  scheduling having had to predict it.
- The trigger carries no `subject`, so it cannot act on an object that has since been replaced
  (CR 400.7). The body it exiles is the body it is on.

`delayedIndexOf` stays, because Thicket Basilisk and Flickerwisp still schedule by index; unearth is
simply no longer one of its callers.

### What the fragment deliberately does not set

`leavesAtEndOfTurn` — the bot's hint that a creature will not be there next turn. For a card with
unearth that depends on **how the body arrived**: a Dregscape Zombie cast from hand stays. Setting it
from the keyword would tell the bot every unearth creature is a Ball Lightning. Hellspark Elemental
still sets it, for its own printed reason: it sacrifices itself at the end of every turn however it
got there.

### The tests

**8 compile rows and 7 runtime rows through `customDeck`.** The runtime describe is built on a
**pair** — Ashen Revenant and Ashen Footsoldier, the same 2/1 body, one printed line apart — and the
row that matters most is the control:

> a body that was **cast** must not be exiled at end of turn.

That row is what the change makes load-bearing. The exile now rides on the card from the moment it
reaches the battlefield however it got there, so the `UNEARTHED` counter is the only thing between a
cast Dregscape Zombie and an exile it never earned. Nothing else in the suite would have noticed if
that gate went.

Three refusal rows, and the third is a real card: **Dregscape Sliver** prints *"Each Sliver creature
card in your graveyard has unearth {2}"*, which grants the keyword to **other cards in a zone this
fragment says nothing about**. Reading it as the Sliver's own unearth would be a wrong card rather
than an unread line (D362), which is why the reader matches a whole line and not the word.

### The break run

**12 breaks, 12 caught.** The two worth naming are the pair the refactor created:

- *the exile is not gated on the UNEARTHED counter* — caught by the control row, which is the whole
  reason that row exists.
- *the exile is delayed again, so the event path never fires it* — restoring `delayed: true` makes
  the trigger unreachable, because nothing schedules it any more. Caught by the end-of-turn row.

And two about the reader rather than the mechanic: accepting a bare `Unearth` with no cost, and
matching the word anywhere in the line rather than as a whole declaration (which is Dregscape
Sliver).

### Coverage

| | before D517 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 22,044 / 56,421 (39.1%) | **22,096 / 56,421 (39.2%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,043 | **11,076** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,817 | **6,842** |
| of those, needing no script at all | 1,192 | 1,192 |

52 printed lines and **25 cards finished** — exactly the 25 the probe predicted, which is what a
keyword family should look like when the mechanic was already there and only the shape was in the
way. Measured on a freshly built `dist` with no stale-engine warning, `LEGAL=1` over the 31,654-row
corpus.
