## D518 — Rank the queue by what a player meets, and the artifact that ranking found

### Why a second queue

`one-line-short.mjs` ranks the unread shapes by how many cards each would finish. That is the right
question for coverage and the wrong one for a beta. **15,887 legal cards are one line short**, and
those lines come in **13,245 distinct shapes with 8,159 printed by exactly one card**. A queue
ordered by cards-finished says the next hundred increments are worth a few hundred cards each and
never says which of them a person at a table would notice.

So `corpus-decks.mjs` gained `UNREAD=1`, which asks the other question. A card only costs a player
anything if they **see** it, and costs more if they try to **play** it. Each game records the
distinct cards that left a library — hand, battlefield, graveyard, exile, stack, command; everything
but the library is a card somebody looked at — and the casts and activations a seat actually took,
crosses both with `unreadLines`, and ranks the shapes by encounters.

Every exit from `play()` goes through one collector, so a stalled game's sightings are counted
exactly as a finished game's are. A game that went badly still showed its players cards, and leaving
those out would measure only the games that went well.

### The beta number

Over **40 four-player pods** of singleton 100-card decks drawn from 28,542 real cards:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| card sightings (a card that left a library) | 1,680 |
| of those, cards with an unread line | **1,180 (70.2%)** |
| casts and activations | 3,119 |
| of those, of a card with an unread line | 2,036 (65.3%) |

So at 39.2% of printed lines read, **about seven in ten cards a player actually picks up** are ones
the engine runs only partly. Games still finish — 40 of 40, no throw, no stall, 0.4 cardboard cards
per 100-card deck — so the table works and the tabletop mode is unaffected. What is not yet true is
the Arena-like promise for the majority of cards in hand.

### The artifact, and the correction

The first run's ranking was wrong, and worth recording rather than quietly fixing. It put Icatian
Infantry's `{1}: ~ gains banding until end of turn` at the top with **360 plays** and Orzhov
Guildmage next with **103** — one card each. That is not what a table meets; it is the bot
activating one free repeatable ability over and over, which a person would not do. **Ranking by raw
plays measures how repeatable a shape is, not how often it is encountered.**

The queue now ranks by **games in which a card carrying the shape was played at least once** — one
vote per card per game, which a loop cannot run up. The raw play count is still printed beside each
row, because "how much of the engine's work is spent on partly-read cards" is a fair question for it
to answer; it is just not the queue.

The sighting figure needed no correction and is the one that matters: it was already one vote per
card per game.

### What the corrected queue says

| games of 40 | shape | cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 18 | `At the beginning of combat on your …` | 18 |
| 15 | `Whenever ~ deals combat damage to a …` | 15 |
| 14 | `At the beginning of your end step` | 14 |
| 14 | `Choose one —` | 14 |
| 12 | `Draw a card` | 12 |
| 10 | `As an additional cost to cast this` | 9 |
| 9 | `At the beginning of your upkeep if` | 8 |

**Trigger prologues, not exotic mechanics** — and the same families the printings queue ranks
highest (`At the beginning of your …` is 946 printings, `Whenever ~ deals combat damage` 298, `At
the beginning of combat on your` 202). The two rankings converging is the useful result: the big
shapes are also the ones players meet, so breadth and experience point the same way for now.

One row is a question rather than an answer: **`Draw a card` on 12 cards**. A bare draw is read, so
that row is a clause the composer refused *in context* — the next probe, not the next reader.

---

## D519 — Correcting myself twice, and finding the actual lever

### The correction that matters

D518's in-play queue put `At the beginning of combat on your turn, …` at the top: 18 of 40 pods, 262
distinct legal printings, **110 of them with it as their only unread line**. I called that four
times D517's haul from one reader. **That was wrong, and wrong twice over.**

First, the prologue was already read — `scripts.ts` has had the `begin-combat` row since the
258-printing family was measured. So the 110 cards are not blocked by the prologue at all; they are
blocked by their **tails**, and the whole line refuses because a line is read whole or not at all
(D487).

Second, and the part that changes the plan: grouping those 110 by the tail's opening verb phrase
gives roughly **sixty** groups, the largest being eleven. There is no reader here worth 110 cards.
The shapes that look big by card count are big because many cards share a *prologue*, not because
they share an *effect* — and the prologues are largely done.

Worth stating plainly because it is the second time this project has been misled by a queue that
counts cards per shape: `one-line-short.mjs` and D518's in-play ranking both group by the line, and a
line's *first seven words* are its prologue. Both queues therefore rank prologue families, which is
why they agreed — and neither was answering "what reader should I write".

### What the measurement says instead

So the question was asked of the clause rather than the line. Of the **16,823 legal cards that are
exactly one unread line from finished**, how many have that line *containing* each recurring
combinator:

| cards | combinator |
| --- | --- |
| **950** | `for each <thing>` |
| **713** | `where X is …` |
| **591** | `you may <verb>. If you do, <effect>` |
| 442 | `. Then <clause>` |
| 364 | `if you control <thing>,` |
| 276 | `up to one target` |
| 194 | `you may pay <cost>. If you do` (a subset of the 591) |
| 162 | `When you do,` |
| 36 | `you may have target …` |
| 30 | `if you've cast … this turn` |

These are **ten to forty times** any card-shape family, and they are upper bounds rather than
promises: a card whose line contains `for each` may be unread for a second reason in the same line.
As a ranking of where effort pays, it is far better evidence than either shape queue.

### The plan this sets

The path to high coverage is **a small number of clause combinators**, not thousands of card shapes.
That is D514's lesson — "a clause is worth more than a line" — generalised, and it is the first
piece of evidence in this project that the long tail is tractable at all: 13,245 distinct shapes is
hopeless, eight combinators is not.

The top two share their machinery. `for each <countable>` and `where X is <count>` are both **a
number read off the board**, which is what `countFrom` already is. So they are one increment, not
two, and it is the next one.

## D520 — Read a quantity off the board

`countOfThing` has been able to count a board since D444. Until this increment exactly **one** caller
asked it: `tokenEffect`, for "create a 1/1 Goblin for each Mountain you control". The count was the
hard part and it was already written; what was missing was every other clause that spends one.

D519 put `for each <thing>` (950 one-away cards) and `where X is …` (713) at the head of the
combinator queue and said they were one increment because they are one number. They are, and the
increment turned out to be three things rather than one.

### 1. The clauses that spend a count

Measured over the legal corpus, the grammars that put a board count in a clause:

| cards | clause |
| --- | --- |
| 140 | `draw N cards for each <T>` |
| 122 | `you gain N life for each <T>` |
| 114 | `deals X damage to <dest>, where X is the number of <T>` |
| 112 | `deals damage to <dest> equal to the number of <T>` |
| 76 | `Add {M} for each <T>` |
| 26 | `you lose life equal to the number of <T>` |
| 25 | `draw cards equal to the number of <T>` |
| 22 | `you gain life equal to the number of <T>` |
| 13 | `you lose N life for each <T>` |
| 11 | `deals N damage to <dest> for each <T>` |
| 8 | `each opponent loses N life for each <T>` |

Magic writes the same number three ways and the difference is not only word order: `, where X is the
number of <T>` announces it and the body's slot is the letter X; ` for each <T>` makes the body's
printed number a **rate**, so "2 life for each card" is two per card; `equal to the number of <T>`
has no slot in the body at all. All three are read in `countScaledEffect`, which is a table of
bodies over one count — the same multiplying shape the trigger prologue table and `composeEffects`
were. Nothing new in the effect vocabulary: `gainLife`, `loseLife`, `draw`, `drawLater` and
`addToPool` are the calls the printed-number readers beside them already make, and the only
difference is that the number is a function of `EffectContext` rather than a constant.

Because a count is read in the **clause**, every prologue that already composes picks it up for
free. Ancestor's Chosen — "When Ancestor's Chosen enters, you gain 1 life for each card in your
graveyard" — reads with no trigger reader changed.

### 2. The damage word order, which was the sharpest statement of the gap

`damageEffect` has read "deals damage equal to the number of `<T>` **to** `<dest>`" since D444, and
**no printed card says that**. All 226 cards that print a counted damage clause put the destination
first. So the machinery was reachable from a grammar nothing printed and unreachable from the two
everything printed. `countedDamageFrom` reads all three orders and hands the destination back
unread, so `damageDestination` stays the single place a destination is understood.

### 3. The vocabulary, and the wrong reading that was waiting inside it

`countOfThing` knew five countables. Widened against the phrases the corpus actually names:
`creature(s) you control` (112 mentions), `card(s) in your hand` (84), the five basic land types (87
between them), `attacking creature(s)` (30), `instant and sorcery card(s) in your graveyard` (29),
`other creature(s) you control` (15), `card(s) in your graveyard` (15), `creature card(s) in all
graveyards` (9). Refused, each for a stated reason: `basic land type among lands you control`
(domain, a distinct-type count), `creature in your party`, `the greatest power among …`, `the amount
of life you gained this turn`, `card exiled this way` — different kinds of fact, and D57's rule says
a count with no reading beats a guessed one.

**The defect this had to fix first.** "Swamps you control" and "Goblins you control" are the same
five printed words and two different counts, and the tribal branch asks `ch.isCreature`. Until now
no card reached that branch with a land type, because Corrupt and Cabal Coffers print their counts in
word orders nothing read — so the bug was latent, and an earlier probe of three synthetic cards
(Swamp, Goblin, Island) recorded that the path was unreachable. Widening the reach makes it
reachable. Reading those orders without `landsOfSubtype` would have made Cabal Coffers tap, resolve
cleanly and add nothing: a card that works and is wrong, which is worse than an unread line because
an unread line is flagged for a human (D362). **"Plains" is the same trap one layer down** — its own
plural (CR 205.3i), so the `-s` rule reads it as "Plain", which is not a land type at all.

### What it moved

| | before D520 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 22,096 / 56,421 (39.2%) | **22,226 / 56,421 (39.4%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,076 | **11,171** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,842 | **6,938** |

**96 cards finished**, the largest single increment since D514, and from one count rather than one
shape — which is D519's prediction holding.

Lotleth Giant is the ground truth for the drain row and is hand-written in the pool, so
`compiled-vs-written.test.ts` reads its printed line through this path and compares it against the
script a human wrote. Cabal Coffers, Battle Hymn, Ground Assault, Feedback Bolt, Ancestral Tribute,
Ancestor's Chosen and Cosmic Epiphany now read end to end. Corrupt still does not, and correctly: its
printed line is two sentences and the second counts "the damage dealt this way", so the line is
refused whole (D487).

**16 of 16 breaks caught**, every one verified to apply against a unique anchor and to revert to a
SHA-256 match. Two were uncaught on the first pass and both were **weak tests rather than vacuous
breaks**, so both were answered with a test rather than counted as a miss:

- removing the Plains case still *read* — it falls through to a creature count of zero — so a compile
  row asserting the line is read passes either way. The discrimination had to be a life total, and
  is now a runtime row with two Plains on the battlefield.
- widening the scaled-mana regex to any symbol admitted `{2}`, generic mana a pool cannot hold, and
  nothing printed it in a test. Answered with a refusal row.

## D521 — A subtype count was counting creatures, and D520 shipped it

A correction to D520, found by the probe written for the increment *after* it.

D520 gave `countOfThing` a branch for the five basic land types and argued the rest of its tribal
branch was safe, because no card had ever reached that branch with a land type. The probe asked the
compiler instead of asking the argument:

```
an artifact type (Food): unread=0  READS
a land type (Gate):      unread=0  READS
a creature type (Goblin):unread=0  READS
```

All three read, and the first two compiled to a count of **creatures** with that subtype — of which
there are never any, because Food is an artifact type and Gate is a land type. So D520 closed the
hole for five words and left it open for every other non-creature subtype. That is the card that
resolves and does nothing, which the whole family exists to refuse: worse than an unread line,
because an unread line is flagged for a human (D362).

**What I got wrong, precisely.** Earlier in the same stretch I had probed three synthetic cards
(Swamp, Goblin, Island), found all three refused, and recorded that the tribal branch was
unreachable. That was true *of D520's readers* and stopped being true the moment their reach
widened — which is the thing D520 itself widened. A reachability finding has a date on it.

### The fix is the rules answer, not a wider net

`landsOfSubtype` became `permanentsOfSubtype`, and the branch for the five basic types went away
because it is subsumed. "The number of Goblins you control" counts **permanents** you control with
that subtype (CR 109.2, CR 205.3), and subtype namespaces are disjoint — a creature type appears
only on creatures, a land type only on lands, an artifact type only on artifacts — so counting
permanents is *equal* to counting within the right namespace and there is no case where it counts
something the card did not mean. That is what makes it one function rather than a table of "which
zone does this word belong to", which the compiler has no vocabulary to answer (#340 and #341 are
open tasks about exactly that missing vocabulary).

For a creature type it agrees with the hand-written `creaturesOfSubtype` permanent for permanent,
which is what keeps a compiled count and Krenko's `goblinCount` the same number. A test pins that
agreement rather than leaving it to the argument.

**Every one of these rows READ before the fix.** What was wrong was the number, so the
discrimination had to be a life total, and the five runtime rows are life totals.

## D522 — A size read off the board, the temporary half

D520 read the one-shot counted clauses and left the counted **size** out, because a size is not
one-shot. Asked of the corpus, the cards one unread line from finished whose line is a counted size
number **355**, and they split by duration into two different jobs:

| | cards | why it is a different job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TEMPORARY (`until end of turn`) | 222 | the amount is locked in as the effect is created (CR 611.2c, pinned by D301), so a count that is a function of `EffectContext` is enough — reader work only |
| STATIC (no duration) | 133 | a continuous effect whose amount is a **live** count, and `state.effects` is serialised to Redis, so a function cannot make the trip |

**That 355 was a ceiling, and the ceiling was not the number.** Of it, only **92** name a count
`countOfThing` can already read — 52 temporary, 40 static. The other 263 are held up by the
*vocabulary* rather than by a size reader, and that tail is genuinely long: `basic land type among
lands you control` 11, `its power` 9, `creature blocking it` 8, `that card's mana value` 6, then
nothing above 4. Worth recording because the first estimate from the shape buckets was ~103, which
undercounted the family by a factor of three for D519's reason — the buckets group by the line, and
a line's first seven words are its prologue.

### What shipped

`countTailOf`, lifted out of D520's `countScaledEffect` so the one-shot reader and the size reader
split the same five words in one place, and `countedPumpOptions`, which turns two printed halves and
a count into the one `PumpOptions` that `pump` takes. Wired into both pump readers: the self-subject
one (which is where the 91 trigger-borne cards land, because the prologue strips the trigger and
hands the clause down) and the targeted one.

Each printed half means something different depending on the grammar, and the table is the reader:

| printed | `announced` (`where X is …`) | `per-thing` (`for each …`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+X` | the count itself | **refused** |
| `+2` | a fixed 2 | 2 **per thing** |

That refusal is the one judgement in it: under `for each`, a printed `X` is a *different* X — the one
chosen at cast time — and multiplying a cast-time X by a board count is not a sentence Magic writes,
so reading it would be inventing a card (D259). It also inherits D252's refusals: a mixed sign is
refused because `+X/-X` cannot say whose creature the clause is for, and a size that is nought
however big the count is refused as `sizeBonus` refuses `+0/+0`.

### What it moved

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 22,226 / 56,421 (39.4%) | **22,264 / 56,421 (39.5%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,171 | **11,204** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,938 | **6,965** |

**27 cards finished against a ceiling of 52**, and the gap is worth stating rather than rounding
away: the rest carry a second unread line, or print the size in a word order this reader does not
take ("Until end of turn, target creature you control gains indestructible and gets +1/+0 for each
card in your hand"), or announce X without the words "the number of". D521 moved no coverage at all,
by construction — those lines already read; what was wrong was the number.

Basilisk Gate and Hunger of the Nim now read end to end. Four refusals I checked by hand are each
correct for a different reason, and each is a different lesson: Charging Hooligan has a second
sentence on the same line (D487), Angelic Exaltation's "it" is the attacking creature rather than the
source, Akroan Hoplite counts "attacking creatures **you control**" (a count the vocabulary does not
have), Elvish Berserker counts "creature blocking it".

**12 of 12 breaks caught**, every one verified to apply against a unique anchor and to revert to a
SHA-256 match. Two came back uncaught on the first pass and they were *different kinds* of result,
which is why they were handled differently:

- **A weak test.** Nothing printed a `+0/+0` counted size, so the guard refusing one was unchecked.
  Answered with a refusal row, and a second for a granted keyword on a counted shrink.
- **A vacuous break.** Dropping `the number of` from the announced tail regex changes nothing,
  because `boardCount` re-checks that prefix itself and returns null without it. The narrower regex
  documents the grammar at the point of the split and costs nothing, so it stays — but it is not
  load-bearing, and the break was replaced with a real one rather than counted as a miss.

## D523 — A static size read off the board, and the constraint that shaped it

D522 shipped the temporary half of the counted size and left the static half, on the stated ground
that a static size needs the count as **data** rather than a function, because `state.effects` is
serialised to Redis. That was true and it was not the hard part.

### The constraint, found before any code was written

`cdaCount` — the function that reads a `definesSize` count — runs **inside** `characteristicsOf`,
so it cannot ask a permanent for its live characteristics. The engine already says so in three
places: *"asking for a permanent's live type line here would re-enter the whole computation for
every other conditional effect on the board, and two conditional effects that read each other's
types would not terminate."* Metalcraft counts **printed** artifacts for exactly this reason and its
docblock records the rules gap that costs (CR 702.105a).

That matters because most of D520's vocabulary is live: `permanentsOfSubtype`,
`creaturesControlledBy`, `otherCreaturesControlled` and `attackingCreatures` all go through
`characteristicsOf`. **None of them can be reused for a static size as they stand.** Had this been
discovered halfway through the implementation it would have meant unpicking the design.

### What the measurement said, and where it corrected me

Of the **133** one-away cards with a static counted size:

| | cards | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a ZONE count | 13 | free — `cardDefs` is printed data, and a card in a hand or graveyard has no continuous effects on it |
| a BATTLEFIELD count | 27 | possible only against the **printed** type line |
| outside the vocabulary | 93 | `its power` 9, `creature blocking it` 8, `that card's mana value` 6, then nothing above 4 |

One row in my own first bucketing was misfiled: `+1/+1 counters on it` reads
`state.instances[id].counters`, which is instance data rather than a characteristic, so it needs no
re-entry at all.

**A probe I wrote and then refused to act on.** To decide whether a subtype count could be answered
from the printed line I classified each counted subtype by namespace, reading the corpus's own type
lines. It put `Forest`, `Mountain` and `Equipment` in the *creature-type* bucket — because one
dual-typed card poisons a word, and Dryad Arbor's printed line is `Land Creature — Forest Dryad`.
The classification was too crude to carry the decision, so it was discarded rather than used. The
answer came from the precedent instead: metalcraft already pays this price in this exact place, and
following it is consistent and testable where inventing a finer rule from an unreliable probe is not.

### What shipped

`ContinuousEffect.sizePerCount` — `{ of: StaticCountable, power, toughness }`, all data — applied in
**layer 7c** beside the fixed modifiers rather than with `definesSize` in 7a. That distinction is the
whole of the design: 7a *sets* a base, 7c *adds* to one, and Adelbert Steiner read through
`definesSize` would be a 1/1 with his printed 3/3 thrown away. A compile row and a runtime row each
pin it.

`PumpOptions` carries the field too, and that is why the attachment half is three lines rather than a
second mechanism: an Aura's or Equipment's bonus is already a `PumpOptions`, so `sizePerCount` rides
it to `staticEffect` and out to `characteristicsOf` the way `power` does. 41 of the corpus's static
counted sizes are printed on an attachment.

`staticCountOf` is deliberately a **narrower** vocabulary than `countOfThing`, and the asymmetry is
the constraint showing through rather than an inconsistency: `creatures you control` is read in a
one-shot clause (D520) and refused in a static size, because a count of creatures cannot be answered
without asking what is a creature. A test asserts both halves of that sentence on the same phrase.

### The cost, stated and asserted

A permanent whose type or subtype comes from a continuous effect is **not counted**. A changeling
(D506) is not seen by a tribal count; a crewed Vehicle is not seen as a creature. The runtime row
that pins this first asserts the Mimic really *is* a Goblin by the live rules, so it fails for the
right reason — a limit nothing tests is a limit nobody will remember.

### What it moved

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed lines read | 22,264 / 56,421 (39.5%) | **22,312 / 56,421 (39.5%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,204 | **11,228** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,965 | **6,993** |

Adelbert Steiner, Blanchwood Armor, Deadeye Plunderers, Dread Slag, Quag Sickness, Exoskeletal
Armor and Runechanter's Pike's sibling shapes now read. Pennon Blade and Bravado are refused, and
correctly: they count creatures.

**10 of 10 breaks caught**, each verified to apply against a unique anchor and revert to a SHA-256
match. One came back uncaught and was a **weak test** rather than a vacuous break: the controller
scoping of `cards in your hand` is real, but the row gave the opponent an empty hand, so a count of
every hand gave the same answer. Fixed by dealing seat 1 a bigger hand, and the row now says in a
comment that this is what the break run found.

**Two stale rows retargeted**, both mine. D522's "leaves a static counted size unread" was the line
between the halves and D523 crossed it; the D474 magecraft row listed Storm-Kiln Artist's
`gets +1/+0 for each artifact you control` as expected-unread. Both now assert the reading, with the
reason recorded in place — D516's rule, that a row recording *when* a shape started reading is worth
more than one that quietly disappears, and that a stale refusal is how a suite starts asserting the
past.

## D524 — The `you may` combinator is worth 33 cards, not 591. A correction to D519's queue

D519 asked the corpus which **clause combinators** recur across the 16,823 cards that are one unread
line from finished, ranked them, and set the plan: `for each` 950, `where X is` 713,
`you may <verb>. If you do, <effect>` 591. D520-D523 spent four increments on the first two and
delivered 123 finished cards against a combined bound of 1,663. That ratio was the warning.

So before building the third, the same question was asked of its **parts** rather than of the line.
A combinator is only worth what its halves are worth: `you may sacrifice a creature. If you do, draw
two cards` needs the may-clause read, the if-you-do clause read, *and* the gating between them. Each
half was compiled on its own, as the whole text of a synthetic sorcery, and counted.

| | cards |
| --- | --- |
| one-away cards whose single unread line says `you may` | **2,216** |
| of those, the `. If you do,` shape | **510** |
| …with **neither** half readable | 350 |
| …with only the **tail** readable | 83 |
| …with only the **head** readable | 44 |
| …with **both** halves readable — the reachable number | **33** |

**So the combinator is worth 33 cards.** D519's 591 counted cards whose line *contains* the shape,
and that figure was published with the words "upper bounds rather than promises" — this is the bound
measured against reality, and it is **18 times** the deliverable.

### What the number says to do instead

The halves are the lever, and they divide cleanly by role: every **head** is a cost and every
**tail** is an effect.

- **The heads that do not read are costs**: `pay {2}{U}`, `exile two cards from your graveyard`,
  `discard your hand`, `exile an enchantment card from your graveyard`. Reading that vocabulary
  turns 83 cards' tails into whole cards *and* makes the combinator worth 116 rather than 33.
- **The tails that do not read are effects** the compiler has no reader for yet, 44 of them.
- **350 cards have neither half**, and no combinator will ever touch them. They are clause work.

The queue therefore inverts: **read the cost vocabulary first, the combinator second.** A combinator
over two unread clauses finishes nothing, which is obvious in hindsight and was not in the ranking.

### The other `you may` shapes, which are a different story again

Only 510 of the 2,216 use `. If you do,` at all. The rest are ranked by shape, and the heads of that
list are mostly blocked by **mechanics rather than grammar**:

| cards | shape | what actually blocks it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 58 | `Whenever ~ deals combat damage to a player,` | the prologue reads; the tails want energy `{E}` and ticket `{TK}` counters |
| 44 | `When ~ enters, you may search your library` | a library search with a choice |
| 37 | `You may have ~ enter as a copy` | copy-on-arrival, which is #94's machinery |
| 29 | `At the beginning of your upkeep, you may` | a mixed bag |
| 20 | `You may exert ~ as it attacks. When you do,` | exert, a keyword the engine does not have |

### The standing lesson, now twice confirmed

D434 said: rank the queue by cards finished, not lines printed. D519 obeyed that for *lines* and
then broke it for *combinators* — it ranked by how many cards contain a shape, which is the same
mistake one level up. The rule generalises: **count what a reader would finish, by compiling the
parts, before believing a bound.** Every increment since D520 has had its ceiling overstated by a
factor of two to eighteen, and in each case the honest number came from compiling rather than
pattern-matching.

## D525 — The whole `you may` reader was unreachable from every path but a trigger

Four increments built the optional-effect family — the bare may (D447), the mana price (D448), the
energy price (D451) and the `. If you do,` sequence (D472) — and all four were written **inside**
`triggerFromLine`, on a closure over the event. Nothing said so, because every card those
increments counted prints its "may" behind a trigger, so the measure could not see the hole.

Asked directly, the compiler read the same clause two different ways depending on what printed it:

```
--- behind a trigger (the path D448 was built on) ---
READS    When ~ enters, you may pay {1}. If you do, draw a card.
READS    When ~ enters, you may discard a card. If you do, draw a card.
READS    When ~ enters, you may pay {E}. If you do, draw a card.
--- the same clause as a SPELL resolution ---
refused  You may pay {1}. If you do, draw a card.
refused  You may discard a card. If you do, draw a card.
--- a bare "you may" as a spell ---
refused  You may draw a card.
```

That is the class of defect D362 is about, read from the other end: not a wrong card, but a line
the compiler *can* read and does not, decided by grammar that has nothing to do with the clause.

### The fix

`optionalEffect(clause, reader)` — the block lifted out whole, parameterised by the **reader** its
caller composes clauses with. The reader is a parameter rather than a reach for the shared
`readEffect` because the trigger needs `eventRelativeEffect` in front of the clause vocabulary ("you
may return **that card** to your hand"), and a function that chose for itself would quietly drop it.

Four callers, each keeping the same order — **read the clause whole first, and strip the two words
only on a refusal**, which is the guard D447 wrote and every caller now inherits:

| path | reader it passes | printed lines of the shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `triggerFromLine` | `eventRelativeEffect ?? composeEffects(…, where)` | unchanged |
| `readResolution` → `optionalResolution` | `composeEffects(…, null)` | 124 |
| the activated-ability path | `composeEffects(…, 'battlefield')` | 95 |
| the loyalty path | `composeEffects(…, 'battlefield')` | 25 |

`optionalResolution` is a **spell-shape** reader (one line, like the four above it) rather than a
clause one, and the reason is `clausesOf`: it splits on the full stop, so by the time the clause
vocabulary sees `you may X. If you do, Y` the two halves have already been cut apart and the
dependency between them is gone.

**The modal path is deliberately left out**, measured rather than forgotten: 15 legal modal bullets
begin with these two words and **one** reads (Witherbloom Charm). A mode's gate would be the first
`payIfChosen`-capable question inside a `ModeDef`, a combination nothing in the pool prints and no
test exercises. One card does not pay for that, and the count is written where the decision lives so
the first card that makes it two can reverse it on evidence.

### Three deletions the lift exposed

- The "the bare may regex is **not** guarded on `priced`" paragraph was in the file **twice**,
  verbatim, once with an extra paragraph about `sequence`. The shorter copy is gone.
- The guard `if ((may !== null || charged !== null) && …)` lost its disjunct. It existed to let a
  clause that read **whole** through untouched, and the whole reading is now the caller's business;
  inside the function the test is vacuously true, because the bare regex matches every shape read
  above. D441 and D438's rule: one statement of one rule.
- `inner`'s `may === null ? clause : …` arm is gone, dead behind the function's own gate.

### What is not carried out of the inner reading, and why

`spellFlags`, `immediate` and `appliesNothing`. One reason covers all three: each is a claim about a
clause that **happens**, and this one may not. `makesMana` would tell the bot's search that "you may
add {R}" produced mana it was free to decline; `immediate` is a reading of the inner effect's
position in a sequence, which the gate in front of it is not part of; `appliesNothing` would let an
assembly drop the effect entirely, and the effect is where the gate lives. A dropped hint is a
play-quality gap and not a wrong card — the right side of D362 to be on.

### What it is worth, measured rather than claimed

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,312 / 56,421 (39.5%) | **22,317 / 56,421 (39.6%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,228 | **11,231** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,993 | **6,994** |

**One card finished: Abandon Attachments** (`You may discard a card. If you do, draw two cards.`),
plus three cards that gained a script with other lines still unread. 244 printed lines are of this
shape across the three new paths, and 239 of them refuse for a reason that has nothing to do with
the wiring: they are **costs**, not resolutions — "you may cast this without paying its mana cost",
"you may discard a Plains card rather than pay this spell's mana cost", "you may put a creature card
from your hand onto the battlefield". The inner half does not read, which is the correct outcome: a
cost read as an effect would be a wrong card.

### What the break run found, including two guards that cannot fail

The first pass was **twelve breaks, six caught** — and four of the six misses were not weak tests.
They were guards with nothing to discriminate on, which is what a break run is for.

- **Three breaks reversed the order** — optional reader before the whole reading, on the spell, the
  ability and the trigger path — and nothing failed. D447 justified that order with a claim about
  the vocabulary ("some clauses already begin with 'you may' and read as one phrase"), so the claim
  was measured rather than argued: of the **2,009 distinct printed clauses beginning with those two
  words, 215 read through the gate and 0 read whole.** The order protects no phrase that exists.
  It is kept all the same, because the asymmetry is real — reading whole first costs one reader call
  on a clause that was going to be read anyway, and the other way round is a stripped clause handed
  to a reader that never saw it the day the vocabulary does gain such a phrase (D362) — and the
  docblock now carries the measurement instead of the stale reason.
- **One break removed the trailing full-stop strip** in `optionalResolution` and nothing failed,
  because `clausesOf` already takes a stop off each clause and `sentence()` takes one off the
  prompt. That guard is **deleted** rather than defended (D441, D438), with the two readers that do
  the work named in its place.
- **Two misses were weak tests, answered with tests**: a two-line spell reaching the one-line reader
  (which compiles the first line and silently drops the second — D487), and a clause that is not a
  "may" at all reaching `may[1]`. Both are compile rows now.
- **Two breaks were added** to pin rules that had no row: the clause's own question not held behind
  the gate (D450), and the priced answer offered before the decline — which would make a bot's
  fallback answer "spend the mana", the opposite of what `extort()`'s docblock settles.

The revised set is **10 breaks, 10 caught**, each verified to apply against a unique anchor and to
revert against a SHA-256. `break525.py` is also where the three order breaks live, so the day the
vocabulary gains a "you may" phrase they start failing instead of staying quiet.

### The lesson, now three deep in the same family

D519 priced this family at 591 cards. D524 compiled the halves and measured 33. D525 wired the
reader to every path and the wiring itself is worth **1**. The same correction keeps arriving from a
different direction, and the generalisation stands: **count what a reader would finish, by compiling
the parts, before believing a bound.**

What makes this increment worth shipping is not the card. It is that the compiler no longer reads one
clause two ways, and that the next reader in the may family — a cost vocabulary, which is what D524
says to build — lands on four paths instead of one the moment it exists.

## D526 — The queue, ranked by cards finished per reader. Three earlier tops were probe artifacts

D434 said rank the queue by cards finished, not lines printed. D519 broke that one level up by ranking
how many cards *contain* a shape, and D524 corrected it for one family. This is the same correction
applied to the whole pool, and it is the first ranking that answers the question directly: **if one
new clause reader existed, how many legal cards would become fully read?**

`probe536.mjs` asks it by taking every legal card that is exactly one `no-reader` line short,
stripping what the compiler itself strips before the clause vocabulary runs (the activation cost
prefix and the `Activate only …` tail), splitting the rest the way `clausesOf` does, and compiling
each clause on its own **under the card's own name**.

| | cards |
| --- | --- |
| legal cards exactly one `no-reader` line short | **16,022** |
| …whose line's clauses all read on their own — the **line shape** blocks it | 499 |
| …short by exactly **one** clause | **10,849** |
| …short by two or more (several readers away) | 4,674 |

### Three artifacts the first run put at the top, and what each one was

Worth writing down because each is a different way a measurement lies.

1. **`Activate only as a sorcery` at 194 cards.** Tested as a standalone clause it refuses; in
   context `activationRestriction` strips it before the clause vocabulary ever sees it, and
   `{2}, {T}: Draw a card. Activate only as a sorcery.` compiles today. The fix is to strip in the
   probe what the compiler strips. (The *older* wording, `Activate this ability only any time you
   could cast a sorcery`, genuinely does not read — a separate, smaller row.)
2. **Three self-naming shapes** — `Exile <self>` at 56, `<self> deals N damage to target creature`
   at 50, `<self> gets +N/+N as long as …` at 38. All artifacts of compiling each clause under a
   placeholder name: `selfRef` matches a card naming **itself**, so "Blastfire Bolt deals 5 damage
   to target creature" refuses under the name "Not A Card" and reads under its own.
3. **`Put the rest on the bottom of your library in a random order` at 129.** Real, but it is one of
   *several* failing clauses on almost every card that prints it — the line is "look at the top five
   … you may reveal … put the rest on the bottom", and reading the last sentence alone finishes
   nothing. Counting a clause once per card rather than once per sighting is what separates the two.

### The ranking, with the top rows verified by hand against the shipping compiler

    25  Return <self> from your graveyard to your hand
    21  Return target creature card from your graveyard to the battlefield
    16  Put target card from your graveyard on the bottom of your library
    13  Return this card from your graveyard to your hand
    13  Exile target card from a graveyard
    ------------------------------------------------------- 88, one zone family  → D527
    33  At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice <self> unless you <cost>
    30  You may have <self> enter as a copy of any creature card in a graveyard
    28  Whenever <self> deals combat damage to a player, that player <does something>
    25  This spell costs {M} less to cast if it targets …
    20  This spell costs {M} less to cast if you control …
    17  This spell costs {M} less to cast for each …
    ------------------------------------------------------- 62, conditional cost reduction
    19  Proliferate                       (the engine has had it since #195)
    18  Untap it
    18  Target creature you control deals damage equal to its power to …
    18  Target creature can't be blocked this turn
    16  Regenerate target creature        (the engine has had it since #37)
    16  The next time a source of your choice would deal damage …
    15  It can't be regenerated
    14  Target creature can't block this turn

Two things stand out and both are about **reach rather than novelty**. The graveyard family needs no
new primitive — `relocate`, `exileCard`, `bottomPile` and `putOntoBattlefield` have all been in
`effects.ts` from the start, and graveyard targeting has been in the engine since #23. And three of
the cheap single clauses name mechanics the engine already implements and the *compiler* cannot say:
proliferate (#195), regenerate (#37) and the blocking restrictions (#133).

## D527 — The graveyard clause family: 94 cards finished, and the scope word that decides the card

D526's ranking put one zone family at the top, and this is it. Five printed clauses, all moves
between a graveyard and another zone, **88 cards predicted and 94 finished**:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,317 / 56,421 (39.6%) | **22,472 / 56,421 (39.8%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,231 | **11,336** |
| cards with every printed line read | 6,994 | **7,088** |

The six over the prediction come from the shared half: `graveyardCardPhrase` is a **target-phrase**
parser, so it lifts every reader that points at a graveyard at once, which is `targetSpecFrom`'s
whole job (D469).

### What was built

**One parser and four readers.** `targetSpecFrom`'s switch had two graveyard phrases written out by
hand (`target creature card in your graveyard`, `target land card in your graveyard`) because each
carries a hand-written `filter` by reference that `compiled-vs-written.test.ts` compares character
for character. Those stay. Everything else goes through `graveyardCardPhrase`, which is a parser for
D469's reason: the printed phrase is **combinatorial** — a run of type words crossed with whose
graveyard it is — and the exile clause alone prints eleven combinations of it.

| reader | printings | wordings read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reanimation — `… to the battlefield`, with or without `tapped` | 82 | 47 |
| graveyard hate — `exile target … card from (a\|your\|an opponent's) graveyard` | 70 | 69 |
| the self-return — `return <this card> from your graveyard to your hand` | 50 | 50 |
| under its own library — `put target … on the bottom of … library` | 20 | 19 |

### The scope word, which is where a wrong card would come from

Not a detail: `your graveyard` is yours, `a graveyard` is **anybody's**, `an opponent's graveyard` is
theirs, and reading one as another changes what the card does rather than whether it reads.
Barkform Harvester read as "a graveyard" would be graveyard hate that puts an opponent's card in
your deck; every graveyard-hate card in the pool read as "your graveyard" could only eat its own.
The hand-written `anyGraveyardCard` already said so in as many words — "'a graveyard' is not 'your
graveyard' and the Ooze is at its best eating somebody else's" — and both directions are now rows.

**One pairing is refused because nobody prints it.** A card in a graveyard is owned by the player
whose graveyard it is (CR 404.3), so `your graveyard … your library` and `a graveyard … its owner's
library` name the same destination — but `a graveyard … your library` would take an opponent's card
and put it in **your** deck. That is a card this compiler would have invented (D259), so the pairing
is checked rather than assumed.

### The one inference, and its bound

`{4}{G}: Return Bestial Bloodline from your graveyard to your hand.` is an ability **activated from
the graveyard**, which the printed line says only by saying "from your graveyard". So the clause
decides something about the *cost*: `AbilityCost.fromGraveyard`, unearth's field, honoured by
`legalActions` since #161 — the engine already knew how to offer an ability to a card in a graveyard
and how to refuse one to a card on the battlefield.

The inference is **one printed shape wide on purpose**, and the bound is a test row rather than a
sentence: Hanna and Scavenging Ooze both say "graveyard" and both are activated from the
battlefield, because there the word is about their *target*. A wider inference would move those
abilities off the board, where they would compile, install and never be offered — which is the
failure `grantedAbilityFrom` already refuses four cost fields to avoid.

It also has to be read **before** the clause vocabulary, not after, and the break run proved that
rather than the docblock asserting it.

### What is refused, with its count

35 of the 82 reanimation printings add a rider the move does not carry — `with a finality counter on
it` (3), `with two additional +1/+1 counters` (1), `attached to ~` (1, Hakim) — or a type run this
vocabulary turns down: `creature or Vehicle` (3, a type mixed with a subtype), `white or black
creature` (1, a colour run), `Pirate` and `Rebel` (subtypes alone; #341 is open about what an
unvalidated subtype target costs — a phrase that compiles and matches nothing). Each refuses the
**line** rather than the rider, which is D487: a reanimation that silently dropped its finality
counter would be a strictly better card than the one printed.

One exile printing is refused for a different reason: Spelltwine exiles **two** cards from two
different graveyards, and two independent target choices cannot share one `targets` list — the same
refusal `composeEffects` gives a two-target fight clause.

### The break run

**12 breaks, 12 caught**, each verified to apply against a unique anchor and to revert against a
SHA-256. Two are worth naming because they are about reading rather than wiring:

- **The self-return read after the clause vocabulary instead of before it** fails, which settles the
  order as a measurement rather than an assertion. The clause vocabulary gets `where` set to
  `'battlefield'` on an ability line, so `selfEffect` answers for a card that is not there.
- **The type run left unvalidated** fails, which is #341's hazard caught in advance: `target Rebel
  card in a graveyard` would compile into a spec that matches nothing, and a card that compiles and
  cannot be aimed is worse than one left unread.

The other ten are each of the four readers not dispatched, `tapped` dropped, the cost flag dropped,
both scope words inverted, the library pairing unchecked, and the card sent to hand instead of under
the library.

## D528 — Four clauses naming mechanics the engine already had: 142 cards finished

D526's ranking is full of a particular kind of row: a printed clause whose **rule** the engine
implemented dozens of increments ago and whose **words** the compiler has no reading for. Four of
them, each with the increment that built the rule:

| cards predicted | clause | the rule, and when it landed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 19 | `Proliferate` | #195, with two hand-written cards already calling it |
| 16 | `Regenerate target creature` | #37, CR 701.15 |
| 18 | `Target creature can't be blocked this turn` | D495, which read it as a *printed* static |
| 14 | `Target creature can't block this turn` | the same |

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,472 / 56,421 (39.8%) | **22,669 / 56,421 (40.2%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,336 | **11,472** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,088 | **7,230** |

**67 cards predicted, 142 finished** — more than double, and for the same reason D527 overshot: two
of the four readings go through `targetSpecFrom`, so every target phrase it already parses comes
free. `up to two target creatures`, `target Merfolk`, `another target creature` and `target
artifact` were never counted in the prediction because the prediction counted one wording each.

### Why these are the cheapest cards there are

Nothing new was built. The two blocking restrictions are a `PumpOptions` with **no size**:
`cantBeBlocked` and `cantBlock` have been `ContinuousEffect` fields since D495 read them off printed
type lines, so granting either until end of turn is `pump` with one flag. `regenerate` is CR 701.15
and refuses a card that is not on the battlefield itself, which is why the readers do not check
`where` — the primitive is the one place that rule lives. `PROLIFERATE` is the hand-written decision
spec **by reference**, so the compiled question is the same object Contagion Clasp and Steady
Progress ask.

### The one place a wrong card could come from

The two blocking restrictions point at **opposite halves of the table**, and the printed word is
what says which: "can't be blocked" is for your attacker (so the spec is `friendly` and carries
`helpsInCombat` — aim it at something that can attack), "can't block" is aimed at a creature of
somebody else's. Guessing that round the wrong way is D252's failure, a bot aiming at the wrong
creature every single time; unlike a mixed-sign pump, here the sentence settles it. Both directions
are rows and both breaks fail.

Neither carries `expiresAtEndOfTurn`, for D412's reason: that flag tells the bot's search it may
hold the spell until blockers are declared, and **both** of these have to resolve before blockers to
do anything at all.

### What is refused

`It can't be blocked this turn` (7 sightings) — "it" is a referent no clause reader is handed, and
in a composition it is the previous clause's subject on some cards and the card itself on others.
`Creatures without flying can't block this turn` (5, Falter) — an untargeted board scope, which is a
different reader. `Target creature with power 2 or less can't be blocked this turn` (10) — the power
clause in the target phrase, which `targetSpecFrom` does not read (the mana-value clause is there,
power is not). And `Target creature gets +1/+0 and can't be blocked this turn` (Distortion Strike) —
a pump and a restriction in one sentence, which is the conjunction reader's business.

Also refused, and this one is about duration rather than vocabulary: **the same words with no "this
turn"**. `Target creature can't be blocked` is a *printed static* (`printedCombatStatics`, D495), not
a one-shot, and reading it here would make a permanent effect out of a sentence that says nothing of
the kind. There is a break for it and it fails.

### Two tests retired themselves, exactly as written

Both had a docblock predicting it, which is the point of writing them down.

- `PARTLY_READ_CARD` was **Contagion Clasp**, whose only unread line was "{4}, {T}: Proliferate." —
  and its constant said in as many words: "When proliferate joins the clause vocabulary this card
  becomes fully read and the test fails loudly, which is the right failure." It did. The constant
  moved to **Obelisk of Urd** (three printed lines: convoke reads, the chosen-type pair does not),
  chosen from the 12 pool cards that satisfy the test's four assertions, with the next two
  candidates named so the move is cheaper next time.
- D525's refusal row used `Proliferate.` as its example of a clause that is not a "may". That
  example started reading one increment after it was written. It moved to `Clash with an opponent.`,
  a keyword the engine does not have at all, with the history in the comment.

### The break run, and the reader it deleted

**12 breaks, 11 caught.** The one that did not fail is the finding: disabling the new
`Regenerate ~` reader changed no test, because `eventRelativeEffect` has read
`^regenerate (?:~|it)$` since the referent machinery was built — and reads "it" as well, which the
new one did not. So this increment **wrote a duplicate and the break run found it**: the newer
reader is gone and a note in its place says why (D441, D438 — one statement of one rule).

That asymmetry is worth stating as a rule. A reader is worth writing when a break on it can fail; a
break that cannot fail means somebody has already written it. The sibling clause two lines below —
`~ can't be blocked this turn` on the card itself — *is* read by this increment, and its break does
fail.

The other eleven: each of the three remaining readers not dispatched, proliferate ignoring the
answer it asked for, the shield not applied, the two restrictions swapped, the unblockable target
not marked as the caster's own, its combat hint dropped, only the first of several targets
restricted, and the duration made optional so a printed static would read as a one-shot.

## D529 — The upkeep tax: echo's question on a card that does not print the keyword

D526's re-ranked queue put this shape at the top with 33 cards, and the measurement behind it is
unusually concentrated for this corpus:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| legal lines printing `… sacrifice ~ unless you …` | **137** |
| …on `At the beginning of your upkeep,` | 74 |
| …on `When ~ enters,` | 42 |
| …whose price is a **mana run** | 52 |

Both prologues already read. The price is the only new reading, and it is **echo** (#196, CR 702.29)
with the keyword taken off.

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,669 / 56,421 (40.2%) | **22,719 / 56,421 (40.3%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,472 | **11,504** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,230 | **7,255** |

**25 cards finished.** Fewer than the 33 D526 predicted, and the gap is the usual one: a card whose
tax now reads may still print something else unread — Binding Grasp's tax reads and "You control
enchanted creature." does not.

### Nothing new was built

- `ChoiceDecisionSpec.payIfChosen` is the price on an answer, paid by the engine between the answer
  and the effect. It carries the rule nobody has to write: **a cost the seat cannot afford is not
  offered**, so one option is left and the engine answers it itself. A player tapped out in their
  own upkeep is never shown a question with a single button; the permanent goes, and the table is
  not stopped. That is the difference between a question and a stuck game, and it is a test row.
- `payIfChosen.energy` is the same price in the other currency (D451), which is Lathnu Hellion's
  `{E}{E}`. It is read **before** the mana parse, for D451's reason: `{E}` matches `\{[^}]+\}`, so a
  mana parse of an energy run reaches `parseManaCost`, is refused, and the whole line reads as
  nothing. That exact mistake cost D448 a whole increment's coverage.
- `moveToGraveyard` is what `echoTrigger` already does on a decline, and a sacrifice is a move to a
  graveyard that cannot be regenerated or replaced.

`'Sacrifice it'` is first for echo's reason: `options[0]` is the engine's fallback, and that fallback
has to be the outcome the rules impose when the price goes unpaid.

### The one `best` a compiled card carries

D448 deliberately wrote **no** `best` for a compiled priced "you may", and the argument was that the
compiler cannot know what declining costs — the same shape covers paying {1} to draw a card and
paying {4} to untap a Mana Vault.

Here the clause says what declining costs: **the permanent**. A permanent already on the battlefield
is worth more than mana in an upkeep nobody else is using, which is echo's own rule and D214's
measurement, and the sentence makes it knowable without knowing the card. So this reader carries
`best: () => pay`, and it is the only compiled hint of its kind. The break that removes it fails:
without it every taxed permanent is sacrificed the first time it is asked.

### What is refused, with its count

21 of the 137 name a price `payIfChosen` cannot express, and each is a **cost**:
`discard a card` (5), `return a non-Lair land you control to its owner's hand` (5),
`sacrifice a land` (4), `discard a card at random` (3), `discard a land card` (3),
`exile the top creature card of your graveyard` (2), and Anurid Scavenger's `put a card from your
graveyard on the bottom of your library`. A cost read as nothing would be a permanent that stays for
free — the worst direction to be wrong in (D362) — so the line stays unread. `parseManaCost` refuses
the rest by recording an unrecognised symbol rather than reading it as generic mana, the same guard
D446's ability costs lean on.

### The break run

**10 breaks, 10 caught**, each verified to apply against a unique anchor and to revert against a
SHA-256. Four of them are about the question rather than the clause, and they are the ones worth
naming: the forced outcome not being `options[0]` (so a question the engine answers itself pays
instead of sacrificing, against the rules), the price not charged at all (the permanent kept for
free **and** a tapped-out seat stopped with a one-button question), the priced answer and the
payment disagreeing about the word (so the engine charges nobody and the effect reads an answer that
was never priced), and `best` removed — without it every taxed permanent is sacrificed the first
time it is asked.

## D530 — A referent subject, read by borrowing the reader that already targets (36 cards)

"That player", "that creature". Before this, the compiler had **six** readers for referent clauses,
each written for one printed sentence: `that player loses N life and you gain N life`,
`~ deals N damage to that player` (both D407), and four for the creature on the other side of a block
(D480). Each is three lines of regex and six of effect, and each only ever answers for its own
wording.

### The measurement, and the two wrong probes before it

Asked how much that style had left on the table, the corpus answered a **long tail**: of the legal
cards one clause short on a "that player" sentence, the rows are `discards a card` 16,
`discards two cards` 4, `mills two cards` 2, `loses N life` 2, then singletons. Writing the next six
readers would buy six rows of a tail that does not end.

Two earlier probes were wrong and both are recorded, because the errors are the instructive part:

- **probe542 answered 8 cards.** It counted clauses rather than cards (against D434), and it split
  each unread line with `clausesOf` and then tested only clauses *starting* with the pronoun — so a
  combat-damage tail sharing its sentence with the trigger prologue was never tested at all.
- **probe545 answered 4 cards.** It compiled each clause standalone, which breaks every clause whose
  reading depends on where it sits: the whole Equipment family refuses on "attach it to target
  creature you control", which only reads inside an ETB trigger. It measured the probe.

The corrected probes strip the prologue the way `triggerFromLine` does, delete the referent clause
from the real card, recompile, and ask whether the **card** finishes:

| referent source | cards finished |
| --- | --- |
| the player the event says was **hit** (`c.attacked.defender`) | 18 |
| the player who **acted** (`c.actor`, the D475 gate) | 9 |
| the target an **earlier clause in the same resolution** chose (`c.targets[0]`) | 9 |

### The mechanism: one borrow, not a seventh reader

"That player discards a card" and "target player discards a card" are **the same effect aimed
differently**, and the clause vocabulary already reads the second. So `referentEffect` swaps the
pronoun for the target phrase, asks the existing reader, and supplies the referent in place of the
chosen target by rewriting `EffectContext.targets` on the way in. Every sentence the vocabulary
learns to target, it now refers to for free.

The gate stays with the caller, because that is D475's whole argument: a referent read off an event
that does not carry it is a *wrong* reading, not an unread line (D362). Three callers, three gates.

### The engine needed one new thing, and the first version of this reader hid it

A discard is a **question asked of the player discarding** — Mind Rot's, chosen by them and not by
the caster. `decisionPlan` resolves `who: 'target-player'` off the **stack object's targets**, and a
trigger has none: the question would be asked of nobody while the ability resolved and said so in
the log. So the first version of `referentEffect` refused any clause carrying a question — and in
doing so refused `that player discards a card`, **the 16-card row at the head of the family it was
written for.**

`CardsDecisionSpec.who` therefore grew two words, matching the compiler's two gates one-to-one:
`hit-player` (`StackObject.attacked.defender`, asking nobody if the object carries no attack) and
`acting-player` (`StackObject.actor`, falling back to the controller — the value and not a guess,
per D474). They are kept **apart** rather than merged into one "the event's player", because merging
needs a fallback between them and that fallback is where a wrong player would hide: a combat-damage
object with no `attacked` would quietly ask the attacking creature's own controller to discard.

### Two defects this increment's own tests caught

- **The licence was checked after an early return.** `composeEffects` returns a one-part composition
  before the borrow licence runs, so a line that is *only* a referent clause borrowed from nothing
  at all: "Whenever another creature enters, that player discards a card" compiled, with
  `c.targets[0]` undefined, and did nothing. A licence checked after an early return is not a
  licence. The check now runs first.
- **`immediate` was refused instead of wrapped.** A clause offering two readings is a deferred draw,
  and a composition picks between them by position. Refusing such a clause lost Dimir Cutpurse,
  "that player discards a card **and you draw a card**", whose second half is that very draw. Both
  readings are now wrapped and the choice survives. Refusing a reading because the wrapper was too
  narrow is the wrapper's bug, not the card's.

`beforeDecisions` stays refused, for `optionalEffect`'s reason, and nothing in the corpus reaches it.

### Not done: the correction that was offered and refused

`eventRelativeEffect`'s docblock named `combat-damage` as a shape it refuses because the event
"passes the watcher's own side". That reason is about where the seat lives, not about whether it is
reachable — and it **is** reachable: `automation.ts` derives `attacked = { defender: event.defender }`
for `combat-damage` before dispatch, for exactly this purpose, and Hellrider's reader has been
reading `c.attacked` off an attack since D480. Chasing the same docblock turned up what looked like a
live defect in a shipped starter-deck card (Mirko Vosk, Mind Drinker reads `c.attacked.defender` and
the raise site at `automation.ts:2567` passes only `defender`), and it is **not** one: the derivation
at `automation.ts:1345` fills `attacked` in before the trigger is dispatched. Recorded as a
non-defect so the next reader of that docblock does not chase it again.

### What it actually bought, against what the probe predicted

| | before D530 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,255 | **7,287** (+32) |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,504 | **11,528** (+24) |
| printed legal lines read | 22,719 / 56,421 (40.3%) | **22,759 / 56,421 (40.3%)** (+40) |

The probes predicted **36** finished cards (27 + 9) and the compiler delivered **32**, so the
measurement over-predicted by four. That is the expected direction and the reason is the probe's
own shortcut: it deletes the referent clause from the card and asks whether the *rest* reads, which
is a weaker condition than the real composer's, since the composer also has to accept the clause
*in place* — under the licence, the question re-aiming, and the one-targeting-part rule. A probe that
over-predicts by 11% is worth keeping; one that under-predicted would have hidden the increment
(probe545 did exactly that, at 4 cards of 36).

### The break run: 18 breaks, 13 caught, and the five that are vacuous

Each break was verified to **apply** against an anchor matching exactly once and to **revert** against
a SHA-256 of the file. Two files are in scope, because this increment changed both the compiler and
the engine: all six engine breaks are caught, including `hit-player` resolving to the controller
(the attacking creature's own side asked to discard) and `acting-player` losing its controller
fallback (D474's absent actor never asked at all).

**One break found a coverage hole in these very tests, and it is the useful result of the run.**
Break 2 removes the aiming — the effect is handed the context unchanged instead of the referent —
and the first run left it **green**. The reason is specific and worth keeping: a discard carries a
`CardsDecisionSpec`, and `who: 'hit-player'` is what routes it, so the engine applies the answer
itself and an effect handed the *wrong* object still produces the right discard. Every row in the
runtime describe was a discard, so none of them could see the aiming at all. A life-loss row
(`that player loses 2 life`, no question, so the seat it takes life from is whatever the effect is
handed) was added, and it catches break 2 and break 9 — the one that aims at the actor instead of the
defender, which is the exact failure this increment exists to prevent.

The five that stay uncaught are **vacuous against the shape table and the corpus**, not untested
behaviour, and each is recorded with what makes it so rather than left as a gap:

- **3 — a null referent treated as present.** `supply` is typed `Target | null` and the guard stops
  a null reaching the effect, but no event this reader is gated on ever produces one:
  `automation.ts:1345` fills `attacked` in for every combat-damage dispatch. The guard is
  type-driven, and nothing in the engine can exercise it.
- **5 — the spec kind not checked inside the borrow.** It would matter for a clause whose swapped
  reading declares a target of some *other* kind, and no printed clause in the corpus does: the
  inserted phrase is what every one of them reads.
- **6 — `immediate` unwrapped.** The field is present on Dimir Cutpurse's reading (that is what made
  refusing it a bug), but a composition only *uses* `immediate` in a non-final position, and no
  printed referent clause sits non-final with a deferred draw inside it. Wrapping is strictly
  better and costs nothing, so it stays.
- **8 — `some` instead of `every` on the hit gate.** This one is **provably** vacuous rather than
  merely unexercised, and the check is cheap: `TRIGGER_SHAPES` has exactly two multi-event shapes,
  `[etb, dies]` and `[etb, to-graveyard]`, and neither mixes a hit event with a player action. The
  two quantifiers agree on every shape that exists. `every` stays because it is the correct form the
  day a mixed shape is added.
- **18 — a player question riding a creature pronoun.** No clause beginning "that creature" has a
  swapped reading that carries a `target-player` question.

Inventing text to exercise the five would be worse than leaving them vacuous (D259), so they are
written down instead. This is the same outcome D525 recorded for three of its order-breaks.

### What this increment did NOT read, said plainly

The referent must be the clause's **subject**. An *object*-position referent is untouched: "Whenever
~ deals combat damage to a player, ~ deals 3 damage to **that player**" (Furnace Scamp) is still
refused on a combat-damage trigger, because the swap only rewrites a leading pronoun. That family is
the one `eventRelativeEffect`'s old `dealt` reader covers, and only under the actor gate. Reading
object position needs the phrase replaced mid-clause and the spec check re-derived, which is a
separate increment and not a line this one can claim.

The six hand-written referent readers were therefore **kept**, not deleted — and the deletion the
task brief called for was *attempted and measured*, not reasoned about. Compiling the swapped
sentences directly answers it:

    Whenever an opponent casts a creature spell, that player loses 2 life and you gain 2 life.  READS
    Target player loses 2 life and you gain 2 life.                                             unread
    Whenever an opponent draws a card, ~ deals 1 damage to that player.                          READS
    ~ deals 1 damage to target player.                                                          unread

So neither `drained` nor `dealt` is redundant, for a reason sharper than "they read object position"
(which is true of `dealt` only — `drained` is subject position like the borrow): **the targeted form
of their sentences does not read at all**, so there is nothing for the borrow to borrow. A borrow can
only reach a sentence the clause vocabulary already understands with a target in that slot, and these
two are exactly the sentences it does not. The four block readers are untouched for a different
reason: they read `c.blocked`, a referent source this increment never wired.

D441 deletes a duplicate statement of one rule. These are not duplicates, and the probe is what
establishes that rather than an argument about it.

### The pod sweep

**40/40 pods finished** at a fresh seed (SEED0=40201) on the clean commit, no engine throw and no
stalled table, 70.3 turns and 382 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across the 160 decks built: 25.0
cards with a hand-written script, 48.0 with at least one line nothing could read, 61.7 playable only
because of the printed data, and 0.5 cardboard. The seed is fresh rather than reused, which is the
D226 rule: one seed is one shuffle wearing many deck pairings.

## D531 — The chosen discard, and the first question whose pool is not the chooser's own

    Target opponent reveals their hand. You choose a nonland card from it.
    That player discards that card.

Dark Inquiry, Distress, Despise, Brainbite, Collective Brutality, Corpse Traders, Deceit, Cerebral
Confiscation, Auntie's Sentence. **95 unread legal lines** contain the third sentence, in 84 distinct
shapes; this increment reads the head of that family — the three-sentence form in its six spellings.

### Why it was unread, which is a fact about the engine and not about the compiler

`CardsDecisionSpec.who` named **both** the chooser and the owner of the zone, because
`decisionCandidates` read `zoneKey(chooser, from)`. So the only expressible reading of this family
asked the *discarding* player to choose — and that card already exists: it is Mind Rot. The whole
point of the printed card is that the **caster** picks, and a reading that lost that would be a card
that works and does the wrong thing, which D362 ranks below leaving the line unread. No regex could
have fixed it.

`fromSeat?: 'chooser' | 'target-player'` splits the two. Default `chooser`, so every question written
before this is unchanged, and `decisionCandidates` is still the **one** place the candidate list is
computed — which is what lets everything else lean on the stored list rather than recomputing a rule
that could disagree.

Two things the brief predicted needing work and which did **not**, both verified rather than assumed:

- **Where the card goes.** `moveToGraveyard` already relocates by `inst.owner`, so a card the caster
  picks out of an opponent's hand lands in the *opponent's* graveyard. A runtime row asserts it, and
  asserts the caster's graveyard does not get it.
- **The answer's authorisation.** All five readers of the candidate list — the `auto:decide` check,
  the bot's `pick`, the scry resume, `canIdentify`, and the scry filter — read
  `pending.candidates`, the list stored when the question was asked. There was never a second
  computation to keep in step.

### Letting the caster *read* the cards, and keeping it that narrow

`canIdentify`'s `hand` case gains the clause the `library` case already had for scry: a card may be
read when the pending decision is **this** question, asked of **this** viewer, and names **this**
card in its candidate list. Three runtime rows hold that line — the caster reads the candidates and
*not* the Swamp in the same hand that the printed "nonland" excluded, a spectator reads nothing new,
and the permission is gone the moment the question is answered.

It is deliberately **not** `inst.revealed`. That flag is a card deliberately shown to the table and
it stays shown; this reveal lasts one resolution, and riding the pending decision is what makes it
expire on its own.

### The read is a group, and the middle sentence is why

`stealPrefix`'s argument (D516): three printed sentences, one play. A reveal without the discard
leaks a hand for nothing, and a discard without the reveal asks the caster to choose out of cards
they were never shown. And the middle sentence is **not an effect at all** — "you choose a card from
it" *is* the question — so there is nothing a clause reader could return for it. Only a reader that
sees all three can produce the one `CardsDecisionSpec` the play is.

The qualifier is read by `graveyardTypeTest`, the same function three other readers use, because a
hand and a graveyard ask the same question of a card's printed types. It grew one case: `nonland`
composed with a second qualifier ("a nonland permanent card"), read as the conjunction the words are
rather than as a fourth hard-coded phrase — one statement of one rule (D441), and its three existing
callers get it for free.

### What it refuses, each left for its own increment

- **"Look at target opponent's hand and choose X cards from it"** (Abandon Hope) — an X chosen as the
  spell is cast, which D399 keeps off this path.
- **"reveals three cards from their hand and you choose one of them"** (Blackmail, Bala Ged Thief,
  Cabal Interrogator) — the pool is a slice of the hand rather than the hand, which `fromSeat` does
  not express.
- **"you MAY choose"** (Cracked Skull) — the offer has to gate the question, which is #337's open gap.
- **"Choose a color. … you choose a card of that color from it"** (Addle) — the filter is an earlier
  answer rather than printed words.

Approximating any of them would be the D362 trade in the wrong direction.

### What the hidden-information audit can and cannot say about this

`scripts/measure/hidden-info.mjs` (#164) drops **any** position with a question outstanding, which is
broader than its name said — it was called `readingLibrary` and has been renamed `readingHidden` with
the reason written in. That rule is right: a pending question means some card is in the middle of
showing somebody something, and scrambling cards the card itself just revealed would report the card
working as the bot cheating.

The consequence is worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be rediscovered: **the audit needed
no change, and the audit therefore does not exercise this permission.** It still confirms nothing was
widened *accidentally*. The checks that actually cover the new path are the three redaction rows in
`scripts.test.ts`, and they exist because the instrument could not.

### The numbers, and the audit's verdict

| | before D531 | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,287 | **7,308** (+21) |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,528 | **11,550** (+22) |
| printed legal lines read | 22,759 / 56,421 (40.3%) | **22,793 / 56,421 (40.4%)** (+34) |

`scripts/measure/hidden-info.mjs` re-run after the change: **0 changed decisions out of 14,293**,
0% on every action type — `auto:cast` 0/3053, `auto:pass` 0/7508, `auto:attack` 0/1476,
`auto:block` 0/586, `auto:activate` 0/1258, and the ten smaller rows. The bot reads nothing it
should not, and nothing was widened by accident. What that run does **not** do is exercise the new
permission, for the reason above, and the three redaction rows in `scripts.test.ts` exist because of
it.

### The break run: 14 breaks, 14 caught — after it found three holes in these tests

Each verified to apply against an anchor matching exactly once and to revert against a SHA-256,
across all three files this increment touched. The first run caught **11 of 14**, and all three
misses were holes in my own tests rather than defensive guards — which is the run paying for itself
a third time in this session:

- **The reveal sentence not required.** The refusal row for "the reveal missing" began
  "You choose a nonland card from it" — no player in that sentence, so loosening the regex to accept
  any first sentence naming a player left the row green. **A refusal row that would still refuse
  with the guard gone is not a check on the guard.** Replaced with "Target opponent loses 2 life.
  You choose … That player discards that card." — a first sentence that does name a player and is
  not a reveal.
- **The discard sentence not required.** That row had only two clauses, so `clauses.length < 3`
  refused it first and the third-sentence regex was never reached. Replaced with a three-clause
  version whose third sentence is "You gain 2 life."
- **`nonland` composed with a qualifier, with the `nonland` half dropped.** Nothing printed
  "a nonland permanent card", and only a card that does can tell `!land && permanent` from
  `permanent` — a land *is* a permanent, so the broken reading would offer every land. A second
  compiled card (Probing Edict) and a runtime row asserting the Swamp stays out of the pool.

Re-run after those three: **14/14**. The two engine breaks that matter most are among them —
`fromSeat` ignored when the candidates are gathered, and `decisionCandidates` reading the chooser
instead of the pool seat — and so are all three on the permission: the chooser unable to read at all,
the permission not limited to the candidate list, and the permission not limited to the viewer being
asked.

**40/40 pods finished** at a fresh seed (SEED0=40401) on the clean commit, no engine throw and no
