## D532 — "This ability triggers only once each turn", and the ranking that said 39 when the answer was 8

`TriggerDef.onceEachTurn`, the triggered-ability counterpart of D508's `AbilityDef.onceEachTurn`.
143 printings across 140 legal cards carry the sentence, and before this increment every one of them
had an unread line.

### The headline is the measurement, not the reader

The queue ranking this increment was picked off (`scratchpad/p549.mjs`) put this row at the head at
**39 cards**. The honest figure, measured by stripping the sentence from all 140 and compiling,
is **8**. The reader shipped and finished exactly 8. A 4.9x over-prediction is worse than D530's
11%, and it is worth writing down because the cause is structural rather than a slip:

1. **The clause probe never tests the prologue.** It splits a line's *body* into clauses and asks
   whether each compiles standalone — and the body is what is left after "Whenever you gain life,"
   comes off. A card whose prologue has no `TRIGGER_SHAPE` is two readers short and counts as one
   clause short. Morbid Opportunist is the example: "Whenever one or more other creatures die, draw a
   card. This ability triggers only once each turn." — its body's only failing clause is the
   restriction, and strip the restriction and the line still does not read. Every trigger row in that
   ranking is inflated by however many of its cards are prologue-blocked, which is a different number
   per row, so the ranking is not even uniformly wrong.
2. **It compiles each clause under a placeholder name**, which is the artifact that bit three
   separate probes this session (D530's and D531's rankings among them): `selfRef(name)` matches the
   card's own name, so "put a +1/+1 counter on Arcbound Crusher" fails under the name "Probe Card"
   for a reason that has nothing to do with any reader. Those artifacts take the whole head of the
   ranking — 58, 37, 25, 16 — and the p549 run was corrected for this one and still wrong by 4.9x
   because of bias 1.

**This is D524's lesson arriving a second time with a second mechanism**, so the instrument is now in
the repository rather than the scratchpad: `scripts/measure/one-blocker.mjs`. For each legal card that
is exactly one line short, it SUBSTITUTES each clause of that line in turn with a clause the compiler
certainly reads ("draw a card") and recompiles the whole card. If the card then reads whole, that
clause is the only thing between it and a finished script — prologue, sibling clauses and the card's
own name all accounted for. Substitution rather than removal, and the difference is 9,459 cards: a
line with one clause has nothing to remove but itself, which is exactly the shape most trigger
printings are.

Run before the change, it predicted this row at **8** and was right. Its head rows for next time are
"untap it" (19) and "it can't be regenerated" (17) — a third and a half of what the old ranking
claimed for its own head, which is roughly the correction factor to expect on the rest of it.

### What the rule needed in the engine

**Enforced where the ability triggers, not where it resolves.** A gate on resolution would put two
copies of the ability on the stack, let an opponent respond to both, and then silently do nothing on
the second: a Morbid Opportunist whose controller sacrifices three creatures would show three
triggers and draw one card. The gate is in `fireTrigger`, after the intervening-if clause (a trigger
whose condition is false never triggered, so it must not spend the turn's firing) and before the
target legality check (a trigger with no legal target *did* trigger, CR 603.3d).

**`triggerFireKey`, namespaced `t:`.** The record goes on `CardInstance.abilityUsedTurn`, which D508
already uses for activated abilities keyed by bare index. A card's triggers and its activated
abilities are indexed separately, so index 0 of each is a different ability on the same permanent and
a bare key would have them share a record — using one would silently lock out the other for the turn.
`triggerFireKey` wraps `abilityUseKey` rather than reimplementing it, so the granted case has one
answer rather than two.

**A printed ability the compiler splits across several events refuses the restriction** rather than
carrying it: each `TriggerDef` gets its own index and so its own record, and one printed ability
firing once per event kind is a different card. Measured cost: of the 140, the 11 whose restricted
line this compiler reads at all emit one event and none emit several, so the refusal costs nothing
today and is right by construction (D487).

Everything else the corpus prints in this position stays unread, which is the behaviour it had
before: "only once" (7 cards — once per *game*, which wants bookkeeping this does not have), "only
twice each turn" (1), "after the clash ends" (3), "only from the battlefield" (1), "only if <card> is
on the battlefield or in your graveyard" (2). `triggerRestriction` returns the text unchanged rather
than refusing, because the refusal already happens one layer down and for the right reason: the
sentence stays in the line and no clause reader matches it. "once per turn" (1 card) is read beside
"once each turn" because they are one rule in two printings (D441).

### What it moved

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,793 / 56,421 (40.4%) | **22,803 / 56,421 (40.4%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,550 | **11,559** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,308 | **7,316** |

8 cards finished (Academy Wall, Battle-Scarred Survivalist, Bloombrute, Flying Octobot, Mary Jane
Watson, Mechan Assembler, Nanoform Sentinel, Whispering Wizard), 11 cards now carry the flag, and a
drop check over all 141 restricted printings found **0 cases where a line the compiler says it read
has no restricted trigger to show for it** — the one failure mode this reader's placement in
`lineScriptFor`'s chain could have had, measured rather than argued about.

### The break run: 12 breaks, 12 caught

Each verified to apply against an anchor matching exactly once and to revert against a SHA-256, over
both files the increment touched. First time this stretch that a run of this size came back clean on
the first pass, and the reason is the test my own first draft failed: see below. The twelve are the
reader never splitting the sentence off, the flag set on every trigger, the flag read and not put on
the `TriggerDef`, "once per turn" dropped, "only once" taken for "only once each turn", the
multi-event refusal dropped, the `t:` namespace dropped, the gate absent, the gate reading but never
refusing, the firing gated but never recorded, the record read as a boolean rather than a turn, and
the live-instance guard inverted.

### Two holes my own tests found before the break run did

- **`passBoth` is not `drain`.** The runtime test's first draft used the file's `cast` helper, which
  is `passBoth(apply(...))` — and `passBoth` stops the moment the stack's contents change, so a
  Spider resolving hands back a board with both entry triggers still waiting. The test read an
  unchanged library and called it a restriction working, which is indistinguishable from a
  restriction that stopped the *first* firing too. It now drains.
- **A refusal row that would still refuse with the guard gone.** The multi-event test's first draft
  used "When ~ enters and whenever you gain life", which has no `TRIGGER_SHAPE` at all — so the line
  was refused by the prologue and the restriction never came into it. Replaced with "When ~ enters or
  dies", a shape that really emits two events, plus a control asserting the same line reads as both
  events once the restriction is removed. This is D531's break-run lesson applied before the run
  rather than after it, and it is why the run came back 12/12.

### What is not tested, and why

- **The firing spent by a trigger with no legal target** (CR 603.3d). The gate sits before the
  target check deliberately, and no printing in the restricted set has a target that can be made
  illegal while the trigger would still fire — Nanoform Sentinel's "untap another target permanent"
  comes closest and needs a board where it is the only permanent, which is a board where it cannot
  become tapped twice. Asserted by construction and by the gate's position, not by a test.
- **The granted case.** `triggerFireKey` passes `grantedBy` through to `abilityUseKey`, and two legal
  cards print the restriction inside quoted granted text (Dionus, Elvish Archdruid and Folk Hero) —
  but those go through the quoted-ability reader, not `triggerFromLine`, so neither compiles with the
  flag today. The key handles them; nothing exercises it.
- **The ordering against a false intervening-if.** The gate is after the condition on purpose, and no
  restricted printing has an intervening-if clause, so a break that moved it before the condition
  would be vacuous.

### The corrected queue, run after the change

`scripts/measure/one-blocker.mjs` over the legal corpus: 15,019 cards are exactly one line short, and
for **2,323** of them exactly one clause of that line is the blocker. (The removal-only version of the
same test found 1,338 — the 985 difference is the single-clause lines substitution can test and
removal cannot.) The head, by cards finished:

| cards | clause |
| --- | --- |
| 19 | `untap it` |
| 17 | `it can't be regenerated` |
| 12 + 10 | `it has "sacrifice this creature: add {m}."` / `they have "…"` — **one reader, 22 cards** |
| 11 | `target creature you control deals damage equal to its power to target creature …` |
| 11 | `if that creature would die this turn, exile it instead` |
| 11 | `its controller loses N life` |
| 11 | `return up to two target creature cards from your graveyard to your hand` |

The 22-card row is the biggest real one and is two printings of the same thing — the Eldrazi Spawn
family's quoted mana ability, singular and plural. Nothing in the corrected ranking is above 19 for a
single spelling, which is the shape of the queue now that the inflation is gone: the honest head of a
40%-read compiler is a row in the high teens, not the high thirties.

## D533 — The pronoun "it", and a referent anywhere in its clause

D530 read a referent in **subject** position by swapping the first two words of the clause for a
target phrase and borrowing the reader that already understands the result. The anchor was the
limitation, and it was costing the head of the family: printed text puts a pronoun in **object**
position at least as often, and `Untap it` was the top row of the corrected queue
(`scripts/measure/one-blocker.mjs`) at 19 cards.

Three changes, all in service of that one:

1. **The pronoun is matched wherever it stands, and must stand exactly once.** Exactly once because
   the swap has to say which occurrence it replaced — "it deals damage equal to its power to it" has
   two referents and nothing here can tell them apart. That count also does the work of a "contains
   no target of its own" test for free: a clause already naming a target ends up with two specs after
   the swap, which D530's guard refuses.
2. **"it" joins the table as a third pronoun**, tried as a creature and as a permanent — so the
   pronoun and the target kind stopped being one parameter. They were one only because D530's two
   pronouns happened to name their own kinds.
3. **The targeting clause has to come earlier in the chain.** D530 shipped without this and its
   licence cannot supply it: that licence counts the targeting parts of the whole line and says
   nothing about where they are. So "Whenever ~ attacks, untap it. Tap target creature." satisfied
   every count it checks — one targeting part, one creature, pronoun names a creature — and means
   the attacker. Bound forwards, the untap lands on the opponent's creature. A wrong card, not an
   unread one, found by writing the test rather than by a break run.

A fourth change came out of the break run's shape rather than from the printings: the loop **filters
the pronoun table by the kind the earlier clause actually points at** instead of taking the first
swap that reads. "Tap target permanent. Untap it." has a correct reading, and without the filter the
creature swap read first, broke out of the loop, and handed the licence a `creature` borrow against a
`permanent` spec — refusing a line that reads perfectly well the other way round.

### What it moved

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,803 / 56,421 (40.4%) | **22,849 / 56,421 (40.5%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,559 | **11,596** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,316 | **7,356** |

40 cards finished — twice the 19 the queue predicted for `untap it` alone, because generalising the
position reads every row in the family at once rather than that one spelling. Four real printings are
in the tests: **Acrobatic Leap** ("Target creature gets +1/+3 and gains flying until end of turn.
Untap it."), **Abyssal Hunter** (borrowing from its own earlier clause inside an activated ability),
**Aether Sting** (the **actor** of a cast, in object position) and **Furnace Scamp** (the player it
**hit**, in object position).

### A stale refusal retired

`compile.test.ts` had a row asserting that "Whenever ~ deals combat damage to a player, ~ deals 1
damage to that player" was **refused**. That was true of D475, which had only the actor to offer, and
the docblock beside it named Furnace Scamp as the card it was protecting. D530 gave the hit player its
own supply and D533 let the pronoun be matched in object position, so the card now reads — correctly,
as the hit player. Keeping the assertion would have been the suite asserting the past (D516). What
replaces it asserts the reading, and keeps the discriminating half: the same clause on an **entry**
trigger, where no player the sentence could mean exists, is still refused.

### The break run: 11 breaks, 7 caught, and all four misses are vacuous

Each verified to apply against an anchor matching exactly once and to revert against a SHA-256.
Scored against `-t D53`, which is D530, D531, D532 and D533 together, because this increment changes
machinery all four are built on.

Caught: "it" removed from the table; the pronoun re-anchored to the start; the pronoun allowed to
refer forward; the kind filter dropped; the swap hard-coded to a creature; the pronoun left in the
swapped text; and the referent not supplied to the effect at all (caught by D530's hit-player rows).

The four misses, each with its reason measured rather than asserted:

- **A clause with two pronouns takes the first.** Provably vacuous: a first-occurrence-only rule
  leaves the *other* pronoun standing in the swapped text, and nothing in the clause vocabulary reads
  a sentence with a bare pronoun in it. Four plausible outputs were compiled directly — "target
  creature deals 2 damage to it", "Untap target creature and it gains flying until end of turn", and
  two more — and all four are unread. The `!== 1` guard is defence in depth that today cannot be
  observed.
- **The word boundary dropped.** The same mechanism: the boundary only matters inside a clause that
  already failed to read, and the swap then produces text no reader takes. Nothing printed
  distinguishes the two.
- **The licence's kind check deleted.** Implied by the new kind filter — the filter only offers a
  pronoun whose kind already equals the spec's, so the licence line cannot fail. It stays, with a
  comment recording it as unfalsifiable rather than presenting it as a live guard.
- **The pronoun table reversed.** Expected to be vacuous and stated as such in its own docblock: the
  filter means at most one entry per pronoun is reachable, so order is immaterial. The first draft of
  that docblock explained an order that had stopped mattering, and the break run is what retired the
  explanation.

## D534 — A triggered ability that divides a quantity is not emitted

D533's pod sweep threw. Seed 40607 of 40 ended with `the engine cannot divide a triggered ability
yet`, and the standing rule is that a throw in a sweep is work now rather than a line in a table.

### What it was

**Gang of Devils** — "When Gang of Devils dies, it deals 3 damage divided as you choose among one,
two, or three targets." `AutoChooseAction` carries no division, so `chooseTargets`
(`autoActions.ts:2465`) throws rather than dealing the whole 3 to the first target. The compiler was
emitting the trigger anyway, so the card went on the battlefield, died, and ended the game with an
engine error.

This is **D463's rule one ability kind over**. That decision stopped the compiler emitting a *divided
activated ability* for exactly this reason, and `dividesAQuantity` has been sitting there with two
call sites since. `triggerFromLine` is the third.

### It is not D533's doing, and the distinction is worth stating

The tempting attribution is that the pronoun work read a line that used to be unread. It did not.
That clause is the only one on its line, so `composeEffects` has nothing aimed before it,
`alreadyAimed` is false and the pronoun table is never consulted — the reading comes from the clause
vocabulary #119 added, and has been there since. What D533's sweep did was **surface** it: the throw
needed Gang of Devils to be in a deck, reach the battlefield and die, which is a seed away rather
than a commit away.

### The cost, measured

Measured over all 31,654 legal rows, **Gang of Devils is the only legal card whose compiled trigger
divided anything.** So the refusal costs exactly one card its script line, and that line did not
work:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,849 | **22,848** (40.5%) |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,596 | **11,595** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,356 | **7,355** |

Seed 40607 re-run after the change: **finished**, 96 turns, no throw.

### What is not done

Division on a triggered ability is a real feature and this is not it — refusing is the honest
placeholder, the same trade D463 made. It is task #375: give the choose action a division the way the
cast action has one, validate it against the budget, and store it on the stack object so
`dividedAmong` reads it on resolution. The same field would let D463's activated-ability refusal be
lifted. The engine's `chooseTargets` throw stays as defence in depth either way: a trigger arriving
from anywhere with a division is still refused rather than resolved wrongly, which is the two-places
rule D67 and D89 share.

### The sweep, re-run on the same seeds

**40/40 pods finished** at SEED0=40601 — the *same* seed set whose 40607 threw, which is the reading
that matters: the fix is confirmed on the games that failed rather than on a fresh set that might
simply not have met the card. No engine throw and no stalled table, 66.5 turns and 437 moves a game.
Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 25.1 cards with a hand-written script, 48.0 with at least one
unread line, 61.9 playable only from printed data, 0.4 cardboard.

D533's own sweep is therefore recorded as **39/40 with one throw, re-run clean at 40/40 after D534** —
not as a clean sweep. The first number is the honest one for that commit.

## D535 — "It can't be regenerated", read as a rider on its sibling clause

The head of the corrected queue at 17 cards, and **134 legal cards print the sentence** across eleven
different destroy shapes: a targeted destroy, four sweepers, an activated ability, an upkeep trigger,
a combat-damage trigger.

### The shape that was missing

It is the first clause this compiler reads that **modifies its sibling rather than doing anything
itself**, and `composeEffects` had no way to say that. The parts run in order and each is handed the
state the one before produced, so a part cannot reach back and change how an earlier part *behaves* —
only what it acts on.

`EffectContext.noRegeneration` is the answer, and the reason it is on the context is the reason the
increment is one reader instead of eleven: the rider is a fact about the **resolution**, not about a
sentence. Every destroy in that resolution reads the flag; the composition is wrapped once to set it.
The two `destroy` call sites in the compiler — the targeted one and `destroy all creatures` — both
read it, so the targeted printings and the sweeper printings come in together.

`destroy` takes `{ regenerates: false }` rather than the rider stripping the shield beforehand, and
the **indestructible early return is why**. A creature that cannot be destroyed keeps the shield it
had; strip-then-destroy would take a shield off a creature the card never touched, and the next thing
to kill it that turn would find it unshielded. A wrong card, in a narrow case nothing else would have
caught — so there is a test for exactly it.

### Two refusals, both deliberate

- **The rider is only read onto a sentence that says "destroy".** Without that, "Draw a card. It
  can't be regenerated." would compile as a draw with a printed sentence silently dropped (D487).
- **The two printings that pair the rider with damage are refused.** "~ deals 2 damage to target
  creature. It can't be regenerated." does not go through `destroy` at all — regeneration there is
  spent where lethal damage is noticed, and the suppression lasts until end of turn on the creature,
  which is a continuous effect this engine has no field for. Reading those two as though the flag
  reached them would be a wrong card (D362). The test for this is a refusal row, and the guard that
  produces it is a test on the *printed text* rather than on the composed reading, deliberately.

### What it moved

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,848 | **22,873 / 56,421 (40.5%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,595 | **11,614** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,355 | **7,375** |

**20 cards finished against a prediction of 17** — the instrument under-counted this time, where
p549 over-counted by 4.9x. `one-blocker.mjs` only attributes a card when *exactly one* clause of its
line is the blocker, so a card whose line the rider unblocks alongside something else is invisible to
it. Under-counting is the direction that instrument's own docblock says it errs in, and this is the
first measurement that confirms it rather than asserting it.

### The break run: 11 breaks, 9 caught, both misses predicted in advance

Each verified to apply against an anchor matching exactly once and to revert against a SHA-256, over
both files. Scored against `-t D53` — D530 through D535 together — because this increment changes
`composeEffects` and `destroy`, which all of them sit on.

The nine: the rider never read; the rider read onto anything rather than only a destroy; the rider
not setting the flag; only "it" read of the four spellings; the targeted destroy ignoring the flag;
the sweeper ignoring the flag; `destroy` accepting the option and ignoring it; `destroy`'s sense
inverted; and the indestructible return moved below the shield.

The two misses were **written into the harness as expected-vacuous before the run**, and the run
confirmed both: `before.length === 0` is unfalsifiable because `composeEffects([])` already returns
null, and the `beforeDecisions` refusal is defence in depth that nothing in the corpus reaches. That
is the first run this stretch where every miss was predicted rather than explained afterwards.

**40/40 pods finished** at a fresh seed (SEED0=40701) on the clean commit, no engine throw and no
stalled table, 61.3 turns and 299 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 25.1 cards with
a hand-written script, 48.2 with at least one unread line, 61.8 playable only from printed data, 0.4
cardboard.

## D536 — The ability a token arrives with

The biggest single row of the corrected queue: 22 legal cards across two spellings, which is the
Eldrazi Spawn family —

> At the beginning of your upkeep, create a 0/1 colorless Eldrazi Spawn creature token.
> It has "Sacrifice this creature: Add {C}."

The second clause this file reads as a **rider on its sibling** (D535 was the first), and the second
new combinator in two increments — which is what the queue has been saying for a while: the lever is
clause combinators (D519), not more sentences.

### Why it is almost free

A token is a `CardDef` like any other card, and `scriptForCard` hands a def with no hand-written
script to the compiler. So **writing the quoted sentence into the token's `oracleText` is the whole
implementation**: the compiler reads it back out when the ability is offered, and the player gets a
real activated ability on a real permanent. The chain is compiler → token def → compiler again, and
only a game can see the second half, which is what the runtime tests are for.

That also explains the shape of the yield. 36 of the 57 legal printings of this shape are the Eldrazi
Spawn sentence; the rest are a tail of quoted triggers ("When this token dies, you gain 1 life"), mana
abilities ("{T}: Add {G}") and one regeneration. They all come for free, because the mechanism is
"write it down and let the compiler read it" rather than a reader per printing.

### The read-back check, and the guard that could not fail

`tokenFrom` already refuses a token whose printed **keyword** list the engine cannot read back —
"a token whose text lies" is its own docblock's phrase. The quoted sentence gets the same treatment:
`lineScriptFor` must produce *something* from it, or the line is refused.

The first draft demanded more than that — an ability or a trigger — and the break run showed it to be
**both untestable and wrong**. Untestable because the refusal row that covers this guard ("Fly over
the moon") is refused by the `null` test one line above, so the second half was never reached. Wrong
because a quoted keyword or static is something the engine applies to a token too. Measured: of the
57 legal printings, **0 put a bare keyword in this position**, and re-measuring the whole corpus after
the widening moved nothing — so the stricter version cost nothing, and was a guard that could not
fail, which is the thing this project does not keep.

Two refusals stand, both measured:

- **A named token cannot take a quoted ability.** "Create a Treasure token" looks the token up in
  `TOKEN_DEFS`, which is shared and fixed; writing text onto one would either mutate the definition
  every other Treasure uses or drop the sentence silently.
- **Exactly two clauses, the token and the rider.** Every legal printing of this shape puts the rider
  immediately after the token sentence with nothing else on the line, because the line is a trigger
  whose prologue has already come off. A longer list would need the token part sequenced after a
  prefix, which `composeEffects` can only do for parts it read itself.

### What it moved

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,873 | **22,899 / 56,421 (40.6%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,614 | **11,635** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,375 | **7,399** |

24 cards finished against a prediction of 22 — `one-blocker.mjs` under-counting again, in the
direction it says it does.

### The break run: 7 breaks, 7 caught — after it found two things wrong with itself

The first pass was 6 of 8, and **neither miss was a hole in the tests**:

- One break deleted the over-strict half of the read-back guard, which proved the guard
  unfalsifiable. That half is gone, and the docblock now records why.
- The other break was **mis-written**: it loosened the two-clause test but still handed
  `clauses[0]` to the token reader, so the hazard it was meant to produce — reading the last two
  clauses and dropping the prefix — never happened. Rewritten as the real thing (`clauses.length - 2`
  with a trailing `last`), it is caught by the existing three-clause refusal row, which was verified
  by patching it in by hand and watching "Draw a card. Create … It has …" compile.

Re-run after both: **7/7**. Scored against `-t D53`, which is D530 through D536 together.

### A third kind of probe artifact, recorded

A smoke test reported Brood Monitor unread while Awakening Zone read, which looked like a plural bug
in the new reader. It was neither: the probe card had `type_line: 'Creature — …'` and **no power or
toughness**, so the card itself was malformed and refused before any line was read. Compiled with its
real printed values it reads. Third distinct probe artifact this session, after the placeholder-name
one (D532) and the clause-compiled-standalone one (D530) — the pattern is the same each time: a probe
that constructs a card instead of using a printed one, and a conclusion about the reader drawn from a
fact about the probe.

## D537 — The possessive referent: "its controller"

The joint head of the corrected queue, and the **third new combinator in three increments** — which
is what the queue has been saying since D519: the lever is clause combinators, not more sentences.

"Destroy target creature. Its controller loses 2 life." is one target and two subjects. The first
clause points at a creature; the second is about a player the board *derives* from that creature.
D530's borrow could only ever hand a clause the object itself, so every possessive printing was
unread — and **139 legal cards put a possessive-controller clause after another sentence**, the
biggest row being this one at 11.

### Three pieces, each forced by something that broke

**`ReferentSupply`.** The pronoun table grew a third column: `'object'` is every pronoun D530 and
D533 read, `'controller'` derives a player. That also split the kind filter in two — matching a
*player* pronoun against a *creature* spec refuses every possessive, so a controller supply is
filtered on whether the earlier clause pointed at something a controller can be read off
(`CONTROLLABLE_KINDS`), and `any` and `player` are excluded for D530's reason.

**`EffectContext.referentSeat`, computed before any part runs.** The first draft looked the
controller up when the clause ran, and the runtime test failed immediately: the printed sentence
**destroys the creature first**, so by then the object has left the battlefield. The game has to use
last known information for it (CR 608.2h), and the only place that can read the board before any
part has changed it is `composeEffects` — the same wrapper shape D535 and D536 use. A supply that
looked it up late would either refuse (the clause silently doing nothing, on the biggest shape in the
family) or read the graveyard's seat, which is the card's *owner*.

**`CardsDecisionSpec.who: 'referent-player'`.** The second draft still failed, and this is **the
D530 hazard arriving in a new place**: `decisionPlan` resolves `who: 'target-player'` off the stack
object's *targets*, and a possessive resolution's target is the creature. "Its controller discards a
card" asked nobody and resolved to nothing. `referentEffect`'s `asks` parameter already existed for
exactly this, and the new word resolves from the stack object's own first card target — read in
**whatever zone it is in**, because the D418 split has already run the destroy by plan time.

### A known limitation, stated

For a card in a graveyard `zoneSeat` is its **owner**, which is its controller for everything but a
permanent that was under another player's control when it left. Closing that needs the controller
recorded as the object leaves, which nothing in this engine does yet. Named in the code and here
rather than left for somebody to find.

Also refused and measured: **the counter path**. "Counter target noncreature spell. Its controller
loses 2 life" — Countersquall and eight legal cards of that shape — has no instance to read, because
a spell's controller lives on the stack object. It wants its own supply; guessing a seat would be a
wrong card (D362).

### What it moved

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,899 | **22,928 / 56,421 (40.6%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,635 | **11,661** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,399 | **7,423** |

### A second stale refusal retired, one increment old

D533's own test asserted that "Destroy target creature. Its controller loses 2 life." stays unread,
with a comment saying it "waits for its own reader". D537 is that reader, one increment later, and
the test now asserts it reads with one target. That is the second stale refusal this stretch after
the Furnace Scamp row — both were true when written, both were notes about a gap, and D516's rule is
that such a note has to be re-read when the gap closes or the suite starts asserting the past.

### The break run: 8 breaks, 8 caught — after it found the hole D530 had already named

The first pass was 7 of 8, and the miss was **the aiming of the effect itself**: every runtime row
was a *discard*, which `CardsDecisionSpec.who` routes, so the engine applies the answer and an effect
handed the wrong seat still produces the right discard. D530's own docblock records this exact hole
and says life loss is the only row that can see the aiming — and I did not carry that forward.
Breaking `referentSeat` left every discard row green.

Added the life-loss row (Bitter Downfall, the real printing, with both life totals asserted). Re-run:
**8/8**. Scored against `-t D53`, which is D530 through D537 together.

## D538 — The freeze: "doesn't untap during its controller's next untap step"

**The primitive has been in the engine since #52 and nothing could reach it.** `freezeNextUntap`
was written for Wall of Frost — a hand-written card — and the clause never got a reader, so all
**73 legal printings** of the sentence compiled with that line unread. This increment is one regex
onto a primitive whose own tests have held since #52, and it is the cheapest kind
of reader there is: no new state, no new rule, nothing to get wrong at the table.

What makes it worth more than one row is that **the referent borrow does the rest**. The printed
sentence almost never names its subject — it says "That creature" (15 printings) or "It" (17) — and
D530 and D533 built the swap for exactly this. The swap had nothing to hand its result to.

|  | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,928 / 56,421 (40.6%) | **22,966 / 56,421 (40.7%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,661 | **11,686** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,423 | **7,445** |

**22 cards finished**, all of them: Barl's Cage, Chillbringer, Crippling Chill, Elvish Hunter,
Frost Lynx, Frost Trickster, Glacial Grasp, House Guildmage, Kor Hookmaster, Niblis of Frost,
Ojutai's Breath, Press for Answers, Quiet Contemplation, Skyline Cascade, Sleep of the Dead,
Sleeper Dart, Spire Patrol, Stitched Mangler, Take into Custody, Watertrap Weaver, Wavecrash Triton,
White Dragon.

### The instrument's fourth calibration, and its largest miss

`one-blocker.mjs` ranked this family at **13** across its two pronoun rows. The real figure is
**22**. Running total: exact at 8 (D532), under by 3 (D535), under by 2 (D536), **under by 9** here.
The reason is the same every time and is in the instrument's own docblock — it counts only a card
that is *exactly one* no-reader line short whose line has *exactly one* blocking clause. Skyline
Cascade names its own target, so its line has no pronoun row to be counted under; Glacial Grasp has
three clauses; and every card two lines short is outside what the probe can see at all. The
instrument under-reads and is still the right instrument: it has never over-read, and a queue that
understates its own head is a queue you can act on.

### What is refused, and why each refusal is a different thing

- **The Aura static, 48 printings** — "Enchanted creature doesn't untap during its controller's
  untap step". Drop the "next" and the sentence stops being a one-shot and becomes a continuous
  effect that holds the creature down for ever. Reading them alike would make Claustrophobia a
  one-turn Frost Lynx: a card that works and is wrong (D259).
- **Dungeon Geists, 2** — the same words with "for as long as you control this creature".
- **The plural referent, 18** — "Those creatures don't untap during their controller's next untap
  step" (11), "...their controllers' next untap steps" (4), "They don't untap..." (3).
  `referentEffect` supplies exactly one borrowed object, so accepting the plural would tap two
  creatures and freeze one. That is the half-read card `foldCardTargets`' docblock calls worse than
  an unread line, because an unread line is badged for a human and a half-read one is not.
- **A pronoun with no antecedent, 3** — Apes of Rath, Lead Golem, Stitcher's Graft: "Whenever ~
  attacks, **it** doesn't untap". The "it" is the attacker itself, so there is no earlier clause to
  borrow from and the pronoun table is never consulted.
- **The blocks-relative referent, 4** — Wall of Frost, Labyrinth Minotaur, Cleric of Chill Depths,
  Shield of the Righteous: "that creature" is the creature this block was *against*, which travels
  on the event as `blocked` and not as a target.
- **"tap that creature and it doesn't untap", 7** — the Kashi-Tribe family: an event-relative
  referent and a conjunction at once.

Those six are the family's own queue, measured by compiling rather than by pattern-matching (D524),
and the plural is the biggest at 18.

### The break run: 7 of 9, and two of my own comments were wrong

The first pass caught **5 of 9** and the two surprises were both coverage holes rather than vacuous
breaks:

- Making `next` optional in the pattern left the suite green. The Claustrophobia row refuses for a
  **different reason than its comment claimed** — "Enchanted creature" is not a target phrase, so
  `targetSpecFrom` turns it down before the "next" is ever consulted. Added a probe row that asserts
  the reader demands the word, with the one-word-different control in the same `it`.
- Removing `pointsAtAPermanent` left the suite green. Added a probe aiming the sentence at a player,
  where without the guard the clause reads and then silently applies nothing.

Both probes are probes on purpose: no card in the corpus prints either sentence, so a real printing
could not have made the guard falsifiable. That is the fourth refusal-for-the-wrong-reason this
stretch has caught (three in D533, one here), and the pattern is always the same — a refusal
asserted as `unread.length === 1` passes whichever line was refused. Two rows were retightened to
name the line instead of counting it.

Re-run: **7/9**. The two that stay uncaught are recorded in the reader's docblock rather than
papered over:

- The literal `target` in the pattern is **redundant with `targetSpecFrom`**. Replacing it with
  `^(.+?)` changes nothing, because every subject the corpus puts here that is not a target phrase
  is refused one line down. It stays because it makes the pattern say what it means.
- `foldCardTargets` rather than the first target is **unfalsifiable today**, for the same reason the
  plural is refused: no printing of this sentence names more than one target. It is the shared fold
  the five open-phrase families use (D469), and it is already right for the day one arrives.

### The possessive is dropped on purpose

"its controller's next untap step" names no new subject — it is English for "the next untap step
that would untap it". `untapAll` runs per seat over that seat's own battlefield, so the controller is
read **at the step** (CR 502.2), which is both what the rules want and what D537's possessive supply
could not have given: a permanent that changes hands between the freeze and the step answers to
whoever controls it then.
