## D539 — "If that creature would die this turn, exile it instead"

**The compiler's first floating replacement effect.** Every replacement the engine had belonged to a
permanent — a regeneration shield, "enters tapped", Kalitas — and was found by the pass that asks
each permanent on the battlefield whether it wants to replace what is about to happen. This sentence
is printed on **spells**: Bleed Dry is in a graveyard by the time the creature it was aimed at dies,
so the thing that must still be there is a `ContinuousEffect` with a duration, and
`replaceZoneChange` reads it.

|  | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,966 / 56,421 (40.7%) | **22,989 / 56,421 (40.7%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,686 | **11,705** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,445 | **7,463** |

**18 cards finished**, all of them: Agate Assault, Bleed Dry, Blitz of the Thunder-Raptor, Bot
Bashing Time, Elspeth's Smite, Fanged Flames, Feed the Flames, Flame-Blessed Bolt, Lava Coil,
Magma Spray, Narset's Rebuke, Ob Nixilis's Cruelty, Obliterating Bolt, Puncturing Blow, Reduce
to Ashes, Scorching Dragonfire, Scorchmark, Suplex. The queue ranked the two referent rows at
16; the instrument's fifth
calibration and under by 2. Running record: exact at 8 (D532), under by 3, 2, 9 and 2.

### The sentence names the same object twice

"If **that creature** would die this turn, exile **it** instead" has two pronouns for one object,
and `referentEffect` swaps one occurrence of one pronoun (D533). So the text that reaches the reader
has the target phrase in whichever slot the pronoun table got to first: swapping "that creature"
gives `if target creature would die this turn, exile it instead`, and swapping "it" — which is the
path Blitz of the Thunder-Raptor takes, because its spec is a *permanent* and the creature entry is
filtered out — gives `if that creature would die this turn, exile target creature instead`.

Both are the same card, so the reader takes either slot: one must parse as a target spec, the other
must be a bare pronoun. The second condition is what stops `if target creature would die this turn,
exile the top card of your library instead` reading as this clause and quietly dropping what the
sentence actually said — a break run found that restriction was otherwise decorative, and it has a
probe row now.

The consequence worth stating: **the raw printed sentence reads as nothing.** Two pronouns, no
target phrase, neither slot parses — so a card that prints it with nothing aimed before it leaves the
line unread rather than arming a replacement over no objects.

### Why an effect rather than a flag on the dying card

A flag on the instance would have worked and would have needed its own line in `endTurnCleanup`.
A `ContinuousEffect` with `duration: 'end-of-turn'` expires there for free, alongside the pumps, and
`pump` already builds exactly this shape. It also gets CR 400.7 right without trying: a creature
blinked and returned is a new object with a new id, so the effect no longer covers it.

`ContinuousEffect.exiledInsteadOfDying` is the first field on that interface that is **not a
characteristic**. Every other member answers "what is this permanent like" and is read by the layer
passes; this one answers "what happens instead when it dies", so `effectApplies` never sees it and
the reader is in `automation.ts`.

### Two rows refused, each for its own reason

- **"If a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, exile it instead"** (8 printings, Anger
  of the Gods). The subject is every creature the *previous clause* damaged, and nothing in
  `composeEffects` hands a clause what its sibling touched. That is a channel to build — the same
  shape `GameState.died`, `drew` and `discarded` already have for other "what just happened"
  questions — not a phrase to match.
- **"If a creature would die this turn, exile it instead"** (2, Flaying Tendrils). Board-wide, and
  it covers creatures that *arrive after it resolves*. The engine snapshots until-end-of-turn scopes
  on purpose (CR 611.2c, #280) — `pumpAll` converts a board-wide pump into a list of ids for exactly
  that reason — so there is no scope here that means "every creature, read when the question is
  asked". Unread rather than half-read.

### The break run: 8 of 9, and the order of two deaths was load-bearing

The first pass caught **6 of 9**, and the miss that mattered was the scope check: deleting
`fx.scope.ids.includes(id)` left the suite green. The reason is a fact about the engine I did not
know and the test now states — **an effect scoped to a card is dropped once that card leaves the
battlefield**, so killing the *named* creature first took the effect with it and left nothing for
the second death to be over-applied to. Killing the unnamed one first catches it. That is the fifth
"my test passed for the wrong reason" of this stretch and the first one where the wrong reason was
the engine's behaviour rather than my own regex.

The one break still uncaught is recorded in the reader's docblock: `on === 'dies'` rather than the
wider `to-graveyard` wording cannot be falsified, because a dying creature is in both lists and the
wide pass runs first.

### The pod sweep

**40/40 pods finished** at a fresh seed (SEED0=41101) on the clean commit, no engine throw and no
stalled table, 66.8 turns and 381 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 25.9 cards with
a hand-written script, 47.4 with at least one unread line, 61.9 playable only from printed data, 0.5
cardboard.

## D540 — The graveyard return, opened up and counted

**The reader was two words wide and the corpus prints eleven.** "Return target `creature|land` card
from your graveyard to your hand" was written for Raise Dead and for Grim Discovery, which prints
both halves of one sentence, and the literal alternation is what every other printing ran into.

|  | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 22,989 / 56,421 (40.7%) | **23,121 / 56,421 (41.0%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,705 | **11,802** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,463 | **7,551** |

**+88 cards with every printed line read**, which is **5.5x** what the queue predicted for the two
rows it could see (11 + 5 = 16). This is the instrument's sixth calibration and by far its largest
miss, and the reason is worth more than the number: the counting quantifier went into
**`graveyardCardPhrase`** rather than into this one reader, so the exile-from-graveyard and
reanimation families got it at the same time. A probe that measures one clause cannot see a change
made one layer down.

Running record of `one-blocker.mjs`: exact at 8 (D532), then under by 3, 2, 9, 2 and **72**.

### None of it needed new vocabulary

`graveyardCardPhrase` has read the type run, the disjunction, the `permanent` list and `nonland`
composed with a second word since D527. The reader simply was not asking it. Opening the phrase is
one regex, and it inherits all of that: `card` with no type at all (12 printings), `permanent` (14
across three quantifiers), `instant or sorcery` (8), `artifact` (6), `enchantment` (3), `sorcery`
(2), `artifact or creature` (2), `artifact or enchantment` (2), `historic` (1).

The count is the other half. "Return **up to two** target creature cards from your graveyard to your
hand" is 17 printings, read with `foldCardTargets` rather than `firstCardTarget` — the pair D469 made
inseparable, because a reader that asks for two targets and moves one of them is a card that resolves
and does half of what it says. The table test asserts **both** cards come back, and the break run
confirms that is the row which catches it.

`up to two` is also two facts and both are load-bearing: `count: 2` and `optional: true`. Dropping
the second makes the spell uncastable with one creature in the graveyard, which is a different and
worse card — its own break, and its own test row.

### What stays refused

- **"two target creature cards that share a creature type"** (3 printings). `TargetSpec.filter` is
  asked about one candidate at a time, so there is nowhere to say "and the same type as the other
  one". A reader that dropped the clause would let a player take any two, which is strictly better
  than the card printed (D259).
- **"X target creature cards"** (5). The engine's X is announced as a cost is paid; `count` is a
  number read when targets are asked for. A count of X is a third thing.

### The break run: 6 of 7, and the seventh is provably unreachable

`POINTS_AT_A_GRAVEYARD_CARD` — the guard that keeps the open phrase honest — can be deleted with the
suite staying green. Rather than leave that as "unfalsifiable", the question was pushed one step:
the callers rebuild the phrase with ` in your graveyard` on the end, and `targetSpecFrom`'s last
resort has **no noun for `graveyard`**, which its own docblock states. So a phrase
`graveyardCardPhrase` turns down is refused outright rather than read as something else, and the
guard cannot fire while that holds.

It is kept, which is the opposite of what D536 did with its unfalsifiable guard, and the difference
is written into the code: there, the unsatisfiable half was a fact about the function's own output;
here it is a fact about a *different* function, one noun away from changing. The day
`parsedTargetPhrase` learns the word, this is what stops `bounceToHand` being handed a permanent off
the battlefield.

The regression that mattered most has its own row: `targetSpecFrom`'s exact-phrase switch keeps
`target creature card in your graveyard` with a hand-written `filter` by reference, which
`compiled-vs-written.test.ts` compares against Raise Dead character for character. Rebuilding the
phrase reproduces exactly that string for the plain printing, and the test asserts the kind, the
description and the absence of a count rather than trusting the other file.

### The pod sweep

**40/40 pods finished** at a fresh seed (SEED0=41201) on the clean commit, no engine throw and no
stalled table, 63.1 turns and 339 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 25.8 cards with
a hand-written script, 47.5 with at least one unread line, 61.8 playable only from printed data, 0.5
cardboard.

## D541 — The mass pump, read by its subject

**Two regexes with one shape between them, and five subjects that had neither.** The compiler read
`creatures you control get +N/+N until end of turn` — plus only — and `all creatures get ±N/±N`.
The corpus prints **492 sentences** in this family and the subject is where they differ.

|  | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,121 / 56,421 (41.0%) | **23,180 / 56,421 (41.1%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,802 | **11,844** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,551 | **7,590** |

**+39 cards finished**, against 45 printings measured across the five missing subjects —
`creatures your opponents control` (22), `attacking creatures` (10), `other creatures you control`
(7), `blocking creatures` (3), `creatures target player controls` (3) — plus the team penalty the
first reader's `\+` had been refusing. The closest the queue has come to its own prediction in six
calibrations.

### The ids are a snapshot, and that is what makes two of the scopes possible at all

Every subject resolves to a **list**, which `pump` freezes into the effect (CR 611.2c, #280): a
creature that arrives later in the turn is not pumped and one that leaves does not take the bonus
with it. `pumpTeam` and `pumpAll` already did exactly that for an until-end-of-turn duration — they
keep a live scope only when the duration is `permanent` — so this reader calls `pump` directly with
the same lists and is behaviour-identical on the two phrases it replaces.

It is also the only way `attacking creatures` and `blocking creatures` can be expressed.
`ContinuousEffect.scope` has no member for "the creatures attacking right now", and it should not:
that set is a fact about `state.combat` at the moment the spell resolves, and a live scope would keep
pumping a creature that had been removed from combat.

### The bot hint, kept where it was calibrated

`expiresAtEndOfTurn` is "hold this for the combat". It is set for a bonus to your own creatures —
D364's trap, where a compiled Inspired Charge otherwise gets cast in a main phase with nothing to
attack with — and for the two combat scopes, which do **nothing at all** outside combat and so want
it more than anything else in the family.

It stays off for `all creatures`, which keeps the sweeper this reader replaced exactly as it was, and
off for the opponents' board: a penalty on their creatures is a combat trick in one light and a sweep
you cast the moment it kills something in another, and which of those the bot should believe is
unmeasured. A hint that points the wrong way plays worse than none, so that waits for a measurement.

Both halves of that preservation are now falsifiable, which took a third row: the two negative
printings are silent about a flag they were never going to have, so a change that flagged every bonus
passed until "All creatures get +1/+1" was asserted to carry none.

### The break run: 9 of 9, and the ninth was a test the suite did not have

The first pass caught **8 of 9**. The miss was the word **other**: deleting the `!== c.source`
exclusion left the whole suite green, because every other subject here is about somebody's entire
board and nothing was asserting the one place the word does work. Bolt Hound — "Whenever Bolt Hound
attacks, other creatures you control get +1/+0 until end of turn" — is that place, and the row now
attacks with the Hound and a Grizzly Bears and asserts the Bears is a 3/2 while the Hound is still a
2/2. Re-run: **9/9**.

That is the seventh break run in eight where what broke was a test rather than the code.

### Refused

`Creatures of the creature type of your choice get +X/+X until end of turn` (Tribal Unity) — a scope
whose membership is chosen as the spell resolves. `massPumpSubject` has no entry for it, so the line
is unread rather than pumped as something else, and the discriminating half is every reading above.

### The pod sweep, and the seed that had to be ruled out first

**40/40 pods finished** at SEED0=41401 on the clean commit, no engine throw and no stalled table,
59.8 turns and 320 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 25.9 cards with a hand-written
script, 47.7 with at least one unread line, 61.8 playable only from printed data, 0.5 cardboard.

**That is the second seed set, and the first one is the finding.** The sweep at SEED0=41301 sat at
100% CPU for twenty-two minutes with nothing printed. A trace found it: game 19 — seed **41319** —
was at **turn 176** on move 2,000, with 39, 49 and 32 permanents on three boards and one seat already
dead, and the moves after that were taking minutes each. Not a loop: the harness's `LOOP` detector
could not fire because life totals, boards and libraries were all still moving. It is the
`unfinished` verdict the harness has a word for, in the #71 / #250 family — a board nobody can break
through, where the bot's lookahead grows with the board it is searching.

**It is not D541's doing, and that was settled by experiment rather than by argument.** The same
seed was run at `MOVES=2000` on the engine built from the **previous** commit's sources (c36f6df)
and on this one: both report `unfinished`, identically. So the long game predates the mass-pump
reader, and the only thing D541 changed about it is nothing.

What this costs, said plainly: there is **no 40/40 reading for seed set 41301**, because the run was
killed rather than left to spend an hour of CPU on one table. The clean reading above is a different
seed set, and the honest summary is "40/40 at 41401, and 41319 is a pre-existing long game".

## D542 — The bite and the fight: two targets pointed at each other

**415 legal printings**, in two shapes that look like one and are not.

The **bite** is one-way: "Target creature you control deals damage equal to its power to target
creature you don't control" (Rabid Bite, Bite Down, Quarrel, Clear Shot, Ram Through). The **fight**
is both ways: "Target creature you control fights target creature you don't control" (Prey Upon, Go
for Blood, Pit Fight, Mutant's Prey), which is a keyword action with a rule of its own (CR 701.12a).

`fight` has been in the engine since Prey Upon and gets right the one thing that matters: both powers
are read **before** either damage is dealt, so a creature that dies to the first half still deals its
own. The bite cannot reuse it — one-way is one-way — but the two readers sit side by side in
`targetedEffect` so the pair stays legible, and the compile table reads them in one describe.

### The damage comes from the creature, not from the spell

This is the whole of the bite's correctness. CR 702.2b and CR 702.15b hang deathtouch and lifelink on
the *source* of the damage, and so do infect and wither. A reader that passed the spell as the source
would compile a card that works — the right creature takes the right number — and silently turn off
four keywords on every printing. So the effect passes `source: mine`, and a row asks a 1/1 Typhoid
Rats to bite a 2/2 and expects the 2/2 dead.

**That row failed, and what it found was not in the reader.** `dealDamage` took `deathtouch` and
`lifelink` as *caller options*, beside `infect` and `wither`, which it read off the source's own
keywords. Of its **41 call sites, exactly one passed them** — `combat.ts` — so deathtouch worked in
combat and nowhere else: not on a bite, not on a ping, not on a trigger, not on anything a card had
ever pointed anywhere. Both are now read from `sourceKeywords` beside `infect`/`withers`, and the two
options are **deleted** rather than kept as an override: an override is a second place for the answer
to live, and the source's keywords are the only place CR puts it. `combat.ts`'s three call sites lost
the arguments, its unused `const lifelink` went, and its `const deathtouch` stays with a note that it
is now read only for the lethal-damage arithmetic (CR 702.2c) while whether the damage is *deadly* is
`dealDamage`'s business.

An increment whose own test finds a four-keyword hole one layer down is the argument for the row
being about behaviour rather than about the compile.

### `friendly` is read off the printed words, and nowhere else

`friendly` is the bot's aim, not a restriction: the printed phrase's own filter already decides what
is legal to target. Almost every bite and every fight names your creature first, so the hint belongs
on the first spec — but the corpus also prints the shape **inverted**: Mutiny and Breaking of the
Fellowship both read "Target creature an opponent controls deals damage equal to its power to another
target creature that player controls", where the same hint would point the bot at a board it may not
choose from. So it is taken from `/\byou control\b/` on the subject phrase and from nothing else.

Prey Upon's hand-written script did not carry `friendly`, which made this a new `compiled-vs-written`
disagreement the moment the reader landed. Settled the way **D419** settled it: `friendly` beside a
filter that already restricts to your side is the aim, not a second restriction, so the flag was
written onto `PREY_UPON` and the standing check's table is empty again.

### Refused: the referent forms

The bigger half of the family is refused on purpose. "It fights target creature you don't control"
(Epic Confrontation, Mage Duel, Savage Smash, Wild Instincts, Chelonian Tackle, ~22 printings) borrows
its first target from the clause before it, and `referentEffect` turns down any reading that declares
more than one target, because it supplies exactly **one** object. Supplying one of two is a real
extension to the borrow, not a wording tweak, so these wait for it rather than being half-read now —
D469, a reader that asks for N targets and moves one is worse than an unread line. The compile row
shows Epic Confrontation with its pump read and its fight unread, side by side.

### The break run: 8 of 9, then 9 of 9, and the ninth needed a probe

The first pass caught 8. The two misses, and what each one was:

- **"the damage comes from the spell, not the creature"** (break 6) — uncaught because nothing
  asserted a keyword on the damage. Answered by **fixing the engine**: see above. The Typhoid Rats row
  is what catches it now.
- **"the first target is always aimed at your own side"** (break 9) — uncaught twice. The first
  answer was a row on "Target creature fights another target creature" (Pit Fight, 2 printings), which
  is real, reads, and carries no aim — but it exercises the **fight** reader, so it stays green while
  the **bite** reader hardcodes the hint. And there is no real printing that can tell them apart:
  every bite in the corpus that reads today says "you control" in its subject, and the two that do not
  (Mutiny, Breaking of the Fellowship) are unread for the phrase after the verb. So this one gets a
  **probe row** — a placeholder name over text no card carries, asserting what a real printing would
  need the day its other phrase reads. Re-run of break 9 alone: **CAUGHT**, 9/9.

Adding a test can only widen what the earlier breaks catch, so breaks 1-8 were not re-run; break 9
was re-verified on its own with the same apply/revert discipline (unique anchor, SHA-256 revert check).

That is the eighth break run in nine where what broke was a test rather than the code.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,180 / 56,421 (41.1%) | **23,228 / 56,421 (41.2%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,844 | **11,875** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,590 | **7,620** |

31 more cards finished. The ratio is the usual one for a two-reader increment on a family whose
bigger half is a referent form: the 415 printings split roughly 1 in 3 readable now, 2 in 3 waiting on
a combinator.

### D542's pod sweep

**40/40 pods finished** at SEED0=41501 on the clean commit (4fdff53), no engine throw and no stalled
table, 66.2 turns and 393 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 26.1 cards with a
hand-written script, 47.5 with at least one unread line, 62.0 playable only from printed data, 0.4
cardboard.

The deathtouch fix is the part of this increment a pod sweep is actually measuring. Reading deathtouch
and lifelink off the source turns both on for every non-combat damage effect in the pool at once —
pings, triggers, bites — so a sweep that finished every game with no throw is the evidence that
widening them did not break the damage path the bot searches through hundreds of times a game.

## D543 — The blink's second half, read as a clause

**18 cards finished**, and a 60-line reader deleted as redundant on the way.

The pair is "Exile another target permanent you control, **then return it to the battlefield under
its owner's control**." The exile half has had a reader since D404. The return half had none, and
because a line is read whole or not at all (D487) the whole line went unread — which was the right
refusal: a compiler that took the exile and stopped would have turned a blink into **unconditional
removal of your own permanent**, a card that works, plays and is the opposite of what it prints.

### Why a clause reader and not a wider `blinkResolution`

`blinkResolution` has read Cloudshift since it was written, and it takes the **whole spell line**. The
cards at the head of the queue are not spells of one line: Felidar Guardian and Wispweaver Angel are
triggers, Distinguished Conjurer and Nephalia Smuggler and Ruin Ghost are activated abilities,
Conjurer's Closet and Teleportation Circle are end-step triggers, Settle Beyond Reality is a mode,
and Justiciar's Portal, Personify and Scrollshift print a third sentence after the blink. A
line-shaped reader can reach none of them.

Read as a clause it reaches all of them at once, because `composeEffects` runs on the clause chain of
a spell, a trigger and an ability alike. Three pieces:

1. **A clause reader** for `return target (creature|permanent) to the battlefield under (its
   owner's|your) control`, which is reachable **only** through the referent swap — no printed card
   says "return target creature to the battlefield", because a creature on the battlefield is already
   there. Every printing names a pronoun.
2. **`that card` as a referent pronoun**, swapping for the same two kinds as "it" and taking the same
   supply. A card the sentence before exiled is a card in exile rather than a permanent, and the
   printings use the two words interchangeably for the same move — Cloudshift and Acrobatic Maneuver
   say "that card" where Ephemerate and Felidar Guardian say "it". It costs two lines because
   `relocate` keeps the instance id across a zone change, so the object the earlier clause chose and
   the card now in exile are the same `c.targets[0]`.
3. **A composition rule**: a chain with a part that `returnsTheObject` is a **blink, not removal**.

### The third piece is the one that matters, and it is a bot fix

The two halves are read by two readers and neither can see the card. To the exile clause's reader,
"exile another target permanent you control" is removal — it is the same sentence Hidden Dragonslayer
prints — so it declares `removesACreature` and leaves the spec's aim hostile. Put the return after it
and every one of those is wrong: nothing is removed, and the reason to cast it is to blink.

`composeEffects` is the only layer holding both parts, so it rewrites the borrowed spec: `blinks` for
what the bot is being asked to price (`TargetSpec.blinks` is #209's whole subject — a token ceases to
exist, counters and Auras and marked damage all go), `friendly` **only when the printed phrase says
"you control"**, and `removesACreature` deleted. Without that last deletion the bot holds Flicker of
Fate as its answer to a threat and then never answers the threat.

The `friendly` condition is D542's discipline applied again, and this family needs it for a real
printing rather than a probe: **Flicker of Fate** says "exile target creature **or enchantment**" and
names no controller. Blinking an opponent's creature to strip the Aura off it is a line a player
takes, so an aim pointing at your own board would be a hint pointing the wrong way (D362). `blinks`
goes on both, because that one is a fact about the effect rather than about the aim.

### `blinkResolution` is deleted, because the general rule subsumes it

Once the clause path read the sentence, the sentence had **two** readers and the suite could not say
which one read Cloudshift. So that was measured rather than argued: the call site was disabled and
**every** compile row and the whole of `compiled-vs-written` stayed green — including the rows that
assert the compiled Cloudshift is character-for-character the hand-written card and carries `blinks`.

Two readers for one sentence is the shape this file keeps collapsing (D441): the one that is correct
and the one somebody will edit. The general rule reads strictly more, so the narrow one goes, and a
note stays in its place saying what it was and why the shape is now covered.

**And the duplicate was masking a test.** The break run's "the return always goes to the owner" break
came back **uncaught** on the first pass, because the probe asserting the your-control wording was a
one-line spell — which `blinkResolution` read, so the clause reader never ran and breaking it changed
nothing. Deleting the duplicate made the same test discriminating with no change to the test. That is
a second argument for the deletion that no amount of reading the code would have produced.

### Refused

The **delayed** return (Flickerwisp, Angel of Condemnation, Abuelo, Aetherling, Long Road Home — 8
cards) needs a delayed trigger (CR 603.7) and is a different card: it exiles a permanent its
controller does not own and gives it back a step later, which is removal for a turn. `tapped`,
`transformed` and `with a +1/+1 counter on it` are riders this does not read, each refusing the line
(D487) — an Aclazotz that came back un-transformed is the wrong card entirely. The **plural**
("return those cards", Displace) waits on the plural referent, which `referentEffect` cannot supply:
it hands the clause exactly one object. That is D538's deferral and it is now the biggest single row
left in this family.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,228 / 56,421 (41.2%) | **23,253 / 56,421 (41.2%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,875 | **11,891** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,620 | **7,638** |

18 newly fully read and **none lost**, checked by diffing the whole list rather than by trusting the
totals: Acrobatic Maneuver, Conjurer's Closet, Distinguished Conjurer, Ephemerate, Felidar Guardian,
Flicker of Fate, Flickering Hound, Justiciar's Portal, Momentary Blink, Nephalia Smuggler, Oji the
Exquisite Blade, Personify, Photon Lady of Light, Ruin Ghost, Scrollshift, Settle Beyond Reality,
Teleportation Circle, Wispweaver Angel.

`one-blocker.mjs` predicted 11 for the two rows aimed at; the extra 7 are cards the "that card"
pronoun opened in passing. **Break harness 9/9** on the second pass, 8/9 on the first — the miss and
its cause are above. Gate green.

### Two stale refusals retargeted rather than deleted

`compile.test.ts` asserted that the owner's-control wording stays unread and that the shape is
refused inside a longer resolution. Both were true of `blinkResolution` and are no longer true of the
compiler, so both rows now assert what is true and say in their own comment what they used to assert
and why it changed (D516: a stale refusal is how a suite starts asserting the past).

### D543's pod sweep

**40/40 pods finished** at SEED0=41601 on the clean commit (85d0e41), no engine throw and no stalled
table, 68.2 turns and 486 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 26.4 cards with a
hand-written script, 46.7 with at least one unread line, 61.9 playable only from printed data, 0.4
cardboard.

The sweep is doing two jobs here. One is the usual check that 18 new readings do not throw. The other
is the deletion: `blinkResolution` was on the spell-casting path of every game, and a sweep that
finished every table is the evidence that the general rule which replaced it reads the same sentence
the same way in play, not only in the compile table.

## D544 — The single-target pump, opened up, with the aim read off the numbers

**70 cards finished**, the biggest single-reader increment since D540, and it is mostly a refusal
being retired with the reason that was missing rather than a new mechanic.

### Three branches and a refusal become one rule

The reader was `+`/`+` in one branch, `-`/`-` in another, and the **mixed** sign refused. The
refusal's own words were the whole problem and also the whole answer:

> what cannot be read off the sentence is which creature it is for, because a card that gives +4/-4
> is removal pointed at them and a trick pointed at your own 1/1 depending on the rest of the card.

Right that the aim must be *read* rather than guessed. Wrong that the sentence is silent.
**Toughness is what kills a creature**, so a size that lowers it is a creature being killed and a
size that raises it is one being saved; when toughness does not move, power decides. One rule, four
quadrants, and it sorts all ten printed mixed sizes correctly — Auger Spree's +4/-4 and Spatial
Contortion's +3/-3 as removal, Alpha Kavu's -1/+1 as a creature of yours being saved.

It also *subsumes* the two branches it replaces: `+`/`+` raises toughness and `-`/`-` lowers it, so
the old friendly/hostile split falls out of the same arithmetic instead of being asserted twice. The
same conclusion D542 and D543 reached from the other direction — read the aim off the printed words,
never from the family — arrived at here by taking the refusal's reason seriously.

### And the subject opened up, which is where the 70 cards came from

The subject was a **fixed list of three phrases** (`target creature`, plus `you control`, `an
opponent controls`, `you don't control`) while `targetSpecFrom` had been parsing a far wider
vocabulary for several increments. It is an open phrase now, guarded by `pointsAtAPermanent` like
destroy and exile, with the quantifier prefix read like every other reader's. That is the same gap
D540 closed on the graveyard return, and it paid about as well: "target creature with flying",
"target creature or Vehicle you control", "another target creature you control", "up to one other
target creature you control".

`(spec.count ?? 1) === 1` rides along because the effect is `firstCardTarget` — D469's pair, a reader
that asks for two and pumps one is worse than the unread line it replaced. No printed plural reaches
it (the plural is "two target creatures **get**", and this reader demands "gets"), so that guard has
a probe row rather than a card.

**The grant refusal is kept, and scoped.** No printed `-`/`-` carries an `and gains` tail, so reading
one would be inventing the only card it could apply to (D259) — but a *mixed* size does print one,
Flowstone Strike's "+1/-1 and gains trample", so the refusal now applies to the sign pair it was
measured on instead of to everything that is not a pump. `helpsInCombat` is set only when the size
helps too: a penalty that grants haste is Flowstone Strike pointed across the table, and the flag
there would aim a removal spell at the bot's own board.

### "Another" costs nothing, and that is a fact about the engine

The old table refused `Another target creature gets -2/-2` with the reason *"another means not the
other target, and a script has one target list"*. The first half is right and the second does not
follow. `permanentFilter`'s `another` excludes the **source**, which for a spell is never on the
battlefield — but `checkTargets` keeps one `seen` set across **every** spec of a resolution and
refuses "the same target cannot be chosen twice". So the engine already forces Leeching Bite's two
creatures apart. The same finding D542 recorded for Pit Fight, now load-bearing.

What is still unread is the *line* Consume Strength prints, and for a different reason:
`composeEffects` refuses two targeting parts in one chain, because a resolution has one `targets`
list. The one-blocker instrument attributed that card's blocker to the clause, which the clause now
reads — the line still does not. Worth stating, because it means **a one-blocker row can name a
clause and be answered without the card moving.** The retargeted test asserts both halves: the clause
reads, the pair does not.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,253 / 56,421 (41.2%) | **23,347 / 56,421 (41.4%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,891 | **11,962** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,638 | **7,708** |

70 newly fully read and **none lost**, checked by diffing the whole list. `one-blocker.mjs` predicted
10 for the two rows aimed at; it was under by 60, for D540's reason exactly — the change went one
layer down into the subject phrase and lifted every family that shares it.

### The break run: 8 of 10, then 10 of 10, and the miss was the harness

The first pass came back **8/10**, with "the grant refusal is dropped" and "the aim is not read off
the words at all" uncaught. Neither was a hole in the tests. Every break harness since D530 has run
`vitest -t 'D5'` to keep the loop quick, and the describe this increment **retargeted** is named
`(D454)` — which that filter excludes. Two breaks read as uncaught for a reason that had nothing to
do with the code or the tests.

Re-run with no `-t` filter at all: **10/10**. The harness keeps it that way, with the reason written
into it. **A filter that scopes the suite can hide the very tests an increment changed**, and an
increment that retargets an old table is exactly when that happens — so the quick filter is wrong
precisely when the run matters most.

### Four stale refusals retargeted rather than deleted (D516)

The `(D454)` table asserted that the mixed sign, the mixed sign with a grant, the pumped-toughness
shrink and `another target creature` all stay unread. All four now read. Each row asserts what is
true, states the aim it must carry, and keeps the old reason above it so the change is legible rather
than silent. Two refusals stay and are unchanged: a grant on a true shrink, and a subtype phrase
(#341).

### D544's pod sweep

**40/40 pods finished** at SEED0=41701 on the clean commit (7f14b15), no engine throw and no stalled
table, 66.7 turns and 324 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 26.2 cards with a
hand-written script, 46.8 with at least one unread line, 61.8 playable only from printed data, 0.5
cardboard.

This is the sweep that most needed running of the last four. The other three added readers; this one
**replaced** the branch structure of a reader that fires on a large share of every deck's tricks, and
a sign error in it would have had the bot aiming its pumps at the wrong half of the table for 40
games without throwing anything. Finishing every table with the usual turn and move counts is the
evidence that the one rule plays like the three branches it replaced.

## D545 — The counter-exile rider, and the path nobody is asked on

**10 cards finished.** `noRegenerationRider`'s sibling, written beside it: the second clause this
compiler reads as a **modifier on another clause** rather than as an effect of its own.

> Counter target spell. **If that spell is countered this way, exile it instead of putting it into
> its owner's graveyard.**

Twenty legal cards print it across six different counter sentences — plain, four target filters, and
"unless its controller pays {N}" — so one flag on `EffectContext` covers what six readers would have
had to. And what it changes is not cosmetic: a buried spell can be recast from the graveyard,
reanimated or dredged back, and exiling it is the whole reason Dissipate costs one more than Cancel.

### Two differences from the regeneration rider, both deliberate

**The rider may stand anywhere in the chain.** Devious Cover-Up and Spelljack print it second of
three, and position cannot matter for a flag set around the whole composition.
`noRegenerationRider` anchors to the last clause because that is where all 134 of its printings put
it; this one does not need to, so it does not pretend to, and a compile row with a sentence after the
rider is what makes that a rule rather than an accident.

**The sibling test is on the printed word "counter".** Without it, "Draw a card. If that spell is
countered this way, exile it instead …" compiles as a draw with a sentence silently dropped — the
half-read line D487 is about. On the text rather than on the composed reading, for
`noRegenerationRider`'s reason: the counters this engine cannot read (a cost computed off the board,
a cost that is not mana) must refuse the whole line rather than have the rider read onto a counter
that is not there.

### The option on `counterSpell` is the right shape, and D542 is why that needs saying

D542 **deleted** two options from `dealDamage` for being exactly the wrong shape, so adding one here
needs its reason written down. The difference is where the fact lives: deathtouch is a characteristic
of the damage's *source*, so a caller passing it was a second place for an answer the game already
held. Whether a countered spell is exiled is a fact about the **countering card's printed text** and
about nothing else on the table — there is nothing in the game state to read it off.

### The path nobody is asked on, which a test found

The flag has to be read in **three** places, and the third is the one that matters most:

1. the plain counter reader, in `scripts.ts`;
2. `settlePayment`'s declining branch, for a controller who could pay and says no;
3. **`automation.ts`'s unaffordable path**, where nobody is asked at all because there is only one
   outcome.

The flag was carried on `pendingPayment` and read in (1) and (2) first, and the table test still
found a Spell Shrivel putting the spell in the graveyard — because a Spell Shrivel aimed at somebody
who has tapped out never reaches (2). That is the common case of the card, and it goes through (3).

Then the **break run found the mirror of the same gap in the tests**: with (3) covered, breaking (2)
changed nothing, because the only payment row exercised an opponent who could not pay. A second row
gives them four untapped Forests and answers `auto:pay { pay: false }`, so both branches are now
asserted. The methodological shape is worth naming: **a question with two answers needs two rows, and
a cost nobody can afford is a third case rather than one of the two.**

### The break run: 8 of 10, then 9 of 10, and the tenth is vacuous

Breaks 5 (the declining branch) and 10 (the pattern's anchor) came back uncaught. The first was a
real hole in the tests, closed above and re-verified **CAUGHT**.

The second is **vacuous, and the probe that settled it is worth more than the break**: loosening the
pattern to accept a tail after "graveyard" changes nothing, because `clausesOf` splits on ", then "
— so Transcendent Dragon's "…, then you may cast it without paying its mana cost" is a *separate
clause*, and what refuses that line is the free cast having no reader rather than the rider's
anchor. Proved rather than argued: the same shape with a readable tail ("…, then draw a card")
compiles, both halves, and now has a row of its own. The compile test's comment claimed the anchor
was doing that work and has been corrected.

### Refused

Thranduil's Decree's "If a **permanent** spell is countered this way" — a condition on the countered
spell's own type, which the flag has no way to express and which would silently exile an instant the
card leaves in the graveyard. Rod of Absorption's "exile it instead of putting it into a graveyard
**as it resolves**" — a replacement on a spell finishing, which a counter is not. Syncopate's `{X}`
cost (D489's standing refusal), Faerie Trickery's subtype target (#341), and No Escape's "target
creature or planeswalker spell", which is a target phrase the vocabulary does not build yet.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,347 / 56,421 (41.4%) | **23,357 / 56,421 (41.4%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,962 | **11,971** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,708 | **7,718** |

Exactly the ten the one-blocker instrument predicted, which is the first exact call since D538 and a
useful calibration point: the instrument is accurate when a reader adds a clause and badly under when
it changes a layer below (D540 by 72, D544 by 60).

### D545's pod sweep

**40/40 pods finished** at SEED0=41801 on the clean commit (86df65e), no engine throw and no stalled
table, 64.6 turns and 407 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 26.8 cards with a
hand-written script, 46.6 with at least one unread line, 61.9 playable only from printed data, 0.4
cardboard.

What this sweep covers that the tests cannot: `counterSpell` and `settlePayment` are on the path of
every counterspell and every ward in every game, and this increment changed the signature of one and
the state shape of the other. Forty tables with no throw is the evidence that the three places the
flag is now read still agree with the thirty-odd callers that do not pass it.

## D546 — Two clauses the engine already had the primitive for

**35 cards finished**, and a defect caught by the break list before it shipped.

Two readers, together because that is what they have in common: the engine could already do both,
and only the sentence was missing. D528's shape.

### The bounce, one zone further back

"Put target creature on top of its owner's library" — Excommunicate's sentence, **23 legal
printings** across seven target phrases (creature, you control, nonland permanent, attacking or
blocking creature, land, permanent, and Jeskai Charm's mode). The bounce reader's mirror in every
respect: an open phrase, `pointsAtAPermanent` as the guard, `foldCardTargets` so a quantifier that
asks for two moves two.

`putOnTopOfLibrary` is its own function rather than an option on `bounceToHand`, because the zone is
the whole difference between the two cards. A Man-o'-War's bounce costs its target's controller a
turn of mana; an Excommunicate costs them **their next draw** as well, and leaves the creature where
a mill can take it away. The table test asserts `ids(state, seat, 'library')[0]` rather than only the
zone, which is the position read the way the player feels it.

### The bite pointed at itself

"Target creature deals damage to itself equal to its power" — Inner Struggle, Kiku, Cut Propulsion:
**7 printings**, the cheapest member of D542's family. Its own pattern rather than a widening of the
bite's, because the bite has two target phrases and this has one: a reader that made the second
optional would accept "target creature deals damage equal to its power to" with nothing after it.

**The sweeper half is refused**, and it is the bigger half by printings — Solar Blaze and The Akroan
War's third chapter say "**Each** creature deals damage to itself equal to its power", which is a
destination with no target and belongs with the sweep readers. Reading it through a target phrase
would ask for a choice the card does not offer.

### The defect the break list found before it shipped

Writing the break "the lifelink goes to the caster" is what exposed it: the reader passed
`controller: c.controller` to `dealDamage`, and `dealDamage` credits lifelink to `opts.controller`
(CR 702.15b, "that source's controller"). The source of a self-bite is the **target** — so an
opponent's Healer's Hawk told to bite itself would have paid *the player who cast Inner Struggle*.
On every printing, because nothing in this sentence filters the target to your own side.

`fight` has read the seat off the instance since it was written — its second half passes
`theirsInst.zoneSeat` — so the fix is that precedent applied rather than a new rule. D542's bite
passes `c.controller` and is correct only because its first target is filtered to "you control"; a
note now says so beside it.

A 1/1 with lifelink biting itself is worth exactly 1 life to its own controller, so the row asserts
both seats: theirs up by one, the caster's unchanged.

### The break run: 9 of 10, then 10 of 10

The miss was the `kind === 'creature'` guard, which had no row — and the failure it allows is the
hardest kind to see: `firstCardTarget` returns nothing for a player target, so the line would
**read** and the effect would silently do nothing, a card that appears to work. Two probe rows (a
player and a land) close it; `pointsAtAPermanent` is not enough here, because a land passes that and
has no power to deal.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,357 / 56,421 (41.4%) | **23,403 / 56,421 (41.5%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,971 | **12,003** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,718 | **7,753** |

**Past twelve thousand cards.** The queue predicted 11 for the two rows (6 + 5) and the outturn is
35 — under by 24, for D540's and D544's reason yet again: the library reader took an *open* phrase
where the queue had measured one. Three of the last four increments have beaten the instrument by
more than twice, and all three opened a phrase rather than adding a clause. That is now a reliable
rule for reading the queue: **a row whose fix is a wider phrase is worth several times its printed
count; a row whose fix is a new clause is worth about what it says.**

### D546's pod sweep

**40/40 pods finished** at SEED0=41901 on the clean commit (aa163fa), no engine throw and no stalled
table, 57.9 turns and 334 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 26.1 cards with a
hand-written script, 47.0 with at least one unread line, 61.9 playable only from printed data, 0.5
cardboard.

**Five increments, five clean sweeps, and the running total for the stretch:** 23,228 → 23,403
printed legal lines read (41.2% → 41.5%), 11,875 → 12,003 cards with a compiled script, 7,620 →
7,753 with every printed line read. 3,321 → 3,380 engine tests, green at every push.

## D547 — The Equipment that arrives already attached

**46 printings that were worse than unread**, and the increment the queue could not have found.

`Living weapon`, `For Mirrodin!` and `Job select` are one mechanic under three names: when the
Equipment enters, its controller creates a creature token and the Equipment attaches itself to it.
Beside them, a fourth shape with the same job: "When ~ enters, attach it to target creature you
control" — 27 printings that put it on a creature you already have.

### Why the instrument was never going to surface this

`living weapon` and `for mirrodin!` are both in `KEYWORD_ABILITY_NAMES`, the list of keyword names
the compiler **recognises as declarations**. So their line did not count as unread — and nothing
implemented it. The Equipment arrived on an empty battlefield with no creature to hold it, the
mechanic did nothing, and no badge told the player anything was missing.

`one-blocker.mjs` counts lines nothing can read. These read. The row it does show, "attach ~ to it"
at 8 cards, is the *reminder text* of the keyword, which is stripped before the compiler sees it.
**A mechanic that is recognised and unimplemented is invisible to the whole measuring apparatus**,
and the only way to find one is to read a family rather than a queue. That is now a standing
caution: the coverage figure counts lines, and a line can be read and still do nothing.

`job select` — the same mechanic under a third name — was missing from that list entirely, so it at
least had an unread line to show for itself.

### Why it lives in `attachmentScriptFor` and not in `keywordScriptFor`

Attaching an Equipment means **applying its bonus**, and the bonus is on a different printed line.
`keywordScriptFor(line, name)` is handed one line and a card name, so a reader there could have
created the token, attached the Equipment and given the creature nothing — the strictly-worse card
D362 rules out. `attachmentScriptFor` is the one function that has the whole card, so the bonus was
hoisted out of `equipFragment`'s argument list and both the equip ability and the arrival trigger now
read it.

The token's body comes from the **rule**, not from any card, which is what makes writing the three
down a reading rather than an invention (D259 is about what a card says; a keyword is not a card).
They are handed to `tokenFrom` as the rule's own sentence — "create a 0/0 black Phyrexian Germ
creature token" — rather than built as a `CardDef`, so the one token parser stays the only one.

### The 0/0 is the whole test

A Living weapon's Germ is a **0/0**. It survives only because the Equipment's +1/+1 is applied as it
attaches; without the bonus, state-based actions bin it immediately (CR 704.5a) and the card does
nothing at all while reading as fully compiled. So the table row asserts the Germ is a 1/1 and that
the Husk is attached to it, and the break that passes `{}` as the bonus is caught by exactly that.

### Two mistakes worth recording

**`self` is a DOM global.** A draft wrote `` `^When ${self} …` `` inside `attachmentScriptFor`,
copying the name from `exileUntilLeavesShapeFor` where it is a local. It typechecked cleanly — `self`
exists in this project's lib — and threw `self is not defined` on the first card measured. The name
is `selfName` now, with the reason beside it.

**A test that looked like it covered a choice.** The targeted row cast the Equipment with one
creature on the board and guarded the `auto:choose` behind `s.pendingTargets`, a field that does not
exist; `tsc -p tsconfig.test.json` caught it in the gate's typecheck. With one legal target the engine
chooses for you, so the row would have passed without ever proving the trigger asks. It has two
creatures now and asserts `pendingChoice.seat` before answering.

### The break run: 7 of 8, and the eighth is vacuous — established in two steps

Deleting `job select` from the vocabulary came back uncaught, so a row was written to catch it: an
Equipment printing the keyword with no `Equip {N}` line, which `attachmentScriptFor` turns down, so
the line should fall through to the per-line path where the list decides. **That row failed.** Not
because the entry is wrong but because such a card does not compile at all — with the attachment
reading refused nothing carries the rest of the text, so D487 makes every line unread and the
keyword's status is invisible.

The entry stays, as rules vocabulary that invents nothing, and the break is recorded as vacuous with
the probe that proved it. Better than a test that passes for the wrong reason.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,403 / 56,421 (41.5%) | **23,464 / 56,421 (41.6%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 12,003 | 12,003 |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,753 | **7,783** |

**The script count does not move at all, and that is the point.** These Equipment already had a
script — the equip ability — so by every number this compiler reports, two of the three keywords
were already "done". What changed is that 46 cards now do what they print. The +30 fully-read and
+61 lines are the Job select printings, the only ones whose line was honest about being unread.

### D547's pod sweep

**40/40 pods finished** at SEED0=42001 on the clean commit (5471f5f), no engine throw and no stalled
table, 59.2 turns and 312 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 26.1 cards with a
hand-written script, 46.6 with at least one unread line, 61.8 playable only from printed data, 0.5
cardboard.

This sweep is checking a path nothing else does: an ETB trigger that **creates a permanent and then
attaches another permanent to it**, on cards the bot casts unprompted out of 160 random decks. Forty
clean tables is the evidence that a 0/0 arriving and being saved by its own Equipment does not trip
the state-based actions, the attachment rules (CR 704.5m) or the bot's search.

### The stretch, in one table

| | start | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,228 / 56,421 (41.2%) | **23,464 / 56,421 (41.6%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 11,875 | **12,003** |

Six increments (D542–D547), six clean pod sweeps, gate green at every push. And one finding that is

## D548 — Audit the keyword list, then read the Evoke line as a whole-card shape

### The audit D547 asked for

D547 found 46 printings whose keyword line **read and did nothing**: `Living weapon` and
`For Mirrodin!` were in `KEYWORD_ABILITY_NAMES`, so `compile.ts` tagged their line
`unimplemented-keyword` rather than `no-reader` — and `one-blocker.mjs` and `one-away.mjs` both
filter to `no-reader`. The whole queue instrument is blind to that family by construction, so the
only way to see it was to ask a different question.

`scratchpad/kwaudit.mjs` asks it: for every legal card, group the unread lines whose `why` is
`unimplemented-keyword`, and count both **printings** and **cards finished** (a card whose only
unread line is that keyword).

| | |
| --- | --- |
| legal cards scanned, by name | 31,654 |
| with an unimplemented keyword line | 2,033 |
| **whose every unread line is one** | **578** |

578 cards are one keyword reader away from a finished script, and none of them was visible to the
queue. The head of the ranking, by cards finished:

| finishes | printings | keyword |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 18 | 30 | evoke |
| 14 | 25 | backup |
| 14 | 23 | improvise |
| 13 | 32 | toxic |
| 13 | 21 | bloodthirst |
| 12 | 42 | disguise |
| 12 | 27 | flanking |
| 12 | 22 | splice onto arcane |
| 12 | 20 | renown |
| 12 | 16 | fabricate |

Two large families are large in printings and **zero** in cards finished, and both are already
explained rather than newly discovered. `kicker` (202) is documented in `keywordScriptFor` as
deliberately unread, because its payoff is printed on another line. `enchant <filter>` (42 for
"enchant player", 22 for "enchant artifact or creature", and a long tail) is a filter-vocabulary
gap on Auras that have other unread lines anyway — a different job from reading a keyword.

### What shipped: evoke, the head row

The cheapest row on the list, because **the engine already had both halves**. `CardScript.evoke` is
read by `collectLegalActions` and `completeResolution` for any script that sets it, and
`evokeSacrifice()` has been written out since #172 for the hand-written Mulldrifter. Thirty cards
carried the declaration as a line nothing implemented.

**The reading is in `wholeCardShapeFor`, not in `keywordScriptFor`, and the reason is order.**
Three facts compose into a bug:

1. Evoke prints **last** on all 30 corpus cards — it is a cost line, and cost lines print at the
   bottom.
2. `compile.ts`'s `merge` **appends** to `triggers`, because a permanent with two printed triggered
   abilities is ordinary and both are real.
3. The engine puts a permanent's triggers on the stack in list order, so the **first listed is at
   the bottom and resolves last** (CR 603.3b).

Read from the per-line loop, the sacrifice would therefore be appended last, go on the stack above
the card's own ETB ability, and resolve **first** — a Mulldrifter that dies before it draws. Nothing
would throw and no line would be reported unread, which makes it the shape of mistake this module is
least able to notice. A whole-card shape runs ahead of the loop, so the sacrifice is listed first.

`wholeCardShapeFor` now holds two different kinds of reader, and its docblock says so: three are
there because **no single line is a unit** (an Aura's enchant line, an exile-until-leaves, soulbond),
and this one because **its one line is a unit but its trigger has to be first**. `evokeShapeFor` is
deliberately last in the chain — a card that somehow matched an earlier shape keeps the reading it
had and its evoke line falls through to be reported, which is the status quo rather than a
regression.

Six printings stay unread: the five Elemental Incarnations ("Evoke—Exile a green card from your
hand.") and Infestation ("Evoke—{1}{B}{B}, Pay 3 life."). `CardScript.evoke.cost` is a mana cost, so
reading either would be inventing a cost the engine cannot pay (D362). Both end in a full stop, so
`isKeywordDeclaration` already refuses them — which is why the audit's row reads 30 and not 36.

### Measured

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,464 / 56,421 (41.6%) | **23,494 / 56,421 (41.6%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 12,003 | **12,014** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,783 | **7,801** |

+18 fully read, exactly what the audit predicted, and +30 lines — one per printing. The audit is
therefore also calibrated: for a keyword row the "cards finished" column is not an estimate.

### The break run, and two entries it sent back

Eleven breaks, each verified to apply against a SHA-256 and to revert to the original bytes, the
whole engine suite run with **no `-t` filter** (D544's rule). **9 caught.** The two that came back
uncaught were adjudicated rather than patched, and they are different cases:

- **The `^` anchor comes off** — uncaught, and probing says why: **zero** printed lines in the legal
  corpus are read by the un-anchored pattern and refused by the anchored one. No real card
  discriminates. But a synthetic line does, and the anchor carries the claim that makes the reader
  safe at all — the line *is* the declaration, not a line that mentions the keyword. A resolution
  sentence ending in a mana cost would otherwise hand the card a free alternative casting, which is
  strictly better than printed. So it gets a row, labelled in the test as a guard against a shape
  the pool does not print rather than a regression test for one it does.
- **`evokeShapeFor` tried first instead of last** — uncaught and **genuinely vacuous**. Of the 30
  legal cards printing a mana evoke cost, **none** also prints an `Enchant` line, an
  exile-until-it-leaves or `Soulbond`, so no card can tell the two orders apart. Recorded as vacuous
  with that count, and `wholeCardShapeFor`'s docblock was rewritten: the ordering claim it used to
  make was a behavioural guarantee it cannot support, so it now says the order is arbitrary against
  the pool as it stands and the position is defensive.

Break 11 is worth naming because it is the one that defends the whole reason this reader is a
whole-card shape: making `merge` **prepend** instead of append reverses every card's trigger order,
and the suite catches it. So the ordering argument in `evokeShapeFor`'s docblock is not decoration —
there is a test that fails when the order flips.

Re-run after adding the anchor row: **10 of 11 caught**, the eleventh recorded vacuous with the
count that proves it. Engine suite 3,402.

### D548's pod sweep

**40/40 pods finished** at SEED0=42101 on the clean commit (6c14b93), no engine throw and no stalled
table, 59.7 turns and 263 moves a game. Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 26.0 cards with a
hand-written script, 47.0 with at least one unread line, 61.8 playable only from printed data, 0.4
cardboard.

What this sweep exercises that nothing else does: an **alternative casting the bot chooses for
itself**, on a creature that then sacrifices itself as it arrives, out of 160 random decks. The
sacrifice is an ETB trigger conditioned on a counter written during resolution, resolving after the
card's own ETB ability — so forty clean tables is the evidence that the counter is written before the
triggers are collected and that a permanent dying to its own trigger does not trip the state-based
actions or the bot's search.

---

## D549 — Renown N, and the audit's second exact prediction

The keyword audit's head row after evoke: **12 legal cards finished, 20 printings** (15 print
`Renown 1`, four `Renown 2`, one `Renown 6`).

Like evoke it needed **no new mechanism**. `TOPAN_FREEBLADE` already carried the whole ability
inline, with the `RENOWNED` counter answering "if it isn't renowned"; that trigger is now
`renownTrigger(count)` and the pool card calls it with 1, so the hand-written card and the compiled
reading are the same code and cannot drift. A compile test asserts they produce the same trigger —
the rule D364 asks of every keyword in this table.

Unlike evoke it reads in `keywordScriptFor` rather than `wholeCardShapeFor`, and the difference is
exactly the one D548's docblock drew: evoke's trigger has to be the card's *first*, so it needed the
stage that runs ahead of the per-line loop. Renown's one line is the whole ability and nothing on the
card orders against it, so the ordinary table is the right place.

### Measured, and the instrument is now calibrated

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,494 / 56,421 (41.6%) | **23,514 / 56,421 (41.7%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 12,014 | **12,031** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,801 | **7,813** |

+12 fully read against a predicted 12, and +20 lines — one per printing. **That is the second exact
hit** after evoke's +18 for 18. For a keyword row the audit's "cards finished" column is a count,
not an estimate, which is a stronger property than the one-blocker instrument has ever had: D532's
head row read 39 and shipped 8. The difference is that a keyword line is a whole line, so finishing
it cannot be partly blocked by a sibling clause.

### Two test defects, both found by the tests failing rather than by reading

- **`drain` settles the stack but does not advance a step.** The first table draft used it after
  declaring attackers, so the attack sat in `declare-attackers` for eighty iterations and renown
  looked broken when nothing had attacked yet. Priority has to be passed through to the postcombat
  main, which is how the pool's own combat tests deal damage. It is a named helper now with that
  reason on it, because the failure mode reads as "the mechanic is broken" rather than "the harness
  is wrong".
- **The blocked row was passing vacuously.** The table helper gave seat 1 no battlefield, so the row
  that proves renown does *not* fire on blocked damage returned early every time. It now puts a
  Grizzly Bears opposite and asserts the Bears died, so the row would read differently if the attack
  had never been blocked.

### The break run

Eight breaks, **7 caught**. The six that matter all are: ignoring the count (every renown becomes
`Renown 1`, which would quietly shrink nineteen cards), dropping the intervening-if so it fires every
swing, never writing the `RENOWNED` marker, never writing the `+1/+1` counters, watching `etb`
instead of `combat-damage`, and Topan Freeblade ceasing to share the factory — that last one is the
drift guard, and it fails as it should.

The eighth, the end anchor, came back uncaught and was adjudicated the way D548's start anchor was:
**zero** printed lines in the legal corpus are read by the un-anchored pattern and refused by the
anchored one, so no real card discriminates. It still gets a guard row, on a sharper argument than
D548's — reading `Renown 1 as long as you control a Knight` as a plain `Renown 1` would take the
trigger and **silently drop the rest of the line**, which is the one thing `readResolution` refuses
by design (D487: a line is read whole or not at all).

## D550 — A free cast was refused on a cost it never pays

**Found by D549's own pod sweep**, which came back 39/40 rather than clean: seed 42201 threw
`Dismember has a mana cost the engine cannot pay yet` and the whole table went down with it.

### The mechanism

`castSpell` parsed the **printed** cost and refused on an unreadable symbol, 300 lines before the
chain that decides which cost this casting actually pays. Dismember is `{1}{B/P}{B/P}` and Phyrexian
mana is a symbol `parseManaCost` does not read yet — so a **cascade** that landed on it threw, even
though a cascade pays nothing at all: `toPay` is overwritten from `pendingOfferedCast.cost` further
down, and for cascade that is absent.

The file had already written down the right rule, for X, forty lines below the bug:

> **X, checked against the cost being paid** (CR 601.2b, CR 107.3b, D481). It sits here rather than
> beside the modes because this is the first line that knows which cost this casting pays.

D481 fixed that question and left this one. Same disagreement between the offer and the payment,
same symptom — one pod in two hundred for D481's Starnheim Unleashed, one in forty here.

### The fix, and what it deliberately does not do

The refusal now reads the cost **being paid**: the offer's cost for an offered cast, the printed one
otherwise. It is narrowed rather than deleted, because for a paid cast it is a real safety net — a
client sending one gets a refusal instead of a half-charged spell, and `legalActions` already
declines to offer those (it checks `unsupported` on the printed cost and on every alternative).

It is **not** widened to the whole chain. A flashback or an escape may replace the printed cost with
one the engine can pay, so the fully correct reading asks this question where `payingCost` is
assembled — a bigger change than the crash needs, and `legalActions` covers those paths. Left as a
note in the code rather than done half-way.

Phyrexian mana itself is still unread. That is the honest state: a card whose cost cannot be
assembled cannot be cast for that cost, and now says so instead of killing the table.

### Verification

A regression test drives the whole chain through a **real cascade** rather than by poking
`pendingOfferedCast`, because the defect lived in the handover between the offer and the payment and
a test that sets the offer by hand would skip exactly that gap: Bloodbraid Elf's hand-written cascade
lands on a compiled Dismember, the offer comes back with no cost at all, the free cast resolves, and
−5/−5 kills the 3/2 it pointed at. **Reverting the fix makes that test fail with the pod's own error
message**, which is the check that it discriminates.

Seed 42201 now finishes: 49 turns, 221 moves.

`corpus-decks.mjs` also gained `STACK=1`, which prints the stack of a throw. Without it the message
alone said only which card died, not which of the three cast paths was on the stack — and the fix
depended entirely on knowing it was the offered one.

### D549 + D550's pod sweep

The honest sequence, because it is the point: D549's sweep at SEED0=42101 came back **39/40**, and
the one throw was D550's defect. After the fix, seed 42201 finishes on its own, and a **fresh** sweep
at SEED0=42301 is **40/40** — no engine throw and no stalled table, 56.4 turns and 250 moves a game.
Per 100-card deck across 160 decks: 26.4 cards with a hand-written script, 46.6 with at least one
unread line, 62.0 playable only from printed data, 0.4 cardboard.

A fresh seed set rather than re-running 42101: re-running the set that found the bug would only prove
the bug is gone, which the named-seed replay already proves. Forty new tables ask whether anything
else is.

**And the sweep earned its place in the loop.** Six increments ran clean before this one; the seventh
caught a defect that had been in the engine since cascade shipped and that the whole 3,414-test suite
never touched, because no test in it cascades into a card with an unreadable cost. The gate proves
the engine does what its tests say; the sweep is what asks whether anything in 160 random real decks
disagrees.

---

## D551 — The relational blocker clause, and #345 corrected while closing it

`characteristics.ts` had recorded for two increments why intimidate and skulk were absent:

> Intimidate (21 lines) and skulk (14) are deliberately absent. Each needs a clause whose answer
> depends on both creatures — "creatures that share a color with it", "creatures with greater
> power" — and `clauseMatches` sees one creature on purpose. They are #345's problem.

So this is the note's own answer. `BlockerClause` gains two **relational** kinds and `clauseMatches`
takes the facing creature:

- `shares-a-colour` — intimidate (CR 702.13a). Fear's shape with the fixed colour replaced by a
  comparison, which is exactly why it had to wait.
- `power-vs` — skulk (CR 702.118a), in both directions, because both occur: the three printed cards
  state it as a **ban** on greater power, and the keyword table as an **allow list** of power at
  most this creature's. The same rule read from either end, and `KeywordBlockRule` has no ban field.

### `other` is required, not optional, and that is the safety argument

An optional parameter would have compiled at all six `canBlock` sites and silently answered a
relational clause against nothing. Worse than silent: these clauses live in **allow** lists, so "no
clause matched" refuses the block — a forgotten argument would make a skulk creature *unblockable*
rather than failing loudly. Required, the compiler named all six, which is how they were found.

### Measured — and the first row to beat its audit figure

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,514 / 56,421 (41.7%) | **23,560 / 56,421 (41.8%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 12,031 | **12,035** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,813 | **7,837** |

The audit predicted 16 (intimidate 10 + skulk 6) and it delivered **24**. Evoke and renown each
landed exactly on their figure; this one beat it, and the reason is the difference between the two
kinds of change — a keyword row adds one reader, while this added two clauses to a **shared
vocabulary** that the printed blocker-filter parser also draws on. So the calibration note needs
one more line: the audit's column is exact for a keyword, and a **floor** for a change to the
vocabulary underneath one.

### #345, closed and corrected

That row was recorded as "nine relative-power printings". Measuring the corpus says **three** cards
print "creatures with greater power" (plus one "…this combat", whose duration this does not read).
The forty-odd power printings the row was sized from — "creatures with power 2 or less" (33),
"power 3 or greater" (9) — are **absolute** comparisons, which the plain `power` clause has read
since D498. So the value here was always the two keywords and never the printed cards, and the file
says so now rather than carrying the inflated figure forward.

Two printed phrases in that family remain, one card each: "creatures with toughness 3 or greater"
(needs a toughness clause beside `power`) and "monocolored creatures".

### Two standing checks refused this before it passed, and both were right

- **`scripts/guards.js`** demanded a player cheat-sheet row for skulk. That guard exists because a
  mechanic the engine enforces and the player doc never mentions is a rule somebody meets at the
  table with no explanation. Both keywords now have one, including the colourless-intimidate case.
- **The "card behind every mechanic" test** flagged intimidate and skulk as pool orphans. No
  hand-written deck prints either, and adding one to a measured deck to satisfy a test is what D442
  forbids. They joined the documented `compilerOnly` set beside fear, shadow and horsemanship — and
  that set's *second* assertion requires they stay orphans, so the exemption cannot outlive its
  reason.

### Two of my own test rows were wrong, and the suite said so (a third is below)

- The intimidate colour-match row first used **Nether Traitor**, which carries shadow — so the block
  was refused for a second reason and the row proved nothing about intimidate. A card that isolates
  a rule has to carry no other restriction; it uses a vanilla black creature now.
- The skulk rows both asserted a **refusal**, which would pass against a clause that refuses
  everything. Both verdicts are asserted now: a 1/1 may block the 1/1 skulker and a 3/3 may not.

### The break harness found a third bad row, and it is the most interesting of the three

10 of 10 breaks caught — but only after a correction, because the first run came back **9/10** and
the survivor was break 1: `shares-a-colour` written with `every` instead of `some`.

Working out why nothing caught it is the whole lesson. Under `every`, a creature with an **empty**
`colors` array is vacuously true, so a colourless creature "shares a colour" with anything. The case
that discriminates the two readings is therefore a **colourless blocker**, not a colourless
attacker: asked of the attacker, a white blocker against a colourless intimidator fails both
readings (`['W'].some(c => [].includes(c))` and `['W'].every(...)` are both false), so that row
cannot tell them apart no matter how it is written.

The block had a row named *"intimidate on a colourless creature lets only artifact creatures
block"*, and it was worthless twice over. It asked the colourless question of the attacker, which
cannot discriminate; and it borrowed **Cybermat** as that attacker, which carries **skulk**, so the
block it asserted was refused for the power comparison and not for anything about colour. A test
that passes for a reason unrelated to its own name is worse than a missing test, because it reads
like coverage.

It is replaced by a fourth row in the intimidate table: **Kobolds of Kher Keep** (`{0}`, Kobold,
colourless, 0/1, no printed text) may not block the black intimidator. No card in the pool or the
corpus prints intimidate on a colourless creature and D259 forbids inventing one, so the
empty-colour case is asked from the side where it has teeth. Break 1 is caught, and the gate is
green at **3,424** engine tests.

Three defective rows in one increment, all three found by the harness rather than by the suite
passing, is the strongest argument yet for running it on every mechanic: a suite only ever reports
that its own assertions held.

## D552 — The Improvise keyword line, and convoke's planner made general

The keyword audit's head row that the engine already had the mechanism for. **23 legal printings,
14 of them finished by reading it**, and the reading is one line:

```ts
if (word === 'improvise') return { improvise: true };
```

Improvise (CR 702.126a) is "each artifact you control can be tapped to pay {1}". Convoke
(CR 702.51) is "each creature you tap pays one generic mana or one mana of that creature's colour".
Those are the same mechanic with two parameters: **what may be tapped**, and **which pips it may
pay**. So `convokePlan` became `tapToPayPlan(state, seat, cost, sources, rule)` with
`rule: 'convoke' | 'improvise'`, and the two differences are two expressions:

```ts
if (!(rule === 'convoke' ? ch.isCreature : hasType(ch.typeLine, 'artifact'))) continue;
available.push({ id, colors: rule === 'convoke' ? ch.colors as readonly ManaType[] : [] });
```

Everything else — mana first, the shortfall only, coloured pips before generic, a tapped permanent
leaving the mana sources, summoning sickness not applying — is shared, because all of it is the
same for both keywords. Writing improvise its own planner would have been that whole argument
copied with one line changed, and the copy is exactly where the two would have drifted.

### The second parameter is where the rules live

An artifact pays **generic and only generic**. There is no colour clause in the keyword, so the
clean way to say it is to hand the planner an empty colour list for an improvising artifact rather
than to add a branch further down: the assignment loop then cannot offer an artifact for a coloured
pip because it never sees a colour to offer. A board of four artifacts against `{3}{R}` is three
pips of four, and that is the test that distinguishes this reading from convoke's.

An **artifact creature** answers to both rules and needs no special case: under `'improvise'` it is
an artifact paying one generic pip, under `'convoke'` it is a creature that may pay a coloured one.
No card prints both keywords, so the two readings never meet on one cast.

### Measured — the third exact keyword prediction in a row

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| printed legal lines read | 23,560 / 56,421 (41.8%) | **23,583 / 56,421 (41.8%)** |
| cards with a compiled script | 12,035 | **12,050** |
| cards with every printed line read | 7,837 | **7,851** |

The audit predicted **14 finishes and 23 printings**; it delivered 14 and 23. Evoke (D548) and
renown (D549) also landed exactly on their figures, and D551 beat its figure because it widened a
shared clause vocabulary rather than adding a keyword. So the calibration note now has three
confirmations of the same rule: **the audit's column is exact for a keyword row** and a floor for a
change to the vocabulary underneath one. That is a property `one-blocker.mjs` has never had, and
the reason is structural — a keyword line is a whole printed line, so reading it either finishes
the card or does not, with nothing left to estimate.

### No pool card, and the two checks that said so

`script improvise` is the fourth entry in `compilerOnly` added on evidence rather than on a card:
23 printings, 14 finished, none in the pool's thirteen measured decks, and the flag cannot be put
on a hand-written card without changing what a measured deck costs to cast (D442). The runtime
evidence is six tests driving printed Foundry Assembler and Sweatworks Brawler through the engine's
own plays. The mechanic-coverage test refused the push until that entry was written with its
evidence, which is the third increment running where a standing check caught the thing I would
otherwise have left undocumented.

### A documentation defect found on the way
