So this is D568 working, not D568 breaking something. The loop is what a correct cleanup step does
with a card that was already wrong; the sweep is what noticed.

**The fix.** The `to-graveyard` event takes `from: 'battlefield'`, answered from the list of
permanents that died in the same pass — the engine already knows exactly which arrivals in a
graveyard came from play. Both rows set it; so do the hand-written Rancor and Ichor Wellspring,
and Rancor's text is the Oracle's.

    legal cards whose trigger this narrows:   55  (37 of them fully read)
    of those, cards that return themselves:   20  (Brilliant Halo, Aspect of Mongoose, Fortitude,
                                                   Despondency, Fallen Ideal, Launch, …)

No count moves — the same lines are read, correctly. Six rows, each card both ways: discarded
from a hand it stays in the graveyard, and leaving the battlefield it does what it says; Ichor
Wellspring draws for the second and not the first; and the pod's own position — an Undying Rage
discarded to hand size — ends the turn. With the filter deleted, four of the six fail. Seed 43821
replayed on the fix: finishes, 212 turns. Engine suite: 3,805.

**The lesson is the same one as D566's Thieving Magpie, a second time in a day.** A hand-written
pool card whose text was typed from memory is not ground truth, and a check that compares two
readings of the same wrong text passes. The compiled-against-written check cannot see this class
of error; only the corpus text can. Worth an instrument: every pool card's text against its corpus
row. Queued as its own task.

## D570 — Sacrifice as an event, and the function that did not exist

"Whenever you sacrifice a permanent" was the largest family left in the event queue, and it could
not be an event because **the engine had no sacrifice**. A sacrifice was a `relocate` to a
graveyard, written out wherever one was needed: the cost of a spell, the cost of an ability, an
ability that sacrifices its own source, a finished Saga, a Treasure spent for mana — five places
in the engine — and behind `moveToGraveyard` at every script that says the word. Afterwards it was
a card in a graveyard, indistinguishable from one a Doom Blade put there.

**One function now.** `sacrifice(state, ids)` in `effects.ts`: for each permanent, record who
controlled it as it left (you can only sacrifice what you control, so that seat did it), then move
it. The five engine sites call it. `moveToGraveyard` hands it any card that is on the battlefield,
because every use of that function on a permanent has always been a sacrifice — an edict's chosen
creature, echo declined, vanishing run out — the other two ways a permanent reaches a graveyard
having functions of their own (`destroy`, and the state-based actions). One rule there instead of
twenty-two call sites each remembering.

**The event.** `sacrifices`, raised once per permanent, before the death it may also be:

| slot | printed | field |
| --- | --- | --- |
| who did it | you / a player / an opponent | `by` |
| the watcher itself? | "another" | `who: 'another'`; the default includes it |
| what | a permanent / creature / artifact / token | `what` |
| | a Clue / Treasure / Food / Blood / … | `ofSubtypes`, from a closed list |

The default **includes the watcher's own sacrifice**: a Korvold fed to an altar still draws its
card, because a zone-change trigger looks back (CR 603.10a). "Another" is the printed word that
rules it out, and Mazirek's row is the one that shows the difference.

Every filter is asked of what the permanent **was**, from the snapshot `relocate` keeps: a
sacrificed token has ceased to exist and a card in a graveyard has no types an effect gave it.

One parsed row reads all of it, with the three slots as named groups, and refuses a thing it does
not know: "a land", "a creature token", "a nontoken creature", "a Goblin", "one or more Foods".

    printed legal lines read:            24,229 → 24,284 of 56,421 (43.0%)
    cards with a compiled script:        12,452 → 12,486
    cards with every printed line read:   8,258 → 8,283

55 triggers on 55 cards, 25 of them now fully read: Korvold, Mayhem Devil, Tireless Tracker,
Mazirek, Smothering Abomination, Body Dropper, Captain Lannery Storm, the five Ordeals' last line.

Tests: 13 runtime rows on eight printed cards, with **the pool's own cards doing the
sacrificing** — Vampire Aristocrat's cost, Fleshbag Marauder's edict, a Clue cracked, a Treasure
tapped for mana — because the claim being tested is that those different paths now say the same
thing. Each filter both ways. With the record disabled, 11 of the 13 fail and the two that pass
are the two that assert nothing happened. 20 compile rows. Engine suite: 3,838.

One thing this does not do: a permanent you **stole** and then sacrificed. The act is recorded
for you, correctly; but a trigger on the sacrificed card itself is matched and controlled from
where the card ended up, which is its owner's graveyard. The same is true of every `dies` trigger
and is not new here.

## D571 — Every built-in card, checked against its Oracle row for the first time

**The built-in pool was typed in from memory, and a great deal of it was wrong.** 336 cards, built
up a few at a time over many sessions, and until now nothing had ever compared what was typed with
what the card says. Two findings in one day pointed at it — Thieving Magpie's text in D566, Rancor's
in D569 — so this is the comparison, done for every card and every printed fact.

What it found, against the corpus row for each card:

| fact | wrong |
| --- | --- |
| mana cost | 59 |
| mana value | 42 |
| type line | 35 |
| toughness | 21 |
| power | 15 |
| colours | 2 |
| rules text, in substance | about 100 |

**174 wrong facts on 107 cards**, before the rules text. Some of what that means at a table:
Murderous Redcap was a 1/1, so the body persist returns died on arrival and the deck built around
it was measured with half its best card missing. Dirgur Nemesis was a 2/6 morph; it is a 6/5
megamorph. Ninja of the Deep Hours cost {1}{U} — the same as its ninjutsu, which is the opposite of
the card. The five cycling lands were typed `Land — Swamp` and so on, and cycled for {2}. Plague
Stinger was an artifact creature. Gelectrode was a Wizard. Terminus, Exsanguinate, Staggershock,
Grapeshot, Explore, Agonizing Demise and Hagra Mauling were all a mana cheap; Twincast, Banishing
Light and Conclave Tribunal a mana or two dear.

### What is fixed in this pass

- **All 174 facts**, mechanically, from the rows.
- **83 rules texts.** 73 were wording only — "enters the battlefield" where Oracle says "enters", a
  different line break, a British spelling — and now read as the row does. Ten changed what the
  card does and were fixed whole, text and script together: the five cycling lands (a plain `Land`,
  cycling for one mana of its own colour) and the five morphs (Dirgur Nemesis and Ainok Survivalist
  are megamorphs; Battering Craghorn turns up for {1}{R}{R}, Master of Pearls for {3}{W}{W}, Zombie
  Cutthroat for five life rather than three).
- **About forty tests** that had been written around the wrong numbers, each re-fitted by hand to
  the real card and not just to the new value: the Redcap's persist test was called "comes back as a 0/0,
  which dies again on its own" and now asserts a 1/1 that shoots for one.

### What is not, and where it is written down

**65 cards still do something other than what they print**, and each is listed by name with the
difference in `KNOWN_DIFFERENT` in `poolOracle.test.ts`: Doom Blade kills black creatures, Preordain
scries one, Walking Ballista grows for {1}, Faithless Looting and Cackling Counterpart have no
flashback, Fireball hits one target, Jace Memory Adept has the wrong abilities. A card's text
changes together with its script and its tests, never ahead of them — a card whose text is right
and whose script is not is a card that lies to the player holding it. That list is the work order
for the next increments.

Two more entries are a convention, not an error: an adventurer's front face quotes its Adventure.

### The standing check

`poolOracle.fixture.json` is the Oracle row for each pool card, and `poolOracle.test.ts` requires
every printed fact of every card to equal its row — cost, mana value, type line, colours, power,
toughness, loyalty exactly; rules text with reminder text removed and nothing else forgiven. It
fails in both directions: on a difference that is not listed, and on a listed one that no longer
differs. Proved by removing an entry and by adding a false one. `scripts/measure/pool-oracle.mjs
--file <corpus> --write` regenerates the fixture.

It caught its own author within the hour: a throwaway `sed` meant to demonstrate a failure rewrote
five mana costs in the real file, and the next full run named all four that have rows. (The fifth,
Ice, has none — see below — and was restored from the last commit.) Experiments go on a copy.

### What this check cannot see

**The corpus carries front faces only**, and is built from a public card-script repository rather
than from Scryfall, which this container cannot reach. So twelve definitions have no row and are
named in `NO_ORACLE_ROW` rather than passed: the back halves of the three split cards (Ice, Wane,
Battery), the two Adventures (Venture Deeper, Shield's Might), the back faces of the two transforming
cards and the two modal ones, and the three whole-split-card names. Those are unverified. So is any
row where the corpus itself is behind Oracle; it is the best source reachable here and it is one
source.

### Three compiler rows that read sentences no card prints

The useful surprise. Putting the printed text on the pool's cards broke seven compiler tests —
because the compiler had been written, and tested, against the pool's wording:

| the compiler read | cards that print it | the printed sentence | cards |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "has protection from **all colors**" | 0 | "from **each color**" | 8 |
| "gains haste until end of turn **and becomes red**" | 0 | "**becomes red and** gains haste until end of turn" | 2 |
| "creature **an opponent controls** with power 4 or greater" | 6 | also "with power 4 or greater **an opponent controls**" | 2 |

All three now read the printed form. The first two had passing tests and read nothing in Magic.

### Tests that passed for the wrong reason

Raising a cost can turn "is not offered" into "cannot be paid", which passes just the same. A scan
of every test that holds a re-costed card and asserts something negative found two: Agonizing
Demise "will not point at a black creature" had three Swamps for a four-mana spell, and the bot's
"holds a ninja" test gave it two Islands for a card that now costs four. Both have the lands to
cast the card now, so the refusal is the one the test is named for.

### What this does to every number measured before it

**Every deck measurement in these docs and in the deck file's comments was taken on the
uncorrected cards.** Win rates, cast counts, slot comparisons — all of it. None has been re-taken
in this pass, and the comments that quote them have not been rewritten; the two I touched (the
Redcap's and the Cutthroat's) say so in place. Re-measuring belongs after the 65 queued cards are
right, not before, or it is done twice.

Also noted and not acted on: the engine refuses a life payment **equal to** the payer's life total
(a Zombie Cutthroat cannot be turned up at five life). I believe the rules allow that payment, and
could not check it here — no rules text is reachable from this container — so it is queued as a
question rather than changed on a recollection, which is the mistake this whole entry is about.

    engine tests: 3,838 → 3,847, all passing
    pool facts that differ from their Oracle row: 174 → 0
    pool rules texts that differ: 154 → 67 (65 queued by name, 2 conventions)

**Break runs owed from earlier.** D566 and D567 together: 41 of 44 caught. One was expected (a
spell's damage raising `deals-damage`, labelled unreached when it was written). One is a guard
nothing reaches — the test that only *combat* damage is one event per creature can be widened to
all damage without a test noticing, because no card damages one creature twice in a single
resolution; the comment at the guard now says so instead of claiming otherwise. The third was a
missing row: "when you cycle **this** card" answered for any card cycled and every existing row
cycled the card itself. A Bant Sojourners on the battlefield while a land is cycled is that row,
and it fails with the break applied. D570's pod sweep (seeds 44001–44040): 40 of 40 finished, no
throw, no stall.

## D572 — A level band is not the card's own text

**Found by D571, in the same hour.** Student of Warfare's Oracle text prints its level bands the
way every leveler does — a header line, a size line, then one ability to a line:

    Level up {W}
    LEVEL 2-6
    3/3
    First strike
    LEVEL 7+
    4/4
    Double strike

The moment the pool carried that text, the Student had first strike with no counters on it. The
reader that did it goes line by line, and to it a band's `First strike` is the card's.

It had always done that to levelers read from the card table. There are **26** of them (25
legal), and on **21** at least one band line was being read as the card's own — 37 lines in all.
Coralhelm Commander flew, Hada Spy Patrol was unblockable with shroud, Kargan Dragonlord flew and
trampled, and Brimstone Mage compiled to a creature that taps for one damage *and* for three *and*
for five. Nothing noticed because the
pool's own two levelers had been typed in a one-line form — `LEVEL 2-6: 3/3, first strike` — that
no reader could parse. The pool's wording hid the bug its real wording would have shown.

**The fix.** From the first `LEVEL n-m` or `LEVEL n+` header to the end of the card, nothing is the
card's own (CR 711.2): the printed-keyword readers stop there, and the compiler reports the whole
tail as unread rather than offering any line under it to a reader. Abilities printed above the
first band are level zero and are read as before.

A leveler from the card table is therefore a creature with its level-zero abilities and a flagged
card, which is honest. What it is not yet is a leveler: nothing reads `Level up {cost}` or fills
`levelBands` from printed text, so it never grows. That is the next step and it is a reading job,
not an engine one — the pool's two levelers already level through `levelBands`.

    printed legal lines read:            24,284 → 24,254 of 56,421 (43.0%)
    cards with a compiled script:        12,486 → 12,481
    cards with every printed line read:   8,283 → 8,287

Lines go **down**, and that is the point of the entry: 37 lines that were counted as read were
band lines read as something they are not. The net figure is smaller than that because the same
measurement includes the sentences D571's three compiler rows newly read.

Tests: four, on two rows copied from the corpus. The keyword above the first band is read and the
ones below are not; Brimstone Mage has one ability; Kargan Dragonlord has none, and on the
battlefield is a 2/2 that does not fly. With either half of the fix removed, they fail.

## D574 — "You may" on five cards that never asked, and the causative the compiler could not read

Five pool cards print "you may" and acted without asking: Gravedigger, Goblin Arsonist, Ninja of
the Deep Hours, Gelectrode and Yavimaya Granger. Each was queued by D571 with its text left at the
pool's wording. All five now ask, and carry their Oracle text.

**One helper, `youMay(prompt, effect, decisions)`**, spread into a trigger. It puts a Yes/No in
front of the trigger's own questions, gates those behind `askOnlyIfChosen: 'Yes'`, and hands the
effect a context with the first answer dropped — which is exactly what the compiler has emitted for
a printed "you may" since D450. Writing it once is the point: the hand-written card and the
compiled card now build the same shape from the same three facts, and `compiled-vs-written`
compares the prompts as well as the effects.

What a player sees: anything the ability points at is still chosen as it goes on the stack
(CR 603.3d); the question is asked as it resolves; No does nothing.

| card | question |
| --- | --- |
| Gravedigger | Return target creature card from your graveyard to your hand? |
| Goblin Arsonist | Have it deal 1 damage to any target? |
| Ninja of the Deep Hours | Draw a card? |
| Gelectrode | Untap Gelectrode? |
| Yavimaya Granger | Search your library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle? |

**The causative.** Goblin Arsonist's line did not compile at all: "you may have it deal 1 damage to
any target" is not "you may" followed by a clause the compiler reads, because the clause is in the
causative. It is the only way a card can print an optional effect whose subject is not the player.
The reader now hands "have X deal N…" on as "X deals N…" and keeps the printed words for the
question. Only on the bare "may": a priced or sequenced one names its effect after "If you do".

    corpus lines printing "you may have … deal": 54
    cards with every printed line read: 8,287 → 8,303 (+16)
    cards with a compiled script: 12,481 → 12,498
    printed legal lines read: 24,254 → 24,274 of 56,421 (43.0%)

The other 38 lines are held up by something else on the line (damage equal to its power, "If you
do", a quoted grant), not by the causative.

**Tests.** Thirteen existing tests met a question they did not answer and were re-fitted; each of
the five cards has a decline row beside its accept row. Three are worth naming:

- Strionic Resonator's copy of a Gravedigger trigger is its own "you may", asked separately. A new
  row declines the copy and takes the original, and gets one card back, not two.
- Gelectrode's question is asked whether or not it is tapped. That is the printed card, and it
  means an untapped Gelectrode now stops the stack for a question with no consequence. Not
  suppressed: an engine that skips a "may" because it judges the answer irrelevant is guessing.
- The compiler comparison row for Goblin Arsonist now gives both readings the same answer first,
  and checks that No leaves the board alone in both. Without that the row compared two no-ops.

The player guide has a new row, "Say no to a 'you may'".

## D575 — Angel of Sanctions, Ophidian Eye and Tandem Lookout as printed

The last three "you may" cards in the queue. Each was more than a question, which is why D574
left them.

| card | the pool had | the card prints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Angel of Sanctions | exiles "another" permanent, always; embalm {3}{W}{W} | "you may exile target nonland permanent an opponent controls"; embalm {5}{W} |
| Ophidian Eye | gives the creature "whenever this creature deals damage to a player, draw a card" | the Aura's own trigger: "Whenever enchanted creature deals damage to an opponent, you may draw a card" |
| Tandem Lookout | the pair draws on combat damage to a player | the pair draws on any damage to an opponent |

**Ophidian Eye is the one that changed kind.** It was written for #230 as the second route into
granted abilities, and the card is not a grant. Three things follow at the table: the Eye's
controller draws whoever controls the creature; a creature that has lost all abilities still feeds
it; and it asks. Any damage to an opponent counts, not only combat damage.

The granted route did not lose its second card. Its four tests (fires for the holder, gone with
the grantor, survives on the stack, respects layer 6 order) now run on **Sixth Sense**, which does
print a granted ability, compiled from its Oracle row and played out of a list of its own. That is
a better test than before: it is the path a pasted deck's Aura takes. A new row beside them proves
the Eye is the opposite case, on the same board, with a Turn to Frog.

**Two compiler readings, so the hand-written cards and the printed text agree.**

- "you may exile … until ~ leaves the battlefield" is the exile-and-return pair with a question in
  front. Angel of Sanctions compiles again; Suspension Field is held up only by its target phrase.
- An Aura that watches its host deal damage to a player or an opponent is aimed at your own
  attacker (`friendly`, `helpsInCombat`). The compiler had refused to guess a side for an Aura with
  no bonus line, rightly: "enchanted creature dies" is printed on cards for both sides. This
  sentence has no second kind. 14 legal Auras print it and all 14 are for the caster's creature.

**The bot.** Its rule for what to feed a sacrifice outlet asked whether a creature has text of its
own or text it was granted. A creature under the printed Eye has neither, and would have been fed
to a Vampire Aristocrat with the Aura on it. The rule now also counts one of your own attachments
that watches the creature. The existing test for it passes unchanged.

**Tests.** Eight re-fitted. New rows: the Angel's embalm is refused with five lands and both
answers to its question are played; the Eye's trigger is the Aura's on the stack, both answers,
and after a Turn to Frog; a Gelectrode's ping draws for the Eye and for the Lookout's pair at a
player's face and not at a creature; the compiler's hint, with "dies" as its control.

### How the work is run, from here

A container restart during this entry cost a 45-minute break run and an in-flight test run. Four
heavy jobs were sharing four cores at the time. Three changes:

- one full engine run per increment, the gate's; iteration uses only the touched test files;
- background measurements run one at a time and never beside the gate;
- the break harness writes each result as it finishes, so a restart keeps what was done.

## D576 — Eighteen cards given the targets and scopes they print

The next group in the queue: cards whose only difference from their Oracle row was who or what
they could touch. Mostly one-line filters. Two were not, and one of those was an engine bug.

| card | the pool had | the card prints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Doom Blade | any creature | nonblack |
| Agonizing Demise | regeneration saves the creature | it can't be regenerated |
| Thicket Basilisk | destroys whatever it fights | not a Wall |
| Mind Sculpt | target player | target opponent |
| Banishing Light | another nonland permanent, yours included | one an opponent controls |
| Impassioned Orator | any other creature entering | another creature you control |
| Bloodthrone Vampire | sacrifice another creature | sacrifice a creature |
| Ravenous Rats | each opponent discards at random | target opponent discards a card they choose |
| Lotleth Giant | each opponent loses life | damage to target opponent |
| Soulherder | a creature you control is exiled | any creature exiled from the battlefield |
| Cruel Celebrant | another creature of yours dies | itself too, and planeswalkers |
| Ruric Thar | every creature must attack | only Ruric Thar |
| Jace Beleren, −1 | you draw | target player draws |
| Swerve | an instant or sorcery | any spell with a single target |
| Rest in Peace | cards | cards or tokens |
| Knight Exemplar | no first strike | first strike |
| Harm's Way, Divine Deflection | "target creature or player" | "any target" (text only; the script already was) |

Counted, not estimated: seven made the pool's card stronger than the real one (Doom Blade,
Thicket Basilisk, Mind Sculpt, Banishing Light, Impassioned Orator, Ravenous Rats, Lotleth Giant),
eight weaker (Agonizing Demise, Bloodthrone Vampire, Soulherder, Cruel Celebrant, Jace Beleren,
Swerve, Rest in Peace, Knight Exemplar), Ruric Thar was a different card, and two changed only
their text. The ones a player would have felt most: a Ruric Thar that forced the whole table to
attack, Ravenous Rats hitting every opponent in a pod with a random discard, and a Doom Blade
that killed black creatures.

**The engine bug: a token under Rest in Peace still died.** The replacement loop skipped tokens
with the comment "every printed version of this effect says nontoken". The pool's own Rest in
Peace was the counter-example: "a card or token". A token is gone either way; what the card
changes is that it was exiled, so it did not die and nothing watching for a death sees one. A
replacement rule can now say `tokens: true`, and Rest in Peace does. Found by a test written for
the new wording, with the same board minus Rest in Peace as its control.

**Swerve and Aura spells.** "Any spell with a single target" includes an Aura on the stack, and
the engine could not find an Aura spell's target: it is declared on the Aura, not in the spell's
target list. Fixed, with a row that sends a Pacifism back at its caster's creature.

**Ruric Thar has no static now.** "Attacks each combat if able" is read off the printed card for
every card that says it, so the hand-written one was a second statement, and the standing
compiled-vs-written check refused it.

**Compiler.** "Target player draws a card" and "target opponent draws N cards" now read (Jace's
printed −1 is the pool's instance; 37 legal lines end in the sentence). Seven of these cards
have a printed line the compiler does **not** read: Cruel Celebrant, Soulherder's first line,
Thicket Basilisk, Swerve, Agonizing Demise, Rest in Peace and Knight Exemplar. For Cruel
Celebrant the pool's invented wording did read, and a compiler test compared against it; that row
is gone and a new one says outright that the printed line is unread. The corpus measure never
counted invented wording, so it does not move.

**New in the type system:** a `dies` trigger can ask for `creature-or-planeswalker`, the two
things the rules say can die (CR 700.4).

**Tests.** The 19 that disagreed were re-fitted or replaced, and 11 rows added, each for the half the old text got wrong: the black
creature a Doom Blade may not point at, the Wall the Basilisk spares, the opponent's creature the
Orator ignores, the planeswalker the Celebrant drains for. Where a re-fit needed a different
card (a regeneration test and a ward test both used Doom Blade on a black creature) it now uses
Murder.

The largest of these in play is Jace, Memory Adept. The pool had the +1 milling ten and the 0
drawing a card, with no ultimate. That is a planeswalker that mills ten every turn and gains
loyalty for it. Hollow Tide is the mill deck and plays it; expect its results to move.

**Four small engine pieces**, each for a clause more than one card prints:

- `escape.counters`, with an `escaped` flag on the stack object, because "escapes with a +1/+1
  counter" is asked as the permanent arrives and by then nothing else remembers how it was cast.
- `setCreatureTypes` on a continuous effect: "becomes a Frog" replaces the creature types and
  leaves any other subtype alone.
- `allCreatureTypes`: a flag, not three hundred subtypes in the game state, and not the
  changeling keyword either, which is an ability a Turn to Frog would remove.
- a fourth kind of conditional static, `source-equipment`, for "as long as two or more Equipment
  are attached to it".

**Compiler.** Two readings added: "~ escapes with N +1/+1 counter(s) on it", read with its Escape
line as one fact (10 corpus cards print it; 3 more say "escapes with" something else and stay
unread), and "becomes a 2/2 creature with all
creature types". Not read, and asserted as unread: Jace's −7, Ajani's −8, Turn to Frog's printed
sentence, and Balan's two lines.

**Tests.** 15 disagreed and were re-fitted; 8 rows added to the script tests and 3 to the
compiler tests. The ones that check a price check it
both ways: Woe Strider's escape is refused with three other cards in the graveyard and offered
with four.

Sunscourge Champion was meant for this group and is not in it: its eternalize costs "discard a
card", and the engine has no discard-a-card cost on an ability yet. It stays queued.

## D578 — Eight more cards as printed: a ward paid in life, a taxed "may", and a creature that assigns no damage

Eight of the last eleven queued cards now carry their Oracle text and do what it says. Three are
left (Toxic Deluge, Fireball, Sunscourge Champion), each needing a cost the engine cannot charge
yet.

**What each card was, and is now.**

| card | the pool had | printed, and now scripted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dragonsguard Elite | ward {1}; two counters a spell | no ward; one counter a spell; `{4}{G}{G}`: double its +1/+1 counters |
| Sedgemoor Witch | ward {3}; a black Pest | Ward—Pay 3 life; a black and green Pest |
| The Birth of Meletis | I a white Wall, II 2 life, III a Plains onto the battlefield tapped | I a basic Plains to hand, II a colorless artifact Wall, III 2 life |
| The Eldest Reborn | creatures only | creature or planeswalker, in chapters I and III |
| Kalitas, Traitor of Ghet | two abilities | the third: `{2}{B}`, sacrifice another Vampire or Zombie: two +1/+1 counters |
| Hagra Mauling | {2}{B}{B} always | {1} less while an opponent controls no basic lands |
| Ophidian | draw, and removed from combat | draw, and it assigns no combat damage this turn |
| Mystic Remora | you may draw two cards | you may draw a card unless that player pays {4} |

**Engine pieces these needed.**

- **A ward paid in life.** `pendingPayment` gains `life`, beside its mana string. One function,
  `paymentWords`, says the cost in the prompt, on the button and in the log (`3 life`,
  `{2} and 2 life`). A player whose life is at or below the amount is not asked, which is the rule
  every other life cost in this engine keeps; whether a payment equal to the life total should be
  allowed is still task #411, for all of them at once.
- **"Assigns no combat damage"** as its own flag on a continuous effect. The existing
  `preventsCombatDamage` stops damage dealt by *and to* a creature, which is a Fog. This one only
  stops what the creature deals; a blocker in front of it still hits it. A test proves the
  difference.
- **A conditional change to a spell's own cost** (`selfCostChange`), computed where affinity is,
  so the offer and the payment agree. The play keeps its printed cost and shows the change and
  its reason beside it.
- **A sacrifice cost narrowed by subtype** (`sacrificeSubtypes`).
- **A "may" somebody else can buy off** (`mayUnlessThatPlayerPays`): the player who cast the
  spell is asked first, with the price on the paying answer, and the controller is asked only if
  they do not pay. A caster who cannot afford it is not asked.

**The compiler reads two of these from printed text**, so they also work on cards from a
pasted list:

- `Ward—Pay N life` and `Ward—{N}, Pay N life`: 19 legal lines (16 and 3). Wards paid by
  discarding (15 lines), sacrificing, or "life equal to its power" (2) stay unread.
- `you may … unless that player pays {N}`: 2 legal cards, Rhystic Study and Mystic Remora.

Measured in the corpus, not yet read by the compiler: 26 legal cards print "assigns no combat
damage", and 108 legal lines print "costs {N} less to cast if …" over 83 different conditions.

**The ward tests moved to real ward cards.** No built-in card prints a ward paid in mana, so
the six mana-ward tests had been standing on two invented wards. They now use Unflinching
Hortimancer (Ward {1}) and Rimeshield Frost Giant (Ward {3}), compiled from their Oracle rows
and played from a custom list, plus Captain Howler, Sea Scourge for the mana-and-life ward.

**Tests.** 18 re-fitted, 21 added, among them one that the engine's own opponent does not
spend six mana doubling no counters. Two stale comments that still called Hagra Mauling a
three-mana instant were corrected (it is four; D571 fixed the cost).

## D579 — The last three: Toxic Deluge, Fireball and Sunscourge Champion as printed

The queue D571 opened is empty. Every built-in card now carries its Oracle text and is scripted
to it; the two entries left in the standing test's list are the adventure-quoting convention,
not differences.

| card | the pool had | printed, and now scripted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Toxic Deluge | the life chosen and paid as the spell resolved | X life paid as an additional cost to cast it |
| Fireball | X damage to one target | X divided evenly, rounded down, among any number of targets; {1} more for each beyond the first |
| Sunscourge Champion | gains 2; eternalize {5}{W}{W} | gains life equal to its power; eternalize—{2}{W}{W}, discard a card |

**Toxic Deluge.** The pool's version was kinder than the card: a countered Deluge cost no
life, and nobody could see how big it was before answering it. X is now announced with the
cast like any other X, the life is paid then, and the stack shows `Toxic Deluge (X=3)`. Two
things were needed so this did not make the card worse to play:

- The table opens the X question on the card's own best number (`bestX`, reported as
  `xDefault`), not on the largest legal one. For this card the largest is "all your life but
  one".
- The bot casts for that number, and does not cast at all when it is nought. The old rule that
  held a Deluge with nothing to kill now reads the same fact from the play.

**Fireball.** One spec, "any number of targets", optional. The split is arithmetic and nothing
is asked: five damage at two targets is two each. The extra {1} a target is charged in the
cast, counted off the targets announced. The table keeps X and the targets inside one budget,
so it will not take a target the mana cannot cover. The bot takes one target (`botTakes`);
without that it filled the spec and divided the damage across the whole table, its own side
included.

**Sunscourge Champion.** A new ability cost, `discardACard`: a card from the hand chosen as the
ability is activated, sent on the action as `discarded`, offered on the play as
`discardOptions`. It is a real discard, so madness and discard triggers see it. The table asks
"tap a card in your hand to discard". The bot discards a land it has no use for (five or more
lands out), then a madness card, then its most expensive card.

**Measured in the corpus, for what these pieces could read later** (legal cards):

    "As an additional cost to cast this spell, pay X life":        7 cards
    "costs {N} more to cast for each target beyond the first":     2 cards
    "Discard a card" as part of an activated ability's cost:     210 cards

The third is the large one. The compiler does not read that cost yet; the engine can now charge
it, so reading it is the next increment. It needs a decision first about when the bot should
pay a card for an effect, which is why it is not in this one.

**Smaller things found on the way.**

- The compiler's "deals X damage to any target" rows had been tested on Fireball, whose text
  that is not. They now use Blaze, which prints exactly that sentence. Fireball's own two lines
  are asserted as unread by the compiler.
- A note in the table's control bar said its "Cast" button for optional targets could not be
  reached by any built-in card. That stopped being true at D577 (Ajani, Jace) and is corrected.
- A target tapped after a ninjutsu or discard cost is now sent with that cost; the reducer had
  been dropping `returned` on that path. No built-in card has both, so nothing was affected.

**Tests.** 12 re-fitted and 15 added in the engine; 7 added to the table client.

## D580 — "Discard a card" read as the cost of a printed ability

D579 gave the engine a cost it could charge — a card from the hand, chosen as the ability is
activated — and used it on one hand-written card. This reads the same cost off printed text, so
it works on any card in a pasted deck.

**What is read.** The three words "Discard a card" as one component of an activated ability's
cost, beside mana, {T}, life, or a sacrifice or discard of the card itself. Counted in the legal
corpus: **206 lines on 204 cards** print it. 114 of those lines now read; the rest have an
effect the compiler does not read yet. Across the whole corpus the build reads 117 more lines
than the last one and finishes 96 more cards (table below). The three lines beyond my 114 reach
the same reader some other way, and I have not itemised them.

D579's record said 210 cards. I could not reproduce that figure; 204 is the count of cards with
the words as a component of an unquoted cost, and it replaces the earlier number.

**What is deliberately not read**, each because the flag cannot carry it:

    "Discard two cards"            16 lines   a count
    "Discard a card at random"     16 lines   not a choice
    "Discard a creature card"      14 lines   a filter
    "Discard a land card"          12 lines   a filter
    "Discard your hand"            11 lines   a count

And one combination: a discard together with "Sacrifice a creature" in the same cost. Both are
choices made as the ability is activated, and the table and the bot each ask for one, so reading
it would offer a play the engine then refuses. One legal card prints it (Bloodsoaked Altar); its
line stays unread.

**Mana abilities.** Three legal cards discard a card for mana (Skirge Familiar, Bog Witch,
Overeager Apprentice). They are read, and offered as an ability the player presses: the card is
discarded and the mana goes to the pool. The auto-tapper never uses one. Without that rule
Overeager Apprentice ("Discard a card, Sacrifice Overeager Apprentice: Add {B}{B}{B}") would have
counted as a free source, because a sacrifice of itself is a cost the auto-tapper accepts — it
would have paid for a spell with no card leaving the hand.

**The bot's rule, which D579 said had to be decided first.** Which card it gives up is
unchanged: a land it has no use for (five or more lands out), then a madness card it can pay
for, then its most expensive card. New is *whether*: an ability that could be paid again in the
same turn is given only the first two. An ability it can use once — {T} in the cost, "only once
each turn", or a cost that exiles or sacrifices the card itself — may take a card it wanted, and
the search decides if that is worth it.

The reason is measured, not assumed. With the rule switched off, a bot holding two Hellriders it
could not cast yet discarded both to Noose Constrictor ("Discard a card: Noose Constrictor gets
+1/+1 until end of turn") in one main phase.

Of the "used once" kinds, {T}, once-each-turn and exile-itself each have a bot test. Sacrifice-
itself and discard-itself are read by the same line and have none: the only board that reaches
them is the bot cashing a creature and a card for one draw, and I did not want that play frozen
into a test as correct.

Sunscourge Champion), 8 compile rows added, 1 retired: an older test listed
"{1}, Discard a card: Draw a card" as a cost the compiler must refuse. It now uses "Discard two

## D581 — Five more ability costs read off the card

D580 read one cost into a field the engine already had. Ranking what was left the same way —
which unread cost components sit in front of an effect the compiler can already read — put
five near the top that each had a field too, added for one hand-written card or keyword and
never given a reader. This reads them.

| printed cost | field | legal lines that print it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remove a (or two, three…) *kind* counter from this card | `removeCounter` | 224, over 44 kinds: 68 +1/+1, 48 charge, 21 oil |
| Exile this card | `exileSelf` | 58 |
| Exile this card from your graveyard | `exileSelf` + `fromGraveyard` | 78 |
| Pay {E}… | `energy` | 45 |
| Sacrifice a (or another) *creature type* | `sacrifice` + `sacrificeSubtypes` | 75, over 29 types: 20 Goblin, 13 Saproling |
| Sacrifice a Food / Treasure / Clue | `sacrifice: 'artifact'` + `sacrificeSubtypes` | 15, 6, 2 |

Nothing in the engine changed. Each field was already checked when the ability is activated,
already kept off the table when it cannot be paid, and already paid before the ability goes on
the stack. The compiler's own note from D446 said three of these costs "have no field"; that
was true then, and the note now says which have gained one.

**Read from the graveyard.** "Exile this card from your graveyard" says where the ability is
used from as well as what it costs, so the ability is offered on the card in the graveyard and
not on a copy in play. A printed "Activate only as a sorcery" still applies there.

**Mana abilities.** Workhorse ("Remove a +1/+1 counter from Workhorse: Add {C}") and Skirk
Prospector ("Sacrifice a Goblin: Add {R}") are read and offered as abilities the player presses.
The auto-tapper does not use them. I checked that claim over the whole legal corpus rather than
reasoning about it: 58 compiled mana abilities carry a discard, a counter removal, an exile of
the card or a sacrifice of something else, and exactly one of them could reach the auto-tapper
— Overeager Apprentice, which D580 already excludes.

**Deliberately not read**, each tested as refused:

- a number of counters chosen as the cost is paid ("Remove X …", "any number of", "all");
- a counter taken off some other permanent;
- "Exile this card from your hand";
- a land or enchantment type ("Sacrifice a Forest", "a Desert", "an Aura") and "Sacrifice a
  land" (38 lines with a readable effect — the largest cost still unread, and it needs a new
  kind of sacrifice in the engine, a bot rule for which land, and a table prompt);
- "Tap an untapped creature you control" (22 lines), which has no field.

## D582 — Channel, and two more tokens: Food and Blood

Two small readers, both found by asking which unread lines sit in front of an effect the
compiler already reads.

**Channel.** A "Channel —" line is an ability you use from your hand by discarding the card:
"Channel — {4}{G}, Discard Bamboo Grove Archer: Destroy target creature with flying." The
compiler kept the label on and left the line unread, on purpose: with the label gone the rest
looks like an ordinary ability and would be offered from the battlefield. But the rest says where
it is used from in its own cost. "Discard this card" is the field the engine already reads as
"used from the hand, and spends the card" (cycling has worked that way since #45). So the label
now comes off on one condition, that the cost under it discards the card; a Channel line whose
cost did not is refused.

has had one since #243. The compiler's own note said why: a named token's text is not in the
sentence that makes it, and writing it from memory was ruled out. The text is in the corpus,
though — every card that makes one quotes the token's ability in its reminder text — so the two
definitions are those quotations:

    Food    {2}, {T}, Sacrifice this token: You gain 3 life.
    Blood   {1}, {T}, Discard a card, Sacrifice this token: Draw a card.

The note that argued against memory had itself remembered Food's text slightly wrong ("this
artifact" for "this token"). Blood could not have been written before D579, because its cost

## D583 — Playing a card out of exile until a deadline

"Exile the top card of your library. You may play that card this turn." Red's version of drawing
a card, and until now a line the compiler left alone: it had no reader, and the engine had nothing
to read it into. A card in exile was castable only if it had been foretold, or was a creature back
from its adventure, or was the one card a cascade was offering.

**What the engine has now.** A card in exile can carry a permission: which seat may play it, and
until when. While it does, it is offered to that seat exactly as a card in hand would be:

- a spell is cast for its printed cost, at its usual time (an instant on anybody's turn, anything
  else in your own main phase with the stack empty);
- a **land** is played as the turn's land, counted against the same one-a-turn limit as a land
  from hand. This is the part neither foretell nor adventure needed, and it is why the wording
  says "play" and not "cast";
- a two-faced card is offered as each face, since neither has been cast;
- nobody else is offered it, and the engine refuses them if they try.

The permission ends at the printed deadline and the card then simply stays in exile. Three
deadlines are read:

    this turn / until end of turn        gone when that turn's cleanup ends
    until the end of your next turn      gone at the end of the first turn of yours that
                                         finishes after the one it was given in
    until your next end step             gone as your next end step begins

It also ends the moment the card leaves exile for any reason, so a card that was played, or that
another effect moved, does not carry it along.

**What the compiler reads.** The two sentences are read as a pair or not at all. The second one
does nothing by itself, and the first one by itself would be a card thrown away, so there is no
reader for either half. The pair is read wherever it sits in a line: on its own (Reckless
Impulse), behind a trigger (Abbot of Keral Keep), behind a cost (Dark-Dweller Oracle), or with
another sentence before or after it.

    legal lines that print the pair with "play":    136, on 132 cards
    read now:                                        53
    of those cards, every line now read:             31

Those three figures match lines by their text, with reminder text removed on both sides, which
is the less reliable of my two ways of counting (see the correction in D582). The totals under
Measurements come from the standing measure and do not depend on it.

Most of the 83 still unread are held up by something else on the same line: a trigger condition
that is not read yet ("whenever a modified creature you control attacks"), a mode bullet, a saga
chapter, a cost. The rest are wordings this increment refuses on purpose, each because it is a
different permission:

- "you may **cast**" it: a land turned over that way stays in exile, and this permission would
  let it be played;
- "without paying its mana cost";
- "you may play **one of** those cards", or a filtered cast "from among them";
- "the top **X** cards";
- the rarer deadlines: until end of combat on your next turn, until your next upkeep, for as
  long as it remains exiled, for as long as you control something;
- another player's library.

One limit to name: a card played this way is cast for its printed cost only. An alternative cost
the card has (evoke, dash, a morph cast face down) is not offered from exile. That is the same
rule the engine already applies to a creature back from an adventure; the rules allow more.

**The computer opponent.** It scored a card in exile as worth nothing, so a Reckless Impulse
looked like one card spent and two library cards lost, and it would not have cast it. A card it
may play from exile now counts as a card in hand. A test has it cast the Impulse, play the land
it turned over and cast the creature. It cannot see what it will turn over: its own library is
shuffled out of its sight before it looks ahead, as it has been since #207.

**Food and Blood, corrected.** D582's break run (below) took away the hand-written script for
each token in turn and no test noticed. The reason is that a card with no script is read from
its printed text, and the two token definitions carry text the compiler reads whole, so each
token had two definitions that happened to agree. I deleted the hand-written pair. A Food and a
Blood are now defined only by their printed text, and the break spec for this increment changes
that text instead (a Food that gains 2, a Blood with no discard) to check the tests notice.

**Tests.** 50 added. In the engine, 32 on five real cards compiled from their Oracle rows
(Reckless Impulse, Act on Impulse, Abbot of Keral Keep, Dark-Dweller Oracle, Yasmin Khan) and on
17 wordings each cast as a spell of its own: what is exiled and how many, each deadline from both
sides of it, the land drop, the other seat refused in its own main phase with its own mana, an
adventurer offered as both faces, a library shorter than the count, the permission dropped when
the card leaves exile, and the bot. In the compiler, 18: the 17 neighbouring wordings above left
unread, and the pair read behind a trigger and a cost.

## D584 — The dig: look at the top cards, take some, the rest leave the top

"Look at the top three cards of your library. Put one of them into your hand and the rest on the
bottom of your library in any order." Blue's and green's card selection, and the largest family
the last probe found: 346 legal lines contain "look at the top N cards of your library", none of
them was read, and 232 of them were their card's only unread line.

**What it is, to the engine.** The same question a scry asks — the top of your own library, shown
to you and nobody else — with two things changed. The cards you pick go to your **hand** instead
of the bottom, so picking is keeping. And the cards you looked at and did not pick **leave the
top**: to the bottom of the library or to the graveyard, as the card says. Two new fields on the
existing question say those two things, and the engine applies the answer itself, as it already
did for scry.

**What the compiler reads.** Two shapes, each several printed sentences read as one question:

    Look at the top N cards of your library. Put K of them into your hand and the rest
      on the bottom of your library [in any order | in a random order] | into your graveyard.

    Look at the top N cards of your library. You may reveal a <type> card from among them
      and put it into your hand. Put the rest on the bottom of your library in <an> order.

The second shape adds a filter, and three things follow from it:

- You are shown every card you looked at, but only the ones of the printed type can be taken.
- The card you take is revealed to the table, which is how the others know it was of that type.
  It stays readable to them while it is in your hand.
- If none of them is of the type, you are still shown them and asked to confirm. The engine
  used to answer a question with nothing to pick by itself, silently; here that would have
  skipped the looking, which is information the card gives you.

`<type>` is a card type, several joined by "or" or listed with commas, "permanent", or "nonland".

    legal lines with "look at the top N cards of your library":   346, on 345 cards
    read now:                                                      90
    of those cards, every line now read:                           69

(Counted by matching line text, as in D583; the totals under Measurements do not depend on it.)

**Three engine faults this would have had, found before it shipped rather than after:**

- *An answer the engine gives itself was never applied to the library.* When a question has
  exactly as many candidates as it must take, the engine answers it without asking. That path
  skipped the code that moves the cards. It never mattered for scry (you may always keep
  everything, so it is always asked), but "put one of them into your hand" over a one-card
  library is that case exactly, and the card would have stayed in the library. Both paths now go
  through one function.
- *The computer opponent would have stopped the table.* Its standing rule for the top of a
  library is the scry rule: bottom a land once it has five. Applied to a dig it takes a land
  when it has plenty and takes nothing when it has few, and "nothing" is not a legal answer to
  "put one into your hand". It now knows a dig from a scry: a land while it holds fewer than
  five lands, otherwise the most expensive card offered.
- *The surveil button said "Bottom 2".* The table had one set of words for every question about
  the top of a library. They are now chosen by where the picks go, in a function with tests:
  bottom (scry), graveyard (surveil), or hand (a dig, where the button reads "Take 1").

**Two simplifications, named.** "In any order" keeps the cards in the order they were already
in; choosing another order needs a question whose answer is a sequence, which scry also does
without. "In a random order" is shuffled by the game's own random numbers.

**Not read, each on purpose:** "then put them back in any order" (20 lines, the sequence
question again); a card put onto the battlefield from among them; a filter that is not a card
type — a creature type ("a Dragon card", the commonest of these and the obvious next step), "historic",
"with power 2 or less"; "up to two" or "any number of" on the filtered shape; "the top X
cards"; and the rider "If you didn't put a card into your hand this way, …".

the Future, Adventurous Impulse, Augur of Bolas, Blood Price, Brightwood Tracker) for what is

Web: six for the words on the row and the button, and for a card that is shown but not offered.

    web tests: 259, all passing

## D585 — More additional costs on spells: a discard, life, and wider sacrifices

"As an additional cost to cast this spell, discard a card." The compiler reads a spell whole or
not at all, so one unread cost line keeps the whole card out, however plain the rest of it is:
Tormenting Voice is "draw two cards" behind a cost the engine could not take. Until now the only
additional cost read was "sacrifice a creature".

**What the engine now takes when a spell is cast:**

- **A card discarded.** The player picks which, as they already do for an ability that costs a
  discard. The spell itself cannot be the card. With no other card in hand the spell is not
  offered, and the reason is given ("it asks you to discard a card, and you have no other card
  in hand").
- **A printed amount of life.** Nothing to choose. Refused unless the player has more life than
  the cost (#411 is the open question of whether paying exactly your life total should be
  allowed; this follows what the engine already does for abilities).
- **A wider sacrifice**: an artifact; an artifact or a creature; a creature of a named type
  ("sacrifice a Goblin"). One shape with the ability costs, so the two cannot drift apart.

Every cost is paid after the mana and before the spell goes on the stack, so a countered spell
has still cost its caster the card, the life or the permanent.

**What the compiler reads**, after "As an additional cost to cast this spell, ": `sacrifice a
creature` (as before), `sacrifice another creature`, `sacrifice an artifact`, `sacrifice an
artifact or creature`, `sacrifice a <creature type>`, `discard a card`, `pay N life`.

    legal cards with a line beginning "As an additional cost to cast this spell":   297
    the cost line is read:                                                           96  (was 54)
    of those, every line is read:                                                    49  (was 21)

(Counted by a probe over the corpus on this build. "Was" is the one cost read before, counted
on the same build; the totals under Measurements are the before-and-after that does not depend
on that.)

**A fault in the table, found by a test written for this.** The table asked which card to
discard and then cast the spell without it: the cast message it sent carried the sacrifice and
left the discard off, because only abilities had ever asked for one. The engine would have
refused every such cast with "choose a card to discard". Fixed, with a test on the message
itself.

**The words on the table** come from one function, `feedWords`, so a spell that eats "an
artifact or creature" says so instead of saying "creature".

**The computer opponent.**

- *A discard.* One function now serves abilities and spells. It gives up a spare land once it
  has five on the battlefield, then a card with madness. For a spell — where the discard is the
  price of the card it has decided to cast — it goes on to the cheapest thing it holds; for an
  ability it still declines rather than throw away a card it wants.
- *An artifact, or an artifact or creature.* It looks at the non-creature options first: a
  token (a Treasure, a Clue, a Food) or an artifact that has nothing left to do. Only then does
  the rule it already had for creatures apply to the bodies.

**Not read, each on purpose**, counted on this build:

    discard X cards                              10    needs X announced with the cost
    exile a creature card from your graveyard     8    a cost paid from the graveyard
    pay X life                                    7    the engine has the payment; the reader
                                                       needs each card's use of X
    sacrifice a land                              6    the obvious next one
    you may collect evidence / reveal a Dragon /
      behold / blight / waterbend                23    optional costs with their own rules
    reveal a creature card from your hand         4
    "A or B" costs (sacrifice a creature or
      pay {3}{B}, discard a card or pay {2})     16    a choice between two costs
    everything else                              rest  one or two cards a wording

And a second family the newly read costs lead straight into: **30 cards whose cost now reads
and whose effect does not**, because the effect measures the thing given up — "Fling deals
damage equal to the sacrificed creature's power to any target", "Draw cards equal to the
sacrificed creature's power", "You gain life equal to the sacrificed creature's toughness".
The engine does not yet remember what was sacrificed once it is gone. That is the next

## D586 — What was sacrificed to pay for it: "the sacrificed creature's power"

"Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creature's power to any target." D585 taught the
engine to take the sacrifice; this is the other half of the same cards, and of the abilities
built the same way (Altar of Dementia, Greater Good, Diamond Valley).

**The rule.** By the time the spell resolves the creature is a card in a graveyard. There it has
no counters, no Aura and no Giant Growth, so the game uses what was true of it as it left the
battlefield (CR 608.2h). The engine now reads three numbers at the moment the cost is paid — the
permanent's power and toughness as they stood, and its mana value — and they travel with the
spell or ability to its resolution.

- A 2/4 under a Giant Growth is thrown for 5. A 3/3 with two +1/+1 counters is thrown for 5.
- A token has mana value 0. So does a face-down permanent, whatever card is under it.
- A copy of the spell has the same numbers as the original, as it has the original's X.

**What the compiler reads.** The measure, in two word orders ("the sacrificed creature's power",
"the mana value of the sacrificed permanent"), wherever a count was already read:

    deals damage equal to <measure> to <target>          Fling, Thud, Brion Stoutarm
    deals damage to <target> equal to <measure>          Final Strike
    deals X damage to <target>, where X is <measure>
    draw cards equal to <measure> / draw X cards, …      Life's Legacy, Greater Good
    you gain | lose life equal to <measure>              Worthy Cause, Diamond Valley
    create X … tokens, where X is <measure>              Carrion
    gets ±X/±X until end of turn, where X is <measure>   Call for Blood, Atogatog

and three it had no counted form of before:

    target player mills cards equal to <measure>         Altar of Dementia
    target player loses life equal to <measure>          Starlit Sanctum
    each opponent loses life equal to <measure>          Jarad's ability

Also the older spelling of a typed sacrifice in an ability's cost, "Sacrifice a Goblin
creature" (Airdrop Condor, Starlit Sanctum), which is the same cost as "Sacrifice a Goblin".

**Where it is refused, which matters more than where it is read.** The same words are printed
where nothing was sacrificed as a cost: "you may sacrifice a creature. If you do, create X
Wolves, where X is the sacrificed creature's toughness" (Feed the Pack), emerge, a
planeswalker's "Sacrifice a creature. When you do, …". There the engine has recorded nothing,
and a reading would be a card that resolves for 0 without saying so. So the measure is a number
only inside text that a sacrifice paid for — the resolution of a spell whose additional cost is
a sacrifice, or the effect of an ability with a sacrifice of another permanent in its cost — and
everywhere else the line stays unread and is flagged. Tests hold each side of that line: a spell
with no cost, a spell whose cost is a discard, an ability that sacrifices its own source, an
ability that only taps, and two abilities on one card where only one of them sacrifices.

    legal cards printing one of these measures:      87
    measure lines read (of 86 on the 85 that compile):  34
    cards with every line read:                      27

**Not read, each on purpose:**

- *Searching by it.* "Search your library for a creature card with mana value equal to 1 plus
  the sacrificed creature's mana value" — Birthing Pod, Prime Speaker Vannifar, Neoform, Eldritch
  Evolution and four more. The most played cards in the family, and they need a search filter
  that is computed, which the search has not got. The next thing worth building here.
- *Mana equal to it* (Sacrifice, Burnt Offering, Priest of Yawgmoth): seven cards.
- *Counters equal to it* (Vish Kal, Forge Armor, Scourge of Skola Vale) and a discard of that
  many cards (Tormented Thoughts).
- *A fact about the creature that is not one of the three numbers*: "if the sacrificed creature
  was a Human", "was legendary", its colours, its creature types.
- *"…then you gain life equal to its toughness"* (Momentous Fall): "its" is the sacrificed
  creature, and the pronoun reader does not know that.

**The computer opponent** pays these costs as it pays every sacrifice, with the creature it
values least. So its own Fling is usually thrown for 1. That is a legal play and a weak one; a
rule for when a big creature is worth throwing is its own piece of work, and is task #424.

**Three lines removed before they shipped.** The first draft also handed the numbers to a mana
ability, to a trigger's condition and to the reader for modal spells. No printed card reaches
any of the three, so nothing could have tested them, and they are gone.

**Tests.** 26 engine tests added (25 here, and one for D578's break run, below). Ten real cards from their Oracle rows (Fling, Life's Legacy,
Worthy Cause, Reckoner's Bargain, Carrion, Call for Blood, Final Strike, Altar of Dementia,

one, counters, a copy, a token, a face-down permanent, an ability, and a draw that happens
before a question. Eight printed grammars, each as an ability that sacrifices a 2/4 costing
four, so that the three measures give three different numbers. And the refusals above.

## D587 — Lands that enter tapped unless…, and the shock lands

"Clifftop Retreat enters tapped unless you control a Mountain or a Plains." The dual lands that
every Commander mana base is built from: check lands, fast lands, slow lands, bond lands, battle
lands and the shock lands. 132 legal lands print one of these lines; for 100 of them it was the
only line the compiler could not read, so one sentence was all that stood between a deck's mana
base and the automated table.

**What the engine does.** The same replacement as "enters tapped" (CR 614.1c), with a condition
asked as the land arrives, of the board it arrives on. The land never counts itself: "two or
fewer other lands" and "you control a Mountain" are about what was already there. The
conditions read, each counted in the corpus first:

    you control a <basic type> [or a <basic type>]   check lands                 25
    you control N or fewer other lands              fast lands                  11
    a player has N or less life                     Abandoned Campground        10
    you have N or more opponents                    bond lands                  10
    you control N or more basic lands               battle lands                10
    you control N or more other lands               slow lands                  10
    you control a planeswalker                                                  10
    your opponents control N or more lands          Turbulent Crater             8
    you control a legendary creature                Barad-dûr                    6
    you control a basic land                                                     5
    you control N or more other <basic type>s       Mystic Sanctuary             5

**The shock lands** ("As Blood Crypt enters, you may pay 2 life. If you don't, it enters
tapped.") are a choice, so the table offers the land twice — *untapped (pay 2 life)* and
*tapped* — and the answer travels on the land play. The life is paid before the land arrives.
The paying row is not offered at 2 life or less, and the engine refuses it there as it refuses
a life payment for a land that asks none. A shock land that arrives any other way (fetched, or
put onto the battlefield by an effect) enters tapped: the rules give the same choice then, and
the table has no question to ask it with yet. Named in the player guide.

**A fault this found.** A land with basic land types — Blood Crypt is a Swamp Mountain — taps
for those colours with nothing printed (CR 305.6). Only the whole-card reader added that mana.
So a typed land with any line the compiler could not read compiled to a land with **no mana
ability at all**. Probed on D586's build, Blood Crypt and Canopy Vista both compiled to no
script whatever: their enters-tapped line was the line nothing could read, and their only mana
is the kind nothing prints. The line-by-line compiler now adds the
mana of the land's types too, skipping any colour the card already taps for, and 51 typed
lands compile that way. A test asserts the mana on Blood Crypt, Canopy Vista and Mystic
Sanctuary.

**The table.** A land that would come in tapped says so on its row before the player picks it:
"Play Clifftop Retreat (enters tapped: you control a Mountain or a Plains)". The log says
"plays Clifftop Retreat tapped", or "pays 2 life and plays Blood Crypt untapped". The client
carries the shock land's choice on the play it sends, with a test that it does.

**The computer opponent.** It already played the land that comes in untapped before one that
does not; that rule now knows about the conditions, asked of the board as it stands. It pays
for a shock land only when the extra mana casts something that turn — a card in hand that costs
exactly one more than its untapped lands — and only above 10 life. Otherwise it plays the shock
land tapped.

**Not read, each on purpose:** "unless you control a Mount or Vehicle" (5 lands), the two that
reveal a card from hand, Starting Town (a turn count), Multiversal Passage (chooses a land type
first), and "When ~ enters untapped, …" on Mystic Sanctuary and three others, which is a
trigger of its own.

    lands printing "enters tapped unless":      120, 110 read
    shock lands:                                 12, 11 read
    lands in the family now read whole:          96 of 132

**Six old faults, now pinned.** D586's entry said the six faults the D574–D577 break run missed
would get a test or a reason before anything new. They were re-run against D586's tree first and
all six were still uncaught, so the code was right and nothing said so. Each now has a test:

- an optional "you may exile … until it leaves" compiled as mandatory (Angel of Sanctions);
- a replacement that names only cards swallowing a token (Kalitas, with Zulaport Cutthroat
  watching the token die);
- a spell with two target specs treated as redirectable when it holds one target (Swerve);
- "target opponent draws" aimed as help, and "target player draws two cards" drawing one;
- Balan counting an Aura as an Equipment.

Re-run with these tests in: 6 of 6 caught. (The harness's "for example" label named the wrong
test on all six, because the mirror it ran in was snapshotted a step early; the counts were
confirmed by re-running on a fresh snapshot and one fault by hand.)

Sanctuary from their Oracle rows, each condition both ways, a land not counting itself, the

a note: the compile test that asserted a conditional arrival is refused now asserts it is read

## D588 — Typecycling: a cycling that searches instead of drawing

"Mountaincycling {2} ({2}, Discard this card: Search your library for a Mountain card, reveal
it, put it into your hand, then shuffle.)" Basic landcycling, the five basic-type cyclings,
artifact landcycling and the creature-type ones (Wizardcycling, Slivercycling, Halflingcycling).
103 legal cards print one; for 58 of them it was the only line the compiler could not read.

**What it is.** The cycling ability the engine already had (D567: a cost paid from the hand,
the card discarded, and an event that cards watching for a cycle hear), with the search the
reminder text prints in place of the draw (CR 702.29e). The search is the one the compiler
already reads for any printed library search (D449), asked the reminder text's own sentence, so
the filter is that reader's: a subtype is matched on the type line, "basic land" needs the
supertype, and finding nothing is a legal answer.

**A guard the old test made me add.** The compile test written when these lines were refused
included plain "Landcycling {1}{G}". The first version of this reader took the capitalised word
in front as a subtype and so read "Landcycling" as a search for the subtype *Land*, which no card
has: a search that always finds nothing, silently. Now only three type phrases are named (basic
land, artifact land, land) and anything else must be a basic land type or a creature type; a
word that is neither ("Lancecycling") stays unread, with a test.

    legal cards printing a typecycling line:   103
    lines read:                                 102
    cards now read whole:                       61

The one left is Tectonic Reformation, "Each land card in your hand has cycling {R}", which
grants cycling to other cards and is a different shape.

**The table and the computer opponent** need nothing new: a cycling ability is offered from the
hand beside the cast, and the search is the question every library search asks.

**Tests.** 11 engine tests added. Four real cards and Drannith Healer from their Oracle
rows (Hill Gigas, Ash Barrens, Fiery Fall, Sojourner's Companion): only cards of the kind are
offered, the one taken goes to hand and the library is one smaller, a nonbasic land is not a
basic land, an instant offers both its cast and its cycling, nothing is a legal answer, the
Healer gains a life, and the computer opponent's moves are ones the engine takes. The compile
test that asserted these lines are refused now asserts they are read as a search and never as
a draw, with a note; two words that are not subtypes are asserted unread. Three more are for
D587's break run, below.

## D589 — "Doesn't untap during its untap step"

"Enchanted creature doesn't untap during its controller's untap step." (Paralyzing Grasp,
Dehydration, Claustrophobia.) "This artifact doesn't untap during your untap step." (Basalt
Monolith, Grim Monolith.) A drawback that lasts as long as the effect does — not the one-shot
"next untap step" that D538 read, which the engine keeps as `frozen` and spends when the step
happens.

**What the engine does.** A continuous-effect flag, `doesntUntap`, read by the untap step: a
tapped permanent with it stays tapped. "Loses all abilities" clears it when the drawback is the
permanent's own, as it clears "can't block" (CR 613.1f); an Aura's or Equipment's grant is the
Aura's, and a Turn to Frog does not take it away.

**What the compiler reads.**

- On an Aura or Equipment: "Enchanted creature …" / "Equipped creature …" with this tail, as a
  harmful bonus, so the computer opponent aims the Aura at somebody else's creature as it does a
  Pacifism. 41 of the 70 Aura lines; the rest say "Enchanted permanent", which the Aura reader
  does not take yet, or pair it with something else ("loses all abilities and …").
- On the card itself: "This creature / This artifact / <its name> doesn't untap during your
  untap step." Read the way the engine already reads "can't block" and "can't be blocked" off
  the printed line (D495) — a base characteristic of the card, with no script involved. 35 of 39.

**A fault this fixed in passing.** A compiled Basalt Monolith untapped every turn. The card's
own drawback was the one line left unread on it (a test said so), and the engine was playing it
as a strictly better card: tap for three, untap for free next turn, and never pay the {3}. The
same was true of every card in this family that printed its own drawback.

    legal lines printing "doesn't untap during":    245
    of them, the lasting kind read now:             77 (41 Aura, 35 self, 1 Equipment)
    the one-shot "next untap step" (D538):          37 of 91, unchanged

**Not read, each on purpose:** "Enchanted permanent …" (the Aura reader takes creatures only);
"…if it has a depletion counter on it" and the other conditional forms; "for as long as ~
remains tapped" (Amber Prison, Mana Leech); Claustrophobia's "When ~ enters, tap enchanted
creature", which is its own line and still unread — so a Claustrophobia on an untapped creature
leaves it untapped until it taps of its own accord.

**Tests.** 9 engine tests added, on Paralyzing Grasp, Basalt Monolith and Brass Man from
their Oracle rows: the Aura holds a tapped creature down and does not tap an untapped one, the bot
aims it at the opponent, the Monolith stays tapped through its own untap step and its {3} still
untaps it, Brass Man is still tapped when its upkeep asks to pay, a Turn to Frog takes the
drawback away, and the "next untap step" Aura printing is left unread. Four older tests changed,
each with a note: the printed-statics table has a fourth field and two new rows; the D456 test
that used Apathy's line as its example of an unreadable Aura line now uses one that still is;
the D505 test that said Basalt Monolith's drawback was its one unread line now says it reads

## D590 — Explore

"When Merfolk Branchwalker enters, it explores." CR 701.44a: reveal the top card of your
library; a land goes into your hand; anything else puts a +1/+1 counter on the creature, and you
may put the card into your graveyard. 46 legal lines print the word outside reminder text; for
35 of them it was the card's only unread line.

**One engine addition: a question asked only if the board says so.** The engine could already
skip a question on an earlier *answer* ("you may search …", D450). Explore's question depends on
a *fact*: whether the revealed card is a land. `askOnlyIf` is that — asked of the board as the
question comes up, and skipped as an empty answer like every other unasked question, so the
positions effects read by do not move.

**How the three pieces are ordered,** which is where explore is easy to get wrong:

- the counter goes on before the question, and only for a nonland card;
- the question (surveil 1 over the top card) is asked only for a nonland card;
- the land goes to hand in the effect, after the answers. Nothing has moved the top card by then,
  so an empty answer with a land on top can only mean the question was skipped for a land. When
  the card was not a land, it is either in the graveyard (an answer with a card in it) or still on
  top and not a land — so the card under a binned one is never taken by mistake, which a test
  checks.

**Who explores.** "<Name> explores" is the card. "It explores" is the trigger's subject, falling
back to the card when there is none. The first draft read "it" as the card everywhere, and a probe
of Path of Discovery ("Whenever a creature you control enters, it explores") put the +1/+1
counter on the enchantment. The probe is now a test.

    legal lines with "explore" outside reminder text:   46
    read now:                                            21 (all new)
    cards newly read whole:                              21

**Not read, each on purpose:** "explores, then it explores again" (Jadelight Ranger) and "explores
X times", which ask twice; "target creature you control explores" and "each Merfolk creature you
control explores"; the cards that watch a creature explore (Wildgrowth Walker, Lurking
Chupacabra, Shadowed Caravel); and Topography Tracker's replacement.

**Tests.** 7 engine tests added, on Merfolk Branchwalker, Seeker of Sunlight and Path of
Discovery from their Oracle rows: a land goes to hand with no counter and no question; a nonland
card puts a counter on and asks; kept stays on top, binned goes to the graveyard and the card
under it is not taken; an empty library does nothing; the activated form; Path of Discovery's
counter on the creature; the computer opponent's answer is one the engine takes; and Jadelight
Ranger's double explore left unread. One more closes D589's break run, below.
