## D591 — Two-faced cards from printed data: adventure, modal double-faced, transform

The largest single gap left was not a sentence but a shape. **622 legal cards were refused
outright** as "layout … has more than one face" — 388 transforming, 136 adventurers, 98 modal
double-faced — so a pasted deck with a Bonecrusher Giant, a Pathway or a Delver got cardboard. The
engine has played all three kinds since #140, #141 and #217, for hand-written cards; nothing could
build one from data.

**Where the faces come from.** The corpus is built from Forge's card files, which keep every face
in one file after an `ALTERNATE` line. The converter (`scripts/corpus/from-forge.mjs`) threw
everything after the first face away. It now writes `card_faces`, Scryfall's own field in
Scryfall's shape, so the same code reads a real Scryfall import when one lands; the regenerated
corpus is identical to the old one in every other field, row for row. The corpus loader writes the
faces to `scryfall_cards.card_faces`, a column that has always been there and always been null.

**What the compiler does with them.** The front face is compiled as the card; every other face is
compiled on its own and put on the definition (`CardDef.faces`), where the engine already looks.
Each face's unread lines are the card's, so an adventurer whose creature reads and whose adventure
does not is not counted as read whole. A transforming card's back face has no cost and the front's
mana value (CR 712.4c); an adventure and a modal back face are cast for their own. A row with
faces missing is still refused, rather than read as its front alone.

**Battles are refused**, and that is new. Five Invasions read whole the moment faces were built —
their text is one enter trigger — but the engine has no defense counters, no protector and no way
to attack a battle, so a compiled one would sit on the board for ever and never turn over. A
reading with nothing left unread to flag it is the worst kind (D362); 36 battles are now refused
with that reason instead.

**And in production.** The realtime card lookup selects `card_faces` and matches a pasted name
against the part of Scryfall's "Akoum Warrior // Akoum Teeth" before the slashes; the pasted-deck
builder indexes such a row under its front face too. A live-Postgres test inserts a Scryfall-shaped
row and builds a deck from "Akoum Warrior".

    two-faced legal cards:                  622
    now compiled:                           582  (transform 350, adventure 134, modal 98)
    still refused:                          40   (36 battles, 4 whose size is a */* nothing reads)
    newly read whole, every face:           72   (adventure 40, modal 32, transform 0)

No transforming card reads whole yet: the line that says *when* it transforms is almost always
unread, so at the table these play as their front face and are turned over by hand. That family
("transform ~" in triggers, daybound and nightbound) is the next lever here.

**The pool's own faces, checked for the first time.** The standing check of every built-in card
against its Oracle row (D571) could not see a back face, because the corpus had none, and listed
nine faces as unverified. With faces in the corpus all nine have rows, and five facts were wrong:
**Venture Deeper costs {U}**, not {1}{U}; **Shield's Might gives +2/+2**, not +3/+3 (its script
pumped +3/+3 too); and Hagra Broodpit and Vastwood Thicket carried the older "enters the
battlefield tapped" wording. All corrected, and the unverified list is down to the three whole
split cards, whose halves are each checked under their own names.

**One convention kept, and kept out of the rules.** The pool writes an adventurer's Adventure on
the creature too ("Venture Deeper {U} (Sorcery) — …"), so a card in hand shows both halves; the
Oracle check already lists it as deliberate. Compiled as the creature's own text that quote became
an unread line on Merfolk Secretkeeper, and the gate's coverage test caught it. At play time the
quote is now left out of the front face, since the face carries those rules itself.

**Not built:** split cards (126 rows; the pool's two are hand-written), flip, meld, prepare,
specialize and omen. Each has its own rules.

**Tests.** 8 engine tests on corpus rows (Curious Pair, Akoum Warrior, Barkchannel
Pathway, Delver of Secrets, Invasion of Belenon): faces built and counted; a back face's unread
line is the card's; an adventurer offers both casts and its adventure resolves and exiles it; a
modal card plays its land back face, which enters tapped from its own text; a pathway is a land
either way; the derived definition compiles again at play time; a battle is refused; a row
without faces is still refused. Plus a live-Postgres test of the lookup and a loader test that
the faces reach the table.

## D592 — Transforming cards turn themselves over from printed text

D591 compiled 350 transforming cards and not one of them read whole: the line that says **when**
the card transforms was unread on every one, so a pasted Huntmaster or Gatstaf Shepherd played as
its front face for the whole game. This reads the commonest of those lines.

**"Transform ~" and "transform it."** An effect clause, through the same `transformPermanent` that
Delver of Secrets and Thing in the Ice use. The name is whichever face the line is printed on,
because each face is compiled under its own name — the front says "transform Gatstaf Shepherd" and
the back "transform Gatstaf Howler", and both mean this permanent. "It" is what the trigger is about
and falls back to the card, explore's rule: on Vildin-Pack Alpha, "Whenever a Werewolf you control
enters, you may transform it", the Werewolf that entered turns over, not the Alpha. The first draft
read "it" as the card, and the corpus listing of every printed "transform it" is what showed the
one card where that is wrong.

**Only if it has not transformed since (CR 701.28f).** The resolving ability carries the face its
source showed when it went on the stack (`EffectContext.sourceFace`, from the stack object's
`cardKey`). Showing another face means something turned it over in between, and the ability does
nothing: "{4}{G}: Transform Kessig Prowler" activated twice in response to itself turns it over
once. A permanent turned over **twice** in between shows the same face again and is not caught;
nothing in the corpus can do that with one ability waiting, and the gap is written beside the code.

**The werewolves' clock.** "At the beginning of each upkeep, if no spells were cast last turn,
transform ~" and the back face's "if a player cast two or more spells last turn". Neither can be
answered from the turn's own tally, which the cleanup step empties before the upkeep, so the
cleanup step now copies it first: `GameState.spellsCastLastTurnBy`, per seat, because "a player
cast two or more" is one seat's count — one spell each from two players keeps the back face up.
Empty before any turn has ended, which reads as no spells, the honest answer on turn one. Plus
"if ~ is equipped" (Avacynian Missionaries), read live off the board.

**"When this creature transforms into <this face>".** The `transformed` event Awoken Horror
already used, now read: alone, as "enters or transforms into" (two events, one effect — Huntmaster,
Brigid, Ashling and eight more), and as "transforms into ~ or dies". The name after "into" has to be
the face the line is printed on; a line naming the other face is left unread rather than looked up.
And "When ~ deals combat damage to a player" now reads with "When" as well as "Whenever" (Uninvited
Geist): the same event.

**An engine bug the tests found.** `settle` only starts a pass when one of its event lists is
non-empty, and the guard listing them had never included `transformed` or `copied`, though the
pass drains both. So a transform **on its own** was never announced until some unrelated event
carried it: Brigid turning back to her front made no Kithkin. Thing in the Ice hid this for every
test since #217 — its trigger is a spell cast, and the instant reaching a graveyard starts the pass
in the same action. The same was true of a copy made by a trigger, which is storm and replicate:
magecraft saw the copy late. Both are in the guard now, each with a test that fails without it.

**Still unread on transforming cards:** daybound/nightbound (36 cards — day and night is a rule of
its own, CR 726), Sagas whose last chapter returns them transformed (28), disturb (24), "More Than
Meets the Eye" and living metal (13), craft (9), and the transform abilities paid with Phyrexian
mana (17). Most "transforms into" lines that remain are blocked by their effect, not the event.

**Tests.** 12 engine tests on corpus rows (Gatstaf Shepherd, Kessig Prowler, Geier Reach Bandit,
Avacynian Missionaries, Uninvited Geist, Huntmaster of the Fells, Brigid): a werewolf turns over
after a turn with no spells and back after one player casts two; one spell keeps the front, one
each from two players keeps the back; the cleanup step keeps the tally and a new game has none;
the double activation turns over once; "it" is the trigger's subject; "if ~ is equipped"; "When"
combat damage; the two-event and one-event "transforms into" shapes and the wrong-face refusal;
Brigid pays to turn over and turning back makes a Kithkin; a storm copy is announced in the action
that made it; and a pasted list finds a card whose data is named "Front // Back" (D591's break-run
miss, below), and every face's read lines are counted. Each of the two guards and CR 701.28f was
removed by hand and its test failed.

    engine tests: 4,204, all passing
    web 264, realtime 60, api 326, all passing (no change there)

**D591's line figure was low, and this corrects it.** Measured first, the line total *fell* by 50
while coverage rose, which cannot happen if every line is counted once. `compileFaces` kept each
back face's unread lines but dropped its read ones, so a back-face line that became readable left
the count instead of moving across it, and the back faces' read lines were never in D591's 25,795
at all. The compiler now returns every face's read lines; the measure is the only consumer. Cards
read whole are unaffected — that count never looked at read lines. On the same build before the
fix the figure was 25,884 of 57,981 (44.6%): under the old count D592's readers added 89 lines to
D591's 25,795, and the 543 between the two counts are back-face lines that were already read and
never counted.

## D593 — Day and night: daybound and nightbound

The second werewolf rule, Innistrad: Midnight Hunt's (CR 726, CR 702.145), and the one 36 legal
transforming cards print instead of D592's upkeep sentence. It is a fact about the **game**, not a
card: `GameState.dayNight` is `day`, `night` or `null`, and every game starts `null`.

**Three rules, three functions** (`effects.ts`):

- `establishDayNight` — the first time a permanent with daybound is on the battlefield and it is
  neither, it becomes day (night for nightbound). Asked in every `settle`, after arrivals.
- `dayNightAfter` — as a turn begins, day becomes night if the **previous turn's active player**
  cast no spells during it, and night becomes day if they cast two or more. That player's count
  only, from D592's per-seat last-turn tally: two instant-speed spells from somebody else do not
  keep it day. Called where `advanceStep` hands the turn on.
- `matchDayNight` — every daybound permanent shows its back by night and every nightbound one its
  front by day. Read off live characteristics, so a werewolf that has lost all abilities stays as it
  is. Turning over because the time changed **is** a transform, and "transforms into" sees it; a
  card that arrives already matching the time of day enters transformed and does not (CR 712.14) —
  `transformPermanent` takes a `record` flag for that one case, and `arrivalReplacements` uses it.

**Daybound and nightbound are keywords**, changeling's reason: the rule asks a permanent whether it
has one. **"Whenever day becomes night or night becomes day"** is a new event, `day-night`, raised
at the change and not when a game that was neither first becomes day. **"If it's neither day nor
night, it becomes day as ~ enters"** is `becomesDayAsItEnters`, applied on arrival. The ten cards
that print the trigger print that line too.

**On the table:** a Day or Night pill in the top bar once it is either, with the rule in its
tooltip, and the same word in the watchers' header. `GameView.dayNight` is optional, so a view
from an older server reads as neither.

**Not read yet:** "it becomes night/day" as an effect (Into the Night, Unnatural Moonrise, The
Celestus's ability, Tovolar's upkeep), "if it's night" conditions (Olivia's Midnight Ambush, Wolf
Strike, Moonrager's Slash), Angel of Eternal Dawn's "it can't become night", and Sunstreak
Phoenix's trigger, which fires from a graveyard and stays unread rather than read as a battlefield
one. CR 702.145b's restriction — a daybound permanent cannot be transformed by anything else — is
not enforced; nothing the compiler reads tries.

**Tests.** 6 engine tests on corpus rows (Bird Admirer, Firmament Sage) and a probe built on Bird
Admirer's shape with a "transforms into" line on each face: the keywords, the line and the trigger
read; a game starts neither and a daybound card makes it day, in the view too; no spells makes it
night and turns the card over, two make it day and turn it back; only the previous active player
counts, and one spell changes nothing either way; a daybound card cast at night enters on its back
face without its trigger, and becoming day turns it over with its front's; the Sage makes it day
without a change and draws on the next one. Three faults were put in by hand — the arrival recorded
as a transform, the change not raised, the wrong seat counted — and each failed its test. The pool's
mechanic check names all four new mechanics as compiler-only, with this evidence.

## D594 — The Clone family from printed text

"You may have ~ enter as a copy of …" was the commonest one-line-short shape left in the corpus,
and it is a Commander staple: Clone, Stunt Double, Phyrexian Metamorph, Sculpting Steel, Copy
Enchantment. The pool has had a hand-written Clone since the layers work; nothing could read one.

**Read into exactly the hand-written Clone's shape**: a "you may" question over the whole
battlefield as the spell resolves (`min: 0`, so declining is legal) and `becomeCopyOf` on the
answer, which points the arriving permanent at the copied card — so its abilities, its statics and
its entry trigger are the copied card's, as the printed card says. What is new is the noun and the
exceptions.

**The noun** is a disjunction of type runs, each word read by `permanentWordMatch` against the
**live** type line: "any creature", "any artifact or creature", "any nonland permanent", "any Ally
creature", "any Equipment", "any land". And the side: "on the battlefield" is anybody's, "you
control" yours, "an opponent controls" theirs. A clone whose noun is creatures only also sets
`copiesACreature`, the hand-written Clone's hint to the computer player.

**The exceptions** are three printed forms joined by commas and "and": "it's a <types> in addition
to its other types" (card types and subtypes both — Synth Infiltrator's "Synth artifact creature"),
"it isn't legendary", and "it has <keywords>". They become a derived definition through
`TokenCopyProfile`, the one embalm and eternalize already use, registered under the copied card's
key plus a suffix so the copied card itself is untouched; a keyword is a line appended to the text,
which `printedKeywords` reads back. Because the exceptions live in the definition, a Clone of the
clone copies them too, which is the rule (CR 707.9b). Anything else after "except" — a quoted
ability, a changed name, counters, "with power 4 or greater", Dack's Duplicate's dethrone (not a
keyword the engine has) — refuses the line rather than copying without it.

**Not built, and the same as the pool's own Clone:** the question is asked when the spell resolves,
so a clone put onto the battlefield another way — reanimated, blinked — arrives as itself. "Enter as
a copy" is a replacement on any entry (CR 707.5); that wants the arrival replacements to be able to
ask a question, which they cannot yet.

**Tests.** 7 engine tests on corpus rows (Stunt Double, Mirror Image, Malleable Impostor, Glasspool
Mimic's front face) and one probe for "isn't legendary", which no card prints alone: all read
whole; "any creature" offers both sides and arrives as the copy with its haste; "you control"
offers only yours; "an opponent controls" with two added subtypes and flying, and the copied card's
own definition unchanged; a Stunt Double copying a Glasspool Mimic is a Shapeshifter Rogue too; a
non-legendary copy of Krenko leaves two Krenkos; an exception it cannot build leaves the line
unread. The exceptions dropped, and the derived definition written over the original's key, were
each put in by hand and failed. Plus the two D593 tests below.

    engine tests: 4,219, all passing; web 264, realtime 60, api 326

## D595 — Restricted mana: "Spend this mana only to …"

179 legal lines print a restriction on what a mana ability's mana may pay for, and the engine had
no way to say it, so every one was unread — and an unread mana line is a land that taps for
nothing. Ancient Ziggurat, Mishra's Workshop, Haven of the Spirit Dragon and the rest arrived in a
pasted deck as dead lands.

**The model: the mana never floats.** A pool cannot tell restricted mana from free mana, and giving
it a second bucket would mean teaching every payment in the engine which bucket it may draw on. So
the restricted mana is made only **while paying** for something it may pay for:

- `AbilityDef.spendOnly` — the restriction, as a test of a `PaymentFor` (a spell's live type line,
  or the live type line of an ability's source) and the printed words.
- `manaSources(state, seat, paying?)` lists a restricted source only for a payment it allows, and
  never when the caller does not say what it is paying for — so every caller that has not been
  taught about it under-offers rather than over-offers. A land with a free row and a bigger
  restricted one (Eldrazi Temple's shape) offers the bigger row where it may be spent and the free
  one elsewhere; one-mana rows are simply more choices.
- `payFrom` takes `paying`; casting a spell passes the spell's type line, activating an ability
  passes its source's. Mana a restricted source made beyond the cost is **lost** rather than left
  in the pool, where it could pay for anything: Mishra's Workshop's three for a one-mana artifact
  leaves nothing floating.
- `legalActions` asks the same question when it offers a cast or an ability, and does not offer a
  restricted mana ability as a button at all; activating one by hand is refused with the reason.

**The vocabulary** (`spending.ts`, shared by the land mana-line parser and the line reader): a
casting half — "to cast creature spells", "an instant or sorcery spell", "a noncreature spell",
"artifact spells", "Dragon spells", "spells" — and an activating half — "to activate abilities",
"of artifacts", "of an artifact source" — either or both. Type words only, read live: lowercase is
a card type, "noncreature" or "legendary"; capitalised is a subtype. Anything else is refused and
the line stays unread: "a multicolored spell", "colorless Eldrazi spells", "the chosen type",
"kicked spells", "costs that contain {X}", and every rider ("and that spell can't be countered").

**Two older tests pinned the old refusal** on purpose — Ancient Ziggurat's line and a land probe
with a creature-spell restriction. Both now pin a restriction that is still refused (a multicolored
spell), with a note that the type-word ones are read since this entry.

**Not built:** the bot's own planning counts mana without restricted sources (it plays what
`legalActions` offers, which does count them, so it casts with them — it just does not plan around
them); the faint "mana you could make" pips count them as if free, which is the optimistic display
they have always been; and convoke, delve and the special payments (morph, foretell, suspend) do
not draw on them.

**Tests.** 5 engine tests on corpus rows (Ancient Ziggurat, Mishra's Workshop) and two probes: the
restriction is read onto the ability and an unknown one leaves the line unread; Ziggurats pay for
Grizzly Bears and not for Lightning Bolt, are not a button, refuse a hand-pressed activation and
are tapped by the cast; Mishra's Workshop casts Bonesplitter and leaves no {C} floating; "to
activate abilities" offers an equip and not a spell; the two-row land offers {C}{C} for a creature
and {C} otherwise. Unused restricted mana kept, and restricted sources counted for any payment,
were each put in by hand: the first failed one test, the second three.

    engine tests: 4,224, all passing; web 264, realtime 60, api 326

## D596 — Protection from more than colours

Protection was modelled as a list of colours, and `printedPart` refused any other quality on
purpose: a card promising more than the engine could check was left to a human. 37 legal lines
promised more, and 27 cards were one line short of it — Beloved Chaplain, Foothill Guide, Baneslayer
Angel, Progenitus, Elite Inquisitor, Enemy of the Guildpact.

**One list beside the colours.** `Characteristics.protectionQualities` holds the qualities that are
not colours, as tags: a card type ("from artifacts", "from creatures", "from instants"), a creature
type ("from Goblins", "from Demons and from Dragons", read against the corpus-derived creature-type
list in its plural), the snow supertype, "multicolored", "monocolored" and "everything". It is a
printed, base characteristic like the colours and cleared with them when a permanent loses all its
abilities.

**One test for all four rules.** `protectionApplies` already answered DEBT (CR 702.16) — damage,
enchanting and equipping, blocking and targeting all call it, directly or through `protectedFrom` —
so the qualities are checked there, against the **live** characteristics of the other object: a
land animated into a creature is a creature to protection from creatures, a spell on the stack is
an instant to protection from instants, a gold card is multicoloured. Nothing else had to change.

**A list printed with commas is one ability.** "Protection from Vampires, from Werewolves, and from
Zombies" split on its commas was three parts, two of them nonsense; the line is joined back into
the "and from" form the part reader already takes before it is split.

**Still refused, each a quality with a condition the tag cannot hold:** "from non-Spirit
creatures", "from permanents with corruption counters on them", and the chosen-colour and
chosen-player forms.

**D595's break run** caught 9 of 10. The miss was "a noncreature spell" read as its opposite, which
no test had asked; a probe land restricted to noncreature spells now casts a Lightning Bolt and not
a Raging Goblin, and fails with the fault in.

**Tests.** 3 engine tests on corpus rows (Beloved Chaplain, Foothill Guide, Enemy of the Guildpact,
Elite Inquisitor) and a probe for protection from artifacts: every row reads, the comma list is
three subtypes, a conditional quality stays unread; a creature cannot damage or block the Chaplain
and a spell can still damage it; Foothill Guide is protected from a Goblin and not from Bears, Enemy
of the Guildpact from Selesnya Charm and not from a mono-red Goblin, and the probe from Bonesplitter,
which then cannot be equipped to it while it still equips Grizzly Bears. The qualities ignored, and
the comma join removed, were each put in by hand and failed.

## D597 — Affinity for anything

Affinity was `'artifacts'` and nothing else, and the type's own docblock said so: "`artifacts` is
the one the pool has cards for. The day another arrives it is a second member of this union rather
than a second field." 38 legal lines print another, and 17 cards were one line short of it.

`CardScript.affinity` is now `'artifacts'` or an `AffinityFor` — the printed phrase and a test of
one permanent — and `costChangeFor` counts the caster's permanents with whichever it has, live, as
the cost is computed. The keyword reader reads "affinity for <phrase>": a card type in the plural,
a subtype in the plural (the basic land types, Equipment, Gates, Foods, Vehicles and every creature
type the corpus knows, through `isCreatureType`), "historic permanents" (legendary, artifact or Saga,
CR 700.6), "outlaws" (Assassin, Mercenary, Pirate, Rogue, Warlock, CR 700.12) and "tokens". A
phrase it cannot count ("blue permanents") stays unread. Only generic mana moves, as before.

**Tests.** 3 engine tests on Razor Golem's corpus row and a probe with affinity for creatures: both
read and an uncountable phrase stays unread; six Plains pay for the Golem entirely, five Forests
take nothing off, three Plains and two Forests take {3}; two Grizzly Bears take {2} off the probe and
the lands do not count. The phrase's test replaced by the artifact count was put in by hand and
failed two of them. Plus the two D596 tests above.

## D598 — Disguise

Murders at Karlov Manor's morph: cast face down for {3} as a 2/2 with **ward {2}**, turned face up
for the disguise cost (CR 702.168). 46 legal lines print a bare "Disguise {cost}", and 12 cards were
one line short of it.

**Read as morph with one flag.** `keywordWithCost` reads Disguise beside Morph and Megamorph and
returns `disguise: true`; `morph.disguise` carries it on the script, in all three places a costed
keyword becomes a morph. The face-down cast and the turn-up are morph's own, unchanged.

**The ward is a granted trigger, and that is the whole design.** A face-down permanent has no
script, which is how the engine keeps morph's rule, and both the place triggers are collected and
the place a trigger is resolved ask the face-down card for nothing. The ward a disguised one has is
the rules' gift rather than the card's text — exactly what a granted trigger is. So `raise` fires
it from a reserved reference, `DISGUISE_GRANT`, and `scriptFor` answers that reserved name with
`DISGUISED_FACE_DOWN`, whose one granted trigger is the pool's `ward(…, '{2}')`. Every site that
fires, aims or resolves a granted trigger already goes through that lookup, so nothing else had to
learn about disguise. The first attempt gave the face-down permanent a script instead; the trigger
fired and then resolved as the card's own first trigger, because the stack looks a trigger up by
the card and its index. Not while it has lost all its abilities.

**Tests.** 3 engine tests on Riftburst Hellion's corpus row and the pool's Battering Craghorn: the
keyword reads as a disguised morph with its cost; face down, the Hellion's ward counters a Lightning
Bolt whose caster has no mana left, and it survives undamaged; a face-down Craghorn has no ward and
the same Bolt kills it. The ward's firing removed was put in by hand and failed. Plus the two D597
tests above.

## D599 — Retrace

"You may cast this card from your graveyard by discarding a land card in addition to paying its
other costs" (CR 702.81). 18 legal lines, 10 cards one line short: Flame Jab, Raven's Crime and the
rest of Shadowmoor and Eventide's cycle.

**Flashback's zone, the printed cost, and D585's discard narrowed to land cards.** `CardScript.
retrace` from the keyword; `castablePlays` lists a retrace card in the graveyard beside the
flashback and escape lists, offers it for its printed cost with the hand's **land cards** as the
play's `discardOptions`, and does not offer it at all with no land in hand. It is kept out of the
paths a hand cast takes (morph, foretell, suspend, the alternative costs) exactly as escape is.
`castSpell` checks the card is in its caster's graveyard and that the discard named is one of
those land cards, and pays the discard through the same field D585's additional cost uses. A card
that prints both retrace and a discard cost would be two discards, which nothing prints; it is not
offered. The spell goes back to the graveyard as it resolves, which is the rule.

**On the table** the play travels a `retrace` flag the web sends with the cast, beside flashback
and escape; the land is chosen with the table's existing discard picker.

**Tests.** 3 engine tests on Flame Jab's corpus row: it reads; it is offered from the graveyard with
only land cards to discard and not at all with none in hand; a non-land discard is refused, and a
land discard casts it, deals its damage, and leaves both the land and the Jab in the graveyard. The
land check removed was put in by hand and failed. The pool's mechanic check names `script retrace`
as compiler-only, with this evidence. Plus the two D598 tests below.

    engine tests: 4,242, all passing; web 264, realtime 60, api 326

## D600 — Mass effects over a scope, and overload by its own rewrite

Overload was the plan: 28 legal lines, 11 cards one line short. CR 702.96b says what paying it does —
"change its text by replacing all instances of the word 'target' with the word 'each'" — and that is
a rewrite the compiler can do literally and then read. Doing it showed the bigger gap underneath: the
rewritten sentences did not read because **no mass effect but "destroy all creatures" did**. "Destroy
all artifacts." was unread. So was "Destroy all lands", "Destroy all enchantments", "Return all
creatures to their owners' hands", "Tap all creatures your opponents control" — 150 legal lines,
118 cards one line short.

**One mass reader.** "Destroy / exile / tap / untap / return … all or each <scope> [to their owners'
hands]", with the scope read by `massScope`: `boardScope`'s controller clause ("you control", "you
don't control", "your opponents control", "each opponent controls") and "other", over a wider noun —
type words plural or singular, "permanent(s)", "non-" plus a type or subtype, and a list of
alternatives joined by commas and "and" ("artifacts, creatures, and enchantments" is any of the
three). Every word has to classify, read live off `characteristicsOf`, so a colour, a size, "with
flying" or "attacking" refuses the line rather than widening it. The board is read once, before
anything moves, as the wrath does; destroy honours "can't be regenerated".

**Overload, by the rewrite.** `spellScriptFor` holds an "Overload {cost}" line back, reads the
resolution as printed, then reads it again with "target" replaced by "each". If that reading comes
back **with no targets** it is `overload.onResolve`, the field the hand-written Mizzium Mortars
already uses, and the line is read; otherwise it is reported unread and the spell plays at its
printed cost. The first version lost the held line on the paths that never read it — the modal
shape and an unread resolution — and the measured line total fell by 15 for it; every path now
reports it.

**And Cyclonic Rift's target.** "Target nonland permanent you don't control" is the same set as
"… an opponent controls", which the target reader already had; it now reads both, as `boardScope`
always has.

**Tests.** 7 engine tests on corpus rows (Vandalblast, Cyclonic Rift, Armageddon, Evacuation,
Akroma's Vengeance, Planar Cleansing) with a second custom deck giving the opponent artifacts and
creatures: every row reads, overloads included; overloaded Vandalblast destroys both of theirs and
not yours; overloaded Rift returns every nonland permanent they control and leaves their land and
your creature; the printed Rift offers only their nonland permanents; Akroma's Vengeance takes every
listed type on both sides and spares lands, and Planar Cleansing spares lands; Armageddon takes
every land; Evacuation returns every creature to its owner's hand and leaves the Equipment; a colour
in the scope stays unread. The controller clause ignored, "non-" read as its opposite, and the
overload rewrite removed were each put in by hand and failed.

    engine tests: 4,249, all passing; web 264, realtime 60, api 326

## D601 — Damage to every creature of a kind, spells that cost less, and the D600 gaps

The unread dump after D600 ranked "~ deals N damage to each …" first among the one-short shapes. The
reason was narrow: `sweepDestination`, the reader for where a damage sweep lands, matched only "each
creature [with/without K] [and each player]". D600 had just written `massScope`, which reads a
scope's type words, controller clause and "non-". So the first half of this increment connects the
two.

**Damage over a scope.** When the fixed shape fails, `sweepDestination` now reads "each <scope>
[and each player | and each opponent]" through `massScope`. That reads "each creature your opponents
control" (Blazing Volley, Cosmotronic Wave), "each nonartifact creature" (Whipflare), "each non-Pirate
creature" (Fiery Cannonade), and overloaded Electrickery. Electrickery's rewrite reads "each creature
you don't control", which D600 had to leave unread. "And each opponent" skips the caster. A scope must
name a creature or a planeswalker: "each artifact your opponents control" would read as a scope and
deal damage to nothing (CR 120.3), so it is refused.

**Spells that cost less.** `CardScript.selfCostChange` had one user, Hagra Mauling, written by hand
(D578). It now has a reader for three shapes:
- "This spell costs {N} less to cast if <condition>": the condition is `interveningConditionFor`'s.
- "… for each <count>": the count is `forEachCount`'s.
- "{X} less …, where X is the number of <count>".

A new optional `per` field multiplies the rate by the count. Both the condition and the count run
against a context whose controller is the caster and whose source is the card being cast.
`costChangeFor` now takes the card's id, so the offer in `legalActions` and the payment in
`castSpell` see the same number.

Four shapes are refused:
- "If it targets …": this engine prices a spell before its targets are chosen.
- A phrase naming the card itself.
- A coloured discount: only generic mana moves.
- "More": dropping a cost increase would make a card better than printed.

**The count learned two things.** First, the party (CR 700.8): one each of Cleric, Rogue, Warrior
and Wizard, where a creature with two of those types fills one slot. That makes it a matching. It
is computed over the sixteen sets of filled roles, so the cost is linear in the number of creatures.
Second, any `massScope` scope, as a last row after every existing one, so a phrase that already
read keeps its reading. "Creature on the battlefield" (Blasphemous Act) and "creature your opponents
control" (Primeval Protector) now count, and so does every "for each" and "where X is" elsewhere in
the compiler. That widened three readings that tests had pinned as refusals:
- Idolized's "nonland permanents you control".
- "Each Bird on the battlefield", which the D520 comment said the vocabulary "could be taught".
- Ral, Caller of Storms's −7.

Each test now uses a count that still has no reader (colours among permanents). Ral's test expects
the +1 and the −7, with the divided −2 still refused. Mizzium Mortars now compiles whole too. The
keyword-without-builder test moves to Angel of Sanctions (Embalm), and the hand-written Mortars gains
the `removesACreature` hint the compiled reading carries, which is what
compiled-vs-written flagged.

**Sweep 46801 threw, and the bot was why.** The game threw at seed 46821 with "that card is not in
your hand". The bot had cast Glamerdye from its graveyard with the land to discard but without
`retrace: true`, because the bot's cast action carries every alternative-cast flag by hand and
retrace (D599) was missing from the list. The line is added. Two tests now pin it:
- The bot, with its land drop spent, retraces Flame Jab and says so.
- A source check: every field that `LegalPlay` and `AutoCastAction` both declare must appear as
  `play.<field>` in `bot.ts`. Thirteen flags have needed that line one by one, and the fourteenth
  will fail this test rather than a sweep.

**The D600 break run: 10 faults, 5 caught.** Four of the five misses are pinned:
- "You control" ignored: Evacuation's row with the clause returns only your creature.
- "Other" ignored: a creature whose enters trigger returns all other nonland permanents stays on the battlefield.
- Exile read as destroy: "Exile all artifacts" puts them in exile.
- Untap read as tap: "Untap all lands you control" untaps them.

The fifth, the overload guard against a rewritten reading that still has targets, is **vacuous**.
The rewrite replaces every "target" with "each", so no reading can still come back with targets. The
guard stays as a check that costs nothing.

**Tests.** 18 new engine tests:
- 6 on damage sweeps, using corpus rows plus one custom row for "and each opponent".
- 6 on cost reductions: Bone Picker, Ghoultree, Blasphemous Act (cast for {4}{R} with four creatures
  out, and resolved), Deadly Alliance with three party shapes, and three refusals.
- 2 on the bot's retrace.
- 4 pinning the D600 break-run gaps.
- 3 existing tests updated for the wider reading.

Every new reader was broken on purpose and its test failed:
- The "and each opponent" seat filter.
- The creature guard on a damage scope.
- The `massScope` fallback in `sweepDestination` and in the count.
- The bot's retrace line, caught by both tests.
- `per` ignored.
- `when` ignored.
- Party as a headcount.

    engine tests: 4,267, all passing; web 264, realtime 60, api 326
